Document dsid_f94b93a4bc7948ddab45c371187dc6c6:
description:
PRD-style acceptance and behavioral specification for: (A) deterministic structured output envelopes during streaming, (B) robust tool/function-orchestration semantics when downstream tool calls fail or time out (soft-fail modes), and (C) observable signal set for debugging degraded emissions. This ticket captures requirements, tradeoffs, and concrete acceptance tests for engineering to implement and QA to validate.

background:
Teams integrating function-calls and streaming structured output have encountered brittle failure modes: partial JSON emissions, stuck streams when a tool times out, and unclear signals in telemetry for root-cause. Previous specs focused on schema handshakes but did not fully specify soft-fail policies (when to continue vs abort), how to surface partial-but-valid objects, or required observability for production troubleshooting.

goals:
1) Define deterministic envelope semantics so consumers can parse incrementally and resume/reconcile partial objects. 2) Specify soft-fail modes for tool invocation: best-effort, fallback-only, and abort. 3) Establish acceptance tests for streaming + tool failures that exercise backpressure, resumability, and idempotent retries. 4) Define telemetry and SLI/alert thresholds to detect degraded emission reliability.

scope:
- Streaming text and structured frames emitted from Redwood API. - Function/tool invocation lifecycle (invoke, success, failure, retry). - Soft-fail policies and configuration. - Acceptance criteria and end-to-end test matrix (simulated tool latencies/failures).

out_of_scope:
- Changes to client SDKs beyond minimal parsing guidance. - New RPC transport protocols. - Billing/quotas changes related to retries (handled by a separate billing review).

tradeoffs:
- Strict abort-on-tool-failure yields highest data correctness but reduces availability; soft-fail increases availability at the cost of accuracy. We recommend defaulting to best-effort-with-degraded-indicators for hosted API and offering strict-abort configuration for enterprise Dedicated/Private deployments. - Emitting placeholder fields vs removing the field: placeholder maintains schema shape for parsers but may surface misleading data. We prefer placeholder objects with explicit 'soft_fail' enum and provenance metadata.

acceptance_criteria:
AC-1: Incremental Envelope Parsing: Streaming responses are emitted as ordered 'frames' where each frame is a top-level JSON object stringified and newline-delimited. Consumers can reconstruct the final object by concatenating frames and applying frame-level 'commit' markers. In tests, a slow client that disconnects and reconnects using resume token can re-sync and reconstruct a consistent object state.
AC-2: Soft-Fail Modes: System exposes three modes: 'abort' (default for strict endpoints), 'best_effort' (continue emitting remaining structured fields, include 'soft_fail' markers), and 'degraded_fallback' (switch to cheaper model or cached result then emit). Implementation must allow per-route configuration. Acceptance tests must validate each mode against simulated downstream tool failures.
AC-3: Partial-Object Validity: When a tool call fails and mode is 'best_effort', the emitted structured object must remain JSON-parseable at frame boundaries and include an explicit 'provenance' map with keys: source_variant, tool_status, tool_error_code, soft_fail=true. Test harness validates JSON validity after each frame and final reconciliation produces a documented 'incomplete' state.
AC-4: Function-Invocation Idempotency & Retry Signals: Tool gateway must return idempotency token on initial invocation. Retries (automatic or client-initiated) must attach token to avoid duplicate side-effects. Acceptance tests include simulated at-least-once delivery and assert idempotent behavior for a provided sample tool (mock webhook that records invocations).
AC-5: Timeouts & Backpressure Behavior: When a tool exceeds configured timeout: - in 'abort' mode, the stream emits an error envelope and closes (status=closed, code=TOOL_TIMEOUT). - in 'best_effort', emit soft-fail metadata and continue. System must not indefinitely block other concurrent streams; load tests will simulate N=500 concurrent streams with 10% slow tool responses and verify 99th percentile latency SLOs remain within target with degraded outputs accounted for.
AC-6: Observability Signals: For every streaming emission that includes a soft-fail, the following telemetry events must be emitted: tool_invocation.start, tool_invocation.end (status), stream.frame.commit, stream.soft_fail.marker, stream.resume.attempt (if consumer reconnects). Each event includes trace_id and frame_offset. Acceptance: Kibana dashboards show these events for a 1-hour test run and an alert rule triggers when soft_fail_rate > 0.5% over 5 minutes for production routes.
AC-7: Compatibility with Existing Schema Negotiation: Handshake must include 'preferred_envelope' and 'resume_token' semantics. Acceptance tests exercise older clients by verifying graceful degradation: if preferred_envelope is unsupported, server falls back to newline-delimited JSON frames and includes a compatibility header explaining the downgrade.
AC-8: Test Harness & E2E Test Cases: Provide automated tests that simulate network partitions, tool errors (500, 429, 504), tool latency spikes, and partial stream consumption. Tests must assert that consumers receive either a valid final object or a documented incomplete object with soft_fail metadata in all tested modes.
AC-9: Docs & Examples: Console docs must include examples for parsing frames, handling soft_fail metadata, configuring per-route mode, and troubleshooting guide with representative log queries. Acceptance: docs reviewed and approved by Developer Experience and Design reviewers and linked in PR.
AC-10: Security & Compliance: When soft-fail includes tool error payloads, sensitive fields must be redacted per PII policy. Acceptance: static analysis and a sample audit record confirm PII redaction for tool error messages containing email/SSN-like patterns.

test_cases:
TC-1: Best-effort tool timeout: Start streaming generation that triggers a tool lookup that sleeps for 8s (config timeout 2s). Mode=best_effort. Expect frames including 'tool_status':'timeout' and 'soft_fail':"true"; final object parseable. Verify telemetry events emitted.
TC-2: Abort mode on rate-limit: Simulate tool returning 429. Mode=abort. Expect error envelope and stream close with code TOOL_RATE_LIMIT. Verify client-observed close code and server-side logs reference idempotency token.
TC-3: Resume after disconnect: Consumer reads first N frames then disconnects. Server persists resume_token. Consumer reconnects with token and receives frames from last commit point through final. Assert final object equivalent to continuous stream.
TC-4: Fallback variant switch: Mode=degraded_fallback. Downstream model returns non-responsive. Server emits warning frame, switches to cached summary variant, emits final object with 'source_variant':'cached-summary' and 'tool_error_code' annotated. Verify SLO accounting attributes.
TC-5: Idempotent webhook verification: Mock tool endpoint records invocations. Trigger multiple retries with the same idempotency token. Verify single recorded invocation and correct response to client of 'duplicate-suppressed' marker.

monitoring_and_telemetry:
Minimum telemetry must include trace_id, route, model_variant, frame_offset, resume_token, tool_invocation.id, tool_status, tool_error_code, latency_ms. Dashboards: streaming-frame-latency, soft-fail-rate, tool-timeout-trend. Alerts: soft_fail_rate>0.5% over 5m, resume_failure_rate>0.1% over 15m.

notes:
Implementation must include a clear config surface (route-level parameter 'tool_failure_policy' with enum values) and safe defaults for public API. Provide migration notes for existing routes currently using legacy streaming format.

description:
Issue summary: Starting ~2026-03-13T18:10Z we observed an elevated 5xx rate from the /v1/embeddings route for customers on dedicated pool dsp-6-us-east. Error surface: predominantly 502/503 returning from the API gateway with upstream runtime exits. Impact: multiple batch embedding jobs for NimbleSearch failing, ~12-18% request error rate for the tenant, visible increases in retries and customer timeouts.

Impact: Customer-reported batch uploads failing; customer-facing retry storms exacerbated backend pressure. Several internal alerts fired: apigw_5xx_rate_high, runtime_unexpected_exit, dsp-6_gpu_util_spike.


steps_to_reproduce:
1) Submit concurrent embedding batches to customer-specific route (tenant id T-NIMBLE-22) with 8 parallel workers and batch size 256.
2) Observe rising 502s at the API gateway within 5-7 minutes.
3) Check runtime pod logs for SIGABRT / 'pthread_create' errors and thread pool exhaustion warnings.


logs_and_metrics:
- apigw: 502 rate rose from baseline 0.4% to 15% between 18:10 and 18:25 UTC.
- runtime rtm-04 (dsp-6-us-east) logged repeated: 'error: pthread_create: Resource temporarily unavailable' and 'fatal: cannot spawn thread' at 18:12:34 UTC.
- kernel/messages show 'task: pid XXXX killed by SIGABRT' around same window.
- GPU util for pool spiked to 92% and NVML reported frequent driver resets for a subset of nodes.


investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: aggressive prefetching + apigw hedged retries caused connection and work-queue pileup leading to thread exhaustion in the serving runtime.
What we checked: thread counts, ulimit/nproc, runtime threadpool settings, recent config sweeps. No recent runtime code deploys in us-east at incident start; a config bump to prefetch.window_size was rolled out globally at 17:55 UTC (INT-331002 linked).
Findings: rtm-04 hit process-level thread limit (nproc soft limit reached) while other nodes showed high accept-queue lengths. The apigw retry backoff was not honoring the reduced capacity threshold; hedged retries amplified work.
Possible contributory factors: customer workload with large batches (size 256) producing many short-lived threads per request path; the dedicated autoscaler lagged behind request surge.


timeline:
2026-03-13T17:55Z - config sweep: prefetch.window_size increased (internal change INT-331002).
2026-03-13T18:08Z - first apigw 5xx alert for dsp-6-us-east.
2026-03-13T18:12Z - runtime rtm-04 logs thread create failures.
2026-03-13T18:20Z - Support engaged SRE, opened temporary rate limit on tenant route.
2026-03-13T18:35Z - Autoscaler scaled up 2 nodes but observed some nodes still in crashloop.
2026-03-13T19:05Z - Hotfix PR merged to add backpressure respect in apigw retry logic (github.com/redwood/infra/pull/3842).


mitigation:
Applied immediate mitigations:
- Scaled dedicated pool dsp-6 by +3 nodes to absorb burst.
- Added tenant-level temporary rate-limit to 60rps for NimbleSearch routine jobs to stop retry spin.
- Rolled back global prefetch.window_size for dsp-6 to previous value to reduce work amplification.
- Enabled apigw soft-backoff so hedged retries won't flood runtimes while autoscaler warms up.


resolution:
Root cause addressed by a two-part fix: 1) runtime hardening to allocate a bounded worker thread pool (prevents unbounded pthread_create) and better nproc fallback handling, and 2) apigw change to honor backend capacity signals and avoid hedged retry amplification. Hotfix (infra PR #3842) deployed into us-east on 2026-03-13 19:05Z and runtime patch rolled on 2026-03-13 19:40Z. Post-deploy: 5xx rate dropped back to baseline ~0.6% within 20 minutes.
Resolution steps recorded and communicated to NimbleSearch. Incident declared mitigated at 2026-03-13T19:50Z; full resolution pending follow-ups.


follow_up:
- Create a runbook entry for 'thread/worker pool exhaustion' and include detection thresholds.
- Adjust autoscaler warmup policy for dsp-* pools to be more aggressive for batch-heavy tenants.
- Add tenant-level preflight checks for large-batch embedding uploads with recommended batch sizes.
- Audit prefetch config rollout gating so we don't apply global prefetch increases without region-specific safety checks.
- Add metric alert to detect 'pthread_create failure' log pattern and auto-throttle affected tenants.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Redwood Product), Samir Patel (NimbusApps CTO), Jordan Lee (NimbusApps Lead Eng), Maya Chen (NimbusApps Security), Terry Huang (NimbusApps PM)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):
Summary: quick hosted demo, show streaming, show params, answer latency/cost questions, clarify security and data flows.
Action items: see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: alright hi everyone, thanks for taking time, this is Alex from Redwood Inference, I'm an AE, with me is Priya our SE and Carlos product, uh hi team
[00:08] Samir: hey thanks Alex, Samir here, quick note we have about 40 minutes, we'd like to see a live sandbox run and understand retry behavior, and also want to confirm we can meet our data residency needs
[00:18] Alex: yep perfect, we'll start with a quick orientation to the hosted API and console, then Priya will run a live sandbox demo showing streaming and parameter tweaks, and we'll finish with security stuff and next steps
[00:29] Jordan: cool, high level our use case is an in-app assistant with short back-and-forth conversations, sub 300ms median latency ideal, but we care about cost — we might favor smaller models if quality is good enough
[00:40] Priya: sounds good, thanks Jordan. quick housekeeping, the sandbox we'll use is rate-limited but mirrors prod behavior for streaming and retries. i'll open the playground now — one sec
[00:52] Speaker 1: (typing sounds)
[01:04] Priya: okay loading, i pasted an example chat payload. first thing — streaming: you'll see tokens arrive incrementally over a single SSE stream, that's what we call streaming; it reduces perceived latency since the client sees tokens earlier even if final generation takes longer
[01:18] Terry: question, does streaming hold any extra state on our side? like session cookies or KV cache?
[01:24] Priya: good question, streaming is just the output transport. the runtime still manages the KV cache per conversation if you enable it; that cache lives on the server side (redwood-managed for hosted) unless you run private. you can pin cache ttl or disable prefix caching if you need strict data controls
[01:39] Maya: when you say cache lives on server side — is it encrypted and is it surfaced in logs?
[01:45] Carlos: short answer: cache is encrypted at rest with KMS, and we do not persist raw user PII in audit logs; you can configure retention windows and we have an option to disable certain debugging logs. we'll follow up with the security docs
[01:58] Jordan: nice. back to streaming — can we do chunking instead? we have a websocket-based client that prefers discrete messages
[02:05] Priya: yes, you can consume via websockets or SSE and you can buffer into logical chunks client-side. the responses are the same, it's just transport. we also support callback webhooks if you want server-to-server delivery for completed outputs
[02:18] Samir: ok demo time if that's cool
[02:20] Priya: yep starting with a simple prompt: "You are an assistant that summarizes user messages in one sentence." i'll set temperature to 0.2 and max_tokens to 60. watch the stream
[02:34] [02:34] Priya: (sends request)
[02:38] [02:38] STREAM OUTPUT BEGIN
[02:38] Priya: "User asks for concise summary of meeting notes — assistant provides one-line recap with action items."
[02:44] [02:44] STREAM OUTPUT END
[02:45] Jordan: that was immediate, was it actually streaming or just small output?
[02:50] Priya: small output but still streaming. for longer outputs you'll see partial sentences come through every, say, 50-150 tokens depending on model and batch timing. the runtime tries to flush tokens frequently to reduce tail latency
[03:03] Terry: curious — how do you tune for cost? is temperature tied to cost?
[03:09] Priya: temperature affects randomness not cost. cost is primarily tokens (input + output) and the model choice/size. we recommend smaller quantized variants for high-volume assistant tasks. also prefix caching and batching help amortize cost across similar requests
[03:22] Alex: quick interjection, for your use case — if you have short back-and-forths, enabling conversation-level KV cache and a compact model often gives a good cost/latency tradeoff
[03:33] Samir: what's your recommended retry/backoff pattern if we see transient 503 or timeouts? we want to avoid duplicate messages in the app
[03:40] Priya: typical pattern: idempotency key per user-turn, exponential backoff with jitter, and use the request status endpoints to reconcile if you need strong exactly-once semantics. Redwood returns partial tokens on timeouts if the runtime was able to produce them; we document best-effort semantics — for critical flows we recommend server-side dedupe and using model-side stop tokens to mark completeness
[03:59] Jordan: can you show an example of a retry where the first attempt times out and we resume without double-processing?
[04:06] Priya: sure — i'll simulate a transient by throttling the sandbox to cause a timeout. i'll include an idempotency key in the header and then re-call. watch the IDs
[04:18] [04:18] Priya: (runs simulated request — network hiccup)
[04:28] Priya: first call returned 504 after 10s (sandbox threshold). our client then waited 1s + jitter and retried, the second call found a cached KV snapshot and continued, returning the missing tail tokens — you can avoid showing the duplicate prefix by reconciling using the last received token id or sequence number
[04:46] Samir: that makes sense. what about streaming partials — if a client disconnects mid-stream, do you keep the generation alive server-side?
[04:54] Priya: for hosted with default settings the generation continues for a short grace window and if the client reconnects with the same idempotency key you can resume; otherwise it may be GC'd. in private deployments customers can tune grace windows and longer-term retention policies
[05:10] Maya: from a security lens we need to make sure session data isn't kept longer than 24 hours — is that configurable?

Purpose:
Run a tightly-scoped customer workshop that produces a validated Zero-to-POC Canvas, draft success criteria, and a concrete 30/60/90 rollout plan. Designed for mid-sized product teams evaluating Redwood Dedicated or Private deployments.

Format options (choose one):
- Rapid (90 minutes): high-level alignment + tech spike plan. Use when customer already has stakeholder alignment but needs a quick validation roadmap.
- Standard (3 hours): full canvas, slide walkthrough, interactive mapping wall, and breakout spike design. Recommended for first full-day engagement.
- Deep Dive (half-day): adds architecture whiteboarding and performance acceptance tests. For technically heavy customers.

Prework (send 4 days ahead):
- Short questionnaire (team, primary use case, expected QPS, latency SLO, data residency constraints).
- Ask for one representative prompt set or a sample conversation flow (for chat use cases) and a small dataset for embedding/retrieval tests.

Agenda (3-hour, standard):
- 0:00–0:10 — Welcome + goals (Facilitator): set expectations; confirm outcomes.
- 0:10–0:30 — Customer context & constraints (Customer leads): product goals, users, privacy/regulatory must-haves. Capture on the canvas.
- 0:30–0:50 — Success Criteria workshop (Group): define 3 measurable success metrics (e.g., 95th p99 latency < 300ms, inference cost <$0.03/token, end-user satisfaction > 4/5). Prioritize.
- 0:50–1:20 — Architecture options & tradeoffs (Facilitator + Eng): hosted vs dedicated vs private; routing/fallback policies; data flow diagram. Use whiteboard.
- 1:20–1:35 — Break (short)
- 1:35–2:05 — Hands-on mapping wall (Interactive): map data sources, privacy touchpoints, and model artifacts to deployment options. Dot-vote risks and unknowns.
- 2:05–2:35 — Experiment design & quick wins (Breakouts): design 2 small validation spikes (one functional correctness, one performance/cost). Document acceptance criteria and estimated effort.
- 2:35–2:50 — 30/60/90 draft plan (Facilitator): align owners and milestones, dependencies, and go/no-go gates.
- 2:50–3:00 — Next steps & commitments (Wrap): agree on deliverables, dates, and communication cadence.

Zero-to-POC Canvas (one-page deliverable — fill during session):
- Use case summary: 1–2 lines.
- Primary personas & business KPIs: list.
- Must-have compliance/controls: list.
- Traffic profile: expected QPS, peak concurrency, avg sequence length.
- Latency & cost targets: hard SLOs and soft targets.
- Recommended deployment mode: hosted | dedicated | private (with rationale).
- Minimal viable model and fallback: model family, quantization/size recommendation, fallback policy.
- Data path & residency: inbound sources, logging, PII handling, retention.
- Success metrics & acceptance criteria (3 items).
- 2 validation spikes (title, owner, success criteria, estimated effort in days).
- 30/60/90 milestones (see below).

Sample slide outline (10–12 slides, short deck to leave with customer):
1) Title + objective (one sentence). Speaker note: what problem we solve together.
2) Agenda & deliverables from today.
3) Customer context snapshot (pulled from prework).
4) Zero-to-POC Canvas (visual one-pager).
5) Deployment tradeoffs (hosted/dedicated/private) — pros/cons table.
6) Measurement & acceptance strategy (latency, cost, quality).
7) Validation spikes (two experiments with owners & timelines).
8) 30/60/90 rollout plan (milestones).
9) Risk register & mitigation (top 5).
10) Operational considerations (observability, rollouts, fallback).
11) Pricing/commitment ask (if applicable).
12) Next steps & owners.

Facilitation notes (tips and micro-scripts):
- Opening: "We’ll leave today with a one-page POC plan and two experiments you can run within 2–4 weeks."
- When getting stuck on scope: use the "no-more-than-3" rule — at most 3 KPIs, 3 stakeholders, 3 technical unknowns for the POC.
- Dot-vote technique: give each participant 3 dots to allocate across risks/unknowns. Use top-3 as spike focus.
- Timeboxing: call out remaining time at 5-minute marks; assign someone as timekeeper.
- Handling disagreements on deployment: refocus on acceptance criteria. Ask "Which deployment lets us test the primary success metric fastest?"

Breakout templates (copy into a doc during workshop):
- Spike title
- Hypothesis (one sentence)
- Data required
- Steps (1–5 bullets)
- Success criteria (explicit measurement)
- Owner & estimate (days)

30/60/90 Example plan (deliverable to leave with customer):
- Day 0–30 (Discovery & fast validation):
  - Finalize POC scope, run spike 1 (functional) and spike 2 (performance), deliver sample outputs.
  - Deliverable: working notebook + perf report (p95/p99, token cost).
  - Owner: Solutions Eng (initial), Customer Eng.
- Day 31–60 (Integration & ops):
  - Integrate model into staging path, add tracing/cost telemetry, run canary with subset of traffic.
  - Deliverable: staging endpoint, alerts, dashboard.
  - Owner: Customer infra + Redwood SRE/Eng.
- Day 61–90 (Scale & handoff):
  - Scale tests to expected QPS, finalize security controls, sign-off on go/no-go gates.
  - Deliverable: runbook, SLA checklist, go-live date recommendation.
  - Owner: Product + Customer Ops.

Acceptance gates (go/no-go):
- Quality gate: model meets baseline precision/recall or user satisfaction target on representative dataset.
- Performance gate: meets latency SLOs at target load with acceptable cost.
- Compliance gate: data handling and encryption meet stated requirements.

Top risks & mitigations (to capture on mapping wall):
- Unknown: sample data incompatibility. Mitigation: sample ingestion spike day 1.
- Unknown: auth/integration complexity (SAML, internal proxies). Mitigation: early security sync and integration checklist.
- Risk: cost overrun on inference. Mitigation: use smaller quantized model for canary + Redwood Optimize recommendations.

Deliverables to produce within 5 business days after workshop:
- Filled Zero-to-POC Canvas (single page).
- Two spike runbooks and owners.
- Draft 30/60/90 with milestones and owners.
- Shared slide deck (10–12 slides) and a short summary email template to reach execs.

Checklist for SE before running the workshop:
- Send prework and collect responses.
- Build a starter canvas and pre-populate known fields.
- Provision a lightweight test harness (notebook + token) to demo quick model outputs.
- Prepare mapping wall materials (virtual Miro board or physical sticky notes).
- Confirm attendees include 1 exec sponsor, 1 engineering lead, 1 product owner, 1 security/infra contact.

Follow-up email skeleton (one-paragraph + attachments):
- Opening line: thank you + one-sentence outcome.
- Attachments: canvas, slides, spike runbooks, 30/60/90 plan.
- Call to action: confirm owners and two-week check-in date.

Notes from recent customer run (lessons learned):
- Customers often under-estimate the cost variance between dev and production traffic patterns — show a cost band example early.
- Early encryption/key management conversations avoid late delays for Private deployments.
- Small, high-confidence spikes build trust faster than large, ambiguous proofs.

Outcomes (intended):
- A signed-off POC scope and timeline.
- Two rapid validation spikes with owners and explicit success metrics.
- A clear 30/60/90 roadmap that ties to business KPIs.

Quick reference (one-liners):
- If asked about latency vs cost: "We trade latency for cost via batching/quantization and routing policies — measure both on your sample workload."
- If asked about model drift: "Schedule a quality regression checkpoint in the 60-day milestone tied to production prompts."

End of document.

Summary:
This page defines the Kernel Snapshot Observability Contract used by the serving runtime to capture lightweight, deterministic kernel-level state for fast post-hoc diagnostics, profiling correlation, and benchmark reproducibility. The contract describes snapshot contents, TTL/retention semantics, collection cadence, storage indexing, query semantics, and the recommended operational playbook for using snapshots during incidents and regressions.

Why we need a formal contract:
- Reduce triage time: snapshots provide a small, self-contained view of kernel scheduling state across shards without requiring full traces.
- Reproducible regression hunts: standardized fields make automated delta comparison (hashes/digests) possible across releases and benchmarks.
- Safe production capture: contract enforces size and cost limits to keep collection cheap and non-disruptive.

Scope and goals:
- Scope: GPU-scheduling kernels, kernel selector hints, active batch queue heads, kvcache hot entries metadata, and per-request token-progress markers. Not intended to replace full GPU traces or perf counters.
- Goals: <= 2KB compressed per snapshot per shard typical, capture latency < 5ms end-to-end, snapshot ingestion availability 99.9%.

Contract: snapshot manifest fields (string names and semantic description)
- manifest_type: "kernel-snapshot-v1" (identifies schema version).
- timestamp_utc: RFC3339 string (origin of capture).
- host_id: runtime host identifier (short hash).
- shard_id: logical shard name/id.
- kernel_hint: canonical kernel name in scheduler (e.g. "attn_sharded_kv_v2").
- active_requests: comma-separated list of up to 8 request_ids with short metadata (see Active Request Encoding below).
- batch_head_shape: concurrency/sequence-length tuple (e.g. "concurrency=12;avg_seq=128").
- kv_hot_prefix_digest: 64-bit hex digest of most-frequent KV prefixes (comma-separated up to 4).
- queue_depth: integer (number of queued kernel tasks).
- slot_usage_pct: integer 0-100 (measured GPU slot occupancy estimate).
- mem_watermark_mb: integer (resident MB attributed to shard at capture).
- fallback_flags: short tokenized list of active degradation flags (e.g. "quantized-fallback,eviction-throttle").
- capture_id: uuid string (unique id for this snapshot).
- sample_hash: sha1 hex of the canonicalized manifest (for fast equality checks).

Active Request Encoding (embedded): up to 8 items, each encoded as colon-separated tokens: request_id|model:ver|priority|est_remaining_tokens
Example: "r1234|redwood/7b:2026-03-01|p2|est32"

Size and performance constraints:
- Uncompressed manifest must be <= 8KB. Producers MUST gzip the payload before upload.
- Capture must be non-blocking for request latency: producers should sample at scheduling safe points (e.g. pre-dispatch / post-eviction) and limit synchronous work to timestamping and copying small metadata.
- Max capture cadence per shard: 1 snapshot / 5s by default; bursts up to 1/second allowed during active debugging windows.

Capture lifecycle and TTL semantics:
- Local ephemeral cache: snapshots are kept in-memory for 30s to enable immediate correlation with live traces.
- Short-term storage: snapshots forwarded to an indexed store with 7-day retention for operational triage.
- Long-term archive: on-demand (by capture_id or sample_hash) snapshots older than 7 days may be kept in cold archive for 90 days if pinned by a runbook or regression alert.
- Automatic eviction: snapshots exceeding store quotas are evicted by oldest-first per-host.

Storage & indexing conventions:
- Index keys: sample_hash, capture_id, host_id, shard_id, kernel_hint, timestamp_utc.
- Tags: release_tag (e.g. "canary-2026-03-10"), experiment_id (if collection was triggered by an experiment), incident_id (if captured during an incident).
- Searchable fields must be text-tokenized and exact-match filterable for sample_hash and kernel_hint.

Producer responsibilities and API contract:
1) Capture API (local agent): POST /v1/internal/kernel-snapshot 
   - Headers: X-Host-ID, X-Shard-ID, X-Capture-Src (auto|manual|diag).
   - Body: gzip'd manifest (UTF-8).
   - Response: 202 Accepted with JSON {"capture_id":"...","sample_hash":"...","ingest_ts":"..."}.
2) Backoff: if remote ingestion errors with 5xx more than 3 consecutive times, agent falls back to local retention only and emits metric runtime.snapshot.ingest.failures.
3) Priority: manual-triggered captures (via runbook) should include X-Capture-Priority: high and are exempt from per-shard cadence limits for a 60s window.

Query and diagnosis workflow (runbook):
1) Triage start: on a latency SLO violation or kernel regression alert, runbook owner initiates "snapshot-hunt".
2) Retrieve matching snapshots by filter: sample_hash, kernel_hint, timeframe, release_tag.
3) Run a delta comparison on sample_hash across canary vs baseline to find divergence.
4) If sample_hash matches but incident persists, escalate to full trace capture: enable continuous tracing for affected shards (see profiling-playbook integration below).

Integration with profiling playbooks and benchmarking suite:
- Profiling correlation: snapshots are lightweight keys to join streaming traces and microbenchmarks. Include capture_id in trace span attribute: runtime.kernel_snapshot.capture_id.
- Benchmark gating: nightly benchmarks must capture a deterministic snapshot for each workload and store sample_hash in benchmark results CSV. Regression rule: any benchmark run where the sample_hash distribution differs from baseline for > 20% of shards triggers a quality alert.
- Kernel scheduler experiments: when rolling out kernel changes, collect snapshot cohorts (baseline/canary) and run a pairwise hash-difference analysis as part of the release checklist.

Release gating checklist (minimum):
- Collect cohort snapshots for baseline and canary for 24 hours with at least 1000 snapshots per cohort.
- Run automated sample_hash cluster analysis and ensure no new kernel_hint set appears in >5% of canary shards unless intentionally rolled out.
- Verify average slot_usage_pct and queue_depth remain within +/- 10% of baseline.
- Sign-off required by runtime-scheduling and profiling owners.

Alerting and SLOs:
- Metric: runtime.snapshot.ingest.latency_p50 < 30ms, p95 < 100ms.
- Metric: runtime.snapshot.size_bytes_p95 < 4096 bytes compressed.
- Alert: snapshot-ingest-error-rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m -> paging to infra-oncall.
- Alert: sample_hash-drift-score > 0.2 across canary vs baseline -> notify runtime-release-team.

Known limitations and mitigations:
- Not a full trace: snapshots are intentionally small and do not include per-kernel GPU counters. Use them to triage and then escalate to detailed tracing.
- Digest collisions: sample_hash uses sha1 of a canonicalized manifest; collisions are possible but extremely unlikely. If collision suspected, attach raw manifest comparison.
- Cost: high-frequency snapshots across all shards increase storage costs; default cadence and burst limits are enforced by agents.

Operational playbook: incident example (step-by-step)
1) Pager fires for high tail latency on model X.
2) Oncall: run "snapshot-query --kernel attn_sharded_kv_v2 --since 5m --format table" across implicated shards.
3) If sample_hash variance high between recently-deployed canary and baseline: run pairwise-diff tool and note differing fields.
4) If mem_watermark_mb spike correlates with queue_depth rise -> trigger immediate spillover rollback (see runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook).
5) Capture extended traces for 10 minutes and mark capture_ids of interest.

CLI examples and snippets:
- Query tool (example):
  # list snapshots matching kernel and timeframe
  snapshot-query --kernel "attn_sharded_kv_v2" --since "2026-05-01T12:00:00Z" --limit 200 --output json

- Minimal producer example (bash curl):
  payload=$(printf '{"manifest_type":"kernel-snapshot-v1","timestamp_utc":"%s","host_id":"h-abc123","shard_id":"s1","kernel_hint":"attn_sharded_kv_v2","active_requests":"r1|m:1|p1|est24","batch_head_shape":"concurrency=8;avg_seq=64","kv_hot_prefix_digest":"%s","queue_depth":12,"slot_usage_pct":72,"mem_watermark_mb":12288,"fallback_flags":"none","capture_id":"%s"}' "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" "deadbeefcafebabe" "$(uuidgen)")
  echo "$payload" | gzip -c | curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Encoding: gzip" -H "X-Host-ID: h-abc123" -H "X-Shard-ID: s1" --data-binary @- https://internal-ingest.redwood/v1/internal/kernel-snapshot

[00:43] Markus Klein: Got it. We can cover both. The offering is basically the same tech, but the commercial wrapper changes.

[00:49] Stephanie Nguyen: Quick agenda: 5 minutes on your intended usage, then we’ll go through SOC posture, audit logs, retention, KMS. We’ll end with action items and what we’ll send.

[01:05] Tom Gallagher: Sounds good.

[01:07] Stephanie Nguyen: Priya, can you give us the one-minute, like, what you’re building and what’s the “red line” for security?

[01:14] Priya Desai: Sure. We’re a fintech. We’re looking at running a set of customer support and doc summarization workflows. Some of it is internal, some could touch customer data. We need to ensure prompts/outputs aren’t retained beyond processing, unless we explicitly opt-in, and we need strong audit logging, SSO, RBAC. Also encryption—ideally customer-managed keys, at least for anything at rest.

[01:41] Evan Brooks: And on the platform side, we’d likely start with hosted API to move fast, but we might need a dedicated pool if latency is spiky or if we need isolation. Private/VPC is not off the table, but that’s heavier.

[01:56] Naomi Feldman: That helps. We’ll talk about how those requirements map to Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.

[02:04] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Olga, do you want to start with compliance posture and what we can share?

[02:09] Olga Petrov: Yep. So Redwood maintains a SOC 2 Type II report. We also have an internal control mapping that aligns to ISO 27001-style control families—access control, change management, vendor risk, incident response, etc.

[02:24] Tom Gallagher: When you say “aligns,” you’re not claiming certified ISO 27001, right? Just mapping.

[02:29] Olga Petrov: Correct, mapping and alignment. We are not representing ISO certification on this call. For SOC 2: we can share the full report through our secure portal once an NDA is in place. If your marketplace reviewer needs a bridge letter depending on timing, we can provide that too.

[02:47] Priya Desai: Okay. And scope—does it cover the hosted service?

[02:51] Olga Petrov: Yes, the in-scope systems include the hosted inference service and the supporting control plane components. If you do Private deployment, there’s shared responsibility—some controls move to your environment. We’ll share that matrix.

[03:08] Markus Klein: We also have a marketplace-focused security overview doc—kind of a packet—so you don’t have to dig through random pages.

[03:16] Mina Cho: That’s the one AWS asks for sometimes, right? Like “data flow diagram,” “encryption,” “audit logs.”

[03:22] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. We have a security documentation bundle for marketplace review. It includes: high-level architecture, data flow, encryption, retention, audit logging, and shared responsibility.

[03:35] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Let’s go into data handling and retention because that’s usually the hot one.

[03:41] Naomi Feldman: Yep. So for the hosted API: prompts and model outputs are processed to generate a response. By default, we’re not using customer content to train models. Content isn’t shared across tenants. We do retain certain operational metadata for observability—latency, token counts, error codes.

[04:02] Priya Desai: Do you store the raw prompts or completions?

[04:05] Naomi Feldman: It depends on configuration and what logging is enabled. Generally, we minimize retention of payload content. In some cases, customers opt in to store request/response samples for debugging or evaluations, and we can also set retention windows. For regulated customers, the default we recommend is payload logging off, and only metadata retained.

[04:30] Evan Brooks: Is “payload logging off” something we can enforce org-wide?

[04:33] Naomi Feldman: Yes, you can enforce at the org level via policy in the console, and we can confirm that in writing. We also have redaction options for certain fields if you do log.

[04:46] Tom Gallagher: What’s the default retention for metadata?

[04:50] Naomi Feldman: For operational metrics, typical retention is on the order of weeks to support troubleshooting and billing reconciliation. For audit logs, it’s longer—months—because enterprises need that. I want to be careful with exact numbers on the call; we’ll send the current defaults and the configurable ranges after I double-check the latest marketplace settings.

[05:14] Priya Desai: Please do. AWS reviewers will ask “how many days,” very literally.

[05:19] Naomi Feldman: Understood.

[05:21] Markus Klein: Also, if you go Dedicated or Private, the retention story changes because you can keep more in your environment or restrict what’s stored in our control plane.

[05:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Residency next. Evan mentioned US vs maybe EU. What do you need?

[05:38] Mina Cho: We’re primarily US, but we have a small EU footprint. We don’t want data unexpectedly processed outside the region.

[05:47] Naomi Feldman: For hosted, you select the region endpoint. Requests are processed in that region. We’ll provide the list of supported regions for marketplace buyers and what data stays in-region versus what’s global in the control plane (for example, account-level billing records).

[06:10] Priya Desai: So the prompt and response stay in the region endpoint? Not bouncing around?

[06:14] Markus Klein: Correct, the inference happens where you send it. There are edge cases like failover if you explicitly enable cross-region fallback. But that’s a policy you control. Default is no cross-region.

[06:29] Priya Desai: Okay, that’s good.

[06:32] Stephanie Nguyen: Encryption. Markus, want to tee it up, and Naomi can fill in KMS details?

[06:38] Markus Klein: Sure. In transit: TLS. At rest: data stored in our systems is encrypted. The question usually becomes: do you need customer-managed keys.

[06:49] Priya Desai: Yes. Ideally CMK. We’re fine if hosted is Redwood-managed KMS at first, but we need to know the roadmap and options.

[06:58] Naomi Feldman: Right. So for Hosted API, encryption at rest uses cloud KMS under our management. For Dedicated and Private we have stronger options. In Private, because it’s in your VPC or on-prem, you can use your own KMS/HSM and key policies. For Dedicated, there are options for customer-managed keys depending on the exact deployment model and cloud account structure. I don’t want to overpromise—so we’ll follow up with the definitive “supported today” and “supported with Private” statement.

[07:30] Tom Gallagher: We need that spelled out. “Possible” doesn’t work for auditors.

[07:33] Naomi Feldman: Totally fair.

[07:36] Evan Brooks: For hosted, is there any at-rest storage of payload content where the key management matters? If payload logging is off, then it’s mostly metadata anyway.

[07:46] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. Key management is still relevant for the metadata, audit logs, and any configuration artifacts, but the sensitivity is lower if payloads aren’t stored.

[08:00] Priya Desai: How about secrets? API keys? Are those encrypted at rest with KMS as well?

[08:05] Markus Klein: Yes. API keys and tokens are stored in an encrypted secrets store. Access is restricted and audited.

[08:12] Olga Petrov: And access to production systems is controlled with least privilege and logged. That’s in the SOC report.

[08:20] Priya Desai: Okay.

[08:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s do audit logging. Priya, what do you need to see? API calls? Admin actions?

[08:28] Priya Desai: Admin actions for sure—org creation, user invites, role changes, API key creation, model changes. Also if there’s any change in retention settings, that needs to be in the audit log. And ideally the ability to export to our SIEM.

[08:46] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We log administrative events in the console and control plane. Typical events: user auth events, SSO changes, role and permission changes, API key create/revoke, workspace/org settings changes, retention policy changes, and deployment/rollout events for models if you’re using those features.

[09:09] Markus Klein: For export: we support pulling audit logs via API and exporting to object storage, and we’ve had customers forward into Splunk. We can share a “how to” and the event taxonomy.

[09:24] Priya Desai: Is the audit log immutable?

[09:27] Naomi Feldman: You can’t edit audit events. Internally we treat it as append-only. For higher assurance, we recommend exporting to your SIEM where you apply your own immutability controls.

[09:39] Tom Gallagher: Retention for audit logs?

[09:41] Naomi Feldman: There’s a default retention and an enterprise option for longer retention. Again, I’ll send the exact days. We don’t want to quote wrong and then have to correct later.

[09:56] Tom Gallagher: Appreciate that.

[10:00] Mina Cho: Does any of this differ because it’s AWS Marketplace? Like, do we get a different tenant or something?

[10:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Commercially it’s billed via marketplace, but it’s still a Redwood org. The key difference is the onboarding flow: subscription → entitlement → org provisioning. Markus, you want to mention entitlement logs?

[10:18] Markus Klein: Sure. Marketplace entitlements are validated via our entitlement verification endpoints. Those checks are logged on our side. If there’s a provisioning delay, we can trace it.

[10:30] Evan Brooks: Provisioning delay is something we’ve seen with other marketplace stuff. How long does it typically take?

[10:36] Markus Klein: Usually minutes. Sometimes there’s propagation delay on the marketplace side. We’ve added retries and alerting. If it’s more than, say, 30-60 minutes, we treat it as an issue and can escalate.

[10:54] Priya Desai: Okay. Not security, but good to know.

[10:58] Stephanie Nguyen: Back to the security packet. Olga, can you explain how we share evidence without emailing PDFs around?

[11:05] Olga Petrov: Yeah. We provide a gated evidence index: SOC 2 report, pen test attestation letters if applicable, policy summaries. We do not email the full SOC report. You get access through a secure portal with named users. For marketplace reviewers, we can also provide a “customer-facing security overview” that’s public-ish and doesn’t contain sensitive internals.

[11:28] Tom Gallagher: That works.

[11:30] Priya Desai: Pen test—do you do regular pentesting?

[11:34] Olga Petrov: We run ongoing vulnerability management and periodic third-party penetration testing. Details and dates are in the evidence pack; we’ll share the attestation letter, not raw findings.

[11:48] Priya Desai: Okay.

[11:50] Evan Brooks: What about SSO? We need SAML.

[11:54] Markus Klein: Yes, SSO/SAML is supported for enterprise plans. You can enforce it and block password login. We also have RBAC.

[12:05] Priya Desai: Is MFA required for console?

[12:08] Naomi Feldman: We support MFA and you can enforce it, plus SSO with your IdP typically meets your MFA policy anyway.

[12:16] Tom Gallagher: Incident response—do you have an SLA for notifying us?

[12:20] Olga Petrov: Our incident response policy includes customer notification timelines based on severity and contractual terms. The SOC report covers our IR process. For Dedicated/Private, contract language can specify.

[12:36] Priya Desai: Okay.

[12:38] Stephanie Nguyen: I’m going to scroll us to the really specific questions AWS sometimes asks. Priya/Tom, anything you know is coming?

[12:46] Priya Desai: They ask: encryption in transit version (TLS 1.2+), encryption at rest, KMS, audit logs, retention, data deletion, subcontractors.

[12:56] Naomi Feldman: We can cover deletion. For hosted: you can delete API keys and users. For data: if payload logging is disabled, there isn’t payload content persisted to delete, aside from transient processing. If you have payload logging enabled, deletion requests can remove stored samples, and retention policies ensure expiry.

[13:19] Tom Gallagher: Subprocessors list—can you provide?

[13:22] Olga Petrov: Yes, we have a subprocessors list as part of our trust documentation. We’ll provide it.

[13:30] Evan Brooks: One thing: do you use our data to fine-tune or train any models?

[13:35] Markus Klein: No, not by default. We don’t train foundation models on customer prompts/outputs. Any opt-in eval or logging is for your own monitoring/debugging.

[13:49] Priya Desai: Okay.

[13:51] (crosstalk)

[13:52] Mina Cho: And contractually, is that in your terms?

[13:56] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, it’s in the data use terms. For marketplace, there are AWS terms plus our EULA/SSA depending on offer type. We can point you to the exact clause.

[14:10] Tom Gallagher: I want to circle back to customer-managed keys. For a fintech, we often require CMK for any system storing sensitive data.

[14:18] Naomi Feldman: Understood. The honest answer is: CMK is straightforward in Private deployment because it’s your environment, your KMS. For Hosted, it’s Redwood-managed keys. For Dedicated, it depends on how dedicated is provisioned—single-tenant cluster but still Redwood-managed cloud account vs customer account. We have patterns for both. We’ll confirm which ones are available in the marketplace SKU you’re considering.

[14:47] Priya Desai: If we start hosted, can we migrate to Dedicated/Private later without changing API?

[14:52] Markus Klein: Yes, the API surface is consistent. There can be endpoint differences and networking changes, but your application code is basically the same.

[15:04] Evan Brooks: Good.

[15:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s capture what we need to send after the call so you can check the boxes. Priya, do you have a questionnaire we can respond to?

[15:14] Priya Desai: Yes, I can send our standard spreadsheet. It’s like 150 questions.

[15:19] Markus Klein: Love those.

[15:21] Priya Desai: Sorry.

[15:23] Markus Klein: No, all good.

[15:24] Tom Gallagher: Also AWS has their own “security review” template sometimes.

[15:29] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. We’ve been through those. We’ll respond with citations to our packet.

[15:35] Naomi Feldman: One more thing: audit log event list. We’ll provide a list of events and fields (timestamp, actor, IP, action, resource, result). That’s typically what auditors want.

[15:51] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[15:53] Evan Brooks: Can you talk about network isolation in Dedicated? Like, is it single tenant.

[15:58] Markus Klein: Dedicated is single-tenant compute capacity. You get isolation at the cluster/pool level, and you can also restrict access via IP allowlists, private connectivity options depending on cloud. Private is the full “in your VPC” option.

[16:16] Priya Desai: If we do hosted via marketplace, can we do private link?

[16:21] Markus Klein: In some cases yes, but it depends on region and SKU. We can follow up.

[16:28] Tom Gallagher: Another question: do you have audit logs for data access by Redwood employees?

[16:34] Olga Petrov: Our internal access to production systems is logged. Customer-facing audit logs cover customer admin actions. For employee access logs, we can describe the controls and provide evidence in SOC 2, but we don’t stream raw employee logs to customers.

[16:52] Tom Gallagher: That’s standard.

[16:54] Priya Desai: Makes sense.

[16:56] Stephanie Nguyen: I’m going to jump to retention again. We keep hearing “weeks” and “months.” We’ll follow up with precise defaults. Naomi, anything else we should note?

[17:07] Naomi Feldman: Just that retention is separated: (1) request/response payload retention (ideally off), (2) operational metrics retention, (3) audit logs retention. Those have different defaults and knobs.

[17:24] Priya Desai: Great. Also deletion workflow—if we need to confirm deletion, do you provide confirmation?

[17:30] Naomi Feldman: For stored artifacts, yes we can provide confirmation through support and audit events for the action. For transient processing, there’s nothing persisted.

[17:43] Evan Brooks: What about backups? If something is stored, does it persist in backups beyond retention?

[17:49] Naomi Feldman: Backups are encrypted and access-controlled. For some systems, backups have their own lifecycle. We account for that in retention policies. We’ll provide a written statement of how deletion and retention interact with backups at a high level.

[18:10] Priya Desai: Okay, thanks.

[18:12] (gap)

[18:14] Markus Klein: While we’re here, can I ask: are you evaluating other providers? Just to understand what you’re comparing.

[18:20] Evan Brooks: We looked at Bedrock, and also direct OpenAI. Bedrock is nice for procurement but the controls are kind of… variable. And cost.

[18:32] Priya Desai: And we looked at Together. We’re trying to balance performance with controls.

[18:38] Markus Klein: Yep, makes sense. Our pitch is: consistent inference runtime plus enterprise controls across hosted/dedicated/private.

[18:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, I want to be respectful of time. Let’s do a quick checklist recap and then we’ll end early if we can.

[18:56] Tom Gallagher: Works.

[18:58] Stephanie Nguyen: 1) SOC 2 Type II report: Olga will share portal access instructions under NDA. 2) Marketplace security packet: Naomi will share the index and we’ll confirm what’s public versus gated. 3) Audit logs: Markus will send event list, export methods, and retention defaults. 4) Retention statement: Naomi will send exact defaults and configurable options. 5) KMS/CMK: we’ll send a deployment-mode matrix (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) with what’s supported today.

[19:32] Mina Cho: And procurement: I’ll confirm whether we need private offer.

[19:36] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect.

[19:38] Priya Desai: Can you also include subcontractors list in that packet?

[19:41] Olga Petrov: Yep. I’ll include that.

[19:44] Evan Brooks: And can you confirm if cross-region failover is off by default? We want that in writing.

[19:50] Markus Klein: Yes. We’ll include that.

[19:54] Priya Desai: Great.

[19:56] Stephanie Nguyen: Before we close: any “no-go” issues if you don’t get CMK in hosted?

[20:02] Priya Desai: Not a hard no-go for a limited pilot if payload logging is off and we’re not sending high sensitivity data. But for production with customer data, we’ll probably need either dedicated with CMK or private.

[20:16] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s fair.

[20:18] Tom Gallagher: Yep.

[20:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. We’ll send the follow-up within two business days. Let’s schedule a 30-minute follow-up next week once you’ve reviewed the materials.

[20:30] Mina Cho: I’ll wait for the pricing path too, but yes.

[20:33] Markus Klein: We can also hop on with your SIEM team if needed.

[20:37] Priya Desai: Might take you up on that.

[20:40] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, thanks everyone.

[20:43] (Call continues with light scheduling chatter; transcription truncated by Fireflies export settings.)

[51:58] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, we’re good. Thanks all.

Question: In some lab notes about reducing few-shot example copying, what tradeoff was noted when rotating the order of exemplars in prompts?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_7a2cfe4b7e574e6995f33e64bbdbf426:
Purpose
Quick personal scratchpad capturing experiments and heuristics for reducing exemplar overdominance in few-shot prompt sets (what I call 'attenuation') — aim: keep exemplar signal useful but avoid literal copying, brittle token-level overfit, and instruction hijacking.

Background / rationale
- Problem: when small numbers of exemplars are highly similar or strongly formatted, model tends to: copy exact phrasing, overfit label tokens, or treat examples as hard rules instead of cues. This shows up as hallucinated metadata, hallucinated reasoning steps, or brittle failures on paraphrase inputs.
- Goal: heuristics that are cheap to test in hosted/Dedicated flows; prefer prompt-side fixes (no fine-tuning) that interact well with Redwood runtime features: prefix caching, batching, and token-budget SLOs.

Experiment log (chronological)
1) baseline 3-shot (A)
- Template: \"Instructions: Paraphrase to plain English. Example 1 -> Q: \"What is the meaning of life?\" A: \"Life means...\"\" (simple exact format)
- Observed: 36% verbatim reuse for unique phrases, 18% hallucinated numeric claims.

2) example-noise (B) — tiny perturbations
- Apply light paraphrase to exemplars (tense swap, synonym replace). Keep labels same.
- Observed: small reduction in verbatim copying (~22%) but occasional polarity flips (because paraphrase introduced negation in two examples).

3) anchor-token dilution (C)
- Insert neutral anchor sentence before each example: \"(Example for style only; ignore facts.)\"
- Observed: Large drop in factual hallucination (13%), but model ignored label formatting more frequently -> answer brevity decreased.

4) exemplar-weighting via explicit meta cues (D)
- Prefix: \"Examples are guides, not rules. Provide your own phrasing.\" and add \"EXAMPLE_START\" tokens between examples (unique sequence).
- Observed: Better paraphrase diversity; lower exact-match. Slight latency + token usage increase (anchor tokens counted).

5) negative-exemplar (E)
- Include 1 negative example showing what *not* to do.
- Observed: helped on structure errors but introduced confusion when negative example had contradictory label tokens.

Quick takeaway: combination of paraphrase augmentation + explicit \"guidance\" prefix seems promising. Anchors reduce hallucination but cost tokens.

Prototype heuristics (to test systematically)
- ShotRotation: rotate order of exemplars per request to avoid position bias (cheap, interacts badly with caching — needs route-aware cache bypass).
- SoftParaphrasePool: maintain pool of 5 paraphrase variants per exemplar; sample 1–2 per prompt. Reduces verbatim reuse.
- AnchorLite: single short anchor token phrase (\"Style guide: be original.\") vs full sentence; measure delta/loss ratio.
- ExampleContrast: for categorical tasks, include 1 borderline example to widen model boundary; for generative tasks include 1 counterexample to show failure modes.
- TokenBudget-aware truncation: if request close to budget, automatically switch to AnchorLite + 1-shot.

Failure modes observed / notes
- Instruction hijacking: too many meta-cues cause model to treat prompt like a multi-step instruction list and follow the wrong step. Keep meta-language short.
- Contradictory anchors: negative examples that contradict label vocabulary can flip final labels. Use neutral phrasing for negatives (show format, not content).
- Caching/cold-start interaction: rotating exemplars defeats prefix caching; for high-QPS routes, prefer static exemplar unless you have hot cache invalidation.

Sample prompt prototypes (short)
1) SoftParaphrase 3-shot (compact)
\"GUIDE: Use your own words. \nExample 1:\nQ: How to reset my router?\nA: Turn it off, wait 30s, turn on.\n--\nExample 2:\nQ: Steps to cancel subscription?\nA: Sign in, go to billing, click cancel.\n--\nNow answer:\nQ: {{user_q}}\n\"

2) AnchorLite + negative (compact)
\"Style: concise, do not echo examples exactly.\nBAD EXAMPLE:\nQ: What is pi?\nA: 3.14159 EXACT (do not mirror)\nGOOD EXAMPLES:\n... (2 positive paraphrased examples)\nAnswer: {{user_q}}\n\"

Measurement plan (automated)
- Metrics: exact-token overlap rate, n-gram reuse, paraphrase-similarity (embedding cosine to exemplars), faithfulness score (task-specific), token cost delta, 95th pct latency.
- Dataset: 400 eval queries per template; include paraphrase + adversarial variants.
- Compare across: baseline static-3shot, SoftParaphrase, AnchorLite, Rotation-once-per-1000, Negative-example. Use Redwood Dedicated for consistent latency measurement.

Open questions / TODOs
- Q1: How much does exemplar diversity interact with model size/quantization? run small-medium-large (ggml/FP16/8-bit) matrix.
- Q2: Should we expose attenuation knobs in the SDK (e.g., sample_paraphrase_count, anchor_level)? sketch API surface.
- Q3: Best practice doc: one-pager for Solutions team summarizing heuristics + when to prefer server-side cache bypass. Draft outline needed.

Action items (short)
- [ ] Run 5k evaluation across two models and log metrics (owner: Jonas) — Linear-4821
- [ ] Prototype SDK flags for AnchorLite and ShotRotation (owner: me) — drop-in param: attenuation: {none, lite, full}
- [ ] Short internal note for Solutions with examples and recommended defaults (owner: Priya)

Rough notes to self (messy)
- prefer 1–2 short anchors instead of long meta paragraphs; long ones break model flow
- negative exemplars should not reuse label tokens; use neutral markers like \"LABEL:X\" to show format only
- consider embedding-cluster sampling to pick exemplars that are diverse w.r.t. user query (but cost is extra lookup)
- remember: batching + shared prompt templates can accidentally leak anchoring if not per-request randomized

Snippets / quick experiments to copy into test harness
- bash pseudo: \nfor MODEL in rwd-xl rwd-medium; do run_eval --template softparaphrase --paraphrases 3 --samples 1; done

References / links for myself
- internal: RFC: fewshot-guidance-patterns (confluence id: 8743)
- external: paper on instruction induction: \"When Prompts Collude\" (noted in reading list)

End of pad.

(Notes intentionally rough — keep evolving. Will move to a more polished playbook if evaluation results look promising.)

description:
Define a lightweight, operational index (Model Resilience Propensity Index, MRPI) to quantify risk of service-impacting model supply events for customers and produce a reproducible field-probe playbook that triggers procurement/rollout actions. The MRPI combines telemetry signals (latency/availability drift, quantization regressions, provenance churn), model compatibility fragility, and regional capacity volatility into a single actionable score with thresholds that map to playbook steps (investigate, canary, procurement alert, fallback activation).

acceptance_criteria:
1) MRPI score spec documented with contributor formulas and sample calculations for three representative customers; 2) Field probe playbook drafted with step-by-step runbook (investigate -> canary -> procurement trigger -> rollback); 3) Two synthetic probe workloads implemented and runnable in CI; 4) Prototype dashboard mock (console) visualizing MRPI by region/model; 5) Stakeholder sign-off from SRE, Sales Ops, and Solutions Engineering.

deliverables:
MRPI spec doc (Confluence)
Field probe runbook (playbook)
2 synthetic workload harnesses (GitHub)
Console dashboard mock (Figma)
Procurement trigger mapping sheet

notes:
Rationale: customers increasingly ask for proactive model-fallback triggers rather than reactive SLAs; MRPI should be lightweight and explainable.
Trade-off: include model-behavioral regressions (quality) vs keeping index operationally simple. Start with telemetry + supply signals, add quality signal v2.
Decision so far: normalize signals to 0-100 and weight by observed incident contribution (initial weights: telemetry 50, capacity volatility 30, compatibility 20). We will recalibrate after 4 weeks of probes.
Link: MRPI skeleton draft: https://redwood.atlassian.net/l/MRPI-draft (confluence)
Link: synthetic probe repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/mrpi-probes (stub)
Potential follow-ups: integrate MRPI into Console alerts and create per-customer tuning profiles for enterprise accounts.

TAB: Summary
Last updated: 2025-03-14 (Nikhil)

Goal
Define a KPI + telemetry spec to measure whether Quickstart Templates (RAG + Agents) improve Hosted API activation, conversion, and reduce support load, without collecting sensitive content.

Scope
- Hosted API self-serve + sales-assisted (but metrics primarily PLG).
- Template-originated traffic only (tagged / identifiable).
- Initial templates: rag-agent-python, rag-agent-typescript.

North Star (v1)
- Time-to-First-Success (TTFS): from first API key created to first successful template-run request (200 + stream completed OR non-stream response completed) within 60 minutes.

Primary KPIs
1) Activation
- TTFS (p50/p90) for template users vs non-template new users
- Activation rate: % of new accounts reaching “First Success” within D0 (same day) / D7

2) Conversion
- % of activated template users converting to paid within 14/30 days
- $: first 30-day revenue per activated template account (median)

3) Retention / quality of adoption
- D7/D30 retention: % of activated template accounts with >= X tokens / >= Y requests
- Share of traffic tagged as template-originated for first 7 days (proxy for “stuck with it”)

4) Support deflection
- Support tickets per 1k new accounts (template cohort vs baseline)
- Template troubleshooting page engagement vs ticket creation (proxy)

Guardrails
- Opt-in telemetry by default for non-essential headers; templates must still function if telemetry is disabled.
- No prompts, completions, retrieved documents, or tool outputs in analytics events.
- Avoid high-cardinality dimensions (don’t log raw request IDs, customer IDs in metrics tags; use internal joins).

Owners
- KPI definitions + targets: Nikhil (Hosted API PM), Henry (Hosted API PM)
- Telemetry platform + analytics plumbing: Logan Wright
- Template implementation: Monica Patel (DevEx)
- Docs funnel + troubleshooting instrumentation: Elliot Price (Docs), Wei Chen (Tech writer)
- Support deflection measurement: Priya Shah (Support feedback loop), Dev Patel (Support ops)


TAB: KPI Definitions

KPI 1 — Time-to-First-Success (TTFS)
Definition
- Start: timestamp of first API key created OR first successful auth handshake (whichever is available reliably in data warehouse).
- End: timestamp of first “template_success” event OR first “api_request_success” with template tag + completion/stream end.

Inclusion criteria
- Accounts created after template launch date.
- Template cohort identified by either:
  (a) CLI init event (qs.cli.init)
  (b) template app event (qs.app.start) with template metadata
  (c) API traffic containing template tag header (see telemetry section)

Success condition
- Any generation/embedding request that returns 200 AND is not immediately followed by a client-abort flagged error. For streaming:
  - Success = stream completed (client received end-of-stream) OR server sent a final chunk.

Reporting
- p50/p90 TTFS by: template_name, language, sdk (py/ts), region (bucketed), and plan type (free/paid)


KPI 2 — Activation rate
Definition
- Activation event: first_success
- Rate D0: % of new accounts that reach first_success within 24 hours of signup.
- Rate D7: % within 7 days.

Activation funnel stages (see “Funnel Events” tab)
- signup_created
- api_key_created
- template_scaffolded
- local_run_started
- first_success
- deployed_success (optional, later)


KPI 3 — Conversion to paid
Definition
- % of accounts in template cohort converting to paid plan within 14 and 30 days of signup.
- Also track: time from first_success -> paid conversion (p50/p90).

Notes
- Separate self-serve paid vs sales-assisted contract conversions.
- For sales-assisted, treat “opportunity created” as intermediate metric.


KPI 4 — Retention / sustained usage
Definition
- D7 retention: activated accounts with >= 10 successful requests OR >= 200k tokens by day 7.
- D30 retention: activated accounts with >= 50 successful requests OR >= 1M tokens by day 30.

Rationale
- We want to avoid counting “one-and-done” template runs as success.
- Thresholds should be revisited after internal beta baselines.


KPI 5 — Support deflection
Definition
- Ticket rate: (# support tickets created by accounts in cohort within first 14 days) / (# accounts in cohort) * 1000
- Compare to baseline cohort (new accounts same time window, non-template identified).

Ticket taxonomy (initial)
- auth (401)
- quota/rate limit (429)
- networking/timeout
- streaming disconnect
- otel exporter/config
- tool schema validation
- retrieval empty/poor relevance

Success metric
- Reduce ticket rate by 15–25% for template cohort vs baseline within 60 days of public launch.


TAB: Funnel Events (Event dictionary)

Conventions
- Prefix “qs.” = template/quickstart specific events
- Prefix “api.” = already-existing API traffic events, with added template tags/dimensions

Required fields for qs.* events
- template_name (enum; e.g., rag-agent)
- template_language (python|typescript)
- template_version (semver string)
- distribution (cli|github)
- telemetry_opt_in (true|false)
- environment (local|ci|prod) — keep as small enum

Event table

| Event name | When fired | Source | Required properties | Optional properties (bounded) | Owner | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| qs.cli.install | CLI installed | CLI | os (mac|linux|windows), arch (x64|arm64) | shell (zsh|bash|fish) | Monica | If we can’t reliably capture, drop. Useful to debug install friction. |
| qs.cli.init | Template scaffolded | CLI | template_name, template_language, template_version, distribution=cli | git_init (true|false) | Monica | Writes a local “version stamp” file; event only if telemetry_opt_in=true. |
| qs.cli.doctor | Doctor run | CLI | template_name, template_language, template_version | checks_failed_count (0-10), primary_failure (enum) | Monica | primary_failure: missing_api_key|bad_model|collector_unreachable|dns|other |
| qs.app.start | App started | App | template_name, template_language, template_version, environment=local | runtime (node|python), framework (fastapi|express|other) | Monica | Used to measure “got it running”. |
| qs.app.first_request | First user request made in app | App | template_name, template_language, template_version | request_kind (chat|embed|rerank), used_retrieval (true|false) | Monica | Avoid logging user input. Just the action category. |
| qs.app.first_success | First successful completion/stream | App | template_name, template_language, template_version | streaming (true|false), used_tools (true|false) | Monica | This is preferred “First Success” marker; fallback to api.request success if missing. |
| qs.app.error | Template error surfaced to user | App | template_name, template_language, template_version, error_category (enum) | http_status (200/400/401/429/5xx), retry_attempted (true|false) | Monica + Priya | error_category aligns with template error taxonomy; keep stable for support. |
| api.request | Any API request | Gateway/SDK | request_id (internal), customer_account_id (internal) | template_tag (string), template_version (string) | Logan | Template tag should be join key for cohorting; do not create high-cardinality metrics tags. |
| api.request.success | Successful API request | Gateway/SDK | status=200 | latency_bucket (enum), tokens_in_bucket (enum), tokens_out_bucket (enum) | Logan | Use buckets to avoid cardinality issues. |
| api.request.error | Failed API request | Gateway/SDK | status (401|429|5xx|timeout) | error_type (enum), retryable (true|false) | Logan | Align with SDK error types. |

Template tag header proposal (for api.* attribution)
- Header: X-Redwood-Template
  - Value: <template_name>@<template_version>;<language>
  - Example: rag-agent@1.1.0;python
- Header: X-Redwood-Template-Opt-In
  - Value: true|false

Notes
- Headers must be optional. Some corporate proxies reject unknown headers; templates should support disabling via env.
- Gateway allowlist required (see linked PRs). If blocked, templates should still work and fall back to qs.* events only (if any).


TAB: Dashboard Spec (What we want in Console/Analytics)

Dashboard 1: Quickstarts Overview
- New accounts (daily)
- Template cohort size (daily)
- Activation rate D0/D7 (template vs baseline)
- TTFS p50/p90 (template vs baseline)
- Top failure categories (qs.app.error) by count

Dashboard 2: Funnel (Template cohort)
- api_key_created -> qs.cli.init -> qs.app.start -> first_success
- Drop-off % at each step
- Median time between steps

Dashboard 3: Reliability + cost signals (Template-tagged traffic)
- 401 rate, 429 rate, 5xx rate
- streaming disconnect rate (if detectable via SDK / client abort signals)
- Latency p50/p95 (bucketed)
- Tokens out per request (bucketed)

Dashboard 4: Support deflection
- Tickets per 1k new accounts (template vs baseline)
- Ticket breakdown by category
- Link-outs: troubleshooting docs views, “helpfulness” votes (if available)

Operational view (internal)
- Filter in Console for template-tagged traffic (required for triage + demos)
- Ability to pivot by template_name + version (low cardinality only)


TAB: Targets (initial strawman; to revisit post-internal beta)

Assumptions
- Templates are production-minded; primary value is reducing onboarding entropy and failure loops.

Targets (first 60–90 days post public launch)
- TTFS p50 <= 20 minutes for template cohort (from api_key_created)
- Activation D0: +10–15pp vs baseline
- Activation D7: +5–10pp vs baseline
- Conversion to paid (30d): +2–4pp vs baseline (small early expectation)
- Support tickets per 1k new accounts: -15% vs baseline

What “baseline” means
- New accounts in same time window that do not have template tags or qs.* events.


TAB: Implementation Notes / Constraints

Privacy
- Do not log prompts, retrieved text, tool inputs/outputs, file paths.
- For error events, include category + short stable error_code only (no full stack traces in analytics).

Cardinality constraints
- Allowed dimensions for dashboards: template_name, template_version (top N only), language, environment, status code, error_category.
- Not allowed as metric labels: account_id, request_id, raw model name if too granular (use “model_family” bucket where needed).

Data quality concerns (known)
- Some users scaffold via GitHub template without CLI; we need API-level attribution via headers.
- Some proxies block headers; telemetry should be resilient/optional.
- Streaming “success” is tricky; we need consistent detection (SDK improvements in flight).

Dependencies
- CLI emits qs.cli.init / qs.cli.doctor (DevEx)
- SDK/gateway header allowlist + safe handling (Platform)
- Console filter for template-tagged traffic (Console/Analytics)
- Support ticket tagging alignment with taxonomy (Support Ops)


TAB: Open Questions
1) TTFS start timestamp source
- API key created is best but not always tied to “first attempt”. Alternative: first 401/200 request timestamp.

2) Opt-in defaults
- Do we default telemetry_opt_in=true for template events but make header tagging opt-in? (current leaning: yes; reduce proxy issues)

3) GitHub template attribution
- If user clones repo, we can still set X-Redwood-Template by default from app config. But we need an obvious “turn off telemetry” switch.

4) Defining “paid conversion” for sales-assisted
- Use opportunity created + stage progression? Or strict paid contract signature only?

5) Support deflection attribution window
- 14 days vs 30 days. Support suggests 14 days captures most onboarding tickets; keep both in reporting.

6) Regions / deployment modes
- For hosted API metrics, we can bucket by region. For Dedicated/Private, separate dashboards later.

Change log
- 2025-02-07: Added support deflection definitions + ticket taxonomy mapping.
- 2025-02-21: Updated template header proposal to be optional due to proxy/header issues found in early trials.
- 2025-03-14: Added funnel step definitions (qs.app.first_success preferred over api.request.success for streaming correctness).

anna: Quick sync — thinking about introducing a cost-aware routing layer that prefers cheaper model variants for lower customer tiers and by region. It should also have automatic fallback to higher-quality variants if we detect quality regressions. High-level idea, not details yet.

sam: Quotas/limits angle: if we route free-tier customers to cheaper variant we should also enforce a per-customer token_budget so they can't blow past cost forecasts. If budget exceeded, either degrade to a lower-rate limit or surface upsell.

mike: Implementation sketch: routing policy lives in the control plane. At request time we compute a cheap estimate: tokens_est = ceil(prompt_len / avg_chunk) + ceil(max_output_len / avg_chunk) then cost_est = tokens_est * variant_unit_cost. If cost_est <= tier_max we pick the cheaper variant, else default. Need to cache avg_chunk per model.

description:
Motivation: reduce alert noise and per-request cost attribution overhead for long-tail token spikes by introducing a 'telemetry lattice' for low-cardinality cross-layer linkage and a deferred aggregation path to compact frequent short-lived series. This PR implements a sample-first path-sampling strategy that preserves token-level latency/cost fidelity for high-value routes while preventing cardinality explosion for low-volume routes.

What changed (summary): added a lightweight trace-linking propagator (rw.telemetry.lattice) to stitch gateway request paths to runtime spans, implemented a deferred aggregator that batches metric writes at host-local level and flushes on configurable windows to the central TSDB, introduced sampled token-cost histograms by request_path, and added a new dashboard + tuned alert rules. Also includes an e2e synthetic spike test and rollout flags for staged canary.

Key design notes: telemetry lattice uses a stable 64-bit path-hash encoded in trace baggage and a short-lived sample ID for high-fidelity attribution when sample==true. Deferred aggregation reduces immediate Prometheus series churn by aggregating micro-bursts into a small set of summarized buckets before export. Path-sampling policy: always-sample for routes with route.metadata.telemetry.priority == high, probabilistic sample (1%) for medium, and adaptive sample for low (rate-limited with burst tokens).

Implementation highlights: 1) observability/metrics: token_latency_by_path (histogram_v2) and token_cost_sampled(counter with labels: path_hash,sample_id), host-local deferred_aggregator that coalesces writes, 2) tracing: propagator/propagator.go adds baggage entry "rw-tele-lattice", runtime side attaches sampled token_cost meta to the trace when present, 3) dashboards: dashboards/request-telemetry-lattice.json shows sampled vs aggregated cost and series-count impact, 4) alerts: alerts/adaptive-slo-rules.yaml replaces a static threshold for token-burn with an adaptive baseline keyed on historical p95/p99 for the route and a minimum absolute floor to avoid missing hard regressions.

Testing and rollout: unit tests added for aggregator flush logic and propagator encoding, e2e test telemetry_spike_test.go simulates synthetic bursts across 50 routes and validates series count reduction and attribution signal retention. Feature gated behind config flag telemetry.lattice.enabled and rollout guideline: 10% canary -> 50% -> all, monitor series_count and alert_firing_rate.

Backwards compatibility: non-sampled requests carry only the path_hash which is low-cardinality; no downstream schema changes required for existing dashboards.

Notes to reviewers: focus on cardinality and exporter performance, confirm that the sampling rates/flags are adequate, and validate the adaptive alert thresholds won't hide emergent regressions.

Related: ENG-4092 (alert noise reduction), ENG-4178 (token-cost attribution), minor docs update to explain operator flags.


review_comments:
Aisha Kapoor: Concerned about cardinality for 'path_hash' + dynamic labels; please ensure path_hash is scoped to a service and truncated consistently.
Jordan Park: Reply: path_hash is 64-bit stable hash of normalized path template and we scope exporter labels to 'service' so series = service:path_hash only. added normalization tests.
Dmitri Petrov: The deferred aggregator flush interval looks safe but we should ensure worst-case memory bounds under sustained bursts.
Jordan Park: Reply: added circuit-breaker to aggregator that forces flush and drops to summarized bucket if memory exceeds threshold; documented in telemetry-lattice.md.
Marisol Chen: Please validate that adaptive alert won't mask regressive p99 spikes where absolute latency increases but relative baseline remains similar.
Jordan Park: Reply: adaptive alert includes an absolute floor (configurable) to ensure hard regressions are still surfaced; added test covering regression scenario.

release_notes:
Introduce telemetry lattice for low-cardinality path linkage, sampled token-cost histograms, deferred aggregation to reduce TSDB series churn, and adaptive SLO alerting. Feature gated and rolled out by canary.

notes:
Observed prometheus series reduction ~18% in canary run and alert firing rate reduced by ~42% on noisy low-volume endpoints. Operators should monitor exporter_queue_size and aggregator_memory.
