release_notes:
Reduced GPU peak workspace by up to 28% on long-context models via adaptive scratch allocator and deferred activation checkpoint scheduling. No API changes. Rollout: opt-in via runtime flag 'adaptive_scratch=on' followed by gradual default enablement after smoke validation.

description:
Motivation: GPU workspace (scratch) and activation memory are significant cost drivers for long-context generation and multi-tenant Dedicated pools. Previous changes (arena tuning, static checkpointing) helped but left headroom for per-request adaptation and better interaction with KV cache and continuous batching. This PR implements two coordinated changes: 1) An adaptive scratch allocator that shrinks kernel scratch reservations on hot paths using real allocation traces and a light-weight eviction policy; 2) A deferred activation checkpoint scheduler that opportunistically delays checkpoint insertion until after the kernel selection pass when sequence-to-sequence and KV cache usage are known. Design summary: The adaptive scratch allocator records per-model per-kernel high-water marks over rolling windows and exposes a soft cap that kernels consult at selection time; if the soft cap would be exceeded we attempt two actions: pick a lower-scratch kernel variant or apply a temporary micro-batch split. The deferred checkpoint scheduler moves most activation checkpointing decisions out of the eager graph transform and into the runtime scheduling stage so decisions can use real batch sizes, kv-cache presence, and current scratch headroom. This reduces over-checkpointing on requests that will hit the KV cache and reduces worst-case workspace pressure. Implementation notes: - runtime/inference/scratch_allocator.cpp: new AdaptiveScratchManager, hot-path lock-free counters, bounded trace buffer. - runtime/inference/checkpoint_scheduler.cpp: new DeferredCheckpointPlanner, heuristics to trade memory vs. compute (default: aim for <=15% additional compute). - runtime/kernels/kernel_selector.cpp: kernel variants now expose 'scratch_estimate' and 'checkpoint_safe' metadata; selection integrates with AdaptiveScratchManager. - runtime/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cc: minor changes to expose batching window to planner. - tests/perf/scratch_memory_bench.py: synthetic long-context scenarios across models (gpt-style, encoder-decoder) and KV cache toggles. - docs/ops/scratch-tuning.md: operational guidance and rollout recipe. Tests and results: microbenchmarks show peak GPU workspace reduction of 18-28% across 4 tested models at 32k context; tail latency impact is +4% median, +9% 95th when the allocator picks lower-scratch kernels; overall token throughput for large batches unchanged within noise. KV cache interplay: requests with warm KV cache see much larger benefits because deferred checkpointing avoids storing activations that are unnecessary for cached steps. Safety/rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag 'adaptive_scratch' and 'deferred_ckpt' (both default off). We added a gradual rollout plan: enable in Canary region, observe memory headroom and OOMs for 72h, then opt-in to Dedicated pools with autoscaler guards. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] perf scripts, [x] docs updated, [x] rollout plan, [x] security review (no secrets). Backwards compatibility: none; internal only. Related: ENG-3245 (workspace reductions initiative), ENG-3299 (kv-cache improvement spike).

Diego Ramos: This looks promising. Can you add a safety circuit for cases where the allocator oscillates and causes repeated micro-batch splits? Suggest a backoff cooldown per-model.
Maya Lin: Added a cooldown mechanism (AdaptiveScratchManager::cooldown_ms) and tested with aggressive allocation spikes. Benchmarks included in bench_results/2026-02-20.
Lucas Nguyen: The deferred checkpointing change is invasive. How does this interact with tiled-kv cache eviction? Please outline any assumptions about KV lifecycle.
Maya Lin: Deferred planner consults KVCache::is_warmed(request_id) during planning. If KV lifecycle indicates eviction in same window, we conservatively keep checkpoints. Documented in scratch-tuning.md.
Serena Park: CI failed on linux-gpu-lint initially, some style fixes needed in scratch_allocator.h.
Maya Lin: Fixed style nits and added clang-format CI enforcement for runtime/* files.

Merged to main after two rounds of review and CI stabilization. Feature gates left off by default; ops will enable in canary on 2026-02-25. No regressions observed in e2e smoke tests; memory headroom improved on Dedicated canary by ~22% on average.

description:
Summary: Since 2026-03-09 ~03:00 UTC a subset of newly provisioned users are getting 403 when calling the ModelObservability API. Initial triage shows users exist in OKTA and have expected groups, but the RBAC role lookup in auth-service fails because group identifiers in the incoming auth claim are integers instead of strings after a recent Okta mapping change. Impact: Affected SREs and ML engineers cannot access model observability dashboards or runbook actions; blocking incident response in us-east for customer-impacting alerts.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Create or modify an Okta user with group assignment via provisioning (SCIM).
2) Wait for scim-sync job to run (0-5m).
3) Login to console and call /v1/model-observability/metrics (or open dashboard).
4) Observe 403 and no role in auth-service logs for the user.
Expected: role lookup succeeds and 200 returned. Actual: 403 denied due to missing role mapping.

logs:
auth-service warning: role-lookup: claim.groups value types: [123456, 234567] (type: integer)
expected mapping key types: "123456"

example token claim (decoded): {
  "sub": "00u1abcXyZ",
  "email": "eng+test@redwood.ai",
  "groups": [123456, 234567],
  "iss": "https://okta.redwood.ai"
}

auth-service debug: mappedRoles=[] for user 00u1abcXyZ at 2026-03-10T03:12:07Z
model-observability-api access denied: headers: { x-rw-user: 00u1abcXyZ } response: 403 {
  "error": "unauthorized",
  "reason": "no-matching-role-for-groups"
}

investigation_notes:
Timeline: change window 2026-03-08 22:00 UTC when Okta admin updated group import mapping to emit numeric IDs (Okta API update). Hypothesis: identity-proxy and scim-sync historically normalized group ids to strings; the new mapping produced integers and our role index uses string keys -> lookup misses.
Findings:
- scim-sync stored groups in DB as strings when coming from canonical SCIM paths, but identity-proxy forwards token claims verbatim.
- auth-service role lookup code compares claim group IDs with role-index map (string keys). No type coercion.
- Reproduced locally by forging token with numeric group values; role lookup returns empty.
- Not all users affected: only those provisioned after Okta mapping change (group ids numeric). Older tokens remain as strings and continue to work.
Evidence: logs above and successful reproduction in staging by creating token with numeric groups.
Mitigation attempted: temporary canary: identity-proxy will coerce numeric claim.groups to strings on ingress; deployed to canary cluster (canary-2) 2026-03-11 18:30 UTC.

comments:
2026-03-10 04:05 - Priya Kapoor (Support): Reported initial customer-facing impact after SRE oncall noted missing access for 3 engineers. Attached sample decoded token and stack trace.
2026-03-10 06:12 - Diego Morales (Auth): Reproduced locally. Hypothesis: type mismatch between Okta claim payload and our role-index typing. Filed quick PR to normalize types in identity-proxy. Linking PR to this ticket.
2026-03-11 19:05 - Samir Patel (SRE): Canary deploy applied to canary-2. Observed two previously-401/403 requests now succeed. Monitoring for 24h to confirm no regressions.
2026-03-12 09:20 - Priya Kapoor (Support): Customer-facing note drafted: "We identified a token group id encoding mismatch caused by an Okta mapping update. A temporary fix has been deployed to canary and will be rolled to prod after validation. Apologize for the disruption."

resolution:
Hotfix: identity-proxy change (PR #498) coerces all group ids in the token claim to strings on ingress and emits a metric for any non-string group values. Auth-service change (PR #1257) added defensive coercion for role lookup as backup. Canary results: successful requests for previously affected users on canary-2. Rollout plan: staged rollout to prod us-east 2026-03-12 15:00 UTC with monitoring and immediate rollback on elevated error rates. Root cause: Okta mapping change that started emitting numeric group ids; our code assumed string typed ids.

1) Add schema validation on identity-proxy (block incoming tokens with unexpected types and alert).
2) Create automated unit test in auth-service for claim type coercion.
3) Ask IAM team to revert or document Okta mapping change and add approver workflow for mapping modifications.
4) Postmortem to be authored in Confluence and linked here after incident closure.

Document dsid_88b39d13bd584ef8b1422d76994808c7:
description:
Motivation: We have diverging streaming ergonomics across Python/TS/Go SDKs and subtle auth-retry edge cases that manifest as half-open streams or token race conditions during refresh. This PR unifies three areas: 1) a minimal, consistent 3-way auth handshake for stream starts and reconnects; 2) a small, opinionated consumer surface that makes backpressure and heartbeats explicit but ergonomic; 3) a single, test-backed retry policy and token-refresh hook that avoids duplicate requests during auth rotation.

Summary of changes (high level):
- Introduce a lightweight stream handshake: CLIENT_HELLO -> AUTH_OK -> SERVER_READY. Implemented in each SDK with shared semantics and compatibility fallbacks for older servers.
- Consumer ergonomics: new thin abstraction that replaces ad-hoc iterators/callbacks. Python exposes StreamConsumer (AsyncIterator + context manager) with buffer_size and heartbeat_ack semantics; TS exposes createStreamConsumer({onMessage, onComplete, bufferSize}) and an async iterable wrapper; Go exposes StreamReader(ctx) that implements io.Reader-like semantics for single-message reads and a Cancel() helper.
- Auth/retries: unified RetryWithAuthRefresh policy across SDKs. Retries are jittered exponential with token refresh hook invoked once per logical request; transparent idempotency guard added for non-idempotent unary calls.
- Backwards compatibility: consumers detect old handshake flows and fall back to legacy behavior for servers that do not return AUTH_OK. Migration warnings are surfaced at runtime (single warn log per process).
- Tests: added unit tests for handshake transitions and integration e2e stream tests in a local harness that simulates mid-stream token expiration.
- Version bumps: python 0.12.0, typescript 1.9.0, go 0.8.3.

Why this shape: the platform-level serving runtime already relies on explicit stream lifecycle events; exposing a small, consistent surface across SDKs reduces footguns (double-sends during reauth, leaked goroutines or pending async generators) and improves observability for consumers.

Migration notes:
- Python: replace raw async for msg in client.stream() with: async with client.stream_consumer() as c: async for msg in c: ...; short-lived code paths still supported but deprecated.
- TS: prefer createStreamConsumer over stream().iterator() when you need backpressure controls.
- Go: use NewStreamReader(ctx) to ensure reads cancel cleanly on token refresh.

Checklist: 
- [x] Cross-SDK API proposals agreed with SDK leads (Raj/Elena)
- [x] Unit + integration tests added
- [x] CI flake triaged and rerun (see CI summary)
- [x] Changelog & migration guide updated

Notes: this PR intentionally keeps signal surface minimal (3 flags + 2 callbacks) to avoid burdening consumers. See linked Linear ENG-2142 for design doc.

review_comments:
Raj: Can we avoid a second token refresh race if two concurrent streams call the hook? Suggest ensuring the hook is single-flight per token_id. Response: implemented singleflight guard in shared retry_policy with metrics (auth_refresh_locks).
Elena: TS consumer ergonomics look good but question on buffer default. Response: default buffer_size changed to 16 and documented rationale (latency vs memory).
Samir: Go Cancel() semantics — will it leak goroutines when Cancel is called mid-read? Response: added explicit test and closed goroutine via consistent context cancellation path; verified in go race run.
CI-bot: e2e streaming failed when simulating token expiry. Author: added extra wait/retry in harness and hardened backoff; reran and passed.

release_notes:
- SDKs: unify streaming handshake semantics across Python/TS/Go; introduce ergonomic StreamConsumer/StreamReader abstractions.
- Auth: single-flight token refresh hook and unified RetryWithAuthRefresh policy to avoid duplicate in-flight retries.
- Backwards compatibility: servers without AUTH_OK are supported with harmless warnings.
- Version bumps: python 0.12.0, typescript 1.9.0, go 0.8.3.
- Migration guidance added to docs/migration/streaming-migration.md

Observed: increases in batch formation time when request arrival bursts are > expected inter-arrival time. KV hit rate dropped ~12% during spikes (suspected misaligned prefix caching keys).

Quant profile rollback might change token-level costs slightly (higher compute cost) — inform billing/sales if long duration.

description:
Summary:
Design and implement a tenant credit allocator that influences region & tier selection for dedicated capacity while enabling controlled hosted spillback. The allocator issues soft "credits" (soft reservations) based on pre-commit, historical consumption, and SLA tier. Credits drive probabilistic routing decisions: prefer dedicated when credits >= cost_estimate, gradually bleed to hosted when credits are low.

Goals:
- Reduce unexpected hosted spillovers for customers with reserved capacity while allowing controlled, observable backfill to hosted for short bursts.
- Maintain latency SLOs for P0/P1 tenants and keep unit cost predictable for reserved customers.
- Provide a transparent, debuggable fallback mechanism to hosted and to lower-cost model variants.

Design highlights:
1) Credit allocator
- Each tenant has a credit balance updated continuously: credits += reserved_rate * time_window - actual_consumption_cost. Credits are bounded and never drop below a soft negative floor.
- Credit tiers: GREEN (>75%), AMBER (25%-75%), RED (<25%). Routing preference score = base_affinity * f(credit_tier) * tenant_priority_scale.

2) Probabilistic routing with hysteresis
- For each request compute P(dedicated) = sigmoid((score - threshold)/temperature). Add request jitter and short-term moving-average smoothing to avoid flapping.
- Hysteresis windows vary by tier: GREEN (30s), AMBER (2m), RED (10m).

3) Variant shadowing and demotion
- If hosted or lower-cost variant is selected, send a shadow copy to a demoted variant for quality monitoring (no charge to tenant). Shadowing includes: prompt/response hashing, deterministic knob to redact sensitive fields, and TTL for cache.
- Maintain per-variant quality deltas; if demoted variant drops below quality delta threshold for >N requests, automatically escalate to human-in-the-loop review and revert demotion if necessary.

4) Graceful hosted backfill policy
- Backfill is allowed for short bursts if predicted dedicated wait time > backfill_threshold and tenant in RED/AMBER. Backfill must carry metadata (origin:dedicated-backfill, credit_balance, fallback_decision_id) for observability and billing reconciliation.
- Introduce a backfill budget per-tenant per-day to limit cost exposure from hosted spillover.

5) Preemption & recovery
- Dedicated slots are preemptible by a request to reclaim credits: reclaiming triggers a soft-fence preventing re-routing to hosted for a brief cooldown, and emits an event to the tenant alerting them to degraded capacity.
- Recovery path replenishes credits based on committed onboarding schedule and usage smoothing.

Telemetry & observability:
- Emit these metrics at request-level and aggregated: routing_decision(reason), credit_balance_gauge, time_in_tier, backfill_event_count, variant_quality_delta, failed_shadow_rate, cost_delta_per_hour.
- Dashboards: tenant-level SLO heatmap, backfill budget burn-rate, variant-regression alerts.
- Traceable IDs: every decision must surface fallback_decision_id and policy_version in logs to enable postmortems.

Acceptance criteria:
- Simulated 48-hour stress test shows >60% reduction in unexpected hosted spillovers for tenants with >50% reserved commits compared to baseline routing.
- No increase in P0 99th p99 latency beyond 5% during simulated burst tests.
- Integration tests for credit accounting, backfill tagging, and variant shadowing coverage >90%.

Rollout plan:
1) Canary: enable credit allocator for 2 internal tenants and one low-risk external tenant (1 week).
2) Monitoring: create dashboards and an automated guardrail that disables backfill when budget burn-rate exceeds 120% of expected.
3) Progressive exposure: +10% of tenants per day with automated rollback on regression.
4) Post-rollout: 2-week observation then adjust tier thresholds and hysteresis windows based on real traffic.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How to reconcile multi-region commitments where tenant reserves span multiple hemisheres? Proposal: maintain per-region credits with cross-region transfer cap. This adds complexity but preserves locality.
- Determining cost_estimate for long-running streaming requests. We propose a moving-window model that predicts token consumption after N tokens.
- Privacy: shadowing preserves request fingerprints but must redact PII; integrate with KMS and redact rules from private deployments.

- Draft PR (routing service): https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/5312
- Runbook stub: https://wiki.redwood.ai/runbooks/dedicated-credit-backfill-runbook

description:
Purpose: create a concise intake lens and a 'minimum implementation slate' (MIS) artifact that Sales/CS can use at first contact to (1) aggregate related feature asks, (2) rapidly classify feasibility and value, and (3) produce a 1-2 slide scope + recommended first-step (prototype/build/decline).

Problem: Sales currently sends heterogeneous ask formats (emails, spreadsheets, slide decks). PMs spend ~4-8 hours per high-touch ask just consolidating signals and building a hypothesis. This slows response time and increases missed opportunities for Dedicated/Private deals.

Goal: reduce PM first-touch consolidation time to <90 minutes per ask and provide a repeatable triage output that supports fast econ estimates for field and an engineering pre-check.

Deliverables:
- Intake Lens (one-page checklist + scoring rubric) to be used by CS AE or Solutions engineer during intake call.
- Minimum Implementation Slate (MIS): templated 1-slide scope with scope sketch, acceptance criteria, rough throughput and latency targets, and two cost levers (batching/quantization) flagged.
- Quick estimate matrix mapping ask types to recommended paths: Self-serve backlog, Prototype + eval, Dedicated sales engineer engagement, Decline/Redirect.

Non-goals: detailed technical spec, PRD, or final engineering estimates. Not intended to replace deep enterprise discovery for negotiated deals.

Success metrics:
- Triage time per ask reduced from median 5h to <=1.5h for high-touch cases.
- 30% faster first-response SLA from PMs to Sales for prioritized asks.
- 20% increase in prototype->paid conversion for requests surfaced via the MIS within 60 days.

Quality guardrails: sample prompts/test-cases, golden outputs, failure modes to avoid

Document dsid_2271ae6c393d409093b11b5a6d5b96ed:
Topline: brain-dump on a lightweight interaction-tiering model for user-facing features. Goal is a small, composable way to classify/route requests into quality/cost tiers with clear developer ergonomics and ops signals. This is rough — notes to self + things to show KD for feedback.

Why: teams keep asking for predictable unit costs and simpler fallbacks they can reason about. Full-blown QoS systems are heavy. We can give product teams a set of interaction tiers (micro, standard, deep) tied to routing policies, response shapes, and model variants so they can opt-in per route.

Problem statements:
- Product teams: need predictable per-interaction cost buckets without lifting infra complexity.
- Platform: wants transparent SLOs + simple rollout knobs to degrade gracefully under load.
- UX: different flows have different tolerance for latency/verbosity. No single "one-size" model fits all.

Design principles (rough):
- Primitive, composable: tiers are small metadata tags attached to a request.
- Declarative routing: config-driven mapping from tier -> model variant, cache behavior, batching policy.
- Observable: pronounced telemetry (p50/p95 latency by tier, cost per token by tier, quality regression alerts per tier).
- Safe defaults: "standard" tier matches current default behavior; micro/deep are opt-ins.

Tiers (first pass):
- micro: cheapest. short max tokens, high quantization profile, aggressive prefix cache, fallback to canned snippet when generation fails. Use for UI hints, autosuggest, quick facts.
- standard: baseline. balanced latency/cost. default model family and mid quantization. good for general chat, assistant replies.
- deep: quality-first. higher token budgets, less quantization, larger model family, enable structured-tool-calls and longer context. Use for long-form writing, code gen, final answers.

User stories:
- As a product engineer, I want to mark route /search/hint as "micro" so my feature stays within the free tier budget and I can cap per-session spend.
- As platform SRE, I want an emergency policy that turns existing "deep" requests to "standard" when GPU queues exceed 80% for 2m.
- As a growth PM, I want to A/B test deep vs standard for onboarding flows to measure conversion lift per dollar.

Acceptance signals / metrics:
- Per-route cost per 1k requests by tier (trendable).
- Latency SLO compliance per tier (p95 < tier-defined target).
- Quality regression alerts: micro/standard/deep compare eval set deltas.
- Adoption: percent of new routes assigned a tier within 30 days of creation.

API surface sketch (for devs):
- request param: interaction_tier: "micro" | "standard" | "deep" (optional, default standard).
- server-side config: route->tier override map, emergency downgrade policy, batch/caching hints.
- response metadata: served_tier, model_variant, quant_profile, billed_tokens.

Operator/Runtime implications:
- routing layer needs fast check for route-level override + per-tenant default. Could be implemented as a small routing cache with TTL.
- autoscaler signals should consider weighted qps by tier (deep = higher GPU weight).
- caching: micro tier should prefer aggressive prefix/KV caching; deep should sometimes disable prefix cache for freshness.

Rollout plan (experiment-first):
- Phase 0: instrument only. Add served_tier metadata in responses for 2 weeks on internal traffic.
- Phase 1: opt-in routes. Provide SDK flag and console toggle for "micro"/"deep" per route. Collect cost/latency.
- Phase 2: allow automatic emergency downgrades via policy engine. Pilot with 2 partners.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How granular should tiers be? 3 seems OK but some teams want a "burst" tier for ephemeral high-latency ops.
- Billing integration: map tiers to rate limits/quotas vs to unit-price multipliers? Need billing touch.
- Evaluation: what representative prompts should we use per tier for regression monitoring? Ask research for a seeded eval set.
- Security: does deep tier change redaction requirements (longer context)? Probably same, but call out.

Edge cases and fallback ideas:
- If model_variant unavailable, fallback priority: cached response -> cheaper model variant in same tier -> downgrade tier -> canned message. Need hill for graceful wording to end users.
- Per-tenant overrides: enterprise customers can have custom tiers with different cost targets. Keep schema extensible.

UX bits to consider:
- Console: show heatmap of tiers across routes, quick toggle, cost delta estimates for switching tier.
- SDK helper: recommend a tier based on sample prompt length + estimated tokens. Tiny heuristic in SDK to suggest micro/standard/deep.

Notes to demo at sync:
- Plot: cost vs p95 latency vs perceived quality (subjective) for 3 sample prompts.
- Quick demo: toggle route X from standard->micro and show billing estimate, logs show served_tier change.

Related docs to review before PRD:
- CONFLUENCE-4583 (routing primitives)
- session-economy-playbook draft (internal)
- jira JIRA-PRD-712 (billing integration backlog)

Next steps (for me):
- Pull telemetry on current routes: top 20 by qps and candidate tier.
- Quick prototype SDK flag and server read path (2 day spike).
- Sync with research (Sana) for eval prompts per tier.

Random scribbles:
- individual api keys could have default tier quotas (e.g., free-tier users locked to micro for some endpoints).
- possible names: "lanes", "lanes and lanes", "interaction lanes" (hate cliches), "response-lanes". Pick something short.
- consider mapping a small set of quality tags in the response for downstream UI (concise|verbose|confidence-low).

End of notes. Will tidy to an actual PRD once anchors + telemetry exist.

Document dsid_3f4010bdd3c44b99bb1c1ad2326f5eda:
description:
Issue summary:
After depot repair (logic board replacement) of Apple Silicon MacBooks, several devices fail to complete DEP/MDM re-enrollment during OOBE. The MDM profile push stalls and the SSO cert/profile does not install. A third-party kernel extension (legacy VPN client kext) is present on the image and appears to intercept network stack initialization during first-boot, preventing MDM from completing.

Impact:
- ~6 devices failed re-enroll in the last week after depot repairs; devices remain unmanaged and cannot receive corporate certs/policies.
- Affected users are blocked from corporate VPN and SSO until manual remediation.

Context/Notes:
- All affected units are Apple Silicon (M1/M2) models returned from repair with a replaced system board.
- Image includes a legacy enterprise VPN that installs a kernel extension for older macOS versions; the kext is code-signed but not notarized for Apple Silicon-specific requirements.
- On Intel Macs this did not present at scale; appears tied to kext load order and the new hardware IDs after logic board swap.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Use depot repair flow; replace logic board on M1 MacBook and restore company image via DEP image tool.
2) Boot device into OOBE with network available (corporate Wi-Fi or ethernet via dock).
3) Device checks in with DEP, Apple MDM push begins but stalls on profile installation step 'com.redwood.mdm:install-profile'.
4) Observe that sysdiagnose shows kernel extension related logs and the mdm-agent log shows repeated network initialization failures.

observed_behavior:
DEP check-in completes but MDM profile push stalls. mdm-agent repeatedly logs: 'network stack init failed - interface not ready' and macOS kernel reports 'kext com.company.vpn attempted unsupported operations on Apple Silicon'.

expected_behavior:
Device should complete DEP/MDM re-enroll automatically during OOBE, install SSO certs and corporate profiles without manual intervention.

logs:
mdm-agent: 2024-11-15T09:12:17Z ERROR network: interface not ready

kernel: Nov 15 09:12:16 kextd[54]: com.company.vpn: attempted to register deprecated network filter (not supported on arm64e)
system.log excerpt: DEP: token validated, pushing profiles (profileID=com.redwood.sso) - stalled at 98%

investigation_notes:
Initial triage by mac-ops: reproduced on staging image with legacy VPN kext present.
Disabling the VPN kext prior to OOBE (via post-image script that removes the kext bundle) allows MDM to complete normally.
Kext is signed by vendor but not notarized for M1-specific requirements; notarization warning appears in kext load messages.
Hypothesis: on new system board hardware IDs, the kext attempts a network-level hook earlier in boot and blocks system network interfaces until degraded, causing mdm-agent timeouts.
Checked DEP portal: device records are correct; no Apple-side MDM flags indicate block.

comments:
Priya Nair (mac-ops): 'I can reproduce on MBP18,1 with the vendor kext present. Removing the kext before runbook upload fixes enrollment. Need to confirm scope of devices with this kext.'
Aaron Kim (SecOps): 'Vendor confirmed they have an M1-compatible signed driver but we require notarization and an updated installer that avoids early network hooks. Asking for vendor ETA.'
Jordan Lee (reporter): 'Opened INT ticket after 4 devices returned from repair this week failed. Will pause autopilot-like reassign workflows until remediation.'

resolution:
Workaround applied: depot imaging pipeline modified to detect and remove legacy VPN kexts on Apple Silicon builds prior to shipping. Mac-ops will reimage affected units and perform manual profile push where needed. Vendor engaged for notarized M1-friendly installer; security requested vendor PR to remove kernel-level hooks and move to NetworkExtension framework.

Follow-up actions:
- Ship a patched image by 2024-11-20 without legacy kexts for Apple Silicon fleet (assigned to mac-ops).
- Vendor action item logged; expect vendor ETA in 5 business days (tracked in related_github_pr).
- Add a post-repair verification step in depot runbook to validate MDM check-in within 10 minutes of OOBE.

2024-11-17: SecOps confirmed vendor engagement; vendor PR submitted to GitHub (see related_github_prs).

Document dsid_d921e1d4282b45a7b4990e2366bedc05:
description:
Introduce a headroom controller that uses short-horizon workload forecasts to proactively provision and maintain throughput guarantees for Dedicated capacity. The controller combines forecasting, conservative step sizing, and circuit-breaker safety limits to reduce SLA violations and avoid oscillatory scale behavior during traffic spikes and diurnal patterns.

background:
Current autoscaler reacts to observed metrics (p95 latency, tokens/sec) and applies conservative steps with cooldowns. We observe two issues: (1) transient spikes cause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.

proposed_solution:
Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.

decisions:
Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use
Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project
Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures
Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller
Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s
No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction

tradeoffs:
Forecasting reduces missed SLOs for predictable patterns but introduces risk if model overestimates — mitigated by hard emergency ceilings
Adding forecasting increases autoscaler complexity and CPU usage; we chose simple ETS to minimize compute and maintenance burden
Longer forecast horizons improve anticipation but increase false positives; default is conservative (5m) and configurable
PI-style controller is easier to reason about than full RL or optimization but may be suboptimal for complex multi-tenant interactions
Canary rollout and strict safety limits increase deployment time but are necessary to prevent fleet-wide regressions

Implement headroom-to-step mapping and PI-inspired controller - Miguel

Dashboard and alerting (predicted_peak, headroom, scale_decisions, circuit_breaker_events) - Observability
Confluence design doc and rollout runbook - Asha

Document dsid_426ca69578a84dd4af512e5a2782086e:
body:
Context and motivation:
This PR addresses a recurring class of incidents where aggressive fast-path kernel selection and lower-precision execution (fp16 / int8) produced rare but hard-to-detect correctness deviations for edge prompts. At the same time, customers expect throughput and lower cost. We need a runtime mechanism that lets us enable high-performance paths without risking silent correctness regressions in production.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a 'safelock' gating layer in the kernel selection path. The safelock prevents switching to a fast path unless a set of runtime validators pass (numerical consistency, kv-cache integrity checks, and recent success window).
- Introduces a precision toggle API (per-model, per-deployment) with three modes: strict (fp32 only), balanced (fp16 with strict validators), aggressive (fp16/int8 allowed once warmed).
- Adds a lightweight runtime validator harness: stochastic correctness probes run as background requests against canary inputs to compute divergence metrics (token-level mismatch rate, logit-delta distribution). Validators are cheap and attach metadata to requests that triggered path selection failures.
- Changes KV cache eviction policy to be conservative when cache-warmness is below threshold; combined with safelock it avoids invalidating cached KV frames that fast kernels rely on.
- Integrates safelock signals with the continuous-batching scheduler: until a deployment's validators reach a success threshold, scheduler prefers conservative batching and disables cross-model micro-batching that can expose interleaving bugs.
- Adds observability hooks: metrics (safelock.blocked_count, validator.mismatch_rate, precision.switch_count, kv.eviction_suppressed) and a dashboard stub.
- Adds a feature flag runtime.enable_safelock (default true for new deploys) and model config fields precision_mode and validator_policy.

Design notes and rationale:
- The safelock is intentionally conservative: it is designed to minimize customer-visible regressions at the cost of initial throughput until a model warms. We prefer false negatives (staying on slow path) over false positives (silent incorrect outputs).
- Validators are probabilistic and run only on a small fraction of traffic (configurable). We do not rely on end-user prompts alone; the system feeds a small canary corpus that includes known edge cases and adversarial tokens used in previous incidents.
- KV-cache eviction suppression is implemented as an additional guard in the eviction worker: if cache_warmness < 0.7 and safelock.enabled, eviction respects a soft TTL and only evicts when memory pressure exceeds a higher threshold. This prevents state churn that invalidates prefix caching assumptions used by some kernels.

Commits (high-level):
- feat(runtime): add safelock kernel gating and validator harness (A. Kumar)
- feat(config): model precision_mode and validator_policy proto + defaulting (A. Kumar)
- fix(kv): conservative eviction path and warmness estimator (R. Patel)

Purpose and scope:
This runbook captures the operational design and step-by-step procedures for key lifecycle management (cloud KMS, HSM-backed keys, and customer BYOK), rotation patterns, and formatted audit export to the SIEM. It is intended for security engineers, platform engineers (private/dedicated), and on-call SREs who will perform rotations, evidence collection, and incident responses related to encryption-at-rest.

Non-goals:
- Specifying vendor-specific API docs (those are linked in the artifacts section).
- Replacing the Verified KMS onboarding checklist — this complements it with operational playbook material.

Overview of crypto hierarchy (recommended model):
- Root/Signer (offline or HSM-protected root key): only used to sign intermediate keys and for bootstrapping. Extremely high entropy, stored in FIPS-validated HSM or offline guard.
- Master Key (MK): KMS-managed single-purpose key used to encrypt/unwrap key-encryption-keys (KEKs). Rotated infrequently; stored in cloud KMS or HSM with strict RBAC.
- Key-Encryption Keys (KEKs): Per- tenancy (customer or environment) keys used to wrap Data Encryption Keys (DEKs). KEKs live in KMS/HSM and are subject to rotation policies independent of DEKs.
- Data Encryption Keys (DEKs): Short-lived keys used for envelope encryption of object data (S3, blockstore, DB column encryption). DEKs are generated by the service, encrypted with KEK, and stored alongside ciphertext.

Why envelope encryption: improved rotation and small blast radius — DEKs are cheap to rotate and do not require re-encrypting blobs when KEK rotates (only rewrap operation).

RBAC v2 for keys (mapping to roles):
- key-admin: create/delete/grant/revoke KEKs and manage key policy metadata. Should be restricted to Security Eng and Platform Admins. (Granting on a per-key resource basis.)
- key-operator: initiate rotate/rewrap operations, request key usage metrics, and run emergency revocations. Intended for SRE on-call + rotation automation service accounts.
- kms-viewer: read-only access to key metadata, audit entries, and rotation history; used by auditors and compliance reviewers.
- crypto-service (machine/account): service principal used by runtime to perform encrypt/decrypt operations — scoped to specific KEKs via least privilege.

Access controls and constraints:
- No human accounts with direct encrypt/decrypt rights on production KEKs unless explicitly approved and logged.
- All changes to key policy must require multi-approver workflow via ticket (JIRA-SEC or ServiceNow) with a signed justification field.

Rotation policy matrix (recommended default):
- Root/Signer: rotate only on explicit key compromise or re-keying cycle every 5+ years (with offline ceremony).
- Master Key (MK): 18–36 months, or immediately on suspected compromise.
- KEK (per-tenant): 6–12 months; automated rewrap of DEKs recommended during low-traffic windows.
- DEK: TTL 24 hours to 90 days based on workload sensitivity; for high-volume object stores, prefer short TTL (7–30 days) and frequent rewraps.

Rotation step-by-step (KEK rotation, automated):
1) Pre-checks:
   - Confirm current KEK metadata and last_rotation in KMS.
   - Verify successful snapshot/backup of key metadata snapshot (S3 location: s3://redwood-sec-key-metadata/yyyymmdd).
   - Check outstanding re-wrap tasks and in-flight writes; consult per-route write-latency dashboard.
   - Ensure automation runbook is in a healthy state (CI job green).
2) Create new KEK version in KMS/HSM using secure API. Tag version with rotation-correlation-id and timestamp.
3) Update service principal grants for the new key version (if using explicit version grants).
4) Enqueue rewrap job that will read ciphertext metadata, call KMS unwrap with old KEK -> DEK, then wrap DEK with new KEK, and write back wrapped value. Jobs are sharded and rate-limited to preserve latency SLOs.
5) Monitor rewrap progress, look for rewrap-failure counts and backoffs. Failures trigger automatic re-try with exponential backoff and eventual pager escalation to on-call.
6) After >= 95% rewrap completion, update key policy primary-version pointer to new KEK version. Keep old version alive for 30–90 days for rollback and emergency decrypt.
7) Post-ops: generate evidence bundle (audit logs, job run IDs, manifest of rewrapped object IDs) and export to secure evidence store.

Manual emergency rotation (compromise suspected):
- Immediate steps: set KEK to disabled state for new wraps (maintain unwrap to allow decrypts if needed), create incident ticket, notify CS/Legal if customer keys involved. For BYOK, escalate to customer contact according to contract.

BYOK specific flows and customer-supplied HSMs:
- Onboarding requires: customer intent form, key rollover policy acceptance, and KMS import key ceremony recorded in Confluence page.
- BYOK keys are treated as external-key IDs — Redwood stores only wrapped DEKs. Key operations with external HSM require dedicated connector host in customer VPC or HSM proxy with mutual-auth TLS.
- Rotation for BYOK: coordinate schedule with customer; do not perform unilateral rotation of a customer-supplied root. Documented SLA window must be observed.

Audit log schema (key events) — canonical fields (JSON log entry):
- timestamp: ISO8601 string
- event_type: one of [KEY_CREATE, KEY_ROTATE, KEY_VERSION_CREATE, KEY_DISABLE, KEY_ENABLE, KEY_DELETE, KEY_UNWRAP, KEY_WRAP, KEY_POLICY_CHANGE]
- resource_id: kms://<region>/<key-id>
- actor: <principal-id or service-account>
- actor_type: human|service|external-customer
- action_id: UUID (correlation across services)
- request_id: cloud-kms-request-id (if available)
- outcome: success|failure|partial
- reason: free text (failure reason / policy change note)
- correlation_tags: list of tags (rotation-correlation-id, ticket-id)
- old_version: version-id (if rotation)
- new_version: version-id (if rotation)
- rewrap_manifest_loc: s3://... or null
- sampled_trace: diagnostic trace id or null
- raw_event: raw provider event (if available)

Example log (single-line JSON):
{
  "timestamp": "2024-11-05T22:14:31Z",
  "event_type": "KEY_ROTATE",
  "resource_id": "kms://us-east1/ke-abc123",
  "actor": "svc-key-rotation@redwood-infra",
  "actor_type": "service",
  "action_id": "b3a85d6f-4c2b-4a9d-8e1c-3d9f7a9d2fbb",
  "request_id": "cloudreq-9922",
  "outcome": "success",
  "reason": "scheduled-rotation",
  "correlation_tags": ["rotation-20241105", "JIRA-SEC-1290"],
  "old_version": "v1",
  "new_version": "v2",
  "rewrap_manifest_loc": "s3://redwood-sec-key-manifests/rewrap-20241105.json",
  "sampled_trace": "trace-7a9e",
  "raw_event": null
}

SIEM export mapping guidance:
- Ingest each canonical audit log into the SIEM as a single event with the following mapped fields: time, src_principal (actor), event_type, resource, correlation_id (action_id), outcome, tags, message.
- Enrich events with identity attributes from IAM (team, manager, risk_score) and with customer ids for tenant-scoped keys.
- Create SIEM detection rules for abnormal activity patterns:
  - Multiple KEY_UNWRAP calls from different service principals for the same resource within a short window.
  - New key-version creation without a preceding JIRA ticket tag.
  - KEK rotates outside maintenance window.
  - Unexpected external-customer key access from internal VMs.

Evidence automation (post-rotation evidence bundle):
- Components to collect automatically after a rotation or emergency action:
  - Audit log slice covering action_id and +/- 24 hours.
  - Rewrap manifest (list of objects rewrapped and shard ids).
  - KMS provider raw response payloads and request IDs.
  - CI/CD job run ids and artifacts (automation run logs).
  - Signed PDF of rotation approvers (if manual approvals present).
- Automation job will package the above into a signed tarball, compute a SHA256, upload to s3://redwood-sec-evidence/<action_id>/evidence.tar.gz and emit an evidence-created audit event.

Testing, validation and rollback:
- Canary run: pick a low-traffic tenant and perform a KEK rotate + rewrap. Validate decrypt success on sampled objects for 48 hours. Use automated smoke tests (github.com/redwood-infra/tests/key-rotate-canary).
- Rollback: if rewrap fails en masse, revert primary-version pointer to previous version and abort further wrap jobs. Keep failure manifest for investigation.

Monitoring and observability:
- Key metrics to publish: rewrap_progress_percent, rewrap_error_rate, key_usage_per_minute, key_latency_p50/p90/p99 for wrap/unwrap calls, key_policy_change_count.
- Dashboards: per-region key counters, tenant-impact view, and a security incidents dashboard that surfaces any disabled keys or rapid version churn.

Operational playbook checklist (pre-rotation):
- [ ] Confirm maintenance window and customer notifications (if tenant scoped).
- [ ] Snapshot key metadata.
- [ ] Ensure rewrap jobs have capacity and throttles configured.
- [ ] Backup evidence store writable.

Post-rotation checklist:
- [ ] Rewrap >= 95% completed or documented exception list.
- [ ] Evidence tarball produced and verified.
- [ ] Post-rotation smoke tests green.
- [ ] Update key inventory and rotation calendar.

Compromise handling (short runbook):
1) Immediately mark key as disabled for new wraps and log action.
2) Create incident ticket with correlation_id and contact list.
3) If customer key (BYOK), notify customer per contract and follow agreed escalation.
4) Start forensic capture: full audit slice, host traces, and rewrap manifest.
5) If necessary, perform emergency rewrap to new KEK and reject old version; expedite evidence export for compliance.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we require HSM for all MKs by default or only high-sensitivity tenants? (propose: high-sensitivity and enterprise with SLA >$Xk/month)
- Retention policy for old key versions beyond rollback window (30/90/365 days?)
- Integration point for RBAC v2 authorization checks in the KMS proxy — pre-check or delegated to provider?

Next steps (action items):
- Lina: draft BYOK onboarding form for customer agreements (due 2024-11-20).
- Diego: implement SIEM enrichment pipeline prototype (P0) and push PR.
- Samir: add rotation canary to infra tests and schedule monthly runs.

References and links:
- KMS provider docs (internal vault): CONFLUENCE-SEC/KMS-Provider-APIs
- Rewrap job implementation: github.com/redwood-infra/rewrap-service (PR-487 linked above)
- Evidence automation template: CONFLUENCE-SEC/Evidence-Automation-Template
- Incident escalation contact list: CONFLUENCE-SEC/Incident-Contacts

Notes and contextual snippets (working):
- Consider adding rate-limit bucketing per-tenant to rewrap workers to avoid noisy-tenant storms.
- We should index rewrap-manifests by tenant and time for quick e-discovery.
- Long-term: explore native HSM signing for root key ceremonies and publish an offline attestation record.

Purpose
This doc is a combined architecture + operational runbook for our routing policy engine and control-plane components across multi-region deployments. It is intentionally practical: short diagnostics, commands, and mitigations embedded in architecture context so on-call engineers can both reason about root cause and act quickly.

Scope
- Components: routing-policy-service (RPS), control-plane-api, policy-store (etcd/consul), route-agent (edge sidecar), regional health aggregator, and the global policy router.
- Cross-region concerns: affinity, KV replication lag, split-brain on leader election, and fallback model variant routing.
- Not included: serving-runtime GPU node-level debugging (see serving-runtime/sre-runbooks).

Architecture notes (brief)
- Control plane (control-plane-api + policy-store) is the single source of truth for routing policies, rollout stages, and region weightings. It exposes a versioned API used by route-agents to fetch policies on startup and at policy-change webhooks.
- Route-agents run in each region and maintain an in-memory policy cache and local evaluation engine for low-latency routing decisions. Agents watch the policy-store via streaming endpoints and apply delta updates.
- Policy evaluation order: explicit-route (customer pin) -> canary -> weighted-routing -> geo-affinity -> fallback. Policies are deterministic and evaluated top-to-bottom.
- Rollouts: canaries are enabled by rollout rules stored in the policy-store. Each rollout has a name, window, and metric criteria (latency and error thresholds).
- Health checks: agents report region-level health via health-aggregator which updates a region-status index used by global router.

Common incident scenarios + runbooks
1) Control plane API unresponsive (HTTP 5xx or timeouts)
- Symptom: config change fails; route-agents show repeated fetch retries; recent deploy of control-plane-api; alerts: PLAT-CONTROL-API-ERR.
- Quick checks:
  - Check SLOs/dashboard: control_plane_api_request_latency_p50/p95, control_plane_api_error_rate (Dash: Platform / Control Plane / API)
  - kubectl -n platform get pods -l app=control-plane-api; kubectl logs -f deployment/control-plane-api -c api --tail 200
  - curl -v https://control-plane-api.internal/healthz || echo "down"
- Quick mitigations:
  - If pods are CrashLoopBackOff: kubectl describe pod <pod> to see OOM or config errors. Revert recent config change (kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-plane-api) if deploy timestamp aligns with incident.
  - If high CPU due to policy-store scan: scale up replicas temporarily: kubectl scale deploy/control-plane-api --replicas=4 (notify infra).
  - If external dependency (auth/KMS) failing: flip maintained feature-flag to allow unauthenticated local reads for emergency: POST to admin toggle endpoint (requires infra approval).
- Recovery steps:
  - Redeploy last known-good image: kubectl set image deployment/control-plane-api control-plane-api=registry.redwood/internal/control-plane-api:stable-20260201
  - Validate route-agents reconnected: check route-agent logs and policy version: kubectl logs -l app=route-agent -c agent | grep "policy_version="
- Post-incident:
  - Open PLAT JIRA ticket, attach timeline and last deploy id (PLAT-CONTROL-API-ERR-YYYYMMDD), run postmortem template, update changelog.

2) Policy drift or incorrect evaluation order deployed (bad rollout rules)
- Symptom: certain traffic unexpectedly hits a fallback model; regression alerts on quality (Rerank/quality evals) or sudden cost increase.
- Quick checks:
  - Check policy versions: curl https://control-plane-api.internal/v1/policies/versions last_3
  - Search for recent policy changes: git log --since="48 hours" -- platform-configs/policies
  - Query route-agent logs for "policy-eval" traces and decision path: kubectl logs -l app=route-agent | egrep "policy_eval|decision_path"
- Quick mitigations:
  - Push emergency policy patch that restores previous rule ordering. Use the policy-store admin UI to revert version or use API: POST /v1/policies/revert {"version":"v123"}
  - If automatic rollouts continue to apply bad policy, disable rollout engine: PATCH /v1/admin/settings {"rollout_enabled":false} (only for <30m).
- Recovery steps:
  - Validate behavior in canary region and run synthetic tests (see linked_artifacts). Promote fix to all regions after 30 minutes of stable metrics.

3) Regional split-brain / KV replication lag causing inconsistent policies across regions
- Symptom: region A has new policies, region B still uses older policies -> inconsistent routing; alerts: PLAT-POLICY-REPL-LAG.
- Quick checks:
  - Check policy-store replication status: kubectl -n platform exec -it statefulset/policy-store -- /bin/psql -c "SELECT * FROM replication_status;"
  - Check agent-sync metrics: route_agent_policy_sync_lag_seconds{region="us-east-1"}
  - Look for leader-election warnings in logs: kubectl logs -l app=policy-store | egrep "leader|raft|election"
- Quick mitigations:
  - If leader elected incorrectly, force leader stepdown to trigger re-election: kubectl exec -it pod/policy-store-0 -- /bin/consul operator raft remove-peer <peer-id> (follow infra runbook) or use etcdctl to promote leader.
  - Temporarily set global routing to prefer region with majority policy consistency: POST /v1/admin/routing/override {"global_prefer":"us-west-2"}
- Recovery steps:
  - Reconcile KV store: run the replication repair script from git (scripts/repair-kv-replication.sh) with oncall approval. Monitor sync lag and then lift routing override.

4) Route-agent high-latency evaluation causing end-to-end latency spikes
- Symptom: route-agent CPU usage high, p99 eval latency elevated, affecting latency SLOs.
- Quick checks:
  - route_agent_eval_latency_p50/p95/p99, route_agent_cpu_usage
  - Check rule set size: POST /v1/admin/policies/size for region to see number of rules loaded
- Quick mitigations:
  - Reduce policy complexity: enable emergency-compact policy set: POST /v1/admin/policies/compact {"reason":"latency_immediate"} to temporarily apply simplified ruleset.
  - Scale route-agent horizontally: kubectl scale deployment/route-agent --replicas=<current*2>
- Recovery steps:
  - Run policy pruning process to remove obsolete legacy rules (ticket PLAT-3120). Re-introduce full rule set gradually via canary.

Investigations / diagnostics cheat-sheet
- Verify control-plane health: curl https://control-plane-api.internal/metrics | egrep "control_plane_api|policy_store"
- Agent status per region: curl https://health-aggregator.internal/regions | jq . (look for last_synced_ts)
- Policy version reported to router: curl https://global-router.internal/status | jq '.policy_version'
- Example kubectl debugging commands:
  - kubectl -n platform exec -it deploy/control-plane-api -- curl -sS localhost:8080/debug/vars | jq .
  - kubectl logs -l app=route-agent -c agent --since=30m | egrep "warn|error|policy_eval"

Escalation and ownership
- First responder: oncall-platform (rotation). If control-plane API >15m, escalate to platform-sre lead and platform eng owner.
- Pager escalation policy: see PLAT-SOP-ESCL (Confluence link in linked_artifacts). Provide timeline, last_playbook_steps, and any admin toggles we exercised.

Safety knobs and feature flags (where to flip things)
- rollout_enabled (boolean) - disables automated rollouts when false. Admin API path: /v1/admin/settings
- policy_store_read_fallback - allows route-agents to use cached policies for longer TTL when set.
- global_routing_override - temporarily forces traffic to a single region or traffic tier. Use only for short windows and record justification.

Templates / quick commands
- Revert control-plane deployment: kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-plane-api -n platform
- Scale route-agent: kubectl scale deploy/route-agent -n platform --replicas=6
- Force policy-store leader election: kubectl exec statefulset/policy-store-0 -n platform -- /usr/local/bin/raftctl transfer-leader --target-id=<id>
- Emergency compact policy (API): curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://control-plane-api.internal/v1/admin/policies/compact -d '{"reason":"latency_immediate"}'

Post-incident checklist
- Create JIRA ticket with affected regions, start/end times, deploy ids, and mitigations taken (labels: incident, control-plane).
- Add timeline to ticket and link to this doc.
- Run policy audit: ensure no manual emergency edits remain. Archive emergency policy versions to policy-store/history.
- Update runbook with any new commands, gotchas, or learned metrics.

Known gaps / follow-ups
- No safe automated rollback from policy migrations that touch more than 500 rules. Action: implement transactional policy-apply with preflight dry-run (PLAT-4010).
- No RBAC approval flow for emergency admin toggles. Action: short-term Slack approval step required; long-term: implement approval queue.

Appendix: useful dashboards and tests
- Dashboards: Platform / Control Plane / Policy Store Replication; Platform / Routing / Agent Latency; Platform / Global Router Health.
- Synthetic tests: per-region policy-eval synthetic (synthetic/policy-eval) that runs every 30s; endpoint: https://synthetic.internal/policy-eval?test=basic-route

Contact list (oncall rotation owners)
- platform-oncall: @platform-oncall (pager), lead: Arjun Patel <arjun@redwood.com>, eng-owner: Maya Chen <maya.chen@redwood.com>

Notes to self (working area)
- Need to add TLS cert rotation steps for policy-store replication (deferred to infra).
- Double-check rollback image tags used in last 3 control-plane deploys.
- Follow up: add example logs for policy-eval decision_path so new oncall can grep them quicker.

End of doc.

Ship a Playbook (one-pager + actionable runbook) for GTM, sales engineering, and SRE to operationalize competitor signals into procurement guidance and customer conversations.

success_metrics:

Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0096
Question: When an employee is marked for immediate termination in Workday, why can a third party SaaS seat stay billable for around two weeks even after Okta deactivates the user?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_8138b96e181940418cc5067b2630064e:
description:
Issue summary:
HR received reports from Finance and IT that when an employee is placed on Immediate Termination (ITerm) in Workday, the seat/license in third-party SaaS (notably the design/legal tool vendor) remains billable for up to 14 days and the assigned corporate laptop sometimes remains tagged as 'active' in our asset management inventory. This ticket seeks clarification of the intended policy (grace windows) and the operational mechanics (which systems enforce the reclaim/return windows).

Impact:
- Potential short-term double-billing for SaaS seats when seats are quickly re-assigned.
- Delays in device recovery leading to inventory inaccuracies and security exposure for high-risk departures.
- Confusion between HR, IT, and Finance on expected timelines and required manual steps.

Environment:
- Identity sync: Okta -> SCIM -> downstream SaaS (prod)
- Asset tracking: FleetOps (prod) with inventory sync to ITSM
- HR system: Workday (prod)

Observed behavior / Steps to reproduce:
1) Create an employee termination in Workday with 'Immediate' flag at 09:00 UTC.
2) Workday emits termination event, HR webhook updates Okta.
3) Okta SCIM provisioning sends deactivation to SaaS vendor; we observe the user status change but vendor maintains seat as billable for a 14-day grace window (vendor policy).
4) FleetOps does not mark the laptop as 'awaiting pickup' until an asset-handback task is created manually by IT; automatic tagging is not triggered by the termination event.
5) Finance reports a new invoice line for an additional seat 3 days later after license reassign because the old seat was not reclaimed yet.

Logs / evidence: 
- Okta SCIM audit (okta-audit-2026-03-09.log) shows deactivation event at 09:02 UTC and response 200 from vendor with response body: {"status":"deprovision-scheduled","grace_days":14}.
- FleetOps event stream shows no asset lifecycle change tied to the Workday termination event (fleetops-events-2026-03-09.ndjson).
- Finance ticket FIN-1189 referencing unexpected seat charge for week of 2026-03-02.

Question / Requested clarification:
- What are the company-wide defaults for SaaS license reclaim windows and how many days are considered 'standard' vs 'exception' requiring manual immediate reclaim?
- For Immediate Terminations, do we have an established exception/accelerated flow that forces vendor-side seat revocation and device pickup tagging?
- Which teams are expected to take manual actions vs which actions should be automated by identity/asset tooling?

Desired outcome:
- A concise policy statement HR/IT/Finance can rely on for immediate-term offboards, including: default reclaim window, criteria for accelerating reclaim, and the single authoritative runbook link for immediate offboards.

comments:
2026-03-10 11:10 — Marco Ruiz (IT): Noted. In our logs the SCIM response includes vendor-side grace window. We don't currently override vendor windows. IT can manually request offboarding escalation with vendor support but that requires a ticket and often 24–48h processing.
2026-03-10 12:02 — Priya Shah (HR): Can we make 'Immediate' terminations trigger a one-click 'accelerate reclaim' in the HR portal? That would reduce churn between teams.
2026-03-11 09:47 — Ethan Park (Identity): Hypothesis: Okta sets user to 'suspended' and vendor interprets that as soft-deactivate and applies a vendor-side grace window. We can attempt to send a 'hard-delete' SCIM call for critical departures but need legal approval and vendor API support confirmation.
2026-03-11 13:15 — Jana Müller (Finance): Current invoices show an average of 2.3 days of overlap per reassign. Shortening reclaim window will materially affect monthly spend forecasts. Please include Finance in policy decisions.
2026-03-12 08:03 — Support Bot (automated): Linked CONFLUENCE: License Reclaim Policy draft updated (v0.4) — https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/HR/pages/License+Reclaim+Policy

investigation_notes:
Okta->SCIM behavior: The connector implementation uses PATCH to set 'active' to false. Vendor accepts this and sets an internal grace policy (14 days) rather than immediate seat relinquish.
FleetOps integration: Asset lifecycle changes are only triggered by ITSM ticket creation at present; there is no webhook or SCIM-driven asset tagging for device pickup. This is a gap for immediate offboards.
Workday mapping: 'Immediate' termination is mapped to Okta attribute 'terminationType=immediate' but that attribute is not propagated to downstream SCIM calls currently; therefore downstream vendors cannot differentiate Immediate vs standard terminations.
Hypothesis: If Okta emitted a 'terminationType' custom attribute or we used a 'hard-delete' SCIM call on certain vendors, seats could be reclaimed faster, but vendor policies and contracts may prohibit forced immediate deletion (data retention concerns).

resolution_notes:
Tentative operational plan agreed on 2026-03-12:
1) Policy clarification: Default reclaim window remains vendor-determined; for 'Immediate' terminations, HR + IT will follow an accelerated flow.
2) Automation tasks: Identity team to add terminationType flag propagation to SCIM (Ethan Park) and to implement a 'hard-delete' option gated behind a documented approval step.
3) Asset tagging: FleetOps to listen for Workday/Okta terminationType events and auto-tag devices as 'awaiting-security-pickup' (IT will still approve pickup).
4) Finance: will be looped into the vendor contract review to identify vendors that support immediate seat removal vs those with mandatory grace windows.
5) Runbook: Create a concise 'Immediate Offboard' runbook in Confluence with decision tree and contact channel (#it-offboarding).
Follow-ups (action items): [INT-821408] implement SCIM terminationType propagation; [INT-821409] FleetOps webhook for immediate offboard tagging; legal to review vendor TOS for forced seat deletion.
Notes: Until automation is in place, manual vendor escalation is the workaround for high-risk departures. This ticket should remain open until the SCIM flag propagation PR (INT-821408) is merged and FleetOps webhook (INT-821409) is live.

Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0097
Question: In the OpenAI Responses v3 compatibility work, how are overly large user-provided seeds handled to keep determinism, and where is the original seed stored for auditing?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_6c58ddb8ecf543d89fca8352351dea29:
description:
Motivation: the OpenAI Responses API v3 introduces a seed/determinism flag and richer per-response metadata fields. Customers expecting parity through our OpenAI compatibility layer were hitting two classes of issues: 1) requests with deterministic seeds sometimes routed to fallback model variants causing non-deterministic behavior, and 2) streaming reassembly and function/tool-calling events lost user-supplied metadata (e.g., trace ids) on intermediate fragments. This PR: - Propagates the new 'seed' and 'determinism' fields from OpenAI-style Requests through our compatibility translation layer so upstream callers can control RNG determinism when we map to compatible model variants. - Adds per-request metadata passthrough: preserves and forwards top-level metadata and nested response-level metadata (user supplied) through streaming frames and the final assembled Response object. - Stabilizes streaming reassembly for mixed partials (text chunks, tool call fragments, structured JSON outputs) by introducing a sequence/frame id and last-frame markers in the compat layer; this avoids interleaving when a single call fan-outs to auxiliary model variants. - Ensures function/tool-calling events are emitted with the original 'metadata' and 'seed' fields intact so SDKs relying on tool traceability continue to work. - Adds exhaustive integration tests against the Responses v3 contract and extends streaming unit tests to emulate packet reorder and intermittent delivery. Implementation notes: - New compatibility translator: redwood/openai_compat/responses_v3_translator.py maps OpenAI fields to internal inference request flags (seed->rng_seed, determinism->sampling_profile). Translator is intentionally minimal: we preserve unknown fields in a passthrough map under compat_metadata for future extensions. - Streaming layer changes: redwood/api/streaming.py: implement frame_sequence_id and final_fragment bool. Reassembly uses (request_id, frame_sequence_id) ordering plus a small re-sequencing buffer gated by latency_slo to avoid head-of-line blocking. - Routing: routing/policy.py updated to prefer exact-architecture variants when determinism is requested; fallback still allowed if pinned variant unavailable. - Tests: tests/integration/test_responses_v3_compat.py includes deterministic-seed repeatability checks, metadata round-trip assertions, and simulated packet reordering scenarios. - Docs: docs/openai_compat.md updated with Responses v3 mapping and guidance for determinism semantics. Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged if seed/determinism not provided. We intentionally do not make determinism true by default because it impacts throughput. Checklist: - [x] Translator for seed/determinism fields - [x] Metadata passthrough in streaming frames - [x] Stable reassembly and ordering buffer - [x] Routing preference when determinism requested - [x] Integration + unit tests - [x] Docs update - [x] CI passing on rerun Rollout/rollback notes: feature gated behind a compatibility flag (OPENAI_COMPAT_V3=true) and an experiment toggle for routing. If customer issues are observed around tail latency with deterministic requests, the routing policy can be relaxed to fallback earlier while preserving seed values in logs for replay/diagnosis.

review_comments:
Amit Patel: The translator looks good overall. One open question: if the requested seed exceeds 64 bits, how should we normalize? Suggest we hash down with siphash and record the original in compat_metadata. Can you add a test for large seeds?
Marisol Vega: Responding to Amit: added normalization using siphash64 in translator and test case in tests/integration/test_responses_v3_compat.py line ~120. Original seed preserved in compat_metadata.seed_raw for auditability.
Claire Nguyen: Reassembly buffer hardens well but we should be conservative with the latency_slo default. Recommend 20ms default or tie it to per-customer SLO config. Also noted minor lint issues in streaming.py.
Marisol Vega: Reduced default re-sequence buffer to 20ms and moved config to per-customer tunables. Fixed lint comments and added comments describing tradeoffs.
Benji Rosen: Verified end-to-end locally including tool call round-trips; approved after Marisol pushed the siphash change and the docs clarification.
CI Bot: Build #2245: lint failed on first run; second run passed (all checks green).

1) Pseudonymization approach
- We propose per-tenant deterministic pseudonymization: each tenant gets a unique KMS-wrapped salt. Inputs (trace/request ID) are hashed with HMAC-SHA256 + salt and then truncated to 16 bytes (base64) for storage. This preserves correlation in your account while preventing cross-tenant correlation by Redwood. Keys can be customer-managed (BYOK) if required.

2) PII redaction pipeline
- Multi-stage: (a) lightweight regex stripping for obvious patterns (SSN, credit card, phone), (b) ML-based PII classifier for contextual detection (names, free-text emails), (c) token-level masking for user message content.
- Failure mode: If both regex and ML confidence are below threshold, the pipeline will: redact the suspect span with a deterministic pseudonym and emit a high-severity alert to your security webhook (configurable). No unmasked value will be persisted.

3) Retention & storage
- Configurable retention per stream: request_logs (default 90d), audit_logs (default 365d). We can support a 180d option for request_logs for the trial period.
- Backups will be region-locked to the POC region (us-east-1) and marked with the same retention policy.

4) Access & key management
- KMS integration: support for customer-managed keys (AWS KMS CMKs), Redwood-managed KMS with strict IAM roles, or HSM-backed keys for enterprise customers.
- Decryption/pseudonymization privileges: by default, only a Red team service account has access to re-identify for support with an auditable workflow (ticket required). For MedSecure we recommend BYOK so only your SREs hold re-identification capability.
