summary:
Intro discovery to map Zephyrus' usage patterns, target latency and strict monthly budget. Main discussion focused on per-token unit economics, batching and KV/prefix caching tradeoffs, hosted vs dedicated cost and private deployment compliance (VPC/KMS/SOC2). Agreed next steps: pilot scope and micro-benchmarks.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Zephyrus Head of ML), Lina Morales (Platform Eng), Rafael Hu (Finance), Amara Singh (CTO)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, Jordan from Redwood. Thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Ethan: Ethan here.
[00:10] Lina: Lina.
[00:12] Rafael: Rafael.
[00:14] Amara: Amara.
[00:16] Priya: Priya from the solutions eng side. Happy to dig into benchmarks.

[00:28] Jordan: High level agenda — understand Zephyrus workloads (qps, typical prompt/response lengths), budget constraints, latency SLOs, and tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private. Then outline a pilot. Sound good?
[00:36] Amara: Yep that's perfect. We're specifically worried about token burn — our legal and finance team are nervous about runaway costs if we spike.

[01:05] Ethan: Quick context: we run an assistant that summarizes internal docs and generates code suggestions. Average request is 750 tokens input, 600 tokens output, peak qps around 8 but most of the day it's 1-2 qps. We want sub-400ms latency for short assistant flows but 1-2s is okay for longer generation. Budget ceiling per month for inference is $45k.

[01:47] Rafael: And just to be explicit — we need predictable unit economics. If we do hosted, how do we cap spend or get alerts? If dedicated, what's the break-even?

[02:12] Priya: Great, those are the right levers. A few concepts to set expectations: per-token pricing (hosted), reserved GPU cost for Dedicated (committed monthly), and private / VPC which adds a platform fee. Then there are runtime levers — batching, prefix/KV cache, and quantization which materially change cost per token.

[02:50] Lina: Can you quantify — like if we enable KV cache and batch to 8 requests, does cost drop 30%? 50%?

[03:12] Priya: It depends on request distribution. For a lot of small repeated queries, prefix/KV caching can be 40-70% savings on recurrent tokens. For our serving runtime with continuous batching, you typically see 20-45% effective token-cost reduction vs naive single-request inference when batching to sizes of 4-8 and keeping latency SLOs. But for long outputs (600 tokens) batching often helps amortize overhead so savings can be smaller per token but large in throughput terms. Those are rough numbers; we'll run a micro-benchmark on your prompt set.

[04:05] Ethan: When you say prefix cache — does that store user context in KV on GPUs? We're concerned about PII persistence and retention.

[04:22] Priya: Good point. We let customers configure cache policies. For hosted we can do ephemeral KV cache not logged to persistent storage; for Dedicated/Private you can point cache to your own managed store or disable it entirely. We also support TTLs and zero-retention modes. We'll include KMS details in the security pack.

[05:10] Rafael: From finance perspective — show us break-even for dedicated. If our peak qps is 8 but steady is 1-2, committed capacity might be wasteful unless autoscaling with burst works.

[05:32] Jordan: Exactly. Dedicated has a committed GPU pool and predictable throughput. We have automatic burst options and routing policies — fall back to hosted variants when reserved capacity is saturated. The break-even is driven by utilization: if you use >~65% of a reserved token throughput for the month, dedicated typically becomes cheaper. But again depends heavily on model size, quantization, and batching.

[06:10] Amara: Can you explain quantization here? We have some internal concerns about quality regressions.

[06:21] Priya: We offer QC profiles — 8-bit and mixed-precision quantization paths. For many of the open models we onboard, 8-bit gives near-parity for most generation tasks, but we'll run evaluations on your eval set to measure delta. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per workload and flag regressions.

[07:00] Ethan: Ok so pilot looks like: run our representative small/medium/large prompts, measure latency, tokens, and quality under three modes: hosted (standard), dedicated reserved pool with autoscale/burst, and private VPC. Also measure with/without KV cache and batching.

[07:28] Priya: That's our usual micro-benchmark. We'll need sample prompts, sample traffic shape (qps histogram), and expected SLOs per route. Also any blocked tokens or redaction rules.

[08:00] Lina: On the private/VPC side — will Redwood manage the control plane or do we need to run anything on-prem?

[08:18] Jordan: For Private we offer a customer-managed data plane, optional on-prem pack, and a private control plane. You can choose the model — VPC peered control plane or fully air-gapped. KMS/HSM integrations are supported. We'll surface the architecture diagram in the security docs.

[08:45] Rafael: SOC2 and audit logs are non-negotiable. We need API-level audit for token lineage and RBAC.

[08:58] Priya: We have per-token tracing and token-level cost attribution in the Console. Audit logs and SSO/SAML with SCIM are supported; we'll attach our SOC2 report and the logging sample.

[09:22] Ethan: Competitor question — how do you compare to Anthropic/openai on pricing?

[09:30] Jordan: On raw hosted per-token, we're competitive on open models, and for dedicated we can beat managed endpoints when utilization is high due to GPU amortization and batching optimizations. Also our routing and fallback gives predictable latency during spikes. We'll include a competitor compsheet.

[10:02] Lina: About throttles and spend controls — can we enforce hard monthly caps or per-route budgets?

[10:12] Priya: Yes — we support per-route quotas, alerts, and hard limits. For hosted we can set quota thresholds and soft limits; for Dedicated we can add caps in the control plane and also route to lower-cost model variants when thresholds are hit.

[10:45] Amara: For our planning, can you give an example calculation? Say 1.5 qps steady, 45k budget, average total tokens per call 1350, what do we look at?

[11:00] Jordan: Quick back-of-envelope: steady 1.5 qps is ~129,600 requests/month (1.5 * 3600 * 24 * 30). At 1,350 tokens per request that's ~175M tokens/month. If hosted per-token = $0.00003 per token (example), that would be about $5.25k — but that per-token number varies by model and context — embedding vs gen different. If using larger model and higher per-token rates, it scales up. The key is batching, caching and model choice can drop effective cost per served token considerably. We'll produce scenarios with realistic per-token rates for the models you want.

[12:10] Rafael: That example number seems low — are you counting both input and output?

[12:18] Priya: Yes both. But remember per-token rates differ for input vs output on some pricing plans; we'll annotate that. Also for long outputs, batching helps less for tail latency so effective cost per user request might be higher; that's why we do the benchmark.

[13:00] Speaker 6 (mumble): question on caching architecture — how is cache invalidation handled?

[13:10] Priya: Cache invalidation is TTL-based and explicit API calls to clear prefix keys. For shared contexts we recommend a short TTL and user-scope keys. We'll document recommended policies.

[14:05] Ethan: On measurement — we want to be able to attribute cost to features and products internally. Can Redwood break down cost per route and per token type?

[14:18] Jordan: Yes the Console provides token-level cost breakdown, route-level dashboards, and traceable request IDs. You can export CSVs for cost allocation.

[15:00] Lina: Any limitations on model pinning across hosted and dedicated? We want consistent behavior when we roll from hosted to dedicated.

[15:12] Priya: You can pin model versions and rollout policies. The same model artifact can be used across hosted and dedicated; kernel selection and quantization may vary but we try to keep behavior consistent. We recommend a canary rollout to validate outputs.

[16:00] Rafael: Inventory question — what's the minimal committed term for Dedicated? Monthly? Annual?

[16:12] Jordan: We have monthly and annual reserved options. Monthly reserves give flexibility; annual reserves give pricing advantages. We'll include a few reserved capacity price points in the pilot materials.

[16:40] Ethan: Tuning question — will Redwood suggest batching configs automatically?

[16:48] Priya: Redwood Optimize recommends batch sizes and cache policies based on observed latency distribution and usage patterns. You can also set hard latency SLOs and it will suggest conservative batch sizes to meet them.

[17:20] Amara: Ok, quality. We need to run our eval set for rouge/bleu and also human spot checks. If quantization drops accuracy for our code suggestions, we need a rollback plan.

[17:33] Priya: Absolutely — we'll run model regression evals and tie alerts to quality thresholds. Rollback is supported and we suggest progressive rollouts.

[18:00] Jordan: Quick risks — unpredictable spikes, long-tail requests that blow up tokens, and data residency/compliance. How important is region residency?

[18:12] Amara: Strongly prefer EU residency for certain customers. We need logs and data at rest in EU for some cases.

[18:28] Jordan: We support region pinning and private deployments in selected regions. We'll note the regions available for Private.

[19:05] Rafael: Financial ask — show a 12-month spend plan for hosted vs dedicated with scenarios Low/Med/High usage.

[19:18] Jordan: We'll prepare a 12-month spreadsheet with break-even points and sensitivity to avg tokens, qps, and batch sizes.

[20:00] Ethan: For the pilot telemetry — what logs do you need from our side?

[20:08] Priya: Representative prompt set, qps histogram, target eval queries, and any per-request metadata you want to propogate like tenant-id so we can show cost attribution. Also a sample of blocked tokens/redaction rules.

[20:45] Lina: How long does a typical pilot take?

[20:52] Jordan: Micro-benchmarking can start in a week and results in 5-7 business days. A fuller pilot with regression evals and dedicated capacity tests is typically 3-4 weeks.

[21:20] Rafael: On procurement — any security questionnaires we can pre-fill?

[21:27] Jordan: We'll send an NDA/security packet, SOC2, and a standardized security questionnaire. We can also fill customer security questionnaires as part of the enterprise process.

[22:00] Ethan: Wanted to raise a potential blocker — our legal might force us to avoid sending PII to hosted endpoints. If so, private on-prem is likely. How much overhead for private?

[22:14] Priya: Private incurs an onboarding and platform fee and possibly on-prem infra. We can give a cost delta and implementation plan. For many customers we do a VPC/private control plane which reduces friction versus full on-prem.

[23:05] Amara: Any quick wins we should try first to reduce token-cost before changing architecture?

[23:12] Priya: Prompt engineering: truncation, instruction tuning to shorten outputs, caching repeated prefixes, and aggressive batching for non-latency-critical routes. Also using a smaller model variant for lower-cost routes.

[24:00] Lina: Are you able to run a quick sim for our 1.5 qps baseline during the pilot to validate queueing/latency under burst?

[24:12] Priya: Yes — we'll simulate steady and burst patterns, and show latency percentiles and cost.

[25:00] Ethan: On reporting — we want monthly alerts if any route goes > 20% above forecast.

[25:08] Jordan: That's doable. We'll configure cost monitors and Slack/webhook alerts.

[26:00] Rafael: Curious — for auditing token lineage, do you store raw tokens? How is redaction handled?

[26:12] Priya: By default we do not persist raw input tokens for hosted customers unless explicitly enabled for debugging. For Dedicated/Private you control persistence. Redaction hooks can filter PII before logs.

[27:20] Ethan: Ok final thing — show us a sample SLA for Dedicated latency targets.

## Summary

This handbook defines a causal-first process for investigating model regressions (quality, latency, and cost) observed after a change (model version, quantization profile, infra, or prompt). It combines signals from the eval harness, production telemetry, and unit-level artifacts to form testable causal hypotheses and rapidly converge on root cause. This doc is intended for ML engineers, SREs, and applied ML owners performing triage on regression alerts.

## Scope

- Applies to regressions discovered via: continuous eval pipelines, production quality alerts, customer escalations, or automated regression bisect results.
- Covers causal graph design, hypothesis generation, experiment design, statistical testing, and actionable rollback/fix patterns.
- Not a replacement for the automated-bisect playbook; rather, this is the manual/analyst layer for ambiguous or cross-cutting regressions.

## Ownership and Escalation

- Primary owner: Applied ML - Model Quality team
- On-call SRE: for runtime/latency regressions
- Escalation: if causal analysis points to infra/serving runtime, escalate to Eng-Serving-Runtime within 4 hours.

## Definitions

- Regression: measurable degradation in an SLO or metric compared to baseline (pre-change).
- Change event: deploy, quantization profile change, router policy update, prompt set modification, or model promotion.
- Primary signals: evaluation harness results, production cost/latency/quality telemetry, example traces, token-level diffs.

## Signals and Data Sources (ordered by priority)

1. Eval harness: stable test-set metrics, per-slice breakdowns, and seed-fixed reruns.
2. Production telemetry: per-route token latency, error rates, kv-cache hit rates, and token counts.
3. Shadow traffic and A/B results (if available).
4. Client traces / transcript samples (anonymized).
5. Deployment metadata: model SHA, quantization profile ID, kernel selection log, GPU type, and routing policy.

## Causal DAG Templates

Use these canonical Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) templates to structure thinking. Draw the DAG and explicitly list assumed causal links before testing. Example templates (textual):

- Template A (Model-change-driven): ChangeEvent -> Weights/Quantization -> ModelBehavior -> OutputQuality
- Template B (Runtime-interaction): ChangeEvent -> KernelSelection/Batching -> Latency -> TimeoutErrors -> Quality
- Template C (Prompt/Context): ChangeEvent -> PromptSet/ContextTruncation -> KV-CacheHits -> EffectiveContext -> OutputQuality

Always annotate nodes that are observable vs latent and list available instrumentation for each node.

## Investigation Checklist (step-by-step)

1. Record the alert context: metric, threshold, time window, impacted slices (routes, languages, long vs short prompts).
2. Snapshot deployment metadata for the time window: model_id, model_sha, quant_profile, runtime_version, host region, and GPU type.
3. Replicate the failure in the eval harness with the same model and quantization profile, using the failing prompt slices. Use deterministic seeds where applicable.

   Example CLI to re-run a failing slice locally:
   
   curl -X POST https://eval-harness.internal/run -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"slice_id":"lang-en-long-context", "model_id":"m-v42", "quant_profile":"q8_4", "seed":42}'

4. Construct a concise causal DAG and list 2–3 competing hypotheses (e.g., quantization introduced a tokenization-sensitive bias; kernel fallback increased latency and triggered truncation).
5. Prioritize hypotheses by plausibility and ease-of-test. Run targeted ablations:
   - A/B run with float32 weights vs quantized profile on the same hardware.
   - Run with and without KV-cache enabled.
   - Run with controlled batch sizes to reproduce kernel selection differences.

6. Apply causal tests: difference-in-differences, regression adjustment, and when appropriate, causal-impact or DoWhy-style causal estimation.

   Minimal SQL snippet to prepare test/control cohorts:

   SELECT request_id, model_tag, quant_profile, prompt_slice, quality_score, latency_ms, kv_cache_hit
   FROM production_prompts
   WHERE event_time BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-02'
   AND prompt_slice IN ('lang-en-long-context', 'lang-en-short')

7. If initial tests are inconclusive, schedule targeted shadow traffic or a canary with enhanced telemetry for 2 hours covering the failing slices.
8. When confident in root cause, prepare remediation: rollback plan, targeted quantization tweak, kernel configuration change, or prompt update. Document the fix in the incident tracker.
9. Close the loop: add failing prompts to the prompt-sets-and-benchmarks suite and create a new quant-eval slice if quantization was causal.

## Statistical Decision Rules

- Minimum sample size: 500 requests per slice for high-variance tasks (chat/long-context); 100 for low-variance embeddings or deterministic reranks.
- Significance: two-sided p < 0.01 for primary SLOs. Use bootstrap CIs for non-normal metrics (BLEU-like or token-level fidelity).
- Effect size threshold: absolute quality-drop >= 2% or relative latency increase >= 20% is actionable by default. Adjust per-SLO tier.

## Example Causal Test (Python pseudocode)

# Example: Use DoWhy to estimate effect of quantization on quality_score

from dowhy import CausalModel
import pandas as pd

# load prepared cohort dataframe
df = pd.read_csv('cohort.csv')
model = CausalModel(data=df, treatment='quant_profile_q8_4', outcome='quality_score', common_causes=['prompt_length', 'route', 'seed'])
identified_estimand = model.identify_effect()
estimate = model.estimate_effect(identified_estimand, method_name='backdoor.propensity_score_matching')
print(estimate)

Note: include diagnostics and sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding.

## Integrations with Automated Bisect and Eval Harness

- When bisect returns candidate change windows, attach a causal-analysis job that:
  - Replays failing trace samples across candidate model variants.
  - Runs the lightweight DoWhy/DiD tests on per-slice cohorts.
  - Produces a short causal report in the bisect output (delta metrics, p-values, suggested root causes).

- Hook names: eval-harness/replay, bisect/causal-report, telemetry/query-cohort.

## Required Instrumentation and Data Schema

Minimum columns for any cohort extract (plain text table):

| column_name | type | description |
| request_id | string | unique request identifier |
| event_time | timestamp | request time |
| model_tag | string | model identifier (e.g., m-v42) |
| quant_profile | string | quant profile id |
| route | string | API route or product feature |
| prompt_slice | string | slice label from prompt catalog |
| quality_score | float | chosen quality metric (0-1 normalized) |
| latency_ms | float | end-to-end token latency |
| kv_cache_hit | bool | cache hit flag |

Ensure all datasets are (a) anonymized, (b) token counts and sample prompts excluded from exported CSVs by default.

## Common Root Causes and Recommended Fixes

- Quantization-precision-bias: Re-run quant profile with per-layer fallback, raise precision on sensitive layers, add per-slice quant-tune.
- Kernel-fallback-latency: Pin kernel to earlier stable runtime for affected model length range; increase timeout SLOs temporarily.
- KV-cache-eviction-regression: Investigate policy, add explicit cache hold for long contexts or move to a larger shard.
- Prompt-truncation-shift: Add guardrail in prompt pipeline to preserve critical prefix tokens; add unit tests in prompt-sets.

## Playbook for Live Mitigation (fast timeline)

1. Within 30 minutes: if customer-facing degradations, enable fallback model variant (float or previous release).
2. Within 2 hours: collect reproducer examples and run targeted canary with enhanced telemetry.
3. Within 24 hours: implement permanent fix or schedule rollback.

## Post-Incident Actions

- Add failing prompts to permanent prompt regression suite.
- Create a quant-eval slice and add to nightly eval for that profile.
- Update the causal DAG library with the final root cause and evidence.
- Run a retrospective with owners (Applied ML, Serving Runtime, SRE) and record action items.

## Templates and Reporting

Use the following one-page template for causal-report attachments to incidents:

- Title: (short)
- Summary: 2–3 sentences
- Candidate hypotheses tested (list)
- Data used (cohort sizes, time windows)
- Statistical tests and results (p-values, CIs)
- Root cause (with confidence: low/medium/high)
- Action taken and follow-ups

## Related Pages

- eval-harness/serving-simulation-eval-harness-2026
- quantization-profiles/kv-cache-quant-stability-audit-playbook-2025
- regression-triage/automated-regression-bisect-and-blame-assistant-2026

## References

- DoWhy documentation and examples
- Google: CausalImpact R package
- Redwood internal: prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/prompt-coverage-matrix-and-annotated-drift-repair-guide-2024

description:
Motivation: Long-tail requests and multi-turn sessions make it hard to correlate expensive tokens with the actual prompt context. Alert noise for cost spikes often stems from superficially similar traces that differ in a few context tokens. This PR introduces two complementary observability primitives: (1) sampled context anchors — compact, privacy-safe snapshots attached to selected traces that let engineers inspect a representative prefix without storing full payloads; and (2) cost-delta annotations — span-level annotations that capture the incremental token cost relative to a baseline (baseline = first N tokens of the session or pinned model variant), enabling per-span cost-attribution and easy identification of regression candidates.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds a lightweight sampled-context store and recorder in the runtime that writes encrypted, k-anonymized anchors for 1% of long-tail sessions (configurable). Anchors include token fingerprints, anonymized prompt length buckets, and hashed prompt-context tags for grouping (no raw PII/token content stored).
- Adds cost-delta annotations into the tracing pipeline: each model-stage span now carries cost.delta and cost.baseline fields (numeric micro-units). These are added as span attributes and surfaced to OTEL and internal trace indexer.
- Dashboard updates: new dashboard panels on Console -> Observability that show per-route cost-delta distribution, anchor-cluster heatmap (session groups), and annotated trace + anchor join views.
- Alert tuning: new alerting rule that groups alerts by anchor-hash first and surfaces a single grouped alert for clusters of similar high-cost traces (reduces noisy duplicates). Added docs and runbook snippets for triage.

Implementation notes and constraints:
- Context anchors are generated at the runtime layer (redwood/service/runtime) before caching/quantization to avoid skew. Anchors emit a deterministic anchor-hash derived from a salted rolling-hash; the salt is customer-scoped to avoid cross-tenant correlation.
- Cost delta math: cost.delta = observed_token_cost - baseline_token_cost, baseline_token_cost is computed using a rolling median of the first 32 tokens for the route/model combo and periodically recomputed by a background aggregator.
- Privacy compliance: anchors are truncated and tokenized into fingerprint sketches; feature flags and customer-level opt-out is supported.
- Performance: profiling showed a 0.2% median p99 added latency on typical requests in our stage perf lab; batching and non-blocking flush paths mitigate the tail impact.

Overview:
This playbook documents the standardized process for converting embedded contractors, consultants, or long-term vendors into Redwood Inference full-time employees (FTEs). It covers hiring approvals, technical and cultural onboarding, role-level competency checks, IT/security provisioning, compensation calibration, and a 120-day ramp to role parity. The goal is a repeatable, transparent conversion that minimizes disruption to delivery and protects security and compliance posture.

When to use this guide:
- A contractor has received a formal offer and accepted moving to an FTE role.
- A long-term vendor engagement is transitioning to an internal headcount.
- The destination team requests a full-time role to replace contractor work.

Key objectives:
- Complete all HR and security provisioning prior to first day as FTE.
- Ensure at least 3 documented artifacts and 2 knowledge-transfer sessions exist before role transfer.
- Achieve role competency checkpoints by day 30, 60, 120.

Primary stakeholders and responsibilities:
- Hiring Manager: sponsor the conversion, define role expectations, run technical and cultural assessment, and own 120-day ramp plan.
- People Ops: lead offer coordination, background checks, compensation calibration, and new-hire admin tasks.
- IT/Security: validate access changes and complete privileged access approval prior to start date.
- Finance: assign budget code and start-date for payroll provisioning.
- Peer Sponsor (Buddy): assigned by hiring manager to provide daily operational support for first 60 days.

Pre-offer checklist (Hiring Manager & People Ops):
1) Validate headcount and budget with Finance.
2) Verify contractor status, IP clauses, and any non-compete implications with Legal.
3) Confirm eligibility for full-time benefits and relocation needs.
4) Calibrate compensation band using banding matrix and recent comp benchmarks.
5) Prepare offer letter template and proposed start date.

Offer and acceptance (People Ops):
- Standard timeline: 3 business days for initial offer response window.
- Include: start date, compensation, title, reporting manager, benefits overview, probation period (if applicable), and relocation/visa contingencies.
- Trigger items on acceptance: background check initiation, payroll onboarding form, corporate email reservation, and badge request.

Security and legal gating (must complete before start):
- Background check clearance.
- IP assignment and contractor termination/contract amendment completed.
- Any vendor/third-party agreements reviewed such that data ownership and access policies are preserved.
- MFA and SSO provisioning plan scheduled.

Technical and operational handoff (Hiring Manager and Peer Sponsor):
- Artifact inventory: code repos, runbooks, dashboards, deployment keys, vendor accounts. List links and owners.
- 2x knowledge-transfer sessions documented (recording or written notes).
- Create an access de-escalation plan if contractor credentials need to be retired.
- Define first 30/60/120 deliverables aligned to an objective success metric (example templates below).

First-week checklist (Day 0-7):
- HR: benefits orientation, payroll confirmation, and new-hire paperwork completion.
- IT: compute device assigned, VPN/SSO access, standard toolchain installed.
- Security: privileged access exceptions (if needed) validated and logged.
- Manager: daily check-ins, buddy pairing, role expectations and success metrics reviewed.
- Team: welcome intro, stakeholder directory, and calendar invites for recurring meetings.

30/60/120 day competency milestones (examples to adapt by role):
- 30 days: Completed onboarding tasks, executed at least one end-to-end code change or deliverable with review, attended key cross-team syncs, and passed a basic ops/runbook walk-through.
- 60 days: Independently delivers on recurring tasks, demonstrates operational ownership in one area (e.g., monitoring, deploys), and contributes to planning.
- 120 days: Reaches parity with peers on productivity and code quality; leads a small project and mentors others on transferred knowledge.

Role parity assessment criteria (used at day 120):
- Technical proficiency: passes a practical review (PRs, feature ownership, incident participation).
- Process adoption: uses team workflows, ticketing, CI/CD pipeline, and observability tools.
- Collaboration: integrates into team rituals, communicates with stakeholders, and receives positive feedback from buddy and cross-functional partners.

Compensation and benefits notes:
- Contractors converting within 6 months: standard band review; manager provides justification for above-band offers.
- Contractors converting after 12+ months: include performance summary and manager endorsement for accelerated banding if applicable.
- Equity eligibility: clarified at offer time per People Ops policy; vesting start date established in offer.

Examples: First 30-day deliverable templates
1) Individual contributor (engineer): "Deliver a small bugfix or feature with automated tests and deployment runbook updated."
2) Product manager: "Author a 1-page customer problem brief and run the first prioritization triage with stakeholders."
3) Designer: "Deliver a prototype and usability notes; present to cross-functional partners for feedback."

Access and credentialing patterns (common scenarios):
- If contractor had vendor-managed credentials, issue new corporate credentials to avoid shared secrets.
- Rotate any keys or tokens used during contractor period on day 0 of FTE status.
- For sensitive systems, escalate privileges in two stages: limited access on day 1, expanded after 30-day review.

Buddy program guidance (Peer Sponsor):
- Buddy time allocation: 1 hour/day for first 2 weeks, tapering to 1-2 hours/week by week 6.
- Suggested activities: guided walkthroughs, shadowing deploys, calendar clean-up, and culture Q&A.
- Feedback: buddies submit a short 1-page onboarding summary at day 30 and day 60.

Risk controls and compliance exceptions:
- If contractor had access to customer data, require an audit of prior access and explicit re-certification before conversion.
- Any unresolved IP or contractual obligations must block offer finalization.
- For visa-sponsored contractors, coordinate early with immigration counsel; do not set start date until visa transfer is confirmed.

Manager checklist for first 120 days (summary):
- Week 1: confirm paperwork, buddy assigned, access validated, first deliverable scoped.
- Week 2-4: weekly 1:1s focused on knowledge gaps and artifacts completion.
- Month 2: 30/60 progress review and calibration with manager and people-ops.
- Month 3: 120-day parity review and final sign-off; determine any ongoing development plan.

Reporting and audit trail requirements:
- People Ops will retain conversion packet (offer, background check confirmation, IP assignment, role activation) in HRIS.
- Hiring Manager must upload artifact inventory and buddy reports to the team's onboarding folder and link to the HR packet.

Escalation paths:
- If critical access or security issues are found, notify Security and People Ops immediately; pause conversion if needed.
- For compensation disputes, People Ops and Finance mediate with documented rationale and final approval by Head of People.

Doc purpose (Product Ops)
========================
We need a consistent set of internal remediation SLAs (time-to-mitigate / time-to-fix expectations) that:
- match what we can realistically execute across tiers (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- align with customer expectations and enterprise commitments (especially Dedicated/Private)
- can be implemented in tooling (ENG-4829 / SLA timers + breach alerts) without constant exceptions
- remains low-cardinality and understandable during live incidents

This is a working evaluation doc of options; final policy will live in Confluence in the Remediation SLA matrix.

Definitions
===========
- Remediation SLAs in this doc are internal operational targets and escalation triggers.
- We track two clocks:
  1) TTM (time-to-mitigate): time from incident declared (Sev assigned) to customer-impact mitigation in place (or credible workaround). Mitigation may include rollback, routing/fallback changes, traffic shaping, or isolating a bad region/model.
  2) TTF (time-to-fix): time from incident declared to a durable fix deployed OR a signed-off plan with committed ship date (depending on severity). For Sev0/Sev1, we typically expect a durable fix, not just a plan.

- “Tier” definitions:
  - Hosted: multi-tenant public API.
  - Dedicated: reserved capacity; stronger expectations for predictability and comms.
  - Private: VPC/on-prem control plane + data plane; sometimes customer-controlled networking and change windows.

- Severity (draft; matches on-call practice):
  - Sev0: broad outage / severe customer impact / safety risk / inability to serve core requests at scale.
  - Sev1: major degradation (e.g., high 5xx, severe latency) affecting meaningful customer set or a major enterprise customer; urgent.
  - Sev2: partial degradation; workarounds exist; limited scope.
  - Sev3: minor; limited impact; typically handled in normal on-call flow.

Decision principles
===================
1) Make the SLA actionable during incidents (what it forces us to do: staff, escalate, decide).
2) Keep differences by tier minimal, but acknowledge Dedicated/Private have different reality (capacity isolation, maintenance windows, customer networking).
3) Avoid a matrix so complex that incident-bot can’t enforce it.
4) “Pause/override” exists but must be auditable and rare.

Where tier differences are real (observations)
============================================
Hosted
- We control infra + routing + runtime deploys; can mitigate quickly via routing policies, throttles, or rollbacks.
- Customers accept “platform-wide” incidents but expect fast mitigation.

Dedicated
- Stronger expectations: named account pressure, high-touch comms, fewer acceptable repeated incidents.
- Mitigation sometimes means reallocating fleet capacity; can be constrained by GPU availability.
- Some mitigations require coordination with specific customer traffic patterns and agreed “degradation mode.”

Private
- Customer networking, DNS/TLS, firewalls, and change windows can dominate.
- “Mitigation” may require customer action; we can provide fix/instructions but can’t always execute.
- On-prem/air-gapped environments may block fast patching.

Key question: Do we set stricter SLAs for Dedicated/Private because customers pay more, or do we set realistic SLAs acknowledging dependencies and shift strictness into comms/escalation?

Option set
==========
Option A — Single SLA matrix (same targets across tiers) + comms escalation tiers
Pros: simple; consistent; easy to implement + dashboard.
Cons: risks being unrealistic for Private; breaches become noisy; forces frequent overrides.

Option B — Tier-adjusted TTF only (TTM consistent, TTF differs)
Pros: keeps the “stop the bleeding” behavior consistent; reflects reality that durable fixes take longer when customers control deploy windows.
Cons: still may be tight for certain Private classes; requires tier in SLA evaluator.

Option C — Tier-adjusted TTM and TTF (Dedicated stricter on TTM; Private looser on TTF)
Pros: matches customer expectation: Dedicated should be mitigated extremely fast; Private fixes can take longer.
Cons: more complex; risk of perceived unfairness (“why does private get longer?”).

Option D — Incident-type-aware SLA within severity (e.g., Private connectivity vs Control plane vs Runtime regression)
Pros: most accurate.
Cons: too complex for v1; high maintenance; taxonomy drift.

Recommendation (draft): Option B for v1
======================================
- Keep TTM targets consistent by severity across tiers (behavior we want in every incident: mitigate quickly).
- Allow tier-adjusted TTF targets (Private often needs customer maintenance window; Dedicated should still be fast but not necessarily faster than Hosted in all cases).
- In addition, define comms/escalation requirements by tier (Dedicated/Private proactive outreach thresholds), separate from remediation timers.

Proposed draft SLA targets (v1 candidate)
========================================
Notes:
- Times are proposed internal targets for breach alerting + leadership escalation.
- TTM measured to: restored SLO or reduced to acceptable degradation mode (documented).
- TTF measured to: fix deployed OR (Sev2/Sev3 only) fix scheduled with owner + date.

TTM (same across tiers)
-----------------------
Sev0: 30 minutes
Sev1: 2 hours
Sev2: 1 business day
Sev3: 5 business days (or next planned release train)

TTF (tier-adjusted)
-------------------
Hosted:
- Sev0: 24 hours
- Sev1: 3 business days
- Sev2: 10 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Dedicated:
- Sev0: 24 hours (same as Hosted; expectation is mitigation is faster, fix can be similar)
- Sev1: 5 business days (slightly longer than Hosted because some fixes involve fleet reshaping or customer-specific config review)
- Sev2: 15 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Private:
- Sev0: 48 hours (some fixes require customer coordination/change window; still want high urgency)
- Sev1: 10 business days
- Sev2: 20 business days
- Sev3: 45 business days

Rationale snapshots (to validate)
================================
- Private Sev0 TTF at 48h is the most controversial number. The intent is: if a Private incident is Sev0, we should be able to ship a fix quickly OR provide a validated workaround package quickly. But we may not be able to deploy it into the customer’s environment inside 48h. Proposed compromise: define “TTF = fix available” vs “TTF = deployed” for Private only.

Proposed adjustment for Private only:
- For Private tier: treat TTF as “fix available + customer delivery completed (artifact + instructions + support handoff)” rather than “fully deployed in customer environment.” Deployment tracking becomes a CS/Support deliverable.

This avoids constant SLA breaches from customer-controlled schedules, while still forcing Redwood to produce the fix quickly.

Edge cases + carve-outs (must be explicit)
=========================================
1) Cloud provider / upstream outage
- If root cause is confirmed upstream (AWS/GCP region/network, managed KMS outage, etc.):
  - TTM still applies (we should mitigate via failover/fallback where possible).
  - TTF may be waived or converted to “post-incident hardening actions” with due dates.
- Implementation requirement: incident-bot must allow “Upstream dependency” as a contributing factor and a “SLA exception reason” (audited).

2) Customer-caused or customer-controlled failures (mostly Private, occasionally Dedicated)
Examples:
- Customer rotated certs incorrectly; firewall blocks new endpoints; DNS misconfig; customer refuses recommended upgrade.
- TTM definition may be “workaround identified + communicated + support engaged.”
- TTF becomes a tracked action plan with customer owner and Redwood owner; SLA breach should not trigger paging.
- Implementation requirement: a controlled “Customer action required” exception reason.

3) Planned maintenance / change windows
- If incident is triggered by a planned change performed by Redwood:
  - SLAs still apply (we own it).
- If fix requires customer change window:
  - Private: allow “Fix available” measurement as above.

4) Multi-cause incidents
- Primary incident_type determines SLA class.
- Contributing systems recorded separately; do not create multiple SLA clocks.
- If reclassified, SLA clock should not reset (only severity changes reset behavior).

Comms and escalation requirements (separate from remediation timers)
===================================================================
We should not bake comms into remediation SLAs, but we do need consistent obligations by tier.

Draft comms rules (for CS alignment; see comms templates doc):
- Hosted
  - Sev0/Sev1: status page + initial update within 30 min; updates at least every 60 min until mitigated.
  - Sev2: case-by-case; internal update; status page optional.

- Dedicated
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach to affected accounts; initial customer-facing update within 30 min; updates every 60 min.
  - Sev2: proactive outreach within 1 business day if single account materially impacted.

- Private
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach; include “customer action required” assessment early.
  - Emphasize safe language: symptoms, mitigations, next update time.

Open issues / questions to resolve before signoff
=================================================
1) Private TTF definition: “available” vs “deployed”
- Need decision from SRE + Product Private (Vivek) + CS.

2) Dedicated Sev1 TTF: 3 vs 5 business days
- Dedicated product (Lauren) asked for realism: some changes require capacity rebalancing + canary.
- Counterpoint: enterprise expectation is faster. Maybe keep 3 BD but allow exceptions for capacity procurement work.

3) Severity-to-tier mapping clarity
- Can a Private incident be Sev0 if it affects only one customer? Yes, if it blocks core use case and is high urgency.
- Need crisp language in the incident process policy so on-call doesn’t under-severity enterprise incidents.

4) Implementation feasibility in tooling (ENG-4829)
- SLA evaluator needs tier + severity + type.
- Ensure we don’t create a combinatorial matrix. Proposed v1: severity x tier only, with optional overrides.

5) Reporting expectations
- Aisha to confirm dashboards will report:
  - SLA breach rate by tier, severity, incident_type
  - Exception counts by reason (upstream, customer-action, force majeure)

Data sanity check (informal)
============================
Based on last 2 quarters anecdotal review (see top-incidents analysis):
- Most Sev0/Sev1 mitigations happen within 15–90 minutes for Hosted when the mitigation is routing/rollback.
- Dedicated mitigations vary: quick when routing-only; slow when capacity constrained.
- Private “fix deployed” often exceeds 1–2 weeks due to customer windows; “fix available” is typically within a few days if we prioritize.

Action items (next steps)
=========================
- Rachel: circulate this doc to Rafael, Nikhil, Lauren, Vivek, Dev for comments (by 2026-02-07)
- Rafael/SRE: confirm if “TTF = plan w/ ship date” is acceptable for Sev2/Sev3 (Hosted/Dedicated) (by 2026-02-10)
- Vivek + CS: propose Private TTF measurement definition language for Confluence (by 2026-02-10)
- Lauren: confirm Dedicated Sev1 TTF target (3 vs 5 BD) and list top constraints (capacity procurement, release trains) (by 2026-02-12)
- Aisha: verify dashboards can label tier correctly and track exceptions without high cardinality (by 2026-02-12)

Appendix: quick matrix (for copy/paste)
======================================
TTM (all tiers):
- Sev0: 30m
- Sev1: 2h
- Sev2: 1 BD
- Sev3: 5 BD

TTF:
- Hosted:   Sev0 24h | Sev1 3 BD | Sev2 10 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Dedicated:Sev0 24h | Sev1 5 BD | Sev2 15 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Private:  Sev0 48h | Sev1 10 BD| Sev2 20 BD | Sev3 45 BD

Appendix: proposed SLA exception reasons (allowlist)
===================================================
- Upstream dependency confirmed (cloud/provider)
- Customer action required (customer-controlled environment)
- Force majeure (rare; requires Director+ approval)
- Mis-severity (initial severity incorrect; adjust and document)

(End)

anya: Quick readiness check — I'm onboarding open-mix-1.2. Weights uploaded to s3://redwood-models/onboard/open-mix-1.2/weights.pt. Can infra/runtime confirm KV cache format & memory sizing before we flip the canary? Also seeing a tokenizer quirk: BOS token seems duplicated when we push beyond 4096 tokens.

mike: Thanks. Couple quick Qs — is the weights file sharded or a single file? Also what's model config: num_layers / hidden_size / max_position_embeddings?

anya: single file, ~5.3GB (fp16). Model config excerpt in repo: max_position_embeddings: 8192, num_hidden_layers: 32, hidden_size: 4096, num_attention_heads: 32.

infra-bot: s3 upload check: permissions OK, object available to redwood-infra role. :white_check_mark:

sara: Re: tokenizer — I dug in; tokenizer.json is missing special_tokens_map and pad_token is null. When we call tokenizer.encode_plus with add_special_tokens it ends up inserting an extra BOS after the prompt for long sequences. Quick workaround: set tokenizer.pad_token = "<pad>" and tokenizer.add_bos = False before batching. I'll open a tiny patch.

thomas: Runtime notes: current KV cache implementation for onboarding expects per-layer serialization (we call it "layer-sharded-fp16"). The runtime stores K and V per layer, contiguous, dtype=fp16. Important for memory calc: for this architecture (32 layers, hidden 4096, 32 heads => head_dim 128) you get ~16KB per layer per token (k+v), so ~512KB per token total across layers. That means: 1 sequence of 8192 tokens => ~4GB KV alone (batch=1). If you bump batch>1 multiply accordingly.

anya: that's super helpful. So for A100-40GB we need headroom for model params (~5.3GB), optimizer/extra (~1GB for profiling), KV (~4GB) — leaves ~29GB free but fragmentation and other buffers matter. Realistically expect OOM if we try batch>2 at 8192.

mike: Good catch. Options: reduce max_context for hosted canary (set to 4096), enable KV sharding across GPUs (requires dedicated nodes), or auto-evict prefix cache for very long sequences. Which is preferred for onboarding?

thomas: For canary, simplest: set max_context to 4096 and confirm tokenizer fixes. If customer needs 8192 we should run on dedicated nodes with KV sharding; runtime flag is `--kv-shard=auto` (requires at least 2 GPUs to be effective). Also can enable `--reserve-mem=0.2` to keep headroom.

anya: I'll update model config in the onboarding repo to `max_position_embeddings: 4096` for the initial canary and open a follow-up to exercise 8192 on dedicated. Pinging @devex for docs update.

devex-bot: PR hint: opened draft PR #3492 to document tokenizer workaround + config recommendations.

sara: Small patch note (snippet):
```python
# onboarding tokenizer fix
tokenizer.pad_token = "<pad>"
tokenizer.special_tokens_map = {"bos_token": "<s>", "eos_token": "</s>", "pad_token": "<pad>"}
# ensure we don't double-add BOS during batching
tokenizer.add_bos = False
```

mike: Also double-check model config key names: runtime validates `max_position_embeddings`, `num_hidden_layers`, `hidden_size`, `num_attention_heads`, and `kv_cache_format`. If kv_cache_format missing it'll default to `layer-sharded-fp16`.

anya: I'll push the config change and run a canary with batch=1 seq=4096 on staging. Will report back with memory profile logs.

thomas: When you run the canary, grab `/metrics/runtime/mem/alloc` and `/traces/kv/cache_size` — that'll give a clear headroom number. If you still see >70% mem on A100-40 we should opt for 4096 prod limit.

anya: Got it. ETA: I'll run canary this afternoon and post results. Thanks all. :pray:

Summary:

This manual defines the safety contracts, verification checks, benchmarking protocols, and operational runbooks we use to validate adaptive degradation and fallback behavior in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and release owners who gate runtime and scheduler changes. The document consolidates architecture contracts, test harnesses, profiling playbooks, measurable acceptance criteria, and incident response steps into a single reference.

Scope:
- Covers adaptive degradation (fidelity staircases, model-variant fallback, burst shedding) and scheduler/kernel interactions.
- Includes verification checks executed in CI, pre-release staging, and canary phases.
- Prescribes profiling and benchmark procedures for SLO verification and performance regressions.
- Provides runbooks for on-call and release owners for graceful rollback and mitigation.

Principles and safety goals:
1) Observable and measurable: every degradation path must have a minimal observable signal (metrics, traces, events) and a single source-of-truth trace ID for forensic replay.
2) Fail open vs fail closed rationale: correctness-critical requests (enterprise-configured) should prefer fail-closed; non-critical/latency-sensitive requests can fail open to preserved throughput.
3) Bounded fidelity loss: fidelity steps should degrade quality predictably (quantified by eval sets) and be reversible.
4) Deterministic rollback: any automated fallback must expose a deterministic rollback path and human-confirmable guardrails.

Architecture contracts (high-level):
- Degradation tiers: primary (full model), degraded-1 (quantized), degraded-2 (short-context variant), fallback (smaller model / cached-embeddings). Each tier has an SLO budget and cost profile.
- Kernel scheduling contract: the scheduler must maintain per-request kernel affinity for the first N tokens and preserve KV cache affinity during tier transition windows (default N=16).
- Eviction and warmup contract: when a session is evicted from KV cache, a warmup window of configurable length (default 60s) is reserved to rehydrate frequently-seen prompts without degrading SLOs.

Verification matrix (summary table):
| Check ID | Purpose | Where executed | Acceptance threshold | Action on fail | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VD-01 | End-to-end tail latency under 95th percentile SLO | CI staging + canary | p95 < 1200ms for interactive path | block release, auto-rollback in canary | runtime-sre |
| VD-02 | Kernel latency jitter for hot kernels | perf-lab | 95th/50th ratio < 3.0 | schedule throttling + revert kernel flags | runtime-kernel-team |
| VD-03 | Fidelity regression on golden prompt set | automated evals | task-specific metric delta < 1.5% | fail gating | applied-ml |
| VD-04 | KV cache hitrate during warmup | synthetic replay | hitrate > 70% after 120s | degrade to cached-response fallback | runtime-sre |
| VD-05 | Correctness of fallback routing (no request loss) | chaos lab | 0 dropped requests during routing switch | incident | runtime-oncall |

Verifiable artifacts for each check:
- Synthetic replay corpus snapshot (sha256) used in CI.
- Expected telemetry schemas (metric names, tags) and trace samples.
- Baseline benchmark outputs (binary artifacts) for diff-based gating.

CI and pre-release harnesses:
1) CI unit stage: microbenchmarks for individual kernels (latency, occupancy, memory). Thresholds are enforced as fast-fail rules.
2) Staging perf run: full-stack replay of production traffic sampled (1:1000) with degraded-tier injection. Output artifacts: histogram dumps, kernel traces, KV cache heatmaps.
3) Canary: traffic ramp with A/B model variants and automated rollback on VD-* failures. Canary policy: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over 30m windows with automated health checks every 5m.

Benchmarking protocol (detailed):
- Workloads to run:
  - Interactive short-chat (mean tokens=40, 90th=128) — target low-latency SLOs.
  - Streaming long-output (mean tokens=800) — target throughput and memory stability.
  - Embeddings burst (large batch sizes) — target batching efficiency and memory footprint.
- Metrics collected:
  - end_to_end_latency_ms (p50/p90/p95/p99), kernel_exec_time_ms per-kernel, gpu_mem_used_mb, kv_cache_hitrate_pct, tokens_per_second_per_gpu.
- Tooling & commands (examples):
  - Run synthetic replay: 
    ./perf-runner --profile=replay --corpus=sha256:abcd1234 --duration=15m --out=artifacts/replay-$(date +%s).tgz
  - Microbenchmark kernel: 
    python tools/microbench.py --kernel matmul --batch 1 --seq 128 --out json --repeat 50
  - Collect trace samples for a request: 
    curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CI_TOKEN" https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"<<golden>>"}' -o /tmp/trace.json
- Acceptance criteria pattern:
  - No p95 regression > 8% vs baseline.
  - Kernel jitter (95/50) <= 3.0.
  - KV cache delta < 5% hitrate loss after warmup period.

Profiling playbook snippets (how-to):
1) Latency fingerprint collection (on perf-lab machine):
  - Start full instrumentation: export PERF_SAMPLER=on; ./runtime --enable-tracing --trace-sample-rate=0.01
  - Run workload for 10 minutes and collect traces: tar -czf traces.tgz /var/tmp/traces/*
  - Post-process: python tools/trace-aggregate.py --input traces.tgz --output traces-summary.json
2) Kernel causality mapping:
  - Use kernel-hint exporter to annotate kernels with request-id and token-index. Example PromQL to find kernel hotpaths: sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (kernel_name)
3) Latency attribution checklist:
  - Confirm p95 skew aligns with a specific kernel or queue time via trace waterfall.
  - Check GPU utilization and eviction events within the window.
  - Validate KV cache hit/miss correlation with session affinity changes.

Runbook: Adaptive Degradation incident triage (short):
1) Detection: Alert triggers if p95 or error-rate breaches gating thresholds (see Verification matrix).
2) Initial triage (first 10 min):
  - Owner: oncall-runtime.
  - Query: run the baseline PromQL dashboards (listed below) and capture current vs baseline.
  - Commands:
    - promql: rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m]) by (route)
    - runtime CLI: runtimectl list-sessions --filter=evicted=true --since=10m
3) Containment (10–30 min):
  - If caused by kernel regression: flip kernel rollout gate to previous stable tag (runtimectl kernel-set active:stable-<tag>) and pause canaries.
  - If caused by cache warmup regression: enable elevated pre-warm (config: prewarm_multiplier=2) and route new sessions to degraded-1 temporarily.
4) Remediation (30–90 min):
  - Roll back flagged config or kernel. Run perf-runner quick replay to validate.
  - If degradation persists, scale dedicated pool capacity for 15 minutes to reduce pressure and collect artifacts.
5) Post-incident verification: Ensure all VD-* checks pass in staging before re-enabling automated rollouts.

Release gating checklist (for runtime and scheduler changes):
- Code owner review and ADR reference.
- Automated CI checks: unit tests, lint, kernel microbenchmarks.
- Perf artifacts present: replay corpus, baseline histograms, and guard thresholds.
- Canary policy configured and health checks defined (list health checks and thresholds attached).
- Rollback plan and human approvers designated in the release ticket.

Instrumentation and metrics schema (quick reference):
- metric names: runtime.request.latency_ms, runtime.kernel.exec_ms, runtime.kv.hits, runtime.fidelity.tier, runtime.eviction.count
- required tags: service, model_name, model_variant, route, region, canary_id
- recommended tracing fields: request_id, session_id, token_index, kernel_name, warmup_phase

Ownership and escalation:
- Runtime architecture owner: runtime-arch@redwood.ai (primary: Sanjay Rao).
- Kernel scheduling owner: kernel-team@redwood.ai.
- Oncall rota: runtime-sre (see internal roster).
- Escalation path: oncall -> SRE lead -> runtime-arch -> Eng Director (timed escalation at 45m).

Appendices:
A) YAML example: adaptive degradation policy (example config to be applied via runtime fleet config)

  degradation_policy:
    tiers:
      - name: primary
        model_variant: v2-full
        slos:
          p95_latency_ms: 900
      - name: degraded-1
        model_variant: v2-quantized
        slos:
          p95_latency_ms: 700
      - name: degraded-2
        model_variant: v2-shortctx
        slos:
          p95_latency_ms: 350
    warmup:
      kv_cache_warmup_seconds: 120
      prewarm_multiplier: 1.5
    fallback:
      strategy: route-to-smaller-model
      max_inflight_fallback: 250

B) PromQL examples (quick):
- p95 latency for route: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- kernel jitter index: (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel)))/(histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel)))

C) Minimal reproduction recipe for regressions:
1) Snapshot failing commit and baseline artifacts.
2) Run perf-runner with the failing kernel flag enabled and the baseline corpus.
3) Collect traces (traces.tgz) and microbench outputs.
4) Upload artifacts to /artifacts/regressions/<ticket-id>.

Related reading and references:
- See routing and fallback architecture ADR (link in related_pages).
- Profiling playbooks and telemetry contract (links in related_pages).

Notes and change log:

description:
High-level PRD to deliver a compact, production-ready 'mini-bundle' that exposes a consistent API surface for chat, completion, embeddings, and rerank use cases. The intent is to offer a single onboarding flow, one billing SKU with per-route knobs, and an operational surge/rollback plan for launch day. This ticket scopes the product requirements, acceptance criteria, risks, and a tactical launch checklist for a targeted GA to early enterprise customers.

background:
We have multiple Large PRDs covering the full hosted API family. This effort is a deliberately constrained bundle (MVP) to speed time-to-value for teams that need a single integration covering the most common patterns: single-turn generation, chat turn sequences, vector embedding generation, and rerank scoring pipelines. Key differences from larger PRDs: tighter acceptance gates, explicit surge controls, and a built-in sampling quality monitor tied to rollout gates.

goals:
Deliver a single, documented API path that supports chat, completion, embeddings, and rerank with consistent authentication and billing
Provide per-route configuration: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, embedding_model, rerank_model and deterministic fallback mapping
Define launch operational plan that prevents capacity overload via adaptive throttles and a tiered fallback to smaller models/regions
Ship a monitoring plan that samples 0.5% of responses for quality evaluation and flags regression against a baseline prompt set

non_goals:
Full multi-modal support (images/audio) in this mini-bundle
Advanced model orchestration policies (A/B weighted routing across unlimited variants) beyond simple canary and fallback
Enterprise-only Dedicated capacity contracts — this targets hosted tier first

requirements:
API: Single endpoint group /v1/inference with mode param: {mode: "chat|completion|embedding|rerank"}
SDKs: Expose identical surface in SDKs (python/js) with clear defaults and per-route overrides
Billing: One SKU 'mini_bundle' with per-token generation and per-embedding unit rates; explicit metering for rerank scoring calls
Routing: Support region preference and a fallback route list; fallback must preserve response semantics within 95% of acceptance tests
Rate limits & quotas: Configurable per-tenant soft-limit + hard-limit; a surge policy that reduces batch size and routes to fallback models under sustained queue growth
Observability: Token-level cost, per-request latency, sample payloads (0.5%), and a regression alert if sampled quality score drops by >= 6% vs baseline
Security/compliance: All requests logged with request_id and redaction rules; ensure KMS integration for customer-managed keys is documented for Private later

acceptance_criteria:
API contract: OpenAPI entry and SDK surfaces pass contract linting and automated smoke tests
Functional tests: Chat single-turn and multi-turn (3 turns) acceptance suite passes with stability >= 99% over 24h soak
Embedding parity: Embedding model produces vectors within 2% cosine similarity of reference embedding for canonical dataset
Rerank correctness: Top-1 rerank precision on benchmark set >= 88% and latency P95 <= 220ms in hosted region
Billing validation: Billing meter events emitted for every request type and aggregated values match simulated invoice within 0.5%
Safety & redaction: Automated PII redaction hooks exercised and verified in 1000 sample requests
Surge behavior: Under load test (2x expected QPS sustained for 30m) the system enforces surge throttle and fallback route within 60s, with successful degradation behavior (no unhandled 5xx spikes >0.5%)
Canary and rollback: Canary cohort (5% traffic) does not regress metrics for 4 consecutive hours, otherwise automatic rollback to previous model happens
Docs & quickstart: Console quickstart, API docs, and example notebooks present and validated by Solutions Engineering

out_of_scope:
Dedicated capacity provisioning flows for this mini-bundle (handled by Dedicated roadmap)
Customer-managed on-prem installation in GA (Private flagged for later cycle)
Complex retraining/inference pipelines or multi-stage retrieval chains — only single call rerank is supported

dependencies:
ENG-22111 (runtime: per-request sampling and trace IDs)
ENG-23780 (billing: embed per-unit meter events)
ENG-24451 (routing: fallback policy primitives)
DES-1987 (docs: quickstart and SDK examples)
PM-582300 (safety: redaction and PII policy)

risks:
Surge underestimation: underestimated launch demand could exhaust GPU pools; mitigated by conservative initial quota and manual surge escalation playbook
Quality regressions due to fallback: cheaper fallback models may produce unacceptable outputs — sampled quality monitor and rollback gates required
Billing mismatch: complexity in metering different call types could produce unexpected invoices for customers; bill validation harness required
Docs/UX confusion: single endpoint with mode param may be confusing; provide strong examples and per-mode templates in SDKs

metrics:
Adoption: number of unique tenants calling mini_bundle endpoint in first 30 days
Latency: P95 latency for each mode (chat/completion/embedding/rerank)
Quality: sampled quality score delta vs baseline prompt set (daily)
Cost: average cost-per-1k-token and per-embedding unit by workload
Reliability: % requests successful (2xx) and 5xx rate under load
Billing accuracy: variance between simulated invoice and production invoices

rollout_plan:
Phase 0 (internal): SDK + API + docs internal preview with Redwood teams only
Phase 1 (alpha): Invite 5 strategic customers, conservative quotas, 1-week canary; active SRE monitoring and daily review
Phase 2 (beta): Open to self-serve signups with default quotas lowered and surge protections enabled; monitor for two weeks
Phase 3 (GA): Full listing in Console, marketing announcement, quotas increased per usage tiers with sustained SLOs

launch_checklist:

SDK releases (python/js) with example notebooks and unit tests
Billing hooks validated end-to-end with sandbox tenants
SRE runbook: surge playbook, escalation matrix, rollback steps
Monitoring dashboards: latency/cost/quality panels configured and alerted
Canary configuration: 5% routing rule and automated rollback triggers

Runload tests: 2x expected QPS sustained 30m without >0.5% 5xx spikes
Smoke tests: end-to-end quickstart validated by two different engineers

Engineering should run an extended 24h soak test on staging with realistic prompt distributions supplied by Solutions Engineering. Coordinate with billing team to ensure meter event shapes are stable before SDK GA.

Goal: quick, intuition-first set of micro-tier experiments for low-touch SMB & hobbyist flows. Keep things cheap/simple for <10k MAU seed projects, but don't incentivize abusive high-throughput workloads. This is a personal scratchpad — lots of heuristics and TODOs.

Assumptions (back-of-envelope):
- GPU cost baseline: use amortized per-token cost from infra team: 1 GPU-hour ~ $3.50 (spot blended) for inference on 8-bit quantized medium model. This maps to ~ 5M tokens/hour in steady streaming workloads (conservative). => infra token-cost = $3.50 / 5e6 = $0.0000007 / token (~0.70 $/M tokens).
- Add infra overhead (orchestration, storage, network, support) x1.6 => unit cost ~ $1.12 /M tokens.
- Payment processor + margins + churn buffer => target gross margin target 65% => suggested price per M tokens = cost / (1 - margin) = 1.12 / 0.35 = ~$3.20 /M tokens. Round to simple numbers.

User behavior estimates (for small tiers):
- Typical hobbyist: 20 API calls/day, avg request 300 tokens in + 200 tokens out = 500 tokens/call => 10k tokens/day ~ 300k tokens/month.
- Small startup dev: 200 calls/day -> 100k tokens/day -> 3M tokens/month.
- Sandbox heavy: spike bursts are important; need burst cap for < 1 hour windows.

Tier sketches (for experiment matrix):
1) Nano (free-ish): 500k tokens/month included, 30 req/min burst to throttle, email-only support. Add-on packs available.
2) Sprout (entry): $5 / month => 1.5M included tokens, soft rate-limit 60 req/min, no SLA, basic analytics. Overage: $5 /M tokens.
3) Builder (most likely convert): $25 / month => 10M included tokens, 250 req/min, basic SLA, webhook retries, monthly usage analytics. Overage: $3 /M tokens.
4) Scale (paid, committed): $250 /mo => 200M included tokens, dedicated burst pool 1k req/min, 99.9% availability target (hosted). Overage: $1.8 /M tokens or discounted add-on reserved capacity.

Rationale behind numbers:
- Nano free cap chosen to cover typical hobbyist exploratory usage (~300k/mo). 500k avoids early-day blocking and increases virality potential.
- Sprout price anchored to $5 because perceived low friction; included tokens priced at ~ $3.33 /M (5$/1.5M) which is slightly above suggested retail $3.2/M but cheap enough. Overage high to nudge to upgrade.
- Builder is the 'trials convert' tier: effective price = $2.5 /M across included 10M at $25 => attractive cost, gets dev teams comfortable.
- Scale is for small teams who want predictable spend and capacity; economically justified vs payg if sustained.

Burst mechanics & abuse control (sketch):
- Each account gets a token refill bucket per minute computed from included tokens * burst factor. For nano/sprout, burst factor lower (x3 of steady qps), for builder x8, for scale negotiable.
- Rate-limit circuit-breaker: sustained QPS > allowed for >10s => throttle to baseline. Spikes <10s allowed.
- Protect free tier via fingerprinting and progressive verification: email -> phone -> card for larger bursts.

Alternate anchoring: session-bundles vs tokens
- Session-bundle: useful for voice/chat where tokens correlate poorly per 'interaction'. A session bundle = 1,000 tokens equiv. Offer small pack pricing (e.g., 50 sessions / month) for UX-focused apps.
- Hybrid: include N sessions + M tokens. Sessions consume tokens once threshold crossed. Complexity tradeoff: easier to think about UX vs harder billing engine.

Experiment matrix to run (short-term):
A) A/B pricing test: Sprout $5 with 1.5M vs SproutPro $8 with 4M included. Measure upgrade rates & retention over 30 days.
B) Free cap change: free 500k vs free 750k (narrow experiment to see activation lift). Watch abuse pattern (ratio of accounts with >1M usage).
C) Overage elasticity: set overage at $5 /M vs $3 /M for Builder and observe churn/upgrade.

Quick sensitivity calcs (for ops):
- Break-even tokens per month per paying account (consider blended margin): if price = $25 and unit cost = 1.12/M tokens => at $25 you can support ~22.3M tokens before cost eats revenue (25 / 1.12 * 1M = 22.3M tokens). But we target usage lower, so 10M included is safe.
- If average Builder payload = 10M tokens/mo and 10k accounts => infra spend = 10M * 10k * 1.12/1e6 = $112k/month. Revenue = 25 * 10k = $250k/month => gross margin ~ 55% (below 65 target) — need to tighten or upsell.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Validate infra token cost with infra team: is 5M tokens/hour realistic across models (mix of short/long seq)? get per-model profiles.
- How to implement session bundles in billing platform? estimate engineering effort.
- Decide whether free tier should persist on account-level or per-project-level (billing vs org).
- Edge-case: chat apps that use large context windows (50k) — how to price? Consider 'context surcharge' or per-context-block pricing.

Notes to self: keep the pricing language simple on the landing page — round numbers, emphasize included tokens and burst capacity. For first experimental launch, keep overage intentionally punitive to push upgrades rather than risk large pay-as-you-go churn.

Slack refs: convo in #pricing from 2025-10-29 — Jonah posted activation benchmarks. See JIRA-PRC-548 for rollout infra work.

End of scratchpad. Will iterate after infra cost check and A/B test results.

description:
Summary: A legacy compatibility proxy and an ad-hoc legacy-flag-mapper were introduced in early rollout phases to accept old client configs and route traffic to fallback handlers. Over time these have become maintenance burden: duplicated telemetry, increased tail latency variance, and brittle conditional logic that blocks safe schema evolution. This ticket removes the compat-proxy and migrates persisted flag keys/configs to a single canonical config-schema v2. The work includes safe migration tooling, operator controls, and a staged rollout with clear observability.

acceptance_criteria:
Legacy compat-proxy binary and all HTTP/gRPC routes removed from the runtime and service mesh
Config-schema v2 is the sole accepted on-disk format; v1 reader deprecated and gated behind operator toggle
Migration scripts can perform idempotent dry-runs and produce a migration report listing changed keys
No customer-facing errors attributable to missing legacy keys during a 72h full-ramp window
Telemetry shows no net increase in P99 latency or error-rate > 0.5% vs baseline after full rollout

migration_steps:
Create operator-only toggle 'allow_v1_configs' default=false
Run discovery job across S3/DB to enumerate v1 configs and generate migration plan
Execute idempotent migration in dry-run mode and publish report to migration-bucket
Perform controlled migration on a small set of non-critical Dedicated clusters
Flip runtime to reject v1 payloads only after all persisted configs migrated
Remove v1 reader code and compat-proxy from runtime in the final release

rollout_plan:
Phase 0: Nightly dry-runs for 3 days and manual review of reports
Phase 1 Canary: Migrate 1-2 canary clusters (approx 3% traffic) for 6 hours
Phase 2 Staged: Expand to 20% traffic over 24h if canary stable
Phase 3 Ramp: 60% for 24h with automated health checks and human-on-call
Phase 4 Full: 100% with deprecation notice and archive of v1 artifacts

testing_plan:
Unit tests for config parser and migration utilities covering edge cases
Integration tests simulating old-client requests against migrated configs
Contract tests for public API to ensure no behavioural deltas after migration
Load tests at 2x expected peak with traffic shapes that previously hit compat-proxy
Chaos test: kill compat-proxy in staging to validate graceful degradation path

risks:
Dedicated customers using custom config loaders may experience failures if not coordinated
Silent behavioural regressions for rare request shapes due to flag-key renames
Alert noise from duplicated metrics during partial rollout could mask true regressions
Edge-case malformed v1 entries may require manual remediation and slow migration

rollback_plan:
If significant regressions: 1) Pause migration jobs and set 'allow_v1_configs'=true; 2) redeploy previous runtime release to affected shards; 3) run remediation to restore original keys for impacted configs; 4) communicate to customers and schedule follow-up fixes; 5) reopen canary after fixes.

2026-02-16: Architecture review — agreed to consolidate mapping logic into config service
2026-02-22: Discovery job run in staging found ~1.3K v1 configs; 12 clusters with custom loaders detected
2026-03-01: Security requested verification for KMS-wrapped keys during migration; added key-rotation checklist
2026-03-08: Dry-run migration executed on two non-customer clusters; small number of malformed v1 entries reported
2026-03-12: Oncall approved canary window; Derek to execute canary on 2026-03-13

notes:
Notify Dedicated customers and Solutions Engineering 72 hours before any migration affecting their clusters. Ensure logs include 'compat_migration' trace ids for at least 30 days. Post-migration, run an analytics job to validate feature-usage metrics and reconcile with pre-migration baseline.

- Hypothesis C: Orchestrator warms up many parallel short-lived flush workers after promotion; our per-route token attribution (edge-side) misattributes some of those against interactive route token pools when path normalization occurs (signed-url/callbacks).

Question: In the PRD about adding managed orchestration for multi-model inference pipelines, what are the rollout milestones and target quarters for alpha, beta, and general availability?
