Purpose
Set an explicit, compact checkpoint to keep day-to-day work tied to outcomes (not just tickets). Use short experiments to surface friction early and make 1% measurable improvements to throughput and focus.

Week snapshot (Mar 8 - Mar 14, 2026)
- High-level outcome: Reduce queuing latency on inference staging by 12% for 8-token priming sequences (customer-sim testing).
- Why this week: We have 2 customers hitting sudden tail latency and it's adding to SLO risk. If I can knock down median queuing by ~10–15% with a config/ops tweak + a small batching policy change, we can avoid an ops escalation.

Signals I care about (leading/lagging)
- Leading: avg queue time at router for 1–8 tokens (per model variant) — goal: 10% down from baseline 28ms -> target ~25ms.
- Lagging: 95th percentile end-to-end latency on staging harness for customer scenario — goal: <240ms.
- Side signals: number of stale KV-cache reuse events, CPU steal during bursts, error rates during autoscale.

What I shipped last week (quick wins)
- Small router change: lowered max batching window by 5ms for small seqs (AB test v21). Observed median queue down 4ms in canary.
- Ran a smoke eval with customer traces (10k requests) — found one model variant spikes when burst concurrency > 120. Filed PLAT-8742.

Hypotheses + micro-experiments this week (ranked)
1) Hypothesis: aggressively favor small-window batch assembly for <12-token requests reduces per-request queue time without hurting throughput.
   Experiment: deploy batcher policy beta-3 to two nodes in staging for 48 hours, 20% traffic. Measure median queue time and tokens/sec.
   Success metric: median queue time <= -8% and tokens/sec drop <= 3%.
   Confounding: if request size distribution shifts (more 32-token requests), batching overhead shifts.

2) Hypothesis: enabling light quantized-kv-cache (8-bit) on the variant reduces memory pressure and lowers CPU swap/steal during peaks, improving tail latency.
   Experiment: spin dedicated small-node pool (beta quant-kv) and run the 10k trace.
   Success metric: 95th percentile latency improves by 10–12% vs baseline.

3) Hypothesis: small changes to routing priority (preferring dedicated reserved pool for seen-client tokens) reduces cross-tenant interference.
   Experiment: short canary of priority flag on 5 reserved sessions, monitor error/queue delta.

Overview

Purpose: This brief consolidates product positioning, high-impact value metrics, competitive battlecards, pricing guidance, a compact case study, and a prospect-facing security FAQ tailored for SaaS platform buyers evaluating LLM inference solutions. Audience: AEs, SEs, solutions engineers, and product marketing running discovery and technical evaluation calls with mid-market and enterprise SaaS buyers.

Executive positioning (one-liner)

Redwood Inference: Predictable, production-grade LLM inference that maximizes performance and minimizes unit cost across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — giving platform teams a single API and operational surface to ship reliable AI features without rebuilding inference infrastructure.

Top 3 buyer outcomes we lead with

- Reduce per-inference cost while keeping sub-100ms tail latency for common interactive flows.
- Move from prototype to SLA-backed production without re-architecting (same API for hosted, reserved, and private).
- De-risk compliance through private deployment and audit-friendly telemetry.

Key value metrics and how to frame them in discovery

- Latency (P95/P99): Typical hosted P95 for chat flows: 80–180ms (short prompts, <256 tokens). P99 target for Dedicated: <250ms. Discuss tail-latency SLOs and fallback routing to smaller quantized models for spikes.
- Throughput: Batch-aware throughput gains: 2–6x cost savings for high-concurrency embedding jobs with batching & caching. Ask about queries/sec (QPS) and average request size.
- Cost per 1k prompt tokens: Provide customer-specific model/quantization comps. Example framing: "Switching from single-instance self-host to Redwood Dedicated saved AcornCRM ~48% per-token on standard 8K-chat workload."
- Availability / SLA: Hosted: 99.9% regional uptime; Dedicated: 99.95% backed by contract. Use these to quantify expected downtime impact on revenue ops.
- Time-to-production: Typical onboarding (hosted) = 1–3 days; Dedicated proof-of-concept = 2–4 weeks (infra & capacity provisioning).

Battlecard: Primary competitors and how to position

- Cloud-managed endpoints (Hyperscaler-managed LLM endpoints)
  - Strengths: deep cloud integration, single-provider billing.
  - Redwood advantage: Superior latency predictability, multi-model catalog (open models + tuned variants), and lower unit cost via continuous batching, quantization profiles, and model routing policies.
  - Messaging: "Like managed endpoints, but tuned for inference economics and predictable tail latency for production apps."

- LLM API providers (simple hosted APIs)
  - Strengths: easy dev experience, low time-to-value.
  - Redwood advantage: Matches dev ergonomics but adds Dedicated / Private lanes and enterprise controls (VPC, KMS, audit logs) so customers don’t have to replatform as they scale.
  - Messaging: "From prototype to SLA-backed production without rewriting your integration."

- Self-hosted inference stacks (open-source runtime + infra)
  - Strengths: maximum control, on-prem fit for regulated data.
  - Redwood advantage: We provide a hardened runtime, autoscaling, cost controls, and rollout tooling—plus optional on-prem packaging and a customer-managed control plane for compliance. Lower TCO for teams that value operational simplicity and performance tuning.
  - Messaging: "Get the benefits of a maintained, optimized inference runtime without hiring a deep infra team."

Pricing guidance (rules of thumb for AEs to use in discovery)

- Pricing levers to highlight: model family, instance type (Dedicated SKU), quantization tier, reserved commit vs burst, embedding vs generative unit pricing.
- Proposal archetypes:
  - Self-serve hosted starter: no commit, pay-as-you-go per-token and per-embedding. Ideal for product/feature proofs.
  - Dedicated entry: 3–6 month reserved capacity (monthly commit), includes capacity reservation, 24/7 priority support, and model access. Typical for midmarket customers expecting consistent QPS.
  - Private Deployment: fixed platform fee + per-node license + premium support and compliance bundle. For regulated customers or those requiring air-gapped environments.

- Example customer scenario (SaaS search & assistant) — ballpark illustration to use during commercial conversations:
  - Baseline: 3M tokens / month, predominantly generation (average 500 tokens/session), 2M embeddings / month.
  - Hosted cost estimate (pay-as-you-go): $6,000–$9,000 / month depending on model family and streaming usage.
  - Dedicated cost estimate (reserved): $3,200–$5,500 / month equivalent (with 12-month commit) — includes better latency SLAs and lower per-token unit economics.
  - Use these numbers as conversation starters and include precise model-match quotes from pricing desk for final proposals.

Pitch deck outline (6 slides, one-line purpose each)

1. Problem: Rising inference costs, tail latency, and operational debt when scaling LLM features.
2. Vision & Value: Unified inference runtime with predictable economics and deployment flexibility.
3. Product: Redwood product map (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private, Console, Optimize).
4. Proof points: Performance benchmarks (P95/P99 numbers), cost comparisons vs self-host & hyperscalers, and a short case study.
5. Security & compliance: VPC, KMS integrations, SOC2 / ISO posture, audit logs, and private deployment options.
6. Commercials & next steps: Pricing archetypes, pilot offer, success criteria and timeline.

Compact case study: AcornCRM (SaaS CRM) — 8-week engagement

- Situation: AcornCRM needed a contextual assistant for sales reps with sub-200ms P95 latency and tight data residency constraints for EU customers. Their prototype used a mix of self-hosted models and occasional hyperscaler endpoints.
- Action: Redwood onboarded AcornCRM to Hosted API for an initial pilot (2 weeks), instrumented prompt caching and prefix KV caching, then migrated them to a Dedicated pool with quantized model variants for EU traffic. Provided rollout plan with canary and automatic fallback policies.
- Results: 
  - Latency: P95 from ~420ms to 160ms after Dedicated + batching optimizations.
  - Cost: Estimated per-token unit cost reduced 48% vs their previous single-instance hosting baseline.
  - Reliability: Achieved 99.96% uptime for critical inference routes over 90 days.
- Quote (paraphrased): "We launched our assistant into production faster than expected and kept response times consistent across our EU and US customers — the cost reduction was material to our unit economics." — Head of Platform, AcornCRM

Security FAQ for prospects (short and direct)

Q: Can Redwood run in my VPC / on-prem?
A: Yes. We offer Private deployment (customer-managed control plane) and an on-prem package for air-gapped environments. Contact sales for deployment checklist and lead time (typically 4–8 weeks depending on network & hardware).

Q: How is customer data protected in Hosted?
A: Data is encrypted in-transit (TLS 1.2+) and at-rest (AES-256). Optional per-customer keying via KMS (bring-your-own-key supported on Dedicated & Private). We retain only transient inference artifacts by default; retention is configurable.

Q: Do you have third-party attestations?
A: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 evidence; customers with enterprise contracts can request evidence under NDA.

Q: How are audit logs surfaced?
A: Redwood Console exposes request-level telemetry, per-token cost breakdowns, model version, and an audit trail for administrative actions. Logs can also be forwarded to your SIEM via secure forwarding.

Q: What controls exist to prevent data leakage in model updates?
A: Model onboarding and updates are gated by the model-onboarding team. We sign model-change notices and provide canary/eval runs tied to your evaluation suites. Private deployments allow complete model binaries under customer control.

Q: How do you handle incident response and notifications?
A: We maintain a documented incident process with dedicated SRE on-call rotation. Customers with Dedicated or Private get a designated technical account lead (TAL) and a post-incident report within 72 hours for Sev1 incidents.

- "We can build this ourselves": Ask about the cost of hiring/retaining ops talent, time-to-first-SLA, and the ongoing tuning effort. Offer a TCO comparison and pilot to prove the economics.

description:
Motivation: under high-concurrency, the paged KV cache freelist would fragment after repeated allocations/frees of mixed-size blocks, increasing allocation latency and causing more frequent slow-path compaction. This PR adds an opportunistic freelist defragmenter that compacts adjacent free pages on free-paths and a lightweight hot-prefix selective pinning policy so frequently-accessed key prefixes avoid costly eviction. Goals: reduce p99 allocation latency, lower background compaction pressure, and improve tail latency for workloads with hot prefixes (chat sessions, long contexts).

Summary of changes:
- Opportunistic freelist defragmenter run inline on frees when a small threshold of contiguous free segments is observed (configurable).
- Compact-on-free path that coalesces adjacent free pages into larger blocks to improve reuse for larger token sequences.
- Adaptive reuse scoring: tracks short-term reuse frequency per page bucket and prefers reuse of high-score pages.
- Hot-prefix selective pinning: a small resident pin set for top-N hot key prefixes with LRU eviction; pins are persisted across ephemeral reconnects to stabilize performance.
- Scheduler hint: allocator exposes a gentle backpressure hint to the request scheduler when fragmentation crosses configured thresholds so the scheduler can delay batch growth and avoid thrashing.
- Tests and microbenchmarks: new unit tests for defragmenter invariants and a throughput/latency benchmark demonstrating behavior across workload mixes.

Compatibility: fully opt-in via runtime config flags (defaults are conservative).

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked in PR
- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Microbenchmark
- [x] CI green after flake fix
- [x] Perf measurements attached

Related tickets: Linear ENG-4823 (KV fragmentation), ENG-4781 (hot-prefix regressions).

description:
Motivation: We have multiple downstream needs that couldn't be satisfied by the legacy model capability schema: (1) lightweight, per-request runtime hints that the routing layer and serving runtime can use without deserializing the full model profile; (2) a transparent metering knob for tool/function calling (customers asked for per-invocation crediting separate from token billing); and (3) richer guidance for streaming fallbacks so clients can degrade more gracefully when a model variant switches to a lower-throughput tier. This PR introduces three related surfaces: capability_headers, function_call_credit, and streaming_degradation_policy, alongside an OpenAI-compatible shim that surfaces structured-output hints in /v1/models list responses.

Summary of changes (high level):
- API: Add optional capability_headers map to /v1/models and /v1/models/:id responses. These are short key/value runtime hints intended for fast routing decisions (examples: "supports_prefix_cache": "true", "max_prefetch_tokens": "256").
- Catalog schema: Deprecate legacy capability_schema.v1 (kept as legacy_capabilities for migration) and introduce capability_schema.v2 that references compact headers + full capability document. Migration docs added.
- Billing: Introduce function_call_credit as a first-class optional numeric field on model profiles and endpoints. This allows the billing system to attribute cost for tool/function call ops independently; SDKs and console will display credits usage.
- Streaming: Add streaming_degradation_policy on model profiles to expose a list of ordered fallbacks and suggested partial-output tokens thresholds (helps clients decide when to switch to a summarized streaming path). Also include preferred_prefetch_hint to suggest prefix caching window.
- OpenAI compat: Update the /v1/models listing returned by the OpenAI-compat shim to include capability_headers and structured_output_hints under the "capabilities" umbrella so downstream OpenAI-compatible clients can discover behavior without touching Redwood-specific endpoints.
- Docs & SDK: Docs page describing migration, examples for reading capability_headers and consuming streaming_degradation_policy; Python and TypeScript SDK surfaces to parse new fields.

Commits (summary):
- commit 1: api: extend model list + get handlers to populate capability_headers and streaming_degradation_policy (handlers and serializers)
- commit 2: catalog: add models_v2 schema, migration script to copy legacy_capabilities into full_profile and generate default headers
- commit 3: billing: record function_call_credit into usage events and expose in billing UI (console changes)
- commit 4: sdk/docs: parse helpers and docs for migration and examples

Files changed (representative):
- src/api/handlers/models_list.go (updated serializer and OpenAI-compat shim)
- src/catalog/schemas/models_v2.json (new compact schema)
- tools/migrations/migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go (migration script)
- services/billing/credits.go (add function_call_credit aggregation)
- console/src/components/model/ModelDetails.tsx (show capability headers and credits)
- sdk/python/redwood/models.py (new fields + helper parser)
- docs/migrations/capability_headers_migration.md (migration and rollback guide)

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests: added for serializer and parser behavior (capability_headers omitted vs present), billing aggregation tests for function_call_credit.
- Integration: end-to-end test in perf-canary that validates streaming_degradation_policy is honored by the router under simulated capacity pressure; canary shows no increase in 95p latency on main model variants.
- Backwards compatibility: /v1/models still returns legacy_capabilities field for consumers that haven't migrated; the OpenAI-compat shim prefers capability_headers but will fall back to legacy_capabilities when capability_headers is absent.

Migration strategy & rollout:
- Stage 1 (canary): populate capability_headers from existing full capabilities via migration script; run canary for 2 days to ensure no regression in routing or billing.
- Stage 2 (gradual): expose new headers to 20% of API responses; monitor routing decisions and SDK parsing errors.
- Stage 3 (opt-in enforcement): allow customers to opt-in to strict schema validation via a console toggle (default off).
- Final: Deprecate legacy schema via announcement; grace period until 2026-06-01, after which legacy_capabilities may be removed for new write operations.

- Lina Gomez: "Need to ensure function_call_credit can't be negative and that default is 0 where absent; also clarify how it interacts with token billing." — Author: "Validation added; billing pipeline will emit both tokens and function_call_credit events. description:
Motivation: Developers repeatedly hit vague runtime errors when streams failed (auth handshake, transient network) and had to implement ad-hoc parsing logic to decide whether to retry, resume, or surface an error. This PR introduces language-native typed error classes across the three SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Go) and a unified ergonomic iterable reconnect API for stream consumers.

What this change does: 
- Introduces TypedError/StreamError subclasses with machine-friendly error_code, retriable, and suggestion fields across SDKs.
- Adds a new StreamIterable API (python: StreamIterable, ts: createStreamIterable, go: StreamIterator) that yields typed result objects and automatically attempts a single reconnect on retriable failures by default with backoff tuning. Reconnect behavior is configurable by the caller.
- Deprecates low-level sync callback hooks (on_chunk/on_error) in favor of async iterables/promises/iterators to improve ergonomics and parity.
- Adds structured telemetry hooks (opt-in) so apps can key metrics by error_code without brittle string matching.
- Small refactors: move common auth-retry utility into internal/sdk-common, update changelogs and bump SDK package versions.

Backward compatibility and migration: 
- Old callback APIs are still present but marked deprecated; they will emit one deprecation log per process and are scheduled for removal in the next major. Migration notes are added to each SDK CHANGELOG.
- Typed error shapes are additive; existing code catching broad exceptions will continue to work but can opt-in to typed handling for clearer logic.

Testing and rollout: 
- Unit tests added for typed error construction, serialization, and iterable reconnect edge cases. Integration tests simulate transient auth failures with a test double of the runtime.
- Canary rollout to Dedicated region us-west-2 for 72 hours before full merge.

Checklist: 
- [x] Python implementation and tests
- [x] TypeScript implementation and tests
- [x] Go implementation and tests
- [x] Changelogs and version bumps
- [x] Docs snippet in quickstarts repo pointing to new API example

References: Linear ENG-1987, SUP-402 (customer-facing incident), internal design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1987/stream-reconnect-typed-errors (internal link).

Overview

This playbook bundles three tightly related areas that frequently cause onboarding friction for new integrations: SDK localization (i18n) readiness, docs-site operational procedures (staging/canary/translation pipelines), and a compact set of canonical fixes for the top support issues we see from developer onramps. The goal is a one-page operational reference that engineering, Docs, and Support can use during new SDK ship weeks and customer trials.

Goals
- Reduce mean-time-to-first-success (MTTFS) for new SDK adopters by 30% through localized examples and a repeatable docs deploy pipeline.
- Provide concise canonical fixes for the top 8 devx support issues so Support can resolve 60% of triageable tickets without engineering intervention.
- Maintain a low-friction docs release process (canary -> staged -> prod) with clear rollback semantics and telemetry hooks.

Audience
- Developer Experience engineers and tech writers shipping SDK examples and docs.
- Support engineers handling integration issues and reproductions.
- Product engineers owning SDKs or client libraries.

Scope and non-goals
- Included: JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, and Go SDK snippets; docs-site content lifecycle; translation handoff and CI checks; canonical fixes for common API/SDK errors.
- Excluded: full localization of legal or marketing copy; mobile SDKs beyond sample snippets.

Prerequisites
1) Repo layout: all SDK examples live under repo: redwood/devx-examples (branch: main).
2) Docs-site: hosted via docs.redwood-inference.internal, uses static site generator with i18n plugin (locales in /i18n/*.json).
3) CI: GitHub Actions with workflows: docs-canary.yml, docs-staged.yml, docs-prod.yml.
4) Telemetry: snippet telemetry.events.example_load, telemetry.tags.locale, and telemetry.context.sdk_version must be emitted by sample harness.

Quickstart: Localized SDK Example Bundle (developer flow)
1. Clone examples: git clone git@github.com:redwood/devx-examples.git && cd devx-examples
2. Install toolchain (node/pip/go): ./scripts/bootstrap-dev.sh
3. Generate locale-specific examples: ./scripts/generate-localized-examples --locales=en,es,fr --sdk=python
4. Run local docs server including translations: npm run docs:local -- --locale=fr
5. Verify telemetry events appear in staging stream (kinesis-devx-staging): 
   - Expected event: {"event":"example_load","locale":"fr","sdk":"python","version":"0.12.0"}
6. Submit PR to docs-examples with i18n diffs and request docs-site canary deploy via label: docs-canary-request

SDK Localization Checklist (per release)
- [ ] Confirm sample text keys are externalized (no hard-coded English strings in code examples).
- [ ] Provide translation-ready README and example captions in /i18n/{locale}.json.
- [ ] Localized code comments: keep English primary, add short localized caption lines under // LOCAL: ... to avoid syntax churn.
- [ ] Add locale-specific smoke tests: tests/smoke/{locale}/example_test.py (asserts example runs and emits telemetry).
- [ ] Bump telemetry schema version if adding fields: TELEMETRY_SCHEMA: v2 -> notify analytics@redwood.com.

Table: Supported Example Locales and Priority
Locale | Priority | Owner | Notes
------ | -------- | ----- | -----
en (English) | high | devx-eng | baseline; all CI gates run against en
es (Spanish) | medium | intl-ops | customer-facing regions: LATAM, EU-ES
fr (French) | medium | intl-ops | EU-FR customers
de (German) | low | intl-ops | add on request
ja (Japanese) | low | intl-ops | APAC pilot only

Docs-site Operating Procedure (canary -> staged -> prod)
1) Authoring and PRs
   - Create content branch in docs-content repo and include locale JSONs under /i18n.
   - Attach smoke test run output to PR (artifact: smoke-{sha}.zip).
   - Tag PR with labels: [docs-canary-request] or [docs-staged-request] as appropriate.
2) Canary deploy (automatic with label docs-canary-request)
   - Action: GitHub Action docs-canary.yml runs build and deploys to docs-canary.redwood-inference.internal.
   - Checks (must pass): build (exit 0), i18n-linter (no missing keys), smoke-tests (artifacts present), telemetry sanity (at least one example_load event during smoke test).
   - Rollback: manual; revert PR or trigger docs-canary-rollback workflow.
3) Staged deploy (after 48h of Canary uptime and signoff)
   - Add label docs-staged-request. Ops lead runs gated promote: ./tools/promote_docs.sh --from=canary --to=staged --approve="<approver>"
   - Staged URL: docs-staged.redwood-inference.internal. Run translation QA with translator team.
4) Prod promote
   - Window: M-F 9:00-17:00 PT. Approvals: 2 reviewers (author + docs eng). Run promote script with --to=prod and monitor SLOs for 30min.

Operational SLOs for Docs-site during promote windows
- Build success rate >= 99% (30-day rolling).
- Canary smoke-tests pass within 15 minutes after deploy.
- No production downtime > 1 minute caused by new docs push.

Canonical Support Issues and Fixes (top issues during onramp)
Issue A: SDK example fails to authenticate (401)
- Detection: error pattern in logs: "error=unauthorized, code=401, hint=apiKey"; Support: run reproduction script with -v flag.
- Root cause: sample uses environment variable REDWOOD_API_KEY unset or using expired demo key.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Confirm env var exists: echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY
  2. If missing, instruct customer to create API key via console (link: internal:product-docs/create-api-key).
  3. For expired keys, rotate and confirm permission scopes: scopes must include: [inference:invoke, metrics:read].
  4. Add small code snippet to sample that fails fast with helpful error message (example below).
- Owner: Support -> escalate to SDK owner if repro fails.

Code snippet: fail-fast auth check (Python)
```python
import os
api_key = os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')
if not api_key:
    raise RuntimeError('Missing REDWOOD_API_KEY environment variable. Create one at https://console.redwood-inference.internal/settings/api-keys')
# proceed with client
```

Issue B: Streaming responses stall mid-stream
- Detection: client receives first tokens then stalls; metrics show open connection but no bytes.
- Root cause: client-level keepalive mismatch or proxy buffering (common with corporate proxies).
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Ask customer to test with curl -N to confirm raw stream: 
     curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -N \"https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/stream?...\"
  2. If curl works, recommend SDK change: prefer chunked transfer decoding and set socket keepalive: true.
  3. Provide fallback example using poll-based generation with polling timeout 5s.
- Owner: SDK eng + DevX docs for the streaming troubleshooting page.

Issue C: Localized examples missing strings or have placeholders ("__MISSING__")
- Detection: i18n-linter failure in CI; smoke test asserts replaceable keys remain.
- Root cause: upstream translations not merged to branch or translation key mismatch after refactor.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Run i18n-linter locally: npm run i18n-lint -- --locale=es
  2. Check missing keys report: ./tools/i18n-report --sha <pr-sha>
  3. If keys changed upstream, rebase PR and run ./scripts/merge-i18n.sh
  4. If translation missing, create placeholder and flag translator for fast-turn merge.
- Owner: Docs + Intl-ops.

Issue D: SDK telemetry not appearing in staging (no example_load events)
- Detection: telemetry dashboard shows zero events for smoke-run timeframe.
- Root cause: SDK example uses wrong telemetry endpoint, or telemetry schema mismatch.
- Canonical fix steps:
  1. Confirm telemetry endpoint env var: TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT points to staging ingestion.
  2. Run smoke tests locally with verbose flag and inspect emitted payloads: ./scripts/run-smoke --verbose | jq .
  3. If schema mismatch, check TELEMETRY_SCHEMA in repo and bump analytics contract.
- Owner: DevX instrumentation owner.

Emergency rollback recipe (docs-site)
- Trigger: Canary or staged build causes widespread example breakage or production regressions.
- Steps:
  1. Revert offending PR or tag immediately. Use GitHub UI or: git revert --no-edit <merge-commit> && push.
  2. Run docs-canary-rollback action: ./tools/docs_rollback --env=canary --commit=<last-good-commit>
  3. Notify #devx and #sre-channels with incident summary template (include commit, author, time).
  4. Run postmortem within 72 hours if > 15 developer-impacting incidents occurred.

Telemetry and Monitoring (what to watch)
- Telemetry events: example_load, example_error, docs_build_status
- Dashboards: DevX -> Examples Overview, Docs -> Build Health, Support -> Top SDK Errors
- Alerts: Build failure rate > 5% in 1h (PagerDuty to Docs oncall), Missing telemetry events for a deployed smoke run (Slack alert to #devx-monitor).

Owner matrix and contact points
- DevX Docs (authoring + i18n): Marisol Vega (owner)
- Intl-ops (translation & QA): Sana Ribeiro
- SDK engineering (runtime fixes): Evan Park
- Support triage lead: Luis Moreno

Appendix: Example file layout (minimal)
- /devx-examples/
  - /python/
    - example_quickstart.py
    - README.md
    - /i18n/en.json
    - /i18n/es.json
  - /js/
    - example_quickstart.js
    - /i18n/en.json

Contact and escalation
- For blocked promotes contact: #devx-ops on Slack and add pager: docs-oncall@redwood-inference.internal
- For telemetry contract questions: analytics@redwood-inference.internal

Revision history
- 2025-09-12: Initial draft by Marisol Vega
- 2025-11-03: Added streaming troubleshooting and telemetry checks (review: Evan Park)
- 2026-02-20: Finalized canary/staged procedure and rollback script path updates

Related artifacts and snippets
- Scripts referenced live in repo: https://github.com/redwood/devx-examples/tree/main/scripts
- Translation handoff template: /templates/translation-handoff.md

End of playbook

Context:
This is a personal scratch for an 'Edge Runner Adapter' that sits on customer/partner edge nodes (VMs or k8s DaemonSet) and mediates between the local inference runtime and Redwood control plane. Goal is a minimal, resilient handshake + lightweight config model that supports KV caching, local batching hints, safe fallbacks to hosted models, and compact telemetry.

Design goals:
- Small binary/API surface — easy to audit for airgapped installs.
- Declarative config (YAML) that control-plane can push; local overrides allowed.
- Explicit lifecycle states to reason about rollouts, drain, and emergency fallback.
- Telemetry with PII-safe sampling + local aggregation.
- Pluggable auth (edge API key, mTLS, short-lived signed tokens).

High-level flow (quick):
1) Runner boots, loads local config; probes hardware, runtime (nvml info, available CUDA, quant libs).
2) Attempt control-plane registration: /v1/edge/register (POST). If offline, keep exponential backoff and write persistent pending queue.
3) Control plane returns assigned tenant(s), model policy, batching hints, kv_cache_policy.
4) Runner starts serving local requests via local unix socket or http. It also opens heartbeat: /v1/edge/heartbeat (PATCH) every 30s (interval configurable).
5) On capacity pressure or model mismatch, Runner consults local fallback policy and may redirect inbound requests to hosted endpoint, or stream partial tokens then fallback.

API sketch (plaintext examples):
- Registration request (HTTP POST /v1/edge/register):
{
  "instance_id": "edge-az1-88f7",
  "host_info": {"cpu_count": 16, "gpus": ["A100:80GB"]},
  "capabilities": ["kv_cache", "quant-int8", "streaming"],
  "config_hash": "sha256:..."
}

- Registration response:
{
  "status": "accepted",
  "tenant_id": "t-acme-corp",
  "policy": {
    "models_allowed": ["redwood-opt-13b-quant"],
    "fallback": {"type": "hosted", "endpoint": "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/hosted/proxy"},
    "kv_cache_policy": "per-tenant",
    "batching": {"target_ms": 8, "max_tokens": 512}
  }
}

- Heartbeat (PATCH /v1/edge/heartbeat) payload summary:
{
  "instance_id": "edge-az1-88f7",
  "uptime_sec": 234123,
  "cpu_pct": 12.3,
  "gpu_mem_free_mb": 64000,
  "active_sessions": 12
}

Config sketch (YAML style — runner reads local + merge from control plane):
---
runner:
  instance_id: "auto" # uuid if not provided
  listen: "/run/edge-runner.sock"
  auth:
    method: "mtls" # options: mtls | api_key | signed_token
  telemetry:
    sample_rate: 0.01
    aggregate_window_sec: 60
  fallback:
    allow_hosted_fallback: true
    hosted_endpoint: "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/hosted/proxy"
  kv_cache:
    mode: "per-tenant" # per-tenant | shared | disabled
    max_size_mb: 2048
  batching:
    target_ms: 5
    max_batch_tokens: 1024
    prewarm: true

Lifecycle states (local finite-state machine):
- INIT: boot, verify dependencies.
- REGISTERING: attempting control-plane join.
- ACTIVE: serving local traffic.
- DRAINING: stop accepting new sessions, finish existing ones.
- DEGRADED: critical resources missing; still serving limited ops or redirected to hosted.
- RETIRED: shutdown by operator.

Transitions: INIT -> REGISTERING -> ACTIVE. From ACTIVE -> DRAINING (operator or rollout). DRAINING -> RETIRED. Any state -> DEGRADED on resource failure; DEGRADED -> ACTIVE after heal.

Local API for host apps (unix socket or loopback api):
- POST /v1/local/dispatch : body {session_id, prompt, model_hint, prefer_local: bool} -> returns stream url or immediate error.
- GET /v1/local/session/:id/status -> session resource state and node affinity (useful for reconnect).
- POST /v1/local/kv/claim -> reserve a kv cache prefix for session (returns lease token + ttl).

Telemetry events (compact examples):
- event_type: request_complete | request_started | fallback_triggered | cache_miss
- payload fields: ts, instance_id, tenant_id, model, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, reason (for fallback)
Notes: always hash any user-identifying id before sending. Keep default sample_rate low (0.01). Aggregate counts locally per-window to reduce cardinality.

KV cache lease model (notes):
- Claim API issues short leases (30s-5min) for session-specific prefix. Runner enforces eviction LRU per-tenant. Control plane can push larger persistence policies for durable caches.
- Lease token is signed by control-plane; runner validates signature locally. This keeps runner stateless about global ownership.

Edge cases and fragility:
- Network partition during rolling update: new runner may register duplicate instance_id — require idempotent registration by full instance fingerprint (machine-id + cert serial).
- Disk pressure: if /var/cache fills, evict kv cache, mark DEGRADED and send urgent heartbeat.
- Model binary mismatch: control-plane policy should include allowed hashes; runner refuses to load models not in whitelist.

Security note:
- Prefer mTLS between runner and control-plane for on-prem. For airgapped installs, allow signed manifests delivered out-of-band (USB) and then runner applies manifest in offline mode. Need small code path to validate signatures and reject malformed manifests.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should policies be merged per-tenant or per-instance? (Prefer per-tenant but allow instance overrides).
- How to surface expensive GPU temp spikes to control-plane without leaking machine identifiers? Anonymized bucketing?
- Local SDK: expose a tiny Go client that uses unix socket; should we support direct Python gRPC? (Go first, then shim).
- Canary rollout: config_push should support label selectors (k8s nodes, instance metadata) and simultaneous canary signals from metrics.
- Rate-limiting enforcement split: local enforcement + control-plane quotas. Need reconciler to avoid double-throttling.

Next tiny steps (me):
- Create minimal HTTP server prototype (Go) that implements register, heartbeat, local dispatch, and fake kv claim.
- Add simple local YAML merge logic and snapshot on disk with hash.
- Wire up heartbeat to simulate DEGRADED->ACTIVE transition in e2e.
- Draft a short ADR for tenancy model (per-tenant vs per-instance cache).

Notes-to-self: keep message sizes tiny, avoid sending prompts in telemetry, when in doubt log locally and only surface aggregate numbers. If we need to rework fallback behaviour later, keep decisions pluggable (policy module).

End of scratch.

model_prompt:
Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0160
Question: What change reduced GPU memory use and improved first-token latency by prepacking INT8 weights and fusing smoothquant dequantization into the GEMM kernel without creating intermediate tensors?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_c84c8581594e47d49e82d024a6da915d:
description:
Motivation: INT8 inference for large decoder models showed suboptimal memory layout overhead and extra dequant steps when combined with smoothquant-style per-channel scaling. This PR introduces a weight prepack path and a small kernel-lane allocator that lets the runtime fuse smoothquant dequantization into the kernel dispatch without materializing intermediate dequant tensors. Goals: 1) lower wall-clock latency for first-token and steady-state by removing memory-bound dequant copies, 2) reduce peak GPU memory for multi-tenant workloads by prepacking int8 weights in a compact layout and sharing lane metadata across batches, 3) keep compatibility with existing KV cache and continuous-batching pipelines. What changed (high-level): - New weight prepack module (src/runtime/kernel/int8_weight_prepack.cc/h) that produces a packed INT8 layout with per-channel scale/zero-point metadata optimized for our vectorized GEMM kernels. - Kernel adapter hooks (src/runtime/kernel/kernel_adapter.cc) to accept packed weights and apply smoothquant per-channel scaling on-the-fly inside the GEMM launcher when the model has smoothquant metadata. - Kernel lane allocator (src/runtime/scheduler/lane_allocator.cc/h) that assigns model weight lanes to worker threads/GPU streams so packed weights can be reused across microbatches without copying. - KV cache coordinator updates (src/runtime/scheduler/kv_cache_coordinator.cc) to pin KV cache blocks to the same lane affinity when the request uses pinned weights, avoiding cross-lane synchronization. - A shortfall fallback: when model uses dynamic shape patterns incompatible with lane reuse, runtime falls back to previous dequant-copy path automatically. Performance: microbenchmarks on a 32B decoder model (batch sizes 1..8, seq len 1..1024) show median token latency improvement of 9-16% at steady state and 18-28% for first-token latency on Ampere A100, with peak memory reduction of ~12% at high concurrency. Compatibility/risks: The change touches low-level kernel dispatch. We limited the surface by gating packed-weight paths behind a model feature flag and added runtime checks for per-channel metadata version. Rolling plan: staged canary rollout on Dedicated pools with a 2-hour canary window, monitor latency, token error-rate regressions, and memory counters. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for weight prepack and kernel adapter - [x] Integration test exercising smoothquant models through hosted API - [x] Performance bench scripts added - [x] Migration doc and feature flag gating - [x] Observability: added counters for lane cache hits/misses, packed-weight size. Related: ENG-3421 (quant kernel latency), ENG-3498 (kv cache affinity).

review_comments:
Marcus Li: Overall this looks solid; can you add a short docstring describing the layout produced by the prepack method? I had to trace through the code to confirm alignment guarantees.
Anika Rao: Added header docstrings and a diagram in prepack_smoothquant_notes.md per Marcus' request.
Diego Torres: The lane allocator is clever. Concern: potential starvation if many small requests contend for lanes. Suggest adding a fairness counter or aging policy.
Anika Rao: Added simple LRU aging policy and a unit test to simulate heavy small-request contention; PTAL.
Priya Nair (SRE): We need an observability signal for fallback-to-copy rate; ops will want to alert if it spikes after rollout.
Anika Rao: Added metrics runtime.quant.packed_weight_fallback_count and added to Console dashboards as part of the rollout task.
Marcus Li: CI failure on clang-format fixed in latest commit; approving pending perf numbers in canary.
Diego Torres: Verified no regression on tokenization edge-case tests; merging after canary.

Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0161
Question: In the OpenAI compatibility adapter update for Redwood deployments, what priority order does the normalizer use to resolve conflicting tool selection hints?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_2fb08b7571444bdf894607549642498f:
description:
Motivation: Several customers and internal evals showed inconsistent behavior when the OpenAI-compat layer returned tool selection signals (e.g. 'tool_choice' with ambiguous metadata) across streaming and non-streaming modes. This caused duplicate tool invocations, incorrect schema inference, and brittle downstream tool routers in Redwood Dedicated/Private deployments.

This PR introduces a deterministic normalization step for the OpenAI invocation envelope, plus stream-resilient framing for tool/message fragments. The goal is to: 1) make the compatibility layer emit a single canonical selection signal for every invocation, 2) map OpenAI tool schemas into a stable internal schema with minimal changes for existing customers, and 3) make streaming fragments idempotent and re-assemblable at the service edge.

What changed (high level):
- New package: pkg/openai/normalize_invocation.go — normalizer that transforms incoming OpenAI-style responses into Redwood's canonical InvocationEnvelope. It collapses multiple tool signals into one selected_tool hint and preserves tool confidence/metadata in a stable metadata map.
- Tool schema mapper: pkg/tooling/tool_schema_mapper.go — conservative mapping rules for OpenAI 'parameters' -> Redwood typed schema, including type coercion rules and a small whitelist for nested objects.
- Streaming: server/streaming/frame_parser.go updated to add fragment IDs and checksum headers for tool/message fragments. Parser now supports out-of-order fragments and dedup by fragment id+checksum.
- API layer: server/api/openai_adapter.go updated to call the normalizer before routing to tool routing pipeline; updates to response shape sent back to clients to maintain OpenAI wire-compatibility while ensuring a single 'selected_tool' semantic in the internal router.
- Docs: docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md with migration notes and examples.

Compatibility notes:
- Outbound API responses remain OpenAI-compatible: we do not change the visible OpenAI fields returned to customers. Internally, however, the runtime will prefer the normalized 'selected_tool' hint to decide which tool to invoke. In the rare case of conflicting tool signals, the normalizer uses (in order): explicit_invocation field, highest-confidence tool_choice, then deterministic fallback to first available tool that matches schema.
- Customers who implemented custom tool routers based on raw tool_choice fragments should migrate to using the new normalized hint or consult the docs which show a 1-line change to switch to the normalized envelope.

Testing and rollout plan:
- Unit tests for mapping rules and type coercions included.
- Integration tests: simulated streaming sessions with fragmented tool metadata; verified idempotent assembler under network reorders.
- Canary rollout: staged to 10% of traffic for hosted API for 48 hours, then to Dedicated nodes behind a feature flag. Private installer includes an opt-in toggle for the first release cycle.

Migration steps for operators (short):
1) Review docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for the mapping table.
2) If you have custom routers, update to read the normalized 'selected_tool' header from the invocation payload.
3) Toggle feature flag if running Redwood Private/Dedicated during rollout.

Related work: links to internal Linear tasks ENG-7421 (tool-selection ambiguity), ENG-7553 (stream-fragment dedup).

Rationale for not changing public wire format: minimize breaking client changes while fixing internal flakiness in tool invocation semantics.

Release notes summary: Normalizes OpenAI invocation envelopes to ensure a single canonical tool-selection signal, improves streaming fragment resilience, and provides safe mapping rules for tool parameter schemas. Operators with custom routing should follow the migration guide in docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md.

Asha Menon (author): Added a 'coercion_mode' config to tool_schema_mapper with 'permissive' and 'strict' options and documented it in the migration guide. Also added unit tests covering both modes.
Maya Singh (comment): CI initially failed on a flaky streaming test — I saw we added a small sleep in the assembler. Can we avoid sleeps and use deterministic signaling?

No public wire-format breaking changes. Operators with custom routers should read docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for migration steps.

model_prompt:
Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0162
Question: What caused the brief period where a few tenants were not being throttled correctly after a shard reassignment happened at the same time as a runtime policy reload?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93:
description:
Intermittent cases where per-key priority overrides combined with per-org and per-route policies result in transient under-enforcement (requests allowed when they should be throttled). Observed as short windows of elevated usage for a small set of tenants after shard reassignment and policy hot-reload. This ticket captures investigation, repro, short-term mitigation, and a long-term fix plan.

impact:
Transient over-allow for small number of tenants leading to underbilling and potential customer perception issues; visible as short-lived bursts up to ~2x expected throughput for affected keys. Affects hosted and dedicated clusters during rolling updates or instance restarts.

reproduction_steps:
1) Create two tenants T1 and T2 sharing a shard (sticky-shard assignment enabled).
2) Configure per-org policy: default priority = low, per-route quota = 1000/min.
3) Configure per-key override for a service key K1 belonging to T1: priority = high, burst credits = +200.
4) Start a steady stream of requests from T1 at near-quota rate; verify enforcement hitting quota windows.
5) Trigger a shard reassignment for one edge node (simulate instance bounce or maintenance) while simultaneously applying a policy hot-reload that changes route fallback behavior.
6) Observe a ~10-30s window where requests for K1 are allowed beyond quota; metrics show credits attributed to the wrong in-memory bucket and enforcement checks returning allow from fast-path cache.
7) Collect tracer spans and edge logs for the window; reproduce locally using the shard-reassignment harness and time-accelerated policy reloads.

logs_snapshot:
edge: allow decision fastpath: key=K1 shard=sh-23 cache_hit=true priority=high quota_window_id=2026-03-12T10:04:00Z
shard-reassign: lease=renewal failover->sh-27 old_owner=sh-23 new_owner=sh-27
policy-hot-reload: version=v2026-03-12-1 route-fallback=enabled
meter-commit: credits_applied target_bucket=org:T2:key:Kx unexpected=true amount=200

hypothesis:
A race between sticky-shard mapping update and policy hot-reload causes fast-path cache entries (priority and credit pointers) to be re-keyed incorrectly. Per-key overrides store a pointer to a tenant-scoped credit bucket; during reassignment we are dereferencing a stale pointer and applying credits to the wrong tenant's bucket. Enforcement uses the fast-path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur.

experiment_results:
Replayed the sequence in staging using the shard-reassign harness. With no policy reload the issue did not occur. When timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over-allow consistently. Enabling stronger pointer validation (temporary patch) eliminated the over-allows in the harness.

root_cause:
Sticky-shard pointer (in-memory bucket reference) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast-path credit application. Policy hot-reload mutates the route/priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant's bucket. Enforcement fast-path accepts the cache without full tenant-level validation.

mitigations:
Short-term patch deployed to staging: on fast-path cache hit, perform tenant-id validation on the cached credit pointer before applying credits. Also increased grace period on shard handoff to reduce overlap. Rolled patch to canary edge fleet.

rollout_plan:
1) Canary for 2 hours on low-traffic region with added telemetry (done). 2) Gradual ramp to 30% of traffic with continued trace sampling for next 24 hours. 3) Full rollout after 48 hours if no regressions. 4) Follow with a database reconciliation backfill job to detect credits misapplied in last 7 days and create accounting fixes if needed.

long_term_fix:
Refactor in-memory credit pointer representation to be immutable and namespaced by tenant+shard+route. Replace pointer dereference fast-path with a lightweight validation token check (versioned binder). Add unit and property tests for concurrent shard handoff + policy reload scenarios.

regression_test_plan:
Add deterministic concurrency tests to runtime-policy-simulator: combinations of shard reassignment, policy hot-reload, per-key overrides, and burst credit application. Add e2e test in CI harness that exercises rolling updates with randomized interleavings. Add a smoke check after canary verifying no over-allow traces in last 10 minutes.

notes:

Purpose: quick, reusable working template to take a candidate through offer acceptance to contribution in 30/60/90 days. Combine a compact hiring plan, a measurable interview rubric, and a pragmatic onboarding checklist that managers and POs can copy-edit for specific roles.

Status and intent: working draft for FY26 hiring sprints (early trials with infra and platform-engineering hiring waves). This is intentionally opinionated about signals we care about (ramp speed, cross-team communication, test-driven ownership). Use as a baseline; annotate with role-specific tasks and replace TODOs.

Quick orientation (one-liner): HyperOnboard is a "launch packet"—a short, shareable checklist + rubric to align hiring, the hiring manager, mentor/buddy, and recruiting operations on acceptance -> day 90 outcomes.

Scope: ICs (IC2–IC5) across engineering, product, and SRE. Not a replacement for full People Ops handbook; intended to accelerate first-90 days and instrument early quality signals for hiring calibration.

Hiring plan snapshot (for manager + recruiter):
- Hiring signal: 2–3 concrete deliverables expected in first 90 days (choose 1 fast win in month 1, 1 impact work in month 2, 1 cross-team deliverable by month 3).
- Timeline: Week 0: offer & logistics; Week 1: shadow + infra access; Week 2–4: small shipable task; Month 2: feature/infra milestone; Month 3: cross-team rollout + owner handoff.
- Interview loop (baseline for eng roles): Recruit screen (30m) -> Hiring manager (45m) -> Two technical rounds (60m each: system design + code pairing) -> Collaboration/communication round (30–45m) -> Exec/skip-level if IC4+ (30m). Total on-site loop time 3.5–4.5 hours.
- Comms: recruiting to post-offer email should include role launch snapshot (this doc), buddy assignment, first-week calendar skeleton, and links to requisite access checklists.

Offer packet checklist (ops items to complete before start):
- Signed offer + I-9 (if applicable)
- Manager assigned, buddy assigned, and initial 1:1 scheduled for day 1
- Infra access requests issued (jira access + repo perms + cloud console)
- Workstation shipped or on-site booking confirmed
- Security & compliance onboarding assigned (if private deployment/regulatory customer)
- Prestart reading pack shared (team RFCs, relevant incidents, current PRs)

Interview rubric (single-page, numerical scale 1–5, with anchor examples). Use for calibration and debrief notes. Keep score fields in ATS but capture qualitative: examples, gaps, and evidence.
- Areas and anchors:
  - Technical correctness (1–5): Can the candidate implement correct, maintainable code during pairing and explain tradeoffs? Anchors: 5 = correct and robust solution with edge cases and tests; 3 = correct but brittle or missing edge cases; 1 = incorrect or major misconceptions.
  - System design (1–5): Ability to decompose requirements, propose measurable SLAs, identify bottlenecks, and consider operational costs. Anchors: 5 = clear architecture + failure modes + rollout plan; 2 = vague tradeoffs, misses core ops concerns.
  - Product sense & impact orientation (1–5): Prioritization, outcome-thinking, ability to tie technical choices to user/business impact. Anchors: 5 = identifies measurable metrics and tradeoffs; 1 = overly academic solutions with no product tie.
  - Collaboration & communication (1–5): Clarity of explanations, receptive to feedback, cross-functional mindset. Anchors: 5 = proactive clarifying, invites feedback; 2 = closed off or unclear.
  - Ownership & learning velocity (1–5): Evidence of shipping end-to-end, learning new domains quickly. Anchors: 5 = repeated examples of shipping and improving systems; 1 = no evidence of ownership.
  - Cultural/values fit (1–5): Evidence of glue work, candidate’s ability to operate in high-performance, ambiguous environments. Anchors: 5 = pragmatic, bias for action, clear examples; 1 = passive.
- Interview debrief template (copy into ATS notes): "Top strengths (2–3): ...
  Top risks (2–3): ...
  Required onboarding supports if hired: ...
  Recommended 30/60/90 milestones: ..."

Onboarding checklist (practical, manager-first):
- Pre-day-1 (recruiting + manager): welcome doc + first-week calendar sent; Slack invite; send buddy intro email; create required infra tickets; create first-ticket for fast-win task (estimate <3 days).
- Day 1: 1:1 with manager (30–60m) covering role context + 30/60/90 goals; team lunch (virtual/in-person); buddy walkthrough of repos and dev flow; confirm access to ticketing and CI.
- Day 2–5: environment setup validation (local dev, tests pass), complete required security trainings, pair on the fast-win task with buddy, first-week retrospective on Friday (30m).
- Week 2–4: ship fast-win (owner signs off), start second deliverable (mentor-guided), scheduled sync with adjacent team leads.
- Month 1 manager check (end of month): evidence review of fast-win, signal check on documentation contributions, feedback conversation and adjustments to 30/60/90.
- Month 2: take ownership of a mid-scale deliverable, lead a small design doc, participate in oncall rotation shadow if applicable.
- Month 3: lead cross-team rollout or ship major milestone; provide retrospective + proposal for ongoing ownership.

Manager checklist and risk mitigations:
- Before start: confirm buddy and first-ticket exist.
- Weekly 1:1 agenda template: 5m personal check-in, 10m blockers, 20m skill-building or project planning, 10m feedback loop.
- Escalation triggers (email to p-ops + hiring manager): not shipping a measurable artifact by day 30, ongoing access blockers >48h, repeated missing meetings.

Buddy playbook (short):
- First 2 weeks: pair 3x for 90–120m on dev flow and codebase.
- Provide curated list of 6–8 reading items (design docs, incidents, coding standards).
- Shadowing: 2 oncall tickets, 1 deploy cycle.

Evaluation signals (early):
- Technical: able to run test suite locally and fix one failing test in week 1.
- Product: articulates impact metric for a fast-win by end of week 1.
- Collaboration: schedules and leads at least one cross-team sync by week 4.
- Ownership: closes owner-assigned ticket with PR and reviewer responses in <2 weeks.

Template: 30/60/90 milestones (copyable):
- 30 days (learn & ship): complete environment, ship small bug/feature, present learnings to team.
- 60 days (own & expand): own a component or endpoint, reduce latency/bug rate or deliver feature scope, mentor newcomer pairing.
- 90 days (integrate & lead): lead a cross-team launch or own SLA for a subservice, propose roadmap items.

Recruiting playbook notes (ops & interviewer hints):
- Recruiter checklist: send role launch snapshot with offer email; collect candidate prestart constraints (visa, hardware needs); confirm buddy availability.
- Interviewers: focus on concrete examples. Ask for "past 2–3 months shipped work" and one code example. Rate on evidence, not potential.
- Calibration: every hiring round should include at least one calibrated interviewer (eng lead who has completed calibration exercise in last 6 months).

Open questions / TODOs (working):
- Define explicit ramp metrics per org (platform vs. product eng) — who owns this? action: Priya to draft baseline by 2026-02-12.
- Should we require a documented 90-day plan in the offer packet for IC4+? pros/cons noted (clarity vs. inflexibility).
- Add a short checklist for Private deployments hires (HSM/KMS onboarding).

Sample email snippets (copyable):
- Pre-start welcome: "Congrats and welcome — attached is a short launch snapshot with your first-week calendar, your assigned buddy (NAME), and a link to our quick-start repo. Please complete the short security training before day 3."
- Manager day-1 note: "Hi NAME — excited to have you. Today we'll cover role context and your first-week goals. Please bring questions about accounts/access. Expect a walking tour of current work and an intro to the fast-win ticket."

Notes-to-self / working artifacts:
- Keep this doc <2 pages for offer attachments. Expanded examples belong in Role Launch Library (linked_artifacts).
- Run a pilot with 6 hires in Q1 2026 and collect manager/buddy NPS at day 30 and day 90.

Version history: 0.1 draft — initial template compiled from hiring interviews, manager feedback, and recent onboarding retros (nov 2025–feb 2026).

Appendix (quick checklist for recruiter to paste into ATS notes):
- OfferStatus: signed/unsigned
- BuddyAssigned: yes/no
- FirstTicketCreated: ticket-id
- WorkstationShipped: yes/no
- SecurityTrainingAssigned: yes/no

End of HyperOnboard template. Copy, edit, and iterate.

Motivation: The monolithic bash pipelines under .github/workflows and scripts/legacy-ci.sh have become brittle and hard to iterate on across services. This PR modernizes the pipeline by introducing reusable GitHub composite actions, a plugin hook system for per-repo policy, and a small cross-platform ci-toolbox binary to compute robust cache keys and talk to the remote cache store. Scope: 1) Add .github/actions/checkout-composite, test-shard-composite, lint-runner-composite. 2) Replace repo-level shell orchestration with composite action calls and a dynamic matrix generator (tools/ci/matrix-gen.js). 3) Remove scripts/legacy-ci.sh and in-repo Docker-in-Docker usage; use buildah/kind where needed. 4) Add ci-toolbox (tools/ci-toolbox/main.go) used by composite actions for cache keying and fast retries. 5) Add .github/ci-config.yml with opt-in staged rollout flags for teams to adopt incrementally. Owners can enable ci-config.yml flags to opt into new flows. Rollback is as simple as switching the workflow reference back to legacy scripts if an issue is detected. Risks and mitigations: Cache-key changes may cause cache misses on first runs; ci-toolbox includes a dry-run mode to preview keys. Matrix reshaping can increase pipeline concurrency; we added a default concurrency limit and a dynamic shard sizing heuristic. description:
Context: Teams repeatedly ask for sensible defaults for batching, cache TTLs and quantization when onboarding models to Redwood. Currently defaults live in multiple places and require manual tuning with evals and internal heuristics. Goal: ship a small, auditable suggestion system that observes recent workload signals and proposes conservative default profiles for batching.window_ms, batch_size caps, prefix/KV cache TTLs, and quantization presets. The suggester is opt-in by default and produces human-readable suggestions surfaced in the Console and via a new API endpoint.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight offline heuristic engine (defaults-suggester) that consumes short-term aggregated telemetry (per-route QPS, median latency, 50/95/99 latency quantiles, token length distribution) and maps to a ranked set of suggested profiles. 2) Introduces a new API: POST /optimize/v1/suggestions which returns JSON suggestions with confidence scores and an explanation string. 3) Wire up Console: a Suggestions panel on per-route settings with an Apply & Preview flow that shows estimated unit-cost delta and latency impact. 4) Add a gated runtime flag so the runtime can accept a profile payload for immediate application (useful for Dedicated/Private workflows). 5) Provide a small set of canonical profiles (conservative, balanced, aggressive) for batching and quantization, plus TTL presets for prefix/KV caches. 6) Add end-to-end test coverage and benchmark harness runs comparing before/after for representative traffic shapes.

Design notes and trade-offs: - The engine intentionally errs conservative: suggestions will never increase batch window beyond a route-level safety cap derived from SLA settings. - Quantization suggestions prefer per-model family presets (e.g., OPT/GPT-like) and include fallbacks; we do not auto-apply quantization in-host, suggestions only. - Telemetry ingestion is opt-in; customers can disable telemetry for suggestions in account settings. For Private installs the suggester can be run locally against their telemetry export. - Suggestions include an estimated unit-cost delta computed from our unit-econ model; we expose the formula in the Console and include the prompt/eval link so teams can validate quality impact.

Files touched: runtime/batching/suggester.go, optimize/suggester/service.go, api/handlers/suggestions.go, console/src/routes/RouteSuggestionsPanel.tsx, console/src/api/suggestionsClient.ts, docs/operations/defaults-suggester.md, config/profiles/default-profiles.yaml, tests/e2e/suggestions_flow.test.ts, bench/harness/suggester_traffic_shapes.yaml, telemetry/migrations/add_suggester_event.sql, scripts/ci/bench-suggester.sh

Testing: - Unit tests for mapping heuristics and profile ranking. - E2E test simulating three traffic shapes (short chat, assistant longform, embeddings micro-bursts). - Benchmarks: microbenchmark harness run on a c6g-xlarge-equivalent cluster with representative models showed median latency change within +3% for conservative profiles and unit-cost reduction up to 24% for balanced profiles on nuclear workloads. Results attached to the CI artifact and linked in the console patch notes.

Rollout plan: feature gated. Step 1: merge behind feature flag and enable suggestions only for internal org and canary customers. Step 2: collect feedback for 2 weeks. Step 3: enable Console UI for self-serve with telemetry opt-in prompt on first usage. Step 4: document caveats and add guided eval for teams that accept aggressive quantization suggestions.

Open questions / TODOs: - Add an explicit opt-out banner in Console per compliance request (tracked in ENG-7922). - Provide an exportable CSV of suggestion history for audit. - Consider a future ML-backed suggestion engine once we have more signal.

References: Linear items ENG-7842, ENG-7901. Internal benchmark dashboards: /dash/bench/suggester/33219.

Context Documents:
Document dsid_21486610d7314d84980518cb355b6a97:
description:
Issue summary:
During a staggered canary rollout for rw-instruct-7b-v3 in us-east-1, NimbleApps reported ~12% of their requests being served by an older model variant despite an explicit tenant-level model pin. The behavior lasted for ~45 minutes and coincided with an autoscaler prewarm burst triggered by a traffic spike.

Impact:
- Customer reported mixed outputs and downstream feature regressions for active users (measured anomalous quality score increase and user complaints).
- Approximately 11k requests affected for the customer across the incident window.

Environment:
- Production, us-east-1, Dedicated pool for NimbleApps (reserved capacity pool id: ded-342)

comments:
2025-11-02 Priya Singh (Support): Customer opened chat reporting that a portion of requests are returning legacy responses after we started the canary. They provided request IDs and timestamps. Asked to triage asap.
2025-11-02 Liam Chen (SRE): Acknowledged; collecting edge logs and routing snapshots. Initial hypothesis: pin commit race between orchestrator commit and edge cookie rotation during prewarm handoff.
2025-11-03 SRE-team (Liam Chen): Found routing mesh epochs where cohort snapshot contained mixed variant entries for tenant nimbleapps-17. Edge logs show affinity cookie TTL renewal at the same second as prewarm probe success; some flows lost pin before orchestrator snapshot completed.
2025-11-04 Support (Priya Singh) -> Customer: Confirmed we are rolling a targeted hotfix that changes prewarm handshake ordering to commit pins before edge cookie rotation. Asked customer for traffic window to cutover safely.
2025-11-05 NimbleApps (Customer): Verified behaviour has ceased after cutover; provided sampling confirming no legacy outputs in a 1h window post-fix. Thanked on call for quick turnaround.

investigation_notes:
What we observed:
- Autoscaler prewarm created N new prewarm nodes at t0+12s in response to surge.
- Prewarm handshake had a non-atomic ordering: node marked healthy -> edge cookie rotation -> orchestrator snapshot commit.
- In ~9% of sampled requests, edge rotated tenant affinity cookie just before orchestrator committed the new pin mapping, causing requests to land on edge shards that still resolved the tenant to the legacy variant.
- Orchestrator snapshots showed an overlapping epoch where two different routing tables were readable by different edge shards for ~18s.
- No GPU OOMs or serving runtime crashes found. Latency remained within SLO except for slight tail increase during the handoff window.

Hypotheses considered and eliminated:
- Tokenization mismatch in the model: rejected after verifying request payloads and embeddings.
- Customer-side pinned version misconfiguration: rejected; tenant manifest showed explicit pin to rw-instruct-7b-v3 prior to rollout.

Contributing factors:
- Prewarm handshake ordering (health -> rotate cookie -> commit) is non-atomic across control-plane and edge.
- Edge cookie rotation TTL is short and coincided with the commit window during a burst.
- Canary scheduling used staggered slice times (0s, +10s, +20s) which increased overlap surface for commit windows across shards.

resolution_notes:
Immediate mitigations applied:
1) Rolled a hotfix to orchestrator to change prewarm handshake ordering: commit pin mapping before issuing edge cookie rotation. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/3184. Deployed to us-east-1 dedicated pools at 2025-11-04T04:00Z.
2) Increased health-probe smoothing for prewarm nodes to reduce transient epoch changes during bursts.
3) Added a guard in edge-proxy to prefer orchestrator pin mapping when epoch differences detected within a 30s window.

Rollout notes:
- Hotfix applied via canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%) over a 3-hour window for dedicated pools; monitored cohort pins and customer telemetry.
- Post-deployment checks (logs + sampling from NimbleApps) showed 0% legacy-routed requests in the 1h stable window.

Follow-ups and action items:
- Engineering to add an orchestrator unit test that asserts prewarm handshake atomicity across control-plane and edge (owner: Liam Chen, target: 2025-11-12).
- Create a capacity-surge playbook to avoid staggered slice overlap during autoscaler prewarm (owner: Product, target: 2025-11-20).
- Postmortem scheduled and linked: https://confluence.redwood.ai/postmortems/SUP-209876-postmortem

Customer communication:
- Notified NimbleApps via support and scheduled an incident review call. Customer confirmed remediation and accepted workaround as final resolution.

Document dsid_04b24bf957c047f4b7d8ceefdfde8290:
Summary

This ADR defines a company-wide standard for declarative contract tests and a complementary "schema fencing" discipline to prevent schema drift between services and the Redwood platform (APIs, telemetry, and model-serving payloads). The goal is to make API and model I/O contracts machine-testable, versioned, and CI-gated, minimizing production surprises and simplifying rollback and compatibility reasoning.

Context and motivation

Recent incidents and near-misses were traced to silent schema changes that allowed malformed or unexpectedly shaped requests/telemetry to flow into the runtime. Ad-hoc unit tests are insufficient for cross-service contract guarantees because:

- Contracts span teams (edge proxies, gateways, runtime, and client SDKs).
- Behavioral compatibility is not captured by type checks alone (e.g., field deprecation with semantic changes).
- Runtime routing fallback and model-variant compatibility require an explicit, testable matrix.

This ADR proposes:

1. A declarative, YAML-first contract-test spec that lives next to service code and in a central conformance repo for cross-service scopes.
2. A "schema fencing" lifecycle that fences allowed shape changes via explicit change proposals, automated conformance checks, and CI gates.
3. A conformance status ledger and telemetry for contract drift and failed-matrix cell SLI.

Scope

Applies to:

- Public and internal HTTP/GRPC REST endpoints (edge, control-plane, telemetry ingestion).
- Model-serving input/output schemas (prompts, structured responses, embeddings metadata).
- Streaming/session protocols where message schemas are negotiated.

Out of scope:

- Internal-only helper functions that are never consumed by other services.
- Ad-hoc developer prototypes until they are promoted to a supported service.

Key concepts

Declarative contract test spec (DCTS):
- A human-friendly YAML format that describes request/response shapes, example inputs, success/failure predicates, and conformance categories (strict, tolerant, deprecated).
- DCTS entries can be unit-run (local), CI-run (service-level), and cross-service-run (integration conformance matrix).

Schema fencing:
- Every change to a DCTS schema field must be accompanied by a Change Proposal (CP) file and an automated compatibility check.
- CPs are accepted automatically if they pass compatibility rules or fail open for manual review if they are breaking.

Conformance matrix and ledger:
- A centrally aggregated matrix that tracks which service versions (and model variants) satisfy which DCTS cells.
- Each matrix cell has a pass/fail history and a conformance SLI aggregated daily.

Rules and compatibility classes

Fields are labeled with one of: required, optional, deprecated, extension. Compatibility rules:

- required -> optional: allowed but requires explicit CP and CI signal.
- optional -> required: breaking change; requires canary/rollout plan and staged opt-in.
- remove deprecated field: allowed only after 3 release cycles and >95% conformance across callers.
- add new field marked extension: always allowed if receivers ignore unknown fields (tolerant mode).

Change proposal workflow (brief)

1. Author creates a CP file in the service repo under docs/contracts/cps/<pr>.yaml describing intent, compatibility class, rollout plan, and rollback criteria.
2. CI runs: unit tests, DCTS local run, contract linters, and cross-service dry-run against the latest conformance snapshot.
3. If auto-check passes (non-breaking or safe extension), merge proceeds. If flagged as potentially breaking, the CP moves to manual review by contract stewards and product owners.
4. After merge, integration conformance jobs run nightly to validate callers and receivers.

Example DCTS snippet (YAML)

# Example: /v1/generate request/response
# Save as service/docs/contracts/dcts/generate.v1.yaml
---
endpoint: POST /v1/generate
scope: public
version: 1.0.0
mode: strict
request: 
  content-type: application/json
  schema: |
    type: object
    properties:
      prompt:
        type: string
      features:
        type: object
        additionalProperties: true
    required: [prompt]
examples:
  - name: simplest
    request: {"prompt": "Summarize the following text..."}
response:
  schema: |
    type: object
    properties:
      id: {type: string}
      output: {type: string}
      tokens_consumed: {type: integer}
    required: [id, output]
predicates:
  - description: output must be non-empty
    jq: ".output | length > 0"
conformance_category: strict

Automation and CI integration

CI responsibilities (service repo):
- Run local DCTS validation (schema validity, example conformance).
- Run contract linter: enforces required metadata fields (owner, risk_level, test_coverage_min).
- Publish DCTS artifact to conformance-bucket/<service>/<version>/dcts.yaml on successful merge.

Cross-repo conformance job (central):
- Nightly job that pulls the published DCTS artifacts and runs pairwise checks across known callers and receivers.
- Failing cells create RFC-style issues in the responsible service repo and update the conformance ledger with failure signals.

Conformance ledger and dashboard

The ledger is a time-series-friendly table with columns described below and exposed in the Redwood Console and an internal dashboard. Store as rows in our metrics DB and index in the conformance service. (Table described in prose below.)

Required columns (ledger row): timestamp, service_a, service_a_version, service_b, service_b_version, endpoint, dcts_version, test_case_id, result (pass|fail), failure_reason, run_id.

Operational SLOs and alerting

- Nightly conformance pass rate for critical public endpoints >= 99.0%. Alert if < 98.0% over a 24-hour rolling window.
- Any new CP that causes a regression in an existing passing matrix cell triggers a P1 review if the affected client is production and >= 10% traffic.

Gating and release policy

- Service merge gating: Non-breaking CPs are mergeable. Breaking CPs require manual approval and a staged rollout with canary conformance verifying client behavior.
- Platform releases (runtime, SDKs): must maintain 100% conformance for official SDK bindings across supported minor versions.

Rollout and rollback playbook (high level)

1. Pre-merge: author runs smoke DCTS locally and creates CP with rollout notes.
2. Merge: DCTS published and cross-repo nightlies scheduled.
3. Canary: route 5% traffic to new service variant for 2 hours while conformance checks run.
4. Monitor: observe ledger and user-facing errors for regressions.
5. If failure SLI breached or critical callers fail, execute rollback to previous version and open an incident review.

Telemetry and observability requirements

Each contract-test run must emit:
- conftest.run_id (UUID)
- conftest.service (service name/version)
- conftest.endpoint
- conftest.test_case_id
- conftest.result (pass|fail)
- conftest.duration_ms

These fields are sent to the conformance-ingest pipeline with low-cardinality sampling for historical debugging. Link failures to trace IDs when available.

Owner and stewardship

- Contract steward role: a cross-functional team (API Platform + SRE + Product) that maintains the conformance harness, linter rules, and central ledger.
- Service owners: must author and maintain DCTS files for each public surface and model variant.

Open questions and tradeoffs

- How strict should default mode be for internal endpoints? Proposal: internal endpoints default to tolerant mode, but any endpoint used by another service must be promoted to strict with a DCTS.
- Cost vs. coverage: nightly full-matrix checks are expensive. We propose prioritized sweeps (critical endpoints every night, others weekly).

Migration plan

1. Pilot: Onboard three services (edge-proxy, runtime-controller, and the embeddings-ingest) to the DCTS and CP workflow over Q2 2026.
2. Expand to all public endpoints and model-serving inputs by Q4 2026.
3. Enforce gate for new public endpoints starting Q1 2027.

Appendix: sample CLI commands and linter config

# Local validation
#   conftest validate service/docs/contracts/dcts/*.yaml

# Publish artifact (CI step)
#   conftest publish --bucket=conformance-bucket --service=$SERVICE --version=$VERSION dcts.yaml

# Central conformance run (dry-run example)
#   conformance-runner --matrix-file=matrix.json --artifacts-dir=artifacts/ --output=ledger.csv

# Linter rules (excerpt)
# required: [owner, risk_level, conformance_category, test_coverage_min]

Notes on documentation style

- Keep DCTS files short and example-driven. Prefer real-world examples over exhaustive machine-generated schemas.
- Use the CP description field to capture rationale and expected client impact.

References

- See canonical request schema and validation playbook: /architecture-and-standards/api-standards/canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025
- Variant compatibility ledger: /architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/variant-compatibility-ledger-and-stewardship-protocol-2026

Approval

Approved by: API Platform leadership, SRE management, and Product for runtime conformance.
