description:
Motivation: We observed intermittent correctness regressions and KV-cache divergence when nodes opportunistically switched to lower-precision kernels under load. These issues were most pronounced during warm-up phases and when continuous-batching mixed short warm-up sequences with steady-state traffic. The goal of this PR is to make the low-precision fast path reliable in production by adding conservative checks and an automatic, observable annealing mechanism that trades small amounts of peak throughput for deterministic correctness.

Summary of changes: add a light-weight per-node kernel stability probe that runs microbenchmarks on model startup and periodically during low-utilization windows; expose a configurable 'kernel_stability_threshold' that gates transitions to low-precision kernels; implement a precision-annealing state machine that steps precision down gradually (fp32 -> fp16 -> int8) only when stability and latency criteria are met; add a kv-sync-guard which attaches short-lived checksums to KV cache snapshots and prevents applying a cache state if checksum mismatch or stale-timestamp detected; update continuous-batching heuristics to avoid batching sequences observed during the warm-up probe and to prefer homogeneous-decoded sequences to reduce cache churn.

Configuration and defaults: default kernel_stability_threshold=0.92 (fraction of microbench runs that must pass), anneal_step_interval=30s, min_stable_window=2m. Operators can override in runtime config or via console per-cluster. Canary rollout automatically enables annealing on 10% of nodes by default.

Design notes: stability probe is intentionally lightweight (per-model token-limited runs) and runs on a background worker with a low scheduling priority. We capture simple metrics: decode latency variance, kernel success/failure, and checksum of produced KV updates. The precision-annealing state machine records a rollback count and will automatically revert to the last-known-good precision if a regression is detected for two consecutive evaluation windows. KV-sync-guard uses a small 64-bit checksum and timestamp to detect divergent updates; it prevents a stale or corrupt cache from being applied and triggers a re-fetch path that is more conservative (sequential KV application with verification).

Performance and correctness: measured on internal perf-lab with a mix of 1k short-chat and 200 long-generation traces: baseline (optimistic fp16 fastpath without probes) showed +12.3% token/sec vs safe fp32 but a 2.8% rare correctness/regression signal on our eval set and occasional KV-invalidation incidents during canary. With this PR enabled (default canary), we observe +9.1% token/sec, p95 token latency improved by 6ms relative to safe fp32, and correctness regressions dropped to 0.12% (within noise). CPU/GPU telemetry indicates a ~7% reduction in wasted kernel restarts during warm-up.

- feat(anneal): implement precision-annealing state machine and runtime flags (maya/commit/2)
- fix(kv): implement kv-sync-guard with checksum verification and fallback path (alex/commit/3)
- perf(scheduler): adjust continuous-batching heuristic to avoid warm-up mixing (noah/commit/4)
- test(perf): new perf harness scenarios and canary harness (sofia/commit/5)
- docs: ops notes and runtime configuration docs (maya/commit/6)

Testing: unit tests added for state machine transitions and kv-sync checksum logic; integration canary runs in perf-lab for 48h; additional chaos test where random kernel failure is injected to validate rollback behavior. CI initially failed on a flaky kv-manager apply test (race in test harness); I fixed the test harness timing and re-ran. Final CI: all checks passed (build, unit, integration-smoke, perf-canary sim).

Review conversation (high level):

- Maya Chen: "Added rollback_count and min_stable_window config to prevent oscillation; updated tests to exercise noisy conditions."

- Andre Patel: approved after minor doc nits.

Backward compatibility and migration: all flags default to conservative values; clusters not opting into canary see no behavior change. Ops doc includes a migration checklist to enable annealing and KV checksum on dedicated clusters.

description:
Issue summary: Customer observed a sudden P99 latency spike for small-batch embedding requests. During the window (~2026-03-12 09:15-09:35 UTC) requests that should have egressed in eu-west were routed to ap-southeast, adding ~220ms network RTT and causing downstream timeouts in their ingestion pipeline.

Impact: Production ingestion pipelines for Streamline Analytics degraded (10% request failures, 25% higher token latency). Affects users pinned to eu-west and using batch-embeds endpoint.

Environment: prod | eu-west (tenant: streamline-prod, customer-tier: enterprise)

Steps to reproduce: 
1) Send concurrent small-batch embedding calls (batch size 8, concurrency 40) to /v1/embeddings with tenant API key from EU.
2) Observe egress path in edge logs and p99 latency in Grafana.
3) Repeat during off-peak — issue appears correlated with higher control-plane heartbeat jitter.

Observed behavior: During burst, control-plane reports for tenant showed delayed residency stamp refresh; edge selected nearest healthy edge (ap-southeast) as fallback for some connections. TLS handshakes and auth token validation retried against APAC edges causing auth retries and additional latency.

Expected behavior: Requests from eu-west pinned tenants should egress through EU edges unless strict residency is unset or explicit fallback policy permits cross-region egress.

Logs/metrics referenced: grafana/dashboard/embeddings/tenant-streamline-p99 (snapshot attached in comments), edge-proxy logs (edge-eu-01, edge-eu-03), control-plane healthcheck timeline (2026-03-12T09:14:50 -> 2026-03-12T09:16:20). Slack thread: #support-streamline-212022

Temporary impact mitigation: Workaround applied to pin tenant to eu-central-edge pool to avoid dynamic fallback while we investigate.


comments:
2026-03-12 09:27 - Maya Patel (Support): Raised ticket after customer reported spike. Attached sample request IDs and Grafana p99 screenshot.
2026-03-12 09:33 - Alex Kim (SRE): Confirmed mixed egress paths in edge logs for token=tsk_streamline_prod_XXXX. Correlating with control-plane heartbeat lag for tenant stamp refresh.
2026-03-12 09:45 - Jamie Ortiz (Networking): Noticed DNS rebinds on eu-edge NATs around 09:15 that could have contributed to session reestablishment to nearest healthy edge.
2026-03-12 10:02 - Support (to customer): Temporary pin applied and connections restarted. Asking customer to validate. They reported immediate improvement to baseline latency around 10:10 UTC.
2026-03-12 15:20 - Alex Kim (SRE): Added preliminary investigation notes and created follow-up engineering task. See PR link in related_github_prs.
2026-03-13 08:05 - Customer (Streamline Analytics): Confirmed mitigation worked for now; asked for RCA and preventive measures.

investigation_notes:
Data collected: edge-proxy traces, control-plane residency refresh logs, DNS logs from eu-edge NAT cluster. Pattern: intermittent delay in control-plane TTL refresh for residency stamp (~35-90s) under high concurrent embed churn. During that window, edge token validation path falls back to 'nearest healthy edge' bucket which currently includes APAC edges by proximity metric when EU edges show transient auth timeouts. Hypothesis: a combination of DNS rebinds at NAT + control-plane heartbeat suppression triggers transient stamp expiry and fallback-routing. Reproduced in staging with synthetic churn at ~40 concurrent batch requests. Correlated with increased control-plane GC pauses in the same timeframe (GC activity in control-plane host cp-14).

resolution:
Mitigation: Reapplied tenant strict pin to a dedicated eu-edge pool and performed graceful connection drain -> immediate latency return to baseline. Root cause: transient control-plane heartbeat lag combined with NAT/DNS rebinds allowed the residency stamp to be treated stale, which triggered fallback routing logic that selected APAC edges. Permanent fixes planned: 1) Increase control-plane heartbeat alerting and reduce stamp expiry threshold; 2) Harden fallback routing policy to prefer region affinity longer when stamp is near-expiry; 3) Network ops to investigate NAT/DNS rebind frequency and patch; 4) Deploy control-plane GC tuning PR (https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/9876). Follow-ups tracked in INT-451900 (engineering task) and SUP-742913 (similar customer case).

body:
Motivation:
We frequently observe that promotes that look good on telemetry during a short canary window still cause edge-case regressions once given full traffic. This PR introduces two complementary primitives: (1) a traffic_escrow service that holds routing decisions and only releases commits once a rehearse pass and smoke policy succeed, and (2) a rehearse_proxy that can inject synthetic canary traffic and replay recorded request traces into candidate serving revisions without affecting production state.

Goals:
- Allow operators to stage promotes with a commit escrow lease that requires an endorsement from rehearse results before full cutover.
- Provide a reproducible, auditable rehearse run that exercises session affinity, header routing, and KV cache warmup without serving user writes to production.
- Reduce time-to-revert via an escrow ledger that records the include/exclude criteria, lease owner, and rehearse outcomes per promote.

What this PR contains (single-string description):
Implemented a TrafficEscrow controller, a RehearseProxy sidecar + router middleware, a small replay harness for synthetic canaries (replay driver + sampler), and related observability (metrics, traces, and a prometheus scrape target). Included an admin API to grant/revoke escrow leases and an operator CLI hook to trigger a rehearse run. The rehearsals are configurable with smoke policies and timeout/rollback thresholds.

Checklist:
- [x] TrafficEscrow controller + database-backed ledger (sqlite for dev, Postgres migration script included)
- [x] RehearseProxy middleware for routing and replay isolation
- [x] Replay driver and synthetic canary harness with pluggable samplers
- [x] Feature flag gating (rollout.traffic_escrow) and integration tests
- [x] Prometheus metrics + tracing spans for rehearse runs
- [x] Operator CLI commands and docs stub

High-level commits:
- commit 1: controller: add TrafficEscrow CRD and schema, controller reconciliation loop with lease lifecycle
- commit 2: middleware: rehearse proxy router and headers + session-affinity passthrough
- commit 3: replay: synthetic canary driver and reservoir sampler, smoke policy evaluator
- commit 4: telemetry: metrics, traces, and prometheus target
- commit 5: migrations: add escrow ledger table and migration script
- commit 6: tests: e2e rehearse integration tests + unit tests for policy evaluator

Changed files (high level):
- services/traffic-escrow/controller.go (new)
- services/traffic-escrow/ledger/migrations/0001_create_escrow_table.sql (new)
- services/traffic-escrow/api/escrow.proto (new)
- runtime/middleware/rehearse_proxy.go (new)
- runtime/replay/driver.go (new)
- runtime/replay/sampler.go (new)
- deploy/helm/templates/escrow-deployment.yaml (mod)
- observability/metrics/escrow_metrics.go (new)
- cli/ops/escrow_cli.go (new)
- docs/ops/traffic-escrow.md (new)
- tests/e2e/rehearse_integration_test.go (new)

Small illustrative snippet (rehearse proxy header handling):

func (rp *RehearseProxy) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if rp.isRehearseRun(r) {
        // tag and route to candidate revision; keep responses sandboxed
        r.Header.Set("X-Rehearse-Run", rp.currentLeaseID)
        rp.routeToCandidate(w, r)
        return
    }
    rp.routeNormal(w, r)
}

(Full diffs are intentionally small here; implementation files are focused and mostly additive.)

Operational notes:
- Default behavior is a no-op until rollout.traffic_escrow is enabled.
- The escrow ledger keeps soft TTLs for leases; expired leases auto-fail after the configured grace period.
- Rehearse runs can be run in parallel for non-overlapping cohorts; controller rejects overlapping leases by default to avoid double-warmup.

Review thread summary (single string):
See reviewers list for full thread. Key points from review: Liam asked for stronger invariants around overlapping leases; addressed by adding overlap detection in the controller and a unit test. Maya requested clearer observability for rehearse runs; added metrics and traces and a prometheus scrape target with labels rehearse_run and cohort_id. Diego recommended a Postgres migration rather than sqlite for staging; added migration and a readme about storage backends. CI flakes on the first run due to a timing issue in the replay sampler; fixed by adding deterministic seeding in tests.

Selected review comments and replies:
- Liam O'Connor (2026-02-16): "Controller needs deterministic behavior when two promotes touch the same cohort. How does reclamation work?"
  - Author reply (Priya): "Added overlap checks and a ReclaimLease method; controller now serializes conflicting lease requests and exposes a metric escrow_conflicts_total."

- Maya Li (2026-02-18): "Can we get a top-level metric that shows rehearse run pass/fail ratio over the last 24h?"
  - Author reply: "Added rehearse_run_result_total{outcome=\"pass\"|\"fail\"} and example dashboard panels in docs/ops."

- Diego Alvarez (2026-02-19): "DB choice: use Postgres in staging. Please include migration and docs."
  - Author reply: "Included migration script and a small switch in config to pick sqlite for dev, postgres for staging/prod."

CI and test summary:
- CI pipeline: unit (go test), linters (golangci-lint), integration (docker-compose rehearse harness), e2e (k8s kind).
- Run 1: unit/lint passed, integration timed out (race in replay sampler), rerun tests after deterministic seeding.
- Run 2: all checks passed.

Post-merge actions:
- Enable rollout.traffic_escrow behind a canary flag for SRE on a single cluster for two weeks (ENG-2401).
- Run a handful of rehearses using recorded traces to validate session-affinity and cache warmups.
- Add a small playbook to run a fast revert if rehearse failures exceed threshold.

Why this is different from existing rollout features:
This PR focuses on the concept of escrowed commits plus a rehearse proxy that allows routing and replay isolation so that candidate revisions can be exercised end-to-end without touching production state. Existing staged promote primitives at Redwood emphasize traffic phasing and shadowing; traffic escrow gives an operator-level commit gating primitive with a ledger and rehearsals that are auditable and replayable.

Risk assessment:
- Low to medium risk: mostly additive components behind feature flags. The largest surface is the rehearse proxy which touches routing; we've guarded it with feature flag gating and unit tests.

Notes for on-call and SRE:
- Metric to watch: escrow_conflicts_total, rehearse_run_result_total, rehearse_run_duration_seconds_bucket, rehearsal_sandbox_errors_total.
- CLI: redwood ops escrow grant --lease-id=<id> --cohort=<name> --owner=<user>

If any follow-ups are requested, they will be tracked in ENG-1024 and ENG-2401.

description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports repeated 429 responses during a nightly bulk ingest run that stages objects via signed cookies. Failures started after a safe restart of their ingest fleet and coincide with a scheduled canary of a proxy-side keepalive change. BrightFleet uses ephemeral worker pools that refresh signed cookies frequently (~every 90s).

Impact:
- ~20% of ingest batch requests receiving 429s intermittently across a 2 hour window (2026-03-09 03:00–05:00 UTC).
- Customer sees backlog and retry storms causing delayed downstream processing and SLA risk for enterprise tier.

Environment:
- Customer tier: enterprise, VPC peering to prod us-west-2, using pooled edge proxy IPs and signed-cookie approach for pre-signed uploads.
- Ingest orchestrator uses 200 concurrent ephemeral workers per region; each worker refreshes cookies from control-plane every ~90s.

Steps to reproduce (reported by customer):
1) Start parallel uploader with 200 workers using signed-cookie refresh schedule identical to production.
2) Observe steady-state for 10 minutes, then trigger a restart of a subset of workers (simulates canary).
3) Measure HTTP 429s from /upload endpoint and ambiguous throttle headers.

Observed logs / telemetry (customer-provided):
- Repeated 429s with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Reset drifting between 10–60s.
- Ingest orchestrator logs show bursts of signed-cookie refresh requests to the auth service clustered at restart time.
- Edge proxy traces show keepalive connections sticky to pooled IPs; some cookie refresh POSTs get routed through a small subset of origin instances.

Hypothesis / initial triage notes (Support):
- Likely interaction between signed-cookie refresh fanout and token-bucket accounting at the route layer. Ephemeral workers renewing cookies simultaneously can concentrate accounting at the ingress proxy and momentarily exhaust per-route refill credits.

description:
Problem: During regional disruptions we currently perform blunt traffic drains or full cutovers that can truncate long-lived streaming sessions and lose in-flight KV state. This causes visible client disconnects, token replays, and SLO violations for tail latency and availability.

Goal: Implement a gateway bifurcation pattern that enables graceful takeover between two active regions that share a coordinated per-connection KV checkpointing mechanism, short token-grace window, and circuit-decay policy. The mechanism should: preserve active streaming attachments where possible, reduce user-visible interruptions, maintain SLOs for p95/p99 latency, and allow progressive traffic rebalancing with automated load-shedding triggers and circuit breakers for overloaded endpoints.

acceptance_criteria:
New gateway bifurcation control plane can execute staged traffic split 100% -> 80/20 -> 50/50 -> 0% with per-connection checkpointing applied during each stage
Active streaming sessions can resume on target region with KV checkpoint replay within token-grace window for >= 95% of test sessions in canary
Circuit-decay policy triggers and drops low-priority background requests while preserving high-priority tokens; measured p99 latency remains within SLO (<= 800ms) during 70% simulated surge
Automated rollback when telemetry shows error-rate delta > 2% or SLA budget burn > 30% in 10m window
End-to-end observability: dashboards for per-connection handoff success rate, checkpoint latency, token-grace expirations, and circuit-breaker activations are available in Console
Runbook updated with step-by-step operator commands and emergency cutover procedure

design_notes:
Bifurcation model: introduce a light-weight control plane API that instructs edge gateways to enter a 'bifurcate' mode where connections are tracked and checkpoints emitted at defined safe boundaries (e.g., sentence boundaries or invocation end for non-streams)
KV checkpointing uses existing prefix cache format but augments with 'handoff-metadata' containing sequence id and minimal opaque resume token
Token-grace window: short TTL (default 45s) during which requests with valid resume token are allowed on destination region before full auth revalidation, configurable per-customer
Circuit-decay: instead of hard reject on threshold breach, reduce priority of non-interactive routes progressively using weighted drop and backoff so that interactive sessions retain headroom
We will avoid synchronous cross-region KV replication; instead use per-connection snapshot + opportunistic async pre-warm on destination to keep overhead low

technical_approach:
Edge changes: gateway will emit checkpoint artifacts to S3-backed artifact store (or internal blob cache) keyed by connection-id and region, with signed short-lived pointer visible to target region
Control plane: bifurcate controller service with APIs: /start-bifurcate, /advance-stage, /rollback, /finalize. Controller computes staged percentages and pushes policies to gateways via gRPC config streams
Resume flow: destination gateway receives resume token, fetches checkpoint, rehydrates KV cache and replay last few tokens to restore deterministic decoder state; if checkpoint unavailable or stale, fallback to canonical stateless retry path
Load-shedding triggers: telemetry-driven rules based on queue depth, GPU headroom, and p99 latency; rules feed into controller which adjusts split and activates circuit-decay rules
Safety nets: global circuit-breaker per-customer that can instant-fail new sessions to protect cluster and prevent cascading failures
Backwards compatibility: non-streaming and stateless flows unaffected; default behavior for customers not opted-in remains original cutover path

rollout_plan:
Phase 0 - Internal Canary: deploy bifurcate controller and edge code to test cluster; run synthetic suite with deterministic streams (2/10 - 2/24)
Phase 1 - Limited Canary: enable feature for internal services only, monitor handoff success and token-grace expirations, iterate on checkpoint size and pre-warm thresholds (3/1 - 3/8)
Phase 2 - Customer Canary: opt-in 3 low-risk customers with long-lived streams; run staged splits with progressive % increases (3/9 - 3/16)
Phase 3 - Ramp: enable auto-split for broad traffic with conservative defaults and telemetry thresholds; maintain human-in-loop for first 48 hours (3/17 - 3/24)
Rollback: emergency commands in runbook to abort and redirect all bifurcate traffic back to original region and invalidate resume tokens

telemetry:
Per-connection metrics: checkpoint_size_bytes, checkpoint_emit_latency_ms, resume_fetch_latency_ms, resume_success_bool
Handoff metrics: handoff_attempts_total, handoff_success_rate, handoff_fallback_rate
SLOs: p95/p99 latency pre/post-handshake, availability per-region, error-rate by route
Circuit metrics: circuit_open_count, average_decay_rate, dropped_requests_by_priority
Alerting: conservative alerts for handoff_success_rate < 90% in 5m and p99 latency regression > 20% vs baseline

test_plan:
Automated unit tests for checkpoint serialization/deserialization and token signing
Integration tests with simulated cross-region resume using local artifact store
Chaos tests: introduce network partitions and verify controller rolling advance/rollback semantics
Load tests: synthetic streams plus background embedding/ingest traffic to evaluate circuit-decay efficacy
Canary dashboards and SLIs tracked during each stage; automatic gates for phase transition

risks:
Resume token leakage: mitigated by short TTLs and signature verification; requires security review
Large checkpoints may add storage/IO pressure during mass handoffs; mitigation: cap checkpoint size and prefer incremental diffs
Checkpoint replay may diverge for non-deterministic model serving paths (e.g., sampling); mitigation: restrict replay to deterministic sampling or force deterministic mode during handoff windows
Increased control plane complexity and blast radius if controller miscomputes split — mitigations: rate limits, circuit-breakers, and manual abort
SLO trade-off: during surge the system may favor availability of interactive sessions by dropping background work; this needs clear product communication

Summary:
This PRD defines the Quantization & Fidelity Experimentation Lab (the Lab): a reproducible, service-backed environment for running targeted fidelity experiments when introducing quantized model variants, pruning, or other cost-saving serving techniques. The Lab's outputs are deterministic experiment artifacts, decision signals (pass/fail/gated), and standardized reports used by Product, Applied ML, and Serving Runtime to decide rollouts and fallback strategies.

Goals:
- Provide a single source of truth for fidelity impact of any automated compression or quantization profile across representative tenant workloads.
- Produce machine-readable experiment results (quality deltas, latency/cost deltas, statistical significance) and a human-readable report with recommended rollout gating (allow, canary, block).
- Support experiment types: full-model quantization, per-layer mixed-precision, activation pruning, low-rank adapters, and forced KV-cache eviction behaviors.
- Integrate with the Optimize and Serving Runtime rollout pipelines to automatically recommend safe rollouts and guardrail thresholds.

Non-goals:
- The Lab will not itself perform live production A/B rollouts. It produces evidence and artifacts consumed by the rollout systems.
- The Lab does not replace long-term model quality monitoring (that remains in Console/Optimize).

Success metrics (first 6 months):
- 90% of candidate quantization profiles produce a deterministic Lab report within 48 hours of submission (on standard profiles).
- >=75% reduction in manual evaluation time for quantization-related rollouts (measured via engineering survey).
- Fallbacks triggered by Lab-approved rollback policies reduce customer-seen quality regressions by >60% vs ad-hoc rollouts.

Stakeholders and owners:
- Product (owner): Ivy Chen (product lead) — defines acceptance criteria and experimental matrix templates.
- Applied ML (owner): Rafael Ortega — curates evaluation sets and quality metrics per workload/domain.
- Eng: Serving Runtime (owner): Arjun Malhotra — provides runtime hooks and cost/latency telemetry, implements automated rollout integration.
- Eng: DevEx — SDK/CLI for experiment submission and artifacts retrieval.

User stories:
1) As an Applied ML engineer, I want to submit a quantization profile and a list of evaluation prompt sets and receive a standardized fidelity report (metrics, significance, artifact links) so I can recommend rollout policy.
2) As a Product manager, I want a summary dashboard showing pass/fail across customer segments, so I can prioritize safe rollouts.
3) As an SRE, I want experiment artifacts to include traceable request IDs and telemetry so I can audit regressions that reach production.

Experiment runner requirements (functional):
- Accept experiment definitions as YAML or JSON via SDK/REST and return a job id.
- Run experiments against: canonical test harness (deterministic RNG seeds), a configurable subset of model variants (float32, int8, 4-bit mixed), and a set of workload slices (chat, code, long-form completion, embeddings).
- Capture and persist: per-example outputs, token-level latencies, resource utilization (GPU RAM, kernels used), and per-example quality scores.
- Produce a structured report containing: aggregated metrics (mean, median, p99), delta vs baseline, 95% confidence intervals, A/B test p-values, and an automated pass/fail recommendation based on policy.

Experiment runner requirements (non-functional):
- Turnaround: typical small experiments complete within 24 - 48 hours; pilot-level experiments (large prompt sets) within 5 days.
- Reproducibility: experiments run with immutable seeds, pinned model binaries, and environment hashes.
- Multi-tenant safety: experiments run in an isolated namespace, with no customer data used unless explicitly authorized and scrubbed.

Quality metrics and gating logic:
- Primary metrics per workload:
  - Chat/Completion: semantic similarity (embedding cosine) vs baseline, normalized F1 when applicable, and response length parity. Gate: mean embedding cosine drop <= 0.012 AND 99th-percentile semantic delta <= 0.02.
  - Code generation: pass@k and compilation success rate. Gate: pass@1 drop <= 1.5 percentage points and compile-failure delta <= 0.5pp.
  - Embeddings: mean cosine similarity drop <= 0.015; downstream retrieval MAP drop <= 0.8%.
  - Latency/Cost: p50 latency must not increase more than 8% for the target serving configuration; cost/unit must be reduced by >= 12% to be considered.
- Automated pass/fail decision algorithm:
  1. Compute per-workload deltas and CIs.
  2. If any primary metric breaches gate thresholds -> FAIL.
  3. If primary metrics pass but secondary metrics (edge-case slices) show regressions above 95th-percentile thresholds -> WARN (manual review).
  4. Produce recommendation: allow | canary (10% traffic) | block.

Experiment definition schema (example YAML):
  ---
  experiment_name: "int4-mixed-prune-v2"
  model_variant: "redwood-open-7b-v2"
  baseline_variant: "redwood-open-7b-fp16"
  profiles:
    - name: "int4-mixed"
      quantization: "mixed-int4"
      per_layer_overrides: ["attn-16:8", "mlp-5:4"]
  workload_slices:
    - name: "customer-chat-small"
      sample_set: "canonical/chat-1000"
      metrics: ["embed_cosine","mean_length","toxicity_rate"]
  eval_repeat: 3
  rng_seed: 41321

Telemetry and artifact requirements:
- Events captured: experiment.submitted, experiment.started, example.{id}.inference.start, example.{id}.inference.end, experiment.completed, experiment.report.generated.
- Telemetry must include: job_id, model_variant, profile_hash, seed, environment_hash, worker_version, and timestamps.
- Artifacts stored: raw outputs (per example), normalized metric table (CSV), aggregated report (JSON and human-readable markdown), and an immutable experiment metadata file.

Data handling and PII policy:
- No customer PII may be used in Lab experiments unless explicitly consented and processed in a restricted workspace.
- When customer data is approved, the Lab will apply automated scrubbing per the Data Management policy: remove names, tokens matching credit-card patterns, and PII heuristics.

Integration points and automation:
- Rollout Integration: Lab will call the Rollout Recommendation API with pass/canary/block and attach experiment artifact links. Serving Runtime will annotate model variants with experiment ids.
- Console: Add a new page type "Experiment Report" where product and applied-ml can browse experiments, filter by model, and export PDFs.
- CLI: redwood-lab submit --file experiment.yaml -> returns job id; redwood-lab report --id JOB -> downloads artifacts.

Operational requirements and infra sizing:
- Baseline test cluster: 8x A100(80GB) equivalent nodes for parallel small experiments; ability to burst to 32 nodes for large sweeps.
- Storage: lifecycle retention of experiment artifacts: 90 days hot, 1 year cold archive.
- RBAC: roles: lab-admin, lab-runner, lab-viewer. lab-runner may execute jobs but cannot delete artifacts.

Reporting and human-readable output (example):
Title: int4-mixed-prune-v2 — redwood-open-7b-v2
Summary: Pass with WARN on edge-case legal prompts. p50 latency -3.4%, cost/unit -18.7%
Primary metrics table:
| workload | baseline | variant | delta | CI95 | decision |
| chat-1000 | 0.872 | 0.861 | -0.011 | ±0.003 | PASS |
| legal-slice | 0.790 | 0.760 | -0.030 | ±0.010 | WARN |
Notes: The legal-slice regression is concentrated in documents with very long citations (see artifact: /artifacts/12345/legal-edge-cases.csv). Recommend a canary to 5% with automated fallback to fp16 for flagged tenant tags.

Rollout gating workflow (recommended):
1. Experiment authorates PRD + attaches Lab report.
2. Applied ML reviews WARNs; if minor, mark canary; if block, require engineer to iterate.
3. If canary approved, schedule a 2-week canary at 5-10% traffic with monitoring alerts configured (quality delta, token-level fraud checks).
4. If canary succeeds (no production quality regression for 14 days), promote to gradual rollout.

Testing, QA, and guardrails:
- Unit tests: experiment runner validation logic, schema conformance.
- Integration tests: end-to-end run against a small synthetic workload with deterministic outputs.
- Chaos test: randomly kill runner nodes; verify retry semantics and artifact integrity.
- Guardrails: experiments that touch PII require approval from Data Governance.

Open questions and risks:
- How to budget the infra cost of large sweep experiments vs. business value? (Mitigation: quota-based submission and cost-credits workflow.)
- Potential overfitting to canonical prompt sets. (Mitigation: require at least one customer representative slice for any production rollout.)

Milestones and roadmap (quarterly):
- Q1: MVP experiment runner, CLI, and basic report generation; integrate with Rollout Recommendation API.
- Q2: Support for mixed-precision per-layer overrides, artifact retention policy, and Console report UI.
- Q3: Auto-recommendations tied to Optimize insights (cost/latency tradeoff visualizer) and canary orchestration link.

Appendix: example CLI usage and minimal SDK snippet
# Submit
redwood-lab submit --file int4-experiment.yaml
# Poll
redwood-lab status --id job-20270322-001
# Fetch report
redwood-lab report --id job-20270322-001 --output ./reports/job-001

Python SDK (pseudo):

client = LabClient()
job = client.submit(experiment_definition)
report = client.wait_and_fetch(job.id)
print(report.summary)

Maria: Also call out latency to EU customers (we need <60ms p95 for chat). eu-west helps avoid cross-region tail latency.
Eli: For embedding-heavy traffic we could mix A10G-like SKUs in ap-southeast for cost, but that hurts long-context gen. Worth considering for regional embedding caches.
billing-bot: FYI: current enterprise discount in eu-west1 = 7% on committed usage (applies to sustained commit only). No guaranteed discounts in ap-southeast in current contract.

eu-west: on-demand 27.0 -> committed 18.9 (≈30% savings)

Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0186
Question: In the notes about keeping long, stop-and-go chat sessions cheap without replaying the whole history, what storage setup and time-to-live were proposed for keeping the compact per-session state for recent sessions versus longer retention?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_0ae9b752fef446ec86e376e2dea49c28:
Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight scratchpad for thinking about 'fractured context' strategies: when a long session is assembled from multiple interleaved short interactions (multi-document chat, task switching, user sessions with gaps) and how to keep latency and cost predictable while preserving retrieval/continuity quality.

Motivation (quick):
- Users expect context continuity across ephemeral turns and across background tasks (e.g., user edits doc A, then does a quick search, comes back).
- Full prefix replay is expensive at 1k+ tokens per turn; naive KV cache growth or repeated retrievals blow cost/latency.
- Need heuristics or micro-protocols to anchor session state cheaply and recover context when needed.

Reading roundup (notes + immediate takeaways):
1) "Session Anchors for Long Conversational State" (arXiv:2403.01234) - skimed
   - idea: create compact anchor vectors at decision points (every N tokens or after topic change).
   - anchors are small (128–512 dims), stored per-session; on context switch, retrieve nearest anchors and rehydrate partial KV cache via learned projector.
   - takeaway: anchor projection noise likely high for factual detail; works better for topical continuity + procedural cues.

2) "KV-summarize: fragment summarization to compress attention state" (internal notes + related work)
   - offline summarization of stale KV segments to 1–2 sentence summaries that are kept in prompt context rather than expanding KV cache.
   - tradeoff: lossy summaries reduce token cost but can break exact retrieval for code/legal stuff.

3) "Interleaved Context Scheduling (ICLR workshop slides)"
   - scheduling requests by urgency: low-urgency turns can be batched and served with cached summaries; high urgency uses full KV rehydration.
   - practical: annotate requests with "urgency" metadata from client SDK.

Open questions / hypotheses:
- H1: Anchors + light projection will preserve >80% topical coherence while cutting rehydration tokens by 60%.
- H2: For factual fidelity (exact names, code), anchors will fail; need hybrid: anchors for discourse, fetch original KV for critical segments indicated by metadata.
- H3: User-visible latency SLO improves if we precompute anchors on idle CPU/GPU cycles and keep a small LRU of recent anchor->KV mappings.

Experiment sketch (priority ordering):
A) Benchmark anchor retrieval vs full KV rehydration (toy dataset)
   - Dataset: 200 synthetic sessions (mix edits, searches, code) assembled from public chatlogs + internal anonymized sessions.
   - Metrics: continuity_score (human-rated 1-5), token_cost, average_latency, factual_precision@k for retrievals.
   - Implementation notes: reuse kv-playground repo branch from linked PR; add anchor projector model (2-layer MLP) and serialization format.
B) Urgency-based scheduler prototype (client + server hooks)
   - Add "urgency" header in SDK, default low. Server policy: if low and session > N tokens, return summary placeholder and queue background rehydration.
   - Measure user-perceived latency and number of follow-up rehydrations.

Edge cases to capture:
- Multi-document merges (two docs referenced across a session) -> anchors need multi-anchor composition, or metadata indicating document ids to pull exact KV when necessary.
- Hallucination risk when relying on compressed anchors for facts; include fallback that detects high-entropy model outputs (logprob heuristics) and triggers full fetch.

Implementation details & quick notes to self:
- Anchor format: {session_id, t_offset, vec_dim=256, topics=[top-3-lda], token_span=[start,end], doc_ids=[...]} but in Drive scratchpad keep minimal: session_id, t_offset, vec (base64) and token_span.
- Storage: per-customer LRU store (Redis) for hot sessions; long-term anchors in S3 with TTL 30d.
- Rehydration pipeline: projector on CPU -> small KV patch assembled and injected to runtime via runtime API (use existing cold-fill path in serving-runtime).
- Metrics to log: anchor_hit_rate, rehydrate_count, rehydrate_tokens, anchor_project_error (cosine diff vs full-KV-embedding).

Acceptance criteria for prototype:
- end-to-end: anchor generation + rehydration path that adds <50ms extra server-side on top of normal inference.
- experiments: demonstrate >=40% token cost savings with continuity_score drop <=0.5 points on 1-5 scale for non-factual tasks.

Notes from sync with Maya (2024-08-27):
- Maya: prefer starting with a purely synthetic corpus to avoid privacy headaches; she will generate 500 sessions with annotated topic boundaries.
- Action: Maya will push dataset to s3://redwood-experiments/anchors/synth-500 by 2024-09-02.

Immediate TODOs (short):
- [ ] Fork kv-playground branch and wire anchor projector (Derek) - target 2024-09-01.
- [ ] Add urgency header to SDK stub (Ivy) - target 2024-08-30.
- [ ] Create evaluation rubric and small Mechanical Turk instructions for continuity scoring (Derek + Maya) - target 2024-09-05.
- [ ] Draft Confluence page describing anchor format + policies (Derek) - link to draft when ready.

Risks / constraints:
- Privacy: anchors derived from user text could leak PII if not filtered; need deterministic redaction before anchor projection.
- Cost: extra storage overhead and CPU for projectors; mitigate by low-dim anchors and LRU eviction.
- Ops complexity: introduces second-tier state (anchors) to manage; require clear TTLs and graceful degradation.

Random brainstorms (loose):
- Use hashed-document-ids in anchors so they are opaque to ops team; store decryption keys per-customer.
- Hybrid anchor+gap-fill: anchors point to compressed diffs; when user asks factual queries, gap-fill is fetched on-demand and stored for future anchors.
- Explore learned gating net (tiny classifier) that predicts when anchors are safe vs need full rehydration based on recent prompt tokens.

References to revisit (read fully):
- arXiv:2403.01234 (session anchors) - deep read
- GitHub PR: kv-playground/pull/72 - runtime hooks for cold-fill
- ICLR slides: "Interleaved Context Scheduling" - follow up author questions

End of notes.

description:
Purpose: Define a prescriptive acceptance matrix and automated remediation paths for Optimize so that model rollouts and runtime changes that impact quality are detected rapidly, attributed to cohorts, and either automatically mitigated or escalated with clear human-in-the-loop steps. Scope covers promptset stratification, metric composition, regression thresholds, A/B stopping rules, automated fallback behavior, alerting semantics, and required instrumentation. Out of scope: model training pipelines and offline benchmark generation (handled by Research).

acceptance_criteria:
AC1: Promptset stratification defined and published: at minimum the system must support labeling prompts into four cohorts (core, long-tail, adversarial, customer-specific) with a mapping file stored in Drive and a canonical JSON schema for ingestion into the Optimize eval runner.
AC2: Minimum sample sizes and MDEs: For each cohort define a default minimum sample and Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE). Defaults: core=2000 samples (MDE 0.5%), long-tail=5000 samples (MDE 1.0%), adversarial=1000 samples (MDE 1.5%), customer-specific=min(300 or 5% of traffic) (MDE 2%). These numbers must be codified in the rollout config UI and respected by the canary harness.
AC3: Composite quality score and decomposition: Implement a composite quality score (0-100) composed of: relevance (40%), correctness (30%), safety/adversarial flags (20%), latency penalty (10%). Each submetric must be reported separately and in cohort view in the Console dashboard and in the canary API response.
AC4: Regression triggers: A canary must be marked as failing if any of the following occur within the observation window: absolute composite score drop >= 1.5 points for core cohort; relative composite drop >= 3% for long-tail; safety flag rate increase >= 2x and absolute increase >= 0.3% for any cohort. Safety regressions have higher priority and bypass soft cooldown gates.
AC5: A/B stopping rules: Implement a sequential Bayesian stopping test with the following rule: stop when posterior probability that candidate is worse than baseline by at least the cohort MDE > 95% OR when posterior probability candidate is better by >=95%. The harness must support an optional frequentist alpha=0.01 override configured per rollout.
AC6: Multi-signal decision lattice: The system must evaluate at least three signals (composite score, safety flags, latency P95) and apply a weighted decision lattice to determine action (continue, hold, partial rollback, full rollback). Weights must be configurable per project and default to composite>safety>latency.
AC7: Auto-remediation flows: If a critical regression (safety or composite drop > threshold) is detected and sustained for two consecutive evaluation windows, the platform must: (a) automatically shift traffic back to the last-known-good model for up to 75% of traffic, (b) open an incident in the tracking system with a pre-filled template, and (c) notify on-call via PagerDuty and the Console alerting channel.
AC8: Safe partial fallback: For non-critical regressions the platform must support partial fallback routing patterns (e.g., 20%, 50%, 75%) with automated cooldown windows (default: 30m, 2h, 24h). Rollout must include a manual override to freeze traffic and require assignee approval to proceed.
AC9: Operational telemetry: Canary runs must emit per-cohort time-series for composite score, submetrics, sample count, variance, posterior probabilities, and action taken. All metric names and units must be documented in the PRD and wired into the Console dashboard and the alerting rules.
AC10: Auditability and forensics: Every automated decision (hold, fallback, rollback) must be recorded in an immutable audit log with keys: rollout_id, model_version, cohort, window_start, window_end, metrics_snapshot, decision_reason, and runbook_link. The audit log must be exportable as CSV/JSON.
AC11: Acceptance test harness: Deliver a small-scale integration harness (GitHub PR) that can simulate injected regressions (synthetic safety flags, relevance drops) per cohort and validate that the stopping rules and auto-remediation fire as expected. Provide test vectors and expected outputs.
AC12: Documentation & runbooks: Publish a Console-runbook template and a short PRD section for product customers describing how Optimize will behave under quality shocks, expected notifications, and recommended customer configuration defaults.
AC13: Backward compatibility: Existing Optimize rollouts without explicit cohort configs must default to a single 'core' cohort with legacy thresholds, and behavior should be equivalent to current baseline unless customer opts-in to new stratified checks.
AC14: Privacy & compliance check: Ensure that storing of customer-specific prompt examples for cohorting conforms to data retention and PII rules; add a flag in the rollout config for 'retain_examples' (default false).

comments:
2026-02-22 - Arielle Chen: Draft PRD posted to Confluence; requesting early engineering review on Bayesian stopping choice. Link above.
2026-02-25 - Daniel Ortega (ENG): Reviewed thresholds. Suggest reducing core MDE to 0.4% for high-traffic customers; proposed opt-in knob in rollout config. See inline comment in PRD.
2026-03-01 - Maya Singh (PM): Accepted opt-in knob approach. Added acceptance criterion for backward compatibility and default legacy behavior.
2026-03-04 - Priya Rao (DS): Recommends Bayesian sequential test with hierarchical priors across cohorts to improve power for long-tail; will provide a notebook by 2026-03-10.
2026-03-07 - Legal (L. Morales): Confirmed that customer-specific prompt retention must be opt-in and documented for contracts; suggested retention defaults to 30 days. Added security_review_required=false for now but flagged for SOC sync.
2026-03-10 - Engineering lead (H. Park): Spike complete. Prototype harness validates auto-fallback for injected safety regressions; opened GH PR #312. Need instrumentation schema before enabling Console wiring.
2026-03-12 - Arielle Chen: Updated PRD with ACs and sample sizes after DS feedback. Ready for design review to surface the config controls in Console.

['The private-installer release index schema v2 is extended to include a per-artifact origins block.'
 'Each per-artifact origins block records the source repository, build system or job ID, and build commit that produced the artifact, and can also include optional SBOM and cosign references.'
 'The indexer populates the origins block by querying an origin-mapper service and cross-referencing artifact digests to upstream build metadata.'
 'The indexer verifies cosign signatures on the origin blobs and records the verification result in the index.'
 'Operators can make missing or failed origin verification a hard failure by running the indexer with --enforce-origin-verification.']
eval_reference.gold_answer: We extend the private-installer release index (schema v2) to include an per-artifact `origins` block that records the source repo, build system/job ID, build commit, and optional SBOM/cosign references, populated by the indexer querying an origin-mapper service and cross-referencing artifact digests to upstream build metadata. The indexer verifies cosign signatures on the origin blobs and records the verification result, and operators can make failed/missing origin verification a hard failure by running the indexer with `--enforce-origin-verification`.

release_notes:
Add cross-repo artifact origin aggregation to release index used by private-installer; includes pipeline changes, index schema extension, signature/verification cross-checks, and docs for operator consumption.

description:
Context and motivation: Private-installer releases consume artifacts produced by multiple build pipelines (core runtime, helm charts, terraform modules, third-party vendor artifacts). Existing release index entries pointed to single build blobs but lost origin metadata (repo/build-job/container image digest). This PR extends the release index generation to aggregate origin provenance across repos/pipelines so operators can inspect where each artifact came from and verify chain-of-custody at install time.

What this PR does: - Adds an `origins` aggregate block to the release index JSON that lists source repository, pipeline job id, build commit, and optional SBOM/cosign references per artifact. - Modifies the private-installer indexer job to query multiple artifact registries and cross-reference artifact digests to upstream build metadata (via the new origin-mapper service). - Adds origin-mapper microservice (lightweight Go lambda) that merges build metadata across internal buildkite/jenkins/job-run APIs and returns a normalized origin statement for an artifact digest. - Updates CI/CD pipelines: new step in release pipeline to call origin-mapper and attach signed origin blobs to TUF/manifest staging area. - Enhances verification: indexer validates cosign signatures on origin blobs (if present) and records signature verification result in the index. - Adds operator docs and an index API example in private-installer docs for auditors to query artifact origins during upgrades/rollbacks.

Files/areas changed (high-level): - private-installer/cmd/indexer: indexer changed to call origin-mapper and persist origins into index JSON - private-installer/internal/index/schema_v2.go: new schema and JSON marshaling changes - tools/origin-mapper/: new Go service and adapters for buildkite/jenkins - infra/ci/pipelines/release.yml: added origin-stage, sign-origin and upload steps - docs/private-installer/origins.md: operator documentation and API examples - charts/private-installer/values.yaml: small annotation for chart provenance - scripts/dev/replay-origins.sh: local dev helper to simulate upstream metadata

Review conversation (summary): - Lina: "Nice; can we guarantee origin-mapper rate limits won't blow up during a large release?" Author: "Origin-mapper queues queries and caches job metadata for 24h; added circuit-breaker and bulk query path. See origin-mapper/README for eviction rules." - Ethan: "Add tests for mirrored artifacts where upstream job metadata is absent." Author: "Added integration test that marks missing upstream metadata and attaches best-effort origin assertion with source:mirror and mirror-ref." - Zoe: "Signature verification path looks good, but require operator flag to enforce failed verification as hard-fail for critical releases." Author: "Added CLI flag `--enforce-origin-verification` to indexer and documented recommended usage in docs." - Security review (internal): "Ensure origin-mapper tokens scoped read-only and short lived." Author: "Confirmed; CI injects ephemeral tokens, and service uses read-only tokens with minimal TTL. Details in infra/ci/README-security.md."

Final ci_status: pass.

Edge cases and limitations: - For artifacts mirrored from external vendors we may not retrieve upstream build job metadata; index will include `source: mirror` and a pointer to mirror provenance where available. - This PR does not change TUF signing policy; origin blobs themselves are uploaded to staging and signed with cosign in the release pipeline. Summary
-------
This document summarizes the Redwood Optimize 1.3 release (GA: 2026-02-20). Optimize 1.3 introduces Performance Profiles, Telemetry-based Cost Estimator, latency-tier presets for the Console, and several SDK/CLI usability improvements. The release targets customers using Redwood Optimize to tune Dedicated and Hosted inference for predictable unit economics and simplified rollout of quantization/batching recommendations.

Highlights
----------
- Performance Profiles (feature flag: optimize.performance_profiles): per-model, per-workload profiles that capture measured latency/throughput/cost at multiple sequence-length distributions. Profiles power auto-suggestion rules and the new cost estimator.
- Telemetry-based Cost Estimator: end-to-end estimator that uses historical request shape telemetry (prefix length, tokens-per-request, hit rates) to produce monthly cost projections and sensitivity analyses.
- Latency-tier Presets in Console: new predefined profiles (S0: <50ms p95, S1: <120ms p95, S2: <250ms p95) that automatically tune batching and cache TTL recommendations.
- SDK v0.18.0: new Optimize client with async estimate_cost() and get_performance_profile() helpers; breaking rename of estimate() -> estimate_cost().
- CLI: redwood optimize export-profile <model> -> writes a reproducible YAML profile used for Dedicated scheduling.
- Migration & compatibility: recommended default quantization profiles unchanged; deprecated optimize.legacy_hint removed (see Migration notes).

What’s new (detailed)
---------------------
1) Performance Profiles
   - Description: Profiles record observed stat distributions for: sequence_length, tokens_generated, request_rate (qps), prefix_cache_hit_rate. Each profile stores measured p50/p95 latencies and per-token GPU time across representative buckets (short/medium/long).
   - Storage: profiles are stored in the customer namespace (s3-backed), versioned, and visible via Console and API.
   - API preview: POST /v1/optimize/profiles {"model":"redwood-7b-v1","workload":"chat-short"} -> returns profile id and recommendations.
   - Owner: Optimize team (owner: Deepa Nair).

2) Telemetry-based Cost Estimator
   - Inputs: time window (default 30d), model(s), deployment mode (hosted/dedicated), commitment tier, sequence-length histogram.
   - Output: month-over-month projection (USD), token breakdown (input/system/output), sensitivity table (how cost changes if average tokens/request increases by +10/25/50%).
   - Accuracy caveats: estimator factors in measured batching efficiency and prefix cache hit rate; for cold-start or sparse telemetry customers, the estimator uses conservative defaults (see config below).
   - Console: new "Cost Projection" panel on Optimize pages with download CSV button.

3) Latency-tier Presets
   - Presets: S0 (ultra-low latency), S1 (balanced), S2 (cost-efficient). Each preset maps to batching window targets, max batch size, and prefix_cache_TTL suggestions.
   - Implementation: presets are applied as heuristics on top of Performance Profiles and can be overridden by route-level policy.

4) SDK & CLI changes
   - SDK v0.18.0: function rename estimate() -> estimate_cost(); new async wrapper; returns structured CostEstimate object. See SDK guide for migration snippet.
   - CLI: new export-profile command produces a YAML suitable for Dedicated scheduler. Example: redwood optimize export-profile redwood-13b-v2 --window 7d --out profile.yaml

Migration notes and breaking changes
----------------------------------
- Deprecated field removed: optimize.legacy_hint (previously used for heuristic-only recommendations). Action: remove any usages in saved route configs. Failure to remove will return 400 in API calls that include the field.
- SDK rename: update code references estimate() -> estimate_cost(). Simple search-and-replace sufficient for most codebases.
- Profile format changes: profile v1 -> v2 adds buckets for "prefix_cache_hit_rate". Dedicated scheduler accepts both v1 and v2, but v1 profiles will be automatically converted on import with a best-effort fill (read-only). We recommend re-exporting profiles after conversion.

Configuration snippets and examples
----------------------------------
- Console: Toggle Performance Profiles via Admin -> Optimize feature flags -> optimize.performance_profiles (default: off for existing tenants; on for new tenants).

- Example API request (cost estimate):
  POST /v1/optimize/estimate_cost
  Content-Type: application/json

  {
    "model": "redwood-13b-v2",
    "deployment_mode": "dedicated",
    "window_days": 30,
    "sequence_histogram": {"short": 0.7, "medium": 0.25, "long": 0.05},
    "commitment_tier": "std-monthly-1"
  }

  Response (truncated):
  {
    "monthly_cost_usd": 11500.32,
    "cost_per_1k_output_tokens": 2.87,
    "sensitivity": {"+10%_tokens_per_request": 12650.35}
  }

- SDK migration example (Python):
  # before
  cost = optimize_client.estimate(model="redwood-7b-v1", window_days=30)
  # after
  cost = await optimize_client.estimate_cost(model="redwood-7b-v1", window_days=30)

Rollout plan
------------
- Canary: 2026-02-18 -> enable Performance Profiles for 10 pilot tenants (selection criteria: medium-sized Dedicated customers with diverse request shapes). Monitor p95 latency impact and console correctness.
- Gradual rollout: 2026-02-20 -> enable for new tenants and opt-in for existing tenants via Console.
- Full enforcement: 2026-03-10 -> deprecate legacy_hint on route configs (400 returned if present).

SLOs and observability
----------------------
- Optimize service SLO unaffected: 99.9% availability for API endpoints.
- Cost estimator-specific: 99% of estimates generated within 2s for inputs with cached Performance Profiles; 95% within 5s for uncached inputs.
- Telemetry metrics exposed: optimize.profile_generation.count, optimize.estimate_latency_ms.p95, optimize.estimate_cache_hit_rate. Dashboards: /dashboards/optimize/1-3-release-estimates

How to opt-in / try it today
---------------------------
1) Console: Admin -> Feature flags -> toggle optimize.performance_profiles -> follow "Enable" flow to accept data-sharing for profile generation.
2) API: POST /v1/optimize/profiles?action=generate with model + window_days.
3) CLI: redwood optimize export-profile --generate redwood-7b-v1 --window 7d --out my-profile.yaml

Owner and support
-----------------
- Product owner: Deepa Nair (Optimize)
- Engineering lead: Samir Gupta (Optimize infra)
- Support: support@redwood.ai (use tag: optimize-1.3)
- Runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/optimize-profile-generation-runbook

Known issues and limitations
---------------------------
- Cold telemetry causes conservative cost projections (noted in UI). We plan a future release (1.4) to add synthetic workload injection to reduce conservatism.
- Some legacy Dedicated accounts with strict region restrictions may see profile import failures due to S3 path policies; workaround: use CLI export/import via local file.

Full changelog (selected)
------------------------
- 1.3.0 (2026-02-20): GA release. Added Performance Profiles, Cost Estimator, Console presets, SDK 0.18.0, CLI export-profile.
- 1.3.0-rc1 (2026-02-10): Canary with 10 tenants; fixed profile-merge race leading to duplicate buckets.

Feedback and next steps
-----------------------
- We're actively collecting feedback via the Optimize workspace channel and customer QBRs. Priorities for 1.4: synthetic workload generation, improved estimator calculus for multi-model ensembles, and automated rollback suggestions when recommendations cause SLA regressions.

Appendix: reproducible profile YAML example
-----------------------------------------
name: redwood-13b-v2-chat-short
version: 2
model: redwood-13b-v2
workload: chat-short
buckets:
  - name: short
    pct: 70
    p95_latency_ms: 42
    tokens_per_request: 28
  - name: medium
    pct: 25
    p95_latency_ms: 120
    tokens_per_request: 160
  - name: long
    pct: 5
    p95_latency_ms: 420
    tokens_per_request: 1024
prefix_cache_hit_rate: 0.34
recommendations:
  batching: {max_batch_size: 128, target_window_ms: 8}
  quantization: {profile: qc-2-8bit, expected_cpu_savings_pct: 18}

If you need help migrating or want the Optimize team to run a custom projection for your account, contact Deepa or open a ticket with support (tag: optimize-1.3).

description:
Issue summary:
During a peak ingest window on 2026-03-10 08:45–09:20 PST, Falkon Systems reported that semantic search results returned incorrect document ids for a subset of recently ingested vectors. Simultaneously, audit logs for ingestion latency and billing counters were missing for a 22-minute interval which prevented Falkon from reconciling billed usage.

Impact:
- Customer-facing search returned stale or mismatched results for ~3.2% of queries routed to the dense-index-service in us-west-2.
- Falkon reported a billing delta (observed vs expected) of ~12% for the ingestion window due to missing audit log events.
- Customer escalated to enterprise support; legal/finance looped in for potential credits.

Environment:
- Dedicated deployment (customer-managed VPC peering) in us-west-2 using embedding-encoder-v2 -> dense-index-service (quantized).
- Autoscale pool scaled up at 08:40 but indexer pod restarts were observed between 08:46 and 08:53.

Steps to reproduce (investigation checklist rather than deterministic repro):
1) Ingest high-throughput batch (approx 18k vectors/min) with mixed small and large payloads.
2) Observe indexer task restarts in the dense-index kube pool.
3) Run sample search for recently ingested document ids and compare to precomputed vector->id map.
4) Check audit-log stream for missing log sequence numbers in the 08:45–09:07 window.

Logs / telemetry pointers:
- Observability trace: https://observability.redwood.internal/traces/2026-03-10/idx-mismatch-08-47
- Grafana panel: embeddings-indexer pod restarts: https://grafana.redwood/internal/d/embeddings/indexer-pod-restarts?from=2026-03-10T08:30:00Z&to=2026-03-10T09:30:00Z
- Billing delta dashboard: https://console.redwood/internal/billing/deltas/falkon/2026-03-10

Temporary workaround provided to customer:
- Switched Falkon to a pinned read-route that bypasses the in-flight indexer shard (read-only replication) while we replayed the missing events into the index.
- Issued temporary billing credit to cover immediately visible delta pending reconciliation.

Customer impact and communication:
- Customer was updated on-call and received an interim timeline within 30 minutes. Finance requested formal reconciliation and credits; CS opened this ticket to coordinate post-incident follow-up and evidence delivery.

comments:
2026-03-10T09:05Z - Lydia Park (Customer Success): Customer on the line; reporting returned results pointing to wrong doc ids. They can reproduce against queries hitting us-west. Asked for immediate mitigation and credit hold. Escalating to SRE.
2026-03-10T09:12Z - Priya Nair (SRE): Observed 3 indexer pod restarts starting 08:46. Restarted due to OOM eviction on node gpu-12. Raising hypothesis: burst ingest + large batch led to memory pressure on indexer causing partial write batches to be lost before durable ack to audit log stream.
2026-03-10T09:30Z - Evan Chen (Engineer, Index Service): Found gaps in RSM (replicated state machine) commit log for shard-7 between 08:46:23 and 08:58:41. Some commit entries were retained in local ephemeral storage but not flushed to the audit-log producer before the process restart.
2026-03-10T10:10Z - Raul Mendez (Falkon DevOps): Confirmed behavior from our side: ~11% of recent ingest batch ids not present when we ran verification against our sidecar map. Appreciate the temp read-route fix. Need formal reconciliation file and proof of replay before we close billing request.
2026-03-11T14:22Z - Marco Ortega (Assignee): Replay completed and verified. Attached reconciliation CSV to customer Slack and Confluence. Initiated billing adjustment flow. Planning a postmortem and longer-term fix (persistent commit flush before ack).
2026-03-12T16:00Z - Aisha Kumari (Support): Customer accepted reconciliation and billing credit. Customer asked for a timeline for persistent fix and a test plan for future peak ingest scenarios. Added to post-incident action items.

investigation_notes:
Timeline and findings:
- 08:40: autoscaler increased indexer pool to handle surge; several indexer pods scheduled onto new GPU node types.
- 08:46: node gpu-12 experienced transient memory pressure; kernel OOM killed indexer process leading to abrupt restart.
- 08:46–08:59: RSM commit log had unflushed entries that were not propagated to the audit-log Kafka topic due to in-memory batching.
- 08:59–09:10: indexer recovered, but some vector->id mappings were written to ephemeral local store only; replication missed the durable ack.
Root cause hypothesis:
- Combination of aggressive in-memory batching in the dense-index-service and a recent change that increased batch size for latency optimization caused larger transient memory usage. When a pod was OOM-killed, in-memory batch in producer was lost before flush to audit log, creating both search inconsistency and missing billing events.
Contributing factors:
- Autoscaler packed pods onto a smaller set of nodes during the burst (bin-packing behavior).
- No enforced pre-ack flush semantics for commit batches on indexer restart.
Evidence:
- Commit log gaps in index shard-7 trace.
- Missing sequence ranges in audit-log topic for 08:46–09:07.
- Pod OOM event records on node gpu-12.
- Replayed entries successfully restored search parity and reduced billing delta to <0.2%.

resolution_notes:
Immediate remediation:
1) Executed controlled replay of missing commit ranges into indexer from durable write-ahead log stored in object storage.
2) Temporarily pinned Falkon read-route to read-only replica while replay completed.
3) Issued pro-rated billing credit covering the measured delta; finance notified and reconciliation file delivered.
Permanent fixes applied (short-term):
- Rolled out indexer v2.1.3 which reduces in-memory batch size under memory pressure and forces flush on SIGTERM.
- Autoscaler safety adjustment to avoid bin-packing sensitive pods onto a single node by setting podAntiAffinity hints in dense-index-service deploy.
- Added alert rule for audit-log sequence gaps and a check for commit-flush duration > 2s.
Follow-up verification:
- Post-deploy canary with synthetic high-throughput ingest (20k vectors/min) passed for 3 consecutive 30-minute windows with no commit gaps.
Customer communication:
- Shared reconciliation CSV, replay proof, and audit-log segment references. Finance accepted credit; customer closed the escalation after verification.

Create a durable flush-on-commit test and add to CI for indexer (owner: Evan Chen) - due 2026-03-20
Adjust autoscaler bin-packing policy for indexer class pods (owner: Priya Nair) - due 2026-03-18
Run a cross-team runbook review session with SRE, Indexing, and Billing to validate audit-log handoff semantics (owner: Marco Ortega) - due 2026-03-25
Provide Falkon with a monthly report for two months showing post-fix ingest parity and billing reconciliations (owner: Lydia Park) - deliver by 2026-04-10
Add an observability dashboard to surface audit-log sequence continuity per-customer and per-shard (owner: Observability Team) - due 2026-03-22

Document dsid_a193f9b7483248ad86c52e684d98a760:
description:
Motivation: observed high peak GPU workspace usage for mixed-sequence inference (short+long requests) and multi-query fanout workloads. Existing arena tuning + static activation checkpointing provided good average memory savings but left headroom in two patterns: (1) transient scratch buffer spikes from kernels that allocate per-op temp buffers, and (2) suboptimal kernel choices when the operator fanout (key/value heads * queries) changes runtime characteristics. This PR implements two complimentary mechanisms to reduce peak workspace: 1) dynamic scratch reuse: a runtime scratch allocator that tracks short-lived temp regions by lifetime buckets and reuses buffers across operators within the same execution frame, avoiding repeated allocations and reducing fragmentation; 2) fanout-aware kernel selection: extend the kernel-selector to consider request fanout and KV cache reshaping costs when choosing between tiled/packed attention kernels and the low-memory fused attention kernels.

Summary of changes: implemented a lightweight scratch manager in runtime/scratch_manager.{cpp,h} with a lock-free free-list per-sizeclass and lifetime-tagging. Hooked the scratch allocation path into the kernel interface and modified critical kernels (attention, rotary, layernorm) to request scratch via the manager. Added a fanout heuristic in runtime/kernel_selector.cpp that uses observed Q*K fanout counters (collected per-model) to pick kernels that trade compute for lower transient memory. Added a compatibility path so that models pinned to older kernel profiles will continue to run the legacy selector. Integrated unit and microbenchmarks under benchmark-lab/ with a new benchmark script fanout_memory_profile.py and an end-to-end e2e memory test that simulates interleaved short/long requests.

Performance results: on A100-40GB with GPT-2 style model (1B params) and mixed workload (50% seq_len=32, 50% seq_len=1024) peak workspace dropped from 16.8GB to 12.1GB (~28% reduction). For high-fanout Q=16 tests the transient peak reduced by ~34% when the fanout-aware kernel was selected. End-to-end latency impact: median latency for long requests increased ~2.3% in a worst-case knob-on scenario where the low-memory kernel is used; this is within the SLA tradeoff and we expose a config flag to prefer latency vs memory at policy-level.

Compatibility and rollout strategy: feature gated behind runtime flag runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled=false by default in this PR; we plan a phased rollout: enable on non-production clusters for 2 weeks, then opt-in for Dedicated clusters with memory pressure, finally flip default after one week of metrics monitoring. Kernel selection heuristic is additive and can be disabled with runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic=false. Added telemetry metrics: runtime.scratch_reuse.alloc_reuse_ratio, kernel_selector.fanout_decision_count and memory.scratch_peak_by_model.

Testing: added unit tests for scratch manager lifecycle and size-class reuse; added integration tests that assert no OOM on synthetic high-fanout scenarios; ran infra e2e-bench and observed stable results. CI: linux-unit-tests, cuda-smoke, and e2e-bench run green in the final run. Created a small fuzz harness to ensure lifetime tagging prevents use-after-free across frames.

Backward compatibility: no breaking API changes; the kernel interface signature extended with an optional scratch_token but remains backward-compatible with default nullptr behavior. Documentation: runtime/README.md updated with configuration knobs, and redwood-docs/ops/gpu-memory-tuning.md includes recommended settings for Dedicated customers.

Notes: this PR intentionally avoids changing global arena sizing heuristics in this iteration — that will be a follow-up to measure impact of scratch reuse on arena fragmentation (ENG-1919). Also, we identified a secondary opportunity to compress KV cache layout when fanout>8; tracked separately under ENG-1875.

review_comments:
Alex Ortega: Nit - please add a short note on concurrency model for the free-lists. Also, can we expose a knob to limit max per-frame scratch?
Maya Chen (author): Added concurrency notes in scratch_manager.h and exposed runtime.scratch_reuse.max_frame_scratch (default large).
Priya Nair: Verified benchmarks locally on p4d; I saw similar 26-30% peak reduction. One request: add a test ensuring legacy kernel path still used when model pinned.
Maya Chen (author): Added model-pinned test and compatibility checks in kernel_selector.
Samir Patel: Approved after CI green. Left a follow-up to audit arena metrics (ENG-1919).

release_notes:
Reduced peak GPU workspace by ~28% for mixed short/long workloads via dynamic scratch buffer reuse.
Added fanout-aware kernel selection which reduces transient memory for high-query fanout workloads.
Exposed runtime knobs to tune memory vs latency tradeoffs: runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled and runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic.

description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that new service account tokens cannot perform delegated admin ops (user management and billing read) after migrating to a private deployment token broker. Impact: Multiple automation jobs and SRE runbooks fail; customer-facing admin UI returns 403 when acting-as a service account. Environment: Private deployment (Aurora private VPC), prod - us-east, Redwood private control plane with identity-proxy v1.9.2 and token-broker v0.8.2. Observed start: 2026-03-09 18:20 UTC. Business impact: Blocks Aurora's automated onboarding and scheduled invoice exports; they are a HIPAA-regulated customer and cannot proceed with several tasks until impersonation works.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Create service account 'onboard-runner@aurora' in Aurora tenant. 2) Request token via Aurora's token-broker that exchanges internal long-lived key for a short-lived access token. 3) Call Admin API /v1/admin/users with X-Redwood-Impersonate header set to 'user:alice@aurora.com' and Authorization: Bearer <token>. 4) Observe 403 'insufficient_scope' returned. 5) Same call with the original human user's token succeeds.

logs_snippets:
identity-proxy (2026-03-09T18:21:12Z) WARN request_id=3fa2ed 'token scope mismatch: expected [admin:impersonate,admin:users] got [service:read,service:write]'; admin-api (2026-03-09T18:21:12Z) ERROR request_id=3fa2ed 'authorization failed for impersonation: missing permission admin:impersonate'; token-broker (2026-03-09T18:20:58Z) INFO 'issued token sub=svc:onboard-runner aud=redwood-api scope="service:read service:write" exp=2026-03-09T19:20:58Z'

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: token-broker is attaching default service scopes rather than tenant-mapped impersonation scopes. Confirmed that tenant mapping rule set 'aurora-mappings' in token-broker was not applied after the private control-plane upgrade (v0.8.0->v0.8.2). Identity-proxy performs additional scope filtering: it strips any scope not in allowed_scope_table for service accounts. Allowed_scope_table for Aurora appears to be stale and only lists 'service:*' scopes. Replayed token exchange locally with debug flags: mapping step returned intended impersonation grant, but the token-broker's caching layer served an earlier cached token profile. Cache invalidation appears tied to last-deploy timestamp; deployment delta on 2026-03-08 likely left cache entries inconsistent. Cross-referenced with INT-4112 where SRE rolled out token-broker config but noted a missing cache-buster flag. Observed related PR that changed default scopes (see related_github_prs).

workaround:
Temporary workaround provided to customer: 1) Use a human admin token for critical admin calls. 2) As short-term automated fix, update identity-proxy config to whitelist the service account 'onboard-runner@aurora' with an explicit mapping to include admin:impersonate and admin:users. Provided steps and a patch snippet to Aurora engineering. Note this bypass is allowed only in their private VPC and will be removed after full fix.

resolution:
Investigating full fix: coordinated deploy sequence to invalidate token-broker cache and roll token-broker + identity-proxy together with a cache-buster flag. SRE to schedule an out-of-band config reload for Aurora's token-broker and then redeploy identity-proxy v1.9.3 which contains a protective check to reject stale cached scope profiles. After reload, verified token exchange returns token with scopes [admin:impersonate,admin:users] and admin API calls succeed. Resolution steps documented in confluence page and will be included in a postmortem. Customer notified and temporary whitelist removed. Planned follow-up: add integration test in CI to simulate config drift and prevent mapping cache staleness.
