Document dsid_de82a5f7140142f89781f2bf2d56cdca:
Purpose:
This is a compact, portable benchmark note that experiments with a 'phase portrait' view of throughput vs latency across three representative interactive workloads. The goal is a lightweight heuristic we can run in-console to quickly show tradeoffs between lower unit-cost throughput and percentile latencies for different model/hardware/batching choices.

Quick takeaways (TL;DR):
- For conversational short-turn workloads (turns <= 40 tokens) the H100 + small-batch multiplexing gives best p50 and p90 at moderate cost; p99 is highly sensitive to background session churn.
- For longer-turn generation (avg 300 tokens), batching (window 25–50ms) on A100-like instances recovers ~20–35% dollars-per-token vs aggressive single-request fastpath.
- Int8-quantized 34B reduces cost 40–50% at a modest p90 increase (~5–15ms) in our configs — good candidate for mid-tier SLAs.

Testbed & assumptions:
- Date: May 2029, quick lab runs in eu-west-1 dedicated test pool (sandbox).
- Models: rw-7b-fp16, rw-34b-int8, rw-70b-fp16 (representative family: small, mid, large).
- Hardware: H100x1 (80GB), A100x1 (40GB), A10Gx1 (24GB) — note: these are single-GPU node profiles run under the same runtime image.
- Network: intra-region, measured client RTT mean 5ms.
- Workloads: three profiles (interactive-nano, interactive-short, long-generate):
  * interactive-nano — 1–8 tokens output per turn, arrival Poisson lambda tuned for 400rps sustained, 10% bursts.
  * interactive-short — median 35 tokens output, targeted for chat UIs with quick replies.
  * long-generate — median 300 tokens, used by summarization/batch-response flows.
- Economic: rough spot-equivalent cost used for dollars-per-1M-tokens (includes amortized GPU runtime + networking overhead); absolute numbers are lab approximations for comparison only.

Measurement method:
- Each workload run for 15 minutes after a 2-minute warmup.
- Metrics collected: throughput (tokens/sec), p50/p90/p99 request latency (ms) measured end-to-end, throughput-utilization (GPU cycles estimated), and estimated $/1M tokens (runtime-only).
- Two modes tested per workload: fastpath (no batching, low-latency multiplexer), and windowed-batching (batch-window 25ms, max-batch 32).

Representative results (aggregated):
Note: numbers are simplified to highlight shape, not a rigorous stat-run.

1) interactive-nano (short token replies)
- rw-7b-fp16 on H100 (fastpath): throughput 9.8k tokens/s, p50 6ms, p90 14ms, p99 42ms, $/1M tok = $4.2
- rw-7b-fp16 on H100 (window25ms): throughput 16.1k tokens/s, p50 9ms, p90 22ms, p99 75ms, $/1M tok = $2.6
- rw-34b-int8 on H100 (fastpath): throughput 6.1k tokens/s, p50 12ms, p90 28ms, p99 90ms, $/1M tok = $6.8
- rw-34b-int8 on H100 (window25ms): throughput 10.9k tokens/s, p50 18ms, p90 38ms, p99 110ms, $/1M tok = $4.1

2) interactive-short (chat-like ~35 tokens)
- rw-34b-int8 on A100 (fastpath): throughput 1.1k tokens/s, p50 22ms, p90 58ms, p99 160ms, $/1M tok = $12.4
- rw-34b-int8 on A100 (window25ms): throughput 1.7k tokens/s, p50 30ms, p90 85ms, p99 210ms, $/1M tok = $8.6
- rw-70b-fp16 on H100 (fastpath): throughput 0.7k tokens/s, p50 45ms, p90 120ms, p99 380ms, $/1M tok = $28.9

3) long-generate (avg 300 tokens)
- rw-70b-fp16 on A100 (fastpath): throughput 430 tok/s, p50 310ms, p90 820ms, p99 2.7s, $/1M tok = $31.6
- rw-70b-fp16 on A100 (window50ms): throughput 560 tok/s, p50 380ms, p90 910ms, p99 3.1s, $/1M tok = $23.8
- rw-34b-int8 on A100 (window50ms): throughput 810 tok/s, p50 240ms, p90 560ms, p99 1.9s, $/1M tok = $12.7

Phase portrait sketches (ASCII) — throughput on X axis (tokens/sec), latency percentiles on Y. Each row is a rough slice per workload/config.

interactive-nano (throughput vs p90):
[ 5k ]  * rw-7b fastpath p90=14ms    * rw-34b fastpath p90=28ms
[10k ]  * rw-7b window25 p90=22ms   * rw-34b window25 p90=38ms
[15k ]  * rw-7b window25 (peak)

interactive-short (throughput vs p90):
[ 0.5k ] * rw-70b fastpath p90=120ms
[ 1.0k ] * rw-34b fastpath p90=58ms
[ 1.7k ] * rw-34b window25 p90=85ms

long-generate (throughput vs p90):
[ 0.4k ] * rw-70b fastpath p90=820ms
[ 0.56k] * rw-70b window50 p90=910ms
[ 0.81k] * rw-34b window50 p90=560ms

Interpretation & guidance:
- The phase portrait exposes two useful decision axes: (1) target throughput band (tokens/sec) and (2) target percentile latency. For super-low-latency UIs (p90 < 30ms), small models on H100 with fastpath are best despite higher $/M tokens at scale.
- For mid-latency SLAs (p90 30–120ms) and cost sensitivity, rw-34b-int8 with windowed batching on A100 becomes attractive — good balance of dollars and p90.
- For heavy long generation, batching recovers material $/token improvements; pick larger batch windows (40–60ms) but watch p99 tail growth.
- p99 remains dominated by session-level jitter (session churn, cache warmups). Improving p99 will likely require admission controls or prioritized fastpaths rather than only kernel-level tuning.

Recommended knobs to surface in Console for quick decisions:
- Phase portrait toggles: select workload archetype + target percentile slider (p50/p90/p99) -> show cost delta and suggested model/hardware/batch-length.
- Quick-sim: run a 2-minute micro-run that returns an annotated portrait with estimated $/1M tok. (Use sandbox cap and fail-safe).
- Presets: low-latency (p90<30ms), balanced (p90 30–120ms), deep-generation (p90>200ms). Each preset maps to a recommended profile (model + hardware + batching).

Next steps / follow-ups:
- Run a controlled 5x repeat for a narrower confidence interval on p99 for the interactive-short profile; measure with enforced synthetic user churn.
- Add memory-pressure tests for A10G vs A100 for cost-sensitive tiers.
- Prototype the Console quick-sim and validate UX with a couple of internal customers (SEs).

Open questions / caveats:
- These runs are single-node. Multi-GPU sharding and memory-pinned tiling will change throughput curves for rw-70b; expect non-linear scaling.
- Cost numbers are lab approximations; company pricing model (Dedicated vs Hosted) will change break-evens.
- Edge region network delta (client RTT > 30ms) will shift the sweet spot toward batching for interactive workloads.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intended as a heuristic artifact for product/console decisions rather than a formal paper. Please flag any obvious omissions or ask for additional per-node profiler traces (we captured GPU utilization and nvlink counters in the raw logs).
- If this heuristic looks useful, I can port it to a small Notebook that runs inside the Console sandbox and emits the phase portrait + recommended knobs automatically.

-- Claire

 'Within 0 to 5 minutes, acknowledge the alert, open the incident bridge call (Zoom or Meet), create the incident channel (for example, #inc-xxxx), and post an initial status update.'
 'Within 5 to 10 minutes, perform quick impact triage by confirming affected services via dashboards, classifying scope (regional vs global and data plane vs control plane), and producing a short impact statement.'
 'Within 10 to 20 minutes, stabilize traffic using graduated controls such as rate limits and routing or dividing traffic to healthy regions, and where available fall back to lighter model variants or reduced sequence-length modes.'
 'Within 20 to 40 minutes, execute a hotfix window by applying validated, small, reversible mitigations from the relevant service runbooks and document all changes in the incident channel.'

eval_reference.gold_answer: Follow the Ten-Step Restoration Sprint: (1) Acknowledge the alert and open the incident bridge (Zoom/Meet), create the incident channel (#inc-xxxx), and post initial status (0-5m). (2) Perform quick impact triage by confirming affected services via dashboards and classifying scope (regional/global; data/control plane), then produce a short impact statement (5-10m). (3) Stabilize traffic using graduated controls (rate limits, routing/traffic division to healthy regions) and, where available, fall back to lighter model variants or reduced sequence-length modes (10-20m). (4) Execute a hotfix window by applying validated, small, reversible mitigations from the relevant service runbooks and document all changes in the incident channel (20-40m). (5) Validate restoration by running synthetic probes and verifying p95/p99 latency and error rates are returning to baseline, capturing pre/post metrics and commands used (30-50m).

Question: During a major production outage, what is the prescribed sequence of actions for the first 60 to 90 minutes, from opening the live coordination call through confirming the service is healthy again?

Document dsid_25b0de9bfa854d3c9acfa961555c9d45:
Overview

Purpose: This handbook describes a focused, repeatable Ten-Step Restoration Sprint used during multi-system outages and pairs that operational flow with a structured shadow-mentor program to accelerate oncall proficiency. It is intended for first responders, bridge operators, service owners, and SRE mentors.

Scope: Applies to production incidents that meet SLO-impacting criteria (see SLO thresholds section). Not intended for low-severity config errors or scheduled maintenance.

Owner: Eng SRE team. Primary contact: oncall-lead@redwood.example.com.

Quick links: runbook library, status page templates, postmortem template, incident evidence checklist.

Audience and roles

- Incident Initiator: the first person to acknowledge the alert and call the bridge.
- Bridge Operator: facilitates the incident bridge, coordinates comms, and enforces the Ten-Step Sprint cadence.
- Primary Resolver: service owner(s) leading technical work for the impacted service(s).
- Secondary Resolvers: cross-functional engineers called in to assist (networking, infra, runtime).
- Shadow: junior responder who observes and documents actions during the sprint.
- Mentor: senior SRE who leads post-incident coaching and retro facilitation.

How to use this document

- Use the numbered Ten-Step Sprint for initial restoration (first 60–90 minutes).
- Run the shadow mentoring checklist in parallel to create training artefacts.
- After containment, follow the Post-Incident Evidence & Draft Postmortem template included below.

SLO thresholds that trigger Ten-Step Sprint

| Severity | Symptom | SLO impact | Trigger |
|---------|---------|------------|---------|
| Sev1 | Total region outage for hosted API | >= 99.5% reduction in success rate for 5+ minutes | Auto-trigger after 3x alert flood or manual bridge |
| Sev2 | Significant latency increase | > 200ms p95 increase across customer requests for 15+ minutes | Review/bridge by oncall |

Ten-Step Restoration Sprint (primary runbook)

1) Acknowledge & Bridge (0–5m)
   - Incident Initiator: acknowledge the alert in PagerDuty and create a bridge (Zoom/Google Meet).
   - Bridge Operator: open the incident channel (#inc-xxxx) and post initial status: impacted services, region, estimated blast radius, primary contact.
   - Shadow: note timestamps, alert IDs, and initial metrics snapshot.

2) Quick Impact Triage (5–10m)
   - Primary Resolver: confirm service(s) affected using dashboards (console/model-serving, ingress, and edge metrics).
   - Bridge: classify impact (regional vs. global, data plane vs. control plane).
   - Output: short impact statement to stakeholders.

3) Stabilize Traffic (10–20m)
   - If applicable, apply graduated traffic control: rate-limits, scaled back routing policies, or traffic-division to healthy regions.
   - Use fallback model variants or reduced sequence length mode where supported to temporarily reduce CPU/GPU pressure.

4) Hotfix Window (20–40m)
   - Primary Resolver and Secondary Resolvers: run validated mitigation steps from specific service runbooks (see related runbook IDs).
   - Keep changes small, reversible, and documented in the incident channel.

5) Validate Restoration (30–50m)
   - Run synthetic probes against restored endpoints. Confirm p95/p99 latency and error-rate trends returning to baseline.
   - Shadow: capture pre/post metric snapshots and the commands used.

6) Customer Status & Tiered Notifications (immediately after validation)
   - Bridge Operator: publish customer-facing status update using the template below.
   - For enterprise customers impacted by the incident, trigger account-level outreach per the escalation matrix.

7) Stabilization Monitoring (50–90m)
   - Maintain increased sampling and tracing for 3x normal volume for 90 minutes.
   - Set temporary alerts at tighter thresholds (e.g., 50% of SLO slack) to catch reversion.

8) Evidence Collection & Triage for Postmortem (start while stabilizing)
   - Collect logs, traces, config diffs, rollout metadata, and full command history. Attach artifacts to the incident ticket.
   - Shadow: curate a short evidence index with direct links.

9) Restore Normal Ops & Runbook Handover (90–120m)
   - Roll back temporary mitigations and revert traffic controls when confident.
   - Primary Resolver: schedule a 60-minute triage deep-dive with the mentor and product owner within 48 hours.

10) Close Bridge & Draft Postmortem (post sprint)
   - Bridge Operator: move the channel to read-only and create a draft postmortem using the included template.
   - Mentor: assign action owners with clear SLAs for mitigation items.

Shadow-Mentor Program (parallel process)

Purpose: Turn incidents into repeatable learning opportunities and accelerate new responder ramp.

Shadow checklist (during sprint):
- Record timestamps for each decision and action.
- Note who is contacted and the exact commands or consoles used.
- Capture any runbook gaps or ambiguous steps.
- Collect a short list of 3 teachable moments for the retro.

Mentor responsibilities (post sprint):
- Within 48 hours: review the evidence index and draft postmortem with the shadow.
- Within 7 days: run a 30–60 minute learning session with the wider oncall rota covering the teachable moments and suggested runbook updates.
- Ensure at least one runbook edit or clarification is merged per incident for which the shadow prepared artifacts.

Escalation matrix (quick reference)

- Local service issue -> Primary Resolver -> Service Lead (15 min)
- Cross-service or infra -> Add Secondary Resolver(s) + SRE oncall (10 min)
- Prolonged SLO loss > 1 hour -> Paging to Eng Director + Product Ops (escalate at 60m)
- Customer-impacting > 4 hours -> Executive status + CS/AE briefing (escalate at 4h)

Status Page & Customer Comms Templates

Public status template (to be posted on status.redwood.example.com):
- Title: Incident - {service} - {brief cause} (Region)
- Impact: Short sentence (e.g., "Customers in us-west experienced elevated errors and increased latency between 12:03–12:45 UTC.")
- Current status: Investigating / Identified / Mitigating / Restored / Monitoring
- Next update: {time + 30m}
- Notes: High-level mitigation steps and workarounds.

Enterprise account brief (email/Slack DM):
- Subject: Incident update — {service} — {short impact statement}
- Body: One-sentence impact, actions taken, ETA for more info, contact person (SRE lead and AM), apologies and credit guidance (if applicable).

Post-Incident Evidence & Draft Postmortem Template

1) Summary (1–3 sentences): What happened and visible customer impact.
2) Timeline: concise, timestamped actions (use ISO-8601).
3) Root cause hypothesis / final root cause: technical summary.
4) Contributing factors: people, process, tooling, and telemetry gaps.
5) Mitigation and long-term fixes: owner and ETA.
6) Customer impact and remediation: crediting plan, customer comms sent.
7) Evidence index: links to logs, traces, recordings, rollout IDs, and config diffs.
8) Retrospective notes and teachable moments.

Runbook governance and ownership

- Each service runbook must list a primary owner, secondary owner, and last-tested date.
- Runbooks must include safe roll-forward and roll-back commands and a quick-impact checklist.
- Runbook review cadence: quarterly for high-risk services, bi-annual for others.

Game-day & Mentored Simulation schedule

- Quarterly Game-Days: 3 planned scenarios per quarter (network partition, kv-cache storm, auth tier regression). At least one scenario must use the shadow-mentor pairing.
- Shadow simulations: monthly 60-minute labs where a shadow leads a mini-restoration and a mentor grades the artifacts produced.

Metrics and KPIs to track program health

- Mean Time To Restore (MTTR) — target: reduce by 20% year-over-year.
- Shadow ramp time — % of shadows qualified to be solo oncall within 4 months.
- Runbook churn — number of runbook edits per incident (target: >=1 edit/incident).
- Postmortem completion rate — 100% for Sev1/Sev2 within 7 days.

Appendices

A. Evidence collection checklist (CLI commands and dashboards)
- curl and synthetic probe examples, steps to download logs from logging cluster, query examples for traces, recommended span sampling rates.

B. Restorative CLI snippets (examples with placeholders)
- Rollout rollback: 
  gcloud run services update-traffic SERVICE --to-revisions REVISION --region REGION
- Temporary rate-limit (kong example):
  curl -X POST https://api-gateway/config -d '{"limit":100}'

C. Customer status example (realistic copy)
- \"12:10 UTC — We are investigating increased error rates for text-generation in us-west. Our mitigation is to route new requests to our fallback model variant which reduces throughput but restores successful responses. Next update: 12:40 UTC.\"

D. Learning outcomes rubric for mentors
- Level 1: Shadow can summarize timeline and reproduce evidence index without guidance.
- Level 2: Shadow can perform 30% of mitigation steps under supervision.
- Level 3: Shadow can lead a mini-sprint with a mentor ready to intervene.

E. Change log
- 2025-11-02: v0.1 created by Priya Nair.
- 2026-01-05: clarified enterprise escalation thresholds (reviewer: Ethan Murphy).
- 2026-03-15: added evidence collection CLI snippets and learning rubric (reviewer: Lina Kovács).

Related resources

- Runbook index (link to internal runbook library)
- Incident postmortem template (link)
- Status page authoring guide (link)

End of document.

description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that when a streaming SSE connection briefly drops during a TLS renegotiation event at the edge, the client receives a truncated final output: the last sentence or final punctuation is missing and no explicit end marker arrives. The server logs show the completion event emitted, but the client-side stream terminates early after reconnect.

Impact:
- Affects Inkling Health's production inference pipelines in eu-west.
- Partial outputs break downstream post-processing and fail schema validation for their clinical note ingestion (automated).
- Observed on ~3% of long-running streaming sessions during peak load windows.

Environment:
- prod (eu-west) behind vendor edge proxy (CloudEdge) + vendor CDN.
- Clients use SSE long-polling from browser and also a Node.js backend that implements reconnect/resume.
- Model: rw-instruct-large-v1, typical max_tokens ~1024, average response length ~600 tokens.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start a long streaming generation from eu-west with prefix that yields a long final sentence.
2) Simulate TLS renegotiation at the edge by triggering a short RST/reconnect (they used their synthetic traffic tool to flip the client IP and trigger a rehandshake).
3) Observe returned stream on client: most of the time it resumes fine, but in a subset the final sentence is cut off and no terminal event arrives.

Expected behavior:
- Client should receive full streamed tokens including terminal metadata (choice completion). Reconnect/resume should either stitch output seamlessly or include an explicit end marker.

Actual behavior:
- Server emits completion and logs show terminal event for the request id, but the client sees an abrupt stop after an earlier chunk. No explicit "[DONE]" or terminal JSON arrives. Reconnect handshake shows success, but resumed stream never emits the missing trailing tokens.

Workaround (customer):
- Increase client-side post-reconnect polling window and re-request tail tokens using non-streaming completion API; this recovers text but adds latency and cost.

Attachments:
- customer provided curl and Node.js reproducer, sample client traces, and a HAR file (attached separately in support portal).

steps_to_reproduce:
Open SSE stream to /v1/stream with a long prompt that generates a long final sentence
From a test machine behind the same edge, flip IP or trigger short RST to force TLS rehandshake at the edge
Allow reconnect to occur and observe client-side stream events and final terminal event presence
Repeat under load to increase probability of occurrence

logs:
2026-03-12T08:23:45Z serving-runtime: request=req_6f3a terminal_emitted=true seq=0x1ee logsize=1024
2026-03-12T08:23:45Z api-gateway: proxy_write returned 0 bytes to edge worker (code=EPIPE) connection_id=conn_9b
2026-03-12T08:23:46Z edge-proxy: TLS renegotiate start connection_id=conn_9b client_ip=203.0.113.45
2026-03-12T08:23:46Z edge-proxy: coalesced-keepalive zero-length write observed, buffering=true
2026-03-12T08:23:46Z serving-runtime: request=req_6f3a connection_lost_event=true, terminal_delivery_confirmed=false

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: edge proxy zero-length write or buffering during TLS renegotiation causes downstream client to interpret stream as complete. Reproduced in lab by enabling 'edge-worker buffering' and forcing a TLS rehandshake; observed identical symptom. Further narrowed to case where proxy coalesces an SSI keepalive packet with the final JSON boundary, then performs connection migration and the client-side SSE parser treats the next boundary as a new stream rather than continuation.

What we checked:
- Server emits final JSON and exits stream (confirmed).
- Gateway recorded a 0-byte write to the edge worker immediately prior to client disconnect.
- Client reconnects and requests resume token, but resume offset points to earlier chunk (off-by-one) because the proxy suppressed the terminal delimiter during buffering.

Immediate mitigation tried:
- Applied an API-gateway config to insert an explicit "event: end" / "data: [DONE]" line before flushing final chunk for eu-west. Reduced occurrence rate from ~3% to ~0.1% in canary traffic.

Next steps:
- Collaborate with edge-proxy vendor to disable coalescing of zero-length keepalives for SSE endpoints, or to preserve final JSON boundaries across renegotiation.
- Add extra server-side terminal marker for SSE (backport to stable) to make client reconcilers robust to proxy buffering.
- Add more robust resume offset verification on server to ensure resume doesn't skip final tokens.

resolution:
Mitigation applied: gateway now injects an explicit SSE end marker before connection handoff in eu-west canary. Customer workaround documented. Root cause vendor coordination required for permanent fix.

resolution_notes:
Applied canary change 2026-03-13 21:12 UTC to eu-west API-gateway fleet: insert explicit terminal SSE event prior to drain. Monitoring shows reduced error rate. Opening a vendor support ticket with CloudEdge (ticket CE-5542) to request fix for zero-length coalescing during TLS renegotiate. Engineering to prepare backport for streaming runtime to include optional double-terminal marker.

Call notes (2024-09-17) — discovery with ValeHealth (CTO: Aaron Li, SecOps: Maya Singh, Arch: Dan Ochoa)

- Context: ValeHealth is a mid-sized digital health provider planning to run conversational triage + discharge-summary generation inside their data center (air-gapped option discussed). They must not send PHI outside their network. Primary asks: private control plane with VPC peering to their corp network, KMS/HSM integration for key material, audit logs for every inference, and 12 month retention for audit records.

- Key constraints called out by customer:
  - PHI: full PHI scope, must meet SOC2 + HIPAA controls.
  - Network: strict egress rules; anything that talks to hosted control plane needs explicit allow list.
  - Hardware: they will provision 2x A100 80GB per zone initially, plan to add 4x after pilot.
  - Throughput target: 12 concurrent triage sessions, average 40 tokens/response, target p95 token latency per token <= 90ms (end-to-end p95 for a 200-token response <= 18s) — customer expects interactive feel.
  - Burst behavior: expect spikes morning 8–10AM and post-op 3–5PM.

- Functional reqs (high level):
  1) On-prem Redwood Private with local model hosting and local KV/prefix caching.
  2) VPC-only control plane connectivity (can run in their VPC or peered) — no public IPs on inference nodes.
  3) KMS or HSM integration: must support AWS CloudHSM or on-prem Thales via KMIP.
  4) Audit logs: immutable tamper-evident logs for each request (user id, route, token counts, prompt hash).
  5) Structured outputs: discharge summary templates + JSON schema enforcement + function-calling hooks.
  6) Streaming WebSocket support for triage chat UI.
  7) Canary deploys and fast rollback; cannot have model drift affecting PHI fidelity.

- Non-functional / ops notes:
  - Warmup: with A100s expect ~20–40s cold start for large Llama-family models to reach peak throughput. Need pre-warm policy for scheduled windows.
  - Batch sizing: small batch sizes to preserve latency SLO; recommend continuous batching with low-latency cutoff (15ms).
  - KV cache: prefix caching will significantly cut token generation for repetitive triage prompts; plan to instrument cache hit rate in pilot.
  - Quantization: they want FP16 or 4-bit quant for cost; warn: 4-bit may slightly degrade token-level probabilities -> risks for hallucination in medical text. We should plan eval prompts + acceptance criteria.
  - Telemetry: customer wants token-level cost/latency breakdown exported to Splunk (on-prem) every 1 minute.

- Gotchas / open technical risks:
  - Network egress policy: Control plane components that check for model updates may require egress. Customer requires whitelisting; need to enumerate IPs and acceptable update cadence. Offline update flow (airgap) must be documented.
  - HSM cert exchange: support for KMIP versions and cert rotation timeline — Ops needs runbook for emergency rotation.
  - Model licensing: some open models require attribution; legal to confirm whether ValeHealth agrees to the model license and distribution in-country.
  - Tokenization mismatch: current front-end uses older tokenizer library; we need to validate prompt/encoding parity to avoid token count surprises and cost overruns.
  - Long output trimming: discharge summaries sometimes exceed 1,000 tokens; need to support streaming + progressive flush to UI and chunked audit records.

  1) PHI redaction test: send synthetic PHI and ensure logs do not contain raw PHI in plaintext except authorized fields.
  2) Latency test: 200-token generation p50 < 2s, p95 < 18s under steady load of 12 concurrent sessions.
  3) Regression test: standard eval suite of 150 prompts for hallucination / clinical accuracy; failure rate < 3% vs baseline model.

- Quick numbers back-of-envelope (for sizing discussion):
  - If we run Llama-3-classic-70B FP16 on A100-80: single GPU peak concurrency for low-latency ~6–8 simultaneous single-stream sessions (depends on context length). With 2 GPUs expect ~12–16 sessions — matches their initial 12 target.

eval_reference.gold_answer:

summary_long:
Request to implement a single, auditable automation that provisions short-lived research sandboxes for Model Eval and Research pods. When a developer requests a sandbox via a JIRA issue, the automation should: 1) create a namespaced Jira project or project-space (scoped to the team), 2) instantiate Confluence child pages from a 'sandbox playbook' template, 3) provision a private Slack channel using enforced naming conventions and invite the requester + approvals group, 4) attach an approval step (Slack or Okta group approver) before the channel becomes active, 5) schedule automatic archival after a configurable TTL (default 30 days) with a grace-renew option, and 6) emit an audit export (S3) of channel membership and Confluence snapshot at archive time. This is intended to replace ad-hoc manual requests and ensure a reproducible, auditable lifecycle with minimal engineering touchpoints.

impact:
Reduces manual overhead for platform team, speeds up Model Eval/Research experiment setup, and ensures required compliance artifacts (audit exports) are captured for internal audits. Current ad-hoc process creates inconsistent naming, missing playbooks, and undocumented Slack channels.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Creating a Jira issue in project 'Sandbox Requests' triggers the automation. 2) A Jira subproject or issue namespace is created with templated issue types (Experiment, Runbook, Cleanup). 3) Confluence page(s) created from 'Sandbox Playbook' template and linked to the Jira project. 4) Private Slack channel created with naming convention (sandbox-{team}-{shortid}), approver group notified, and channel remains muted until approver accepts. 5) Archive job triggers after TTL and stores an S3 snapshot of Confluence pages + membership CSV. 6) Logs of all steps appear in the central ops log index, and a sample audit export passes security review. 7) Automated renew (extend TTL) works from within Slack with a single command by the owner.

implementation_notes:
Preferred approach: a lightweight orchestration Lambda (or internal worker) that calls the Jira REST API for project/issue templates, Confluence API for page creation, Slack SCIM / Conversations API to create channels, and Okta API to validate approver membership. Use a single service account with scoped permissions and rotate keys via KMS. Store TTL config in a small DynamoDB table keyed by sandbox id. Emit CloudWatch (or our existing observability pipeline) metrics for success/failure. See PRs referenced in related_github_prs for initial scripts.

notes_for_security:
Security review required for: service account scope, S3 bucket lifecycle and encryption, Confluence page export sanitization (make sure secrets are redacted), Slack membership export handling. Proposed S3 path: s3://redwood-audit/sandboxes/{sandbox-id}/. Use SSE-KMS with restricted access and retention per compliance team guidance.

description:
Motivation: customers using function/tool-calling and structured output have limited ability to correlate tool calls to per-route metrics, and streaming JSONL outputs lack stable tags for downstream log processors. This PR attaches per-route metric tags to function-call events, enriches JSONL streaming output with consistent telemetry headers, and adds trace propagation across the OpenAI-compat adapter layer. Changes aim to improve observability without changing public API semantics. Summary of changes: 1) Add per-route "route.tags" metadata to function-call events emitted by the gateway and runtime; 2) Emit a compact telemetry header ("rwid, srv, route, call_idx") at the start of streaming JSONL chunks to enable log reassembly; 3) Propagate distributed trace context and span IDs into function-call instrumentation and structured logs; 4) Update openai-compat adapter to translate OpenAI-style "request_id" into rwid and include route tags for compatibility; 5) Add unit and integration tests covering streaming reassembly and metric label cardinality limits; 6) Add doc comments and console notes for admins about limiting custom route tags. Checklist: - [x] Add telemetry header and tests - [x] Preserve streaming shape for openai-compat clients - [x] Ensure route tag cardinality cap (100) enforced - [x] Add end-to-end smoke test against mock tool runner - [x] Update docs and changelog Impact: no user-facing API change; observability improvements are additive. Rollout plan: feature gated behind experiment flag "obs.route_tags_tool_calls" for three days in canary, then staged rollout to 25% traffic, then full rollout assuming no regressions. Monitoring: added alerts for spike in unique route tags and increased rate of incomplete streams.

Document dsid_b4bd83b46612452e858bc02b380082e2:
Summary
-------
This document defines a reproducible protocol to convert probe heatmaps (telemetry-driven failure density views) into rollout decisions for model promotions, quantization migrations, and configuration changes. The goal is to make decisions auditable, time-bounded, and aligned with SLOs so product and ops can act consistently across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope
-----
- Applies to any promotion or rollout that is gated by probe-driven quality signals: model promotions, quantized rollouts, prompt rewrites, and routing policy changes.
- Focuses on probe heatmaps produced by the eval harness and live shadow probes (not human labelling pipelines).
- Excludes legislated/regulatory decisions (finance/compliance) - see separate compliance approval flow.

Key definitions
---------------
- Probe heatmap: a time-windowed 2D histogram where rows are probes (slice identifiers) and columns are failure modes (fidelity, hallucination, latency, embeddings drift). Each cell contains count and a severity score.
- Decision score (DS): a normalized scalar computed from heatmap aggregates that maps to GO / CAUTION / HOLD / ROLLBACK actions.
- Tiered slice: pre-defined group of probes that share an SLO (e.g., CriticalTenantFlows, BillingIntents, LowRiskExplorations).

Inputs required
---------------
1) Heatmap snapshot covering the last N hours (default N=24) with per-probe metrics: total_calls, failure_count, avg_severity, median_latency_ms, embedding_drift_score.
2) Active rollout plan metadata: target model id, variant (quantized/float16), percent_traffic, scheduled_start.
3) Baseline reference heatmap from the control population (previous model or canary).
4) SLO manifest for target slices (SLO window, allowed error budget, latency SLO).
5) Operational constraints: maintenance windows, capacity headroom, and dependency map.

Decision scoring algorithm (summary)
----------------------------------
We compute three sub-scores and aggregate them into DS (range 0..100):

- StabilityScore (SS): weighted failure density normalized by probe priority. Formula: SS = 100 * sum_p (w_p * (failure_count_p / max(1,total_calls_p))) / sum_p(w_p)
- LatencyPenalty (LP): 10 * max(0, (median_latency_ms - latency_slo_ms) / latency_slo_ms) clipped at 30
- DriftFactor (DF): 50 * embedding_drift_score_95pct_quantile normalized against baseline drift

Final Decision Score: DS = clamp(SS + LP + DF, 0, 100)

Action mapping (recommended)
---------------------------
- DS <= 15: GO (promote / continue rollout)
- 15 < DS <= 35: CAUTION (slow rollout to 10% and schedule targeted human review within 4 hours)
- 35 < DS <= 60: HOLD (pause rollout; trigger automated bisect & focused probes)
- DS > 60: ROLLBACK (automatically revert to baseline variant and open incident ticket)

Configuration table (defaults)
-----------------------------
- heatmap_window_hours: 24 -- Time window to compute the snapshot
- probe_priority_weights: CriticalTenantFlows:10, BillingIntents:8, UXTextGen:3 -- Priority map used in SS
- latency_slo_ms: 250 -- latency SLO used for LP calculation
- drift_baseline_window_days: 7 -- Days used to compute baseline drift
- slow_roll_threshold: 35 -- DS threshold to switch to slow rollout
- human_review_timeout_hours: 4 -- Max time to complete targeted review

Ownership and roles
-------------------
- Eval Oncall (primary): validates heatmap integrity, runs automated bisect and approves/requests human review.
- Model Owner (secondary): responsible for quick triage of failing slices and submitting patch/rollforward.
- Release Engineer: executes percent traffic adjustments and rollbacks in the serving control plane.
- Oncall Platform SRE: monitors capacity/latency regressions and authorizes emergency rollbacks for tail latency incidents.

Procedure: from snapshot to decision (operational runbook)
------------------------------------------------------
1. Fetch heatmap snapshot and baseline. Verify telemetry completeness (missing probes < 5% of expected).
2. Run validation script to confirm probe schema and timestamps: 'python tools/heatmap_validate.py --snapshot /tmp/heatmap.json'
3. Compute DS using the scoring algorithm and emit a decision document to /incidents/probe-decisions/YYYYMMDD-HHMM.json. Example: curl -X POST 'https://ops-api.internal/decisions' -d '{'ds': 27, 'action': 'CAUTION', 'top_slices': ['BillingIntents:charge-failure'] }'
4. If action == GO: continue rollout. Log event and schedule a 24h follow-up check.
5. If action == CAUTION: cap rollout at 10% for 6 hours, assign Model Owner and Eval Oncall for targeted human validation, and run automated bisect on top 5 degrading slices.
6. If action == HOLD: pause rollout, mark the release as blocked in release tracker, and create a regression investigation ticket with pre-populated triage fields.
7. If action == ROLLBACK: trigger automated rollback playbook and notify the incident channel #regression-ops with summary and rollback links.

Automated bisect integration
---------------------------
- The decision pipeline calls the bisect service with the top N probes by (failure_count * avg_severity). The bisect run ID is included in the decision document.
- If bisect identifies a single suspect change (probability > 0.7) the Model Owner must decide to either patch or rollback within human_review_timeout_hours.

Telemetry contract (minimal required fields)
-----------------------------------------
Emitters must provide a compact heatmap JSON with the following fields (example snippet):

'{'
  'snapshot_ts': '2025-01-08T08:00:00Z',
  'window_hours': 24,
  'slices': [
    {
      'slice_id': 'BillingIntents:charge-failure',
      'total_calls': 12450,
      'failure_count': 312,
      'avg_severity': 2.8,
      'median_latency_ms': 430,
      'embedding_drift_score': 0.34
    }
  ]
}'

Required export fields (flat): snapshot_ts, window_hours, slices[].slice_id, slices[].total_calls, slices[].failure_count, slices[].avg_severity, slices[].median_latency_ms, slices[].embedding_drift_score. Optional: host_cluster, model_variant, tenant_id.

Safety checks and hard gates
---------------------------
- If any CriticalTenantFlows slice has failure_rate > 0.5% AND avg_severity >= 3.0 the system must ROLLBACK regardless of DS.
- If more than 10% of probes lack current telemetry, mark decision state as INCONCLUSIVE and require human approval.
- For private/on-prem customers with per-customer SLO overrides, consult the customer SLO manifest before automatic rollback - use the per-customer override endpoint.

Rollback criteria and runbook steps
----------------------------------
1. Lock the rollout in the control plane: 'redwoodctl rollout lock --id <rollout-id>'
2. Execute the variant revert: 'redwoodctl rollout revert --id <rollout-id> --target <baseline-model>'
3. Post-rollback verification: run a 2-hour fast-probe sweep across top 20 slices and confirm DS falls below 20.
4. Create incident with severity mapping: DS>80 -> Sev2, DS 60-80 -> Sev3.

Example: case study (short)
-------------------------
- Scenario: Quantized v1.2 was promoted to 20% across US-hosted tenants. After 12 hours heatmap snapshot showed elevated embedding_drift_score in 3 billing-related slices. Computed DS = 42 -> HOLD. Automated bisect pointed to a tokenizer change in the preprocessor. Model Owner rolled back quant patch and re-run priming probes; DS dropped to 12 within 3 hours and rollout resumed at a slow cadence.

Appendix A: configuration YAML sample
------------------------------------

probe_priority_weights:
  CriticalTenantFlows: 10

  UXTextGen: 3
latency_slo_ms: 250
drift_baseline_window_days: 7
slow_roll_threshold: 35
human_review_timeout_hours: 4'

Question: In our hosted chat streaming, a corporate gateway forces the stream into a polling style connection and after a reconnect the assistant reply consistently loses the last couple sentences and the final completion status never arrives; what is the recommended short term mitigation for customers until a server side fix is deployed?

description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when their corporate edge rewrites Streaming SSE to a long-poll fallback path, the last ~1-2 sentences of responses are consistently missing after a reconnect.

Impact: Intermittent data loss for streaming responses behind certain proxies; affects customer-facing assistant content (missing trailing sentences). Reported by a Dedicated customer (NimbusDocs) using the hosted API through a corporate proxy that downgrades SSE to HTTP long-polling.

Observed behavior: Client receives streamed tokens, then connection is torn down by edge for long-poll fallback. When the session resumes the service returns an early 204/OK and the final trailer event (closing marker/end metadata) is not delivered to the client. Result: truncated final paragraph and absent terminal metadata (choice.finish_reason).

Expected behavior: Fallback path should replay or proxy through the complete trailing chunks or the server should re-emit terminal events after reconstitution so the client receives the full final sentence and closing metadata.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Customer environment: desktop app behind corporate proxy that strips SSE and does long-polling; use proxy that rewrites HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/1.0 and closes keepalive after 15s.
2) Open a streaming chat session against the Redwood hosted API with Accept: text/event-stream and keepalive enabled; send a prompt that yields a 60-120 token final paragraph.
3) Trigger a controlled network interruption to force the proxy to close and re-establish the HTTP connection (simulate edge path change or probe).
4) Observe on the client: streaming resumes but final 1-2 sentences are missing; server logs show a short-lived long-poll request that returns without the closing trailer event.
5) Reproduce reliably by toggling the proxy keepalive interval in synthetic lab; behavior observed ~7/10 runs.

logs:
[2026-03-10T14:08:12Z] proxy edge: Upstream accepted, id=xyz-7
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] client -> proxy: Connection close by proxy (keepalive expiry) (15s)
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] proxy -> rt-proxy: new long-poll /v1/stream?session=abc returning 200 OK (early-close)
[2026-03-10T14:08:26Z] rt-proxy: stream-session abc resumed; last-kv-checkpoint=0x7f1; trailer_flag=false
[2026-03-10T14:08:27Z] serving-runtime: produced final-choice tokens, emitted trailer meta (choice.finish_reason=length)
[2026-03-10T14:08:27Z] rt-proxy: upstream write failed: client closed connection; skipping trailer emission on long-poll path

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis 1: Long-poll fallback path short-circuits trailer emission when client socket indicates close; race between runtime's trailer write and proxy long-poll response commit.
Hypothesis 2: Proxy/edge performs an extra connection-level close that causes rt-proxy to treat resumed session as ephemeral and drop final metadata to avoid blocking write (backpressure handling path).
Repro steps validated in internal staging with our test proxy (haproxy) reproducing 80% of runs when keepalive <= 20s.
Observed difference vs normal SSE: SSE code path uses chunked transfer with streaming flush; long-poll path uses buffered response commit and currently lacks explicit trailer re-synthesis when the client reconnection occurs.
Logs indicate serving-runtime did emit finish trailer but rt-proxy logged upstream write failure before it could sink to the client long-poll response body.

eval_reference.gold_answer:
Use a slice-first observability design: build dashboards and alerts around high-value slices (e.g., enterprise customer_tier, /chat/stream vs /chat/batch, model_variant, and kv_cache_warmth hot/warm/cold) rather than global aggregates, and instrument canonical metrics like first_token_ms (p50/p90/p99), error rate, kv_cache.hit_rate/warmth_index, queue.wait_ms, and model.exec.gpu_ms. On the dashboard, include operational anchors (request rate, latency percentiles, errors), causality suspects (KV hit rate/warmth, queueing, GPU time), and investigation hooks (sample trace list, recent prompt snapshot IDs), so oncall can jump from a spike to a trace quickly.

For tracing, enforce a lightweight span contract (ingress.request → scheduler.queue → model.exec → emitter.stream → exporter.kv_lookup) with required tags including request_id, tenant_id, route, model_variant, kv_hit, batch_id, prompt_sha (hash only), and token_count; keep raw prompts out of traces and link any prompt snapshots as external secure artifacts by prompt_sha. Define KV warmth context via heuristics (warm if warmth_index ≥ 70 and hit_rate ≥ 0.8 over 5m; cold if warmth_index < 50 or hit_rate < 0.6) so responders can correlate cache state with TTF and GPU time.

For low-noise tiered paging, implement graded per-slice alerts instead of a single global threshold: P2 warning when 10m rolling first_token_ms p95 exceeds baseline×1.5 for 15m; P1 degradation when p95 exceeds baseline×2 for 10m or error_rate rises 5× for 5m; and P0 incident on SLA breach (e.g., enterprise p99 > SLA) or sustained 50% request loss. Add noise controls such as requiring at least 3 tenants impacted (or sustained absolute request growth) and enrich alerts with top tenants/routes, the last prompt_shas, and a link to a prebuilt investigation query to support alert → hypothesis → remediation in ~15 minutes.

Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0212
Question: How should we set up low-noise oncall dashboards and tiered paging for a streaming text generation service so that responders can jump from a latency spike to a trace with hashed prompt references and cache hotness context and resolve issues within about 15 minutes?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_5085c9f4b4484f298dabd02c99d9ce03:
Purpose:
This doc captures a slice-first approach for designing dashboards, metric definitions, and alert tuning for tokenized LLM inference flows. It prioritizes operator workflows (fast triage, low-noise alerts) and investigative artifacts (trace anchors, prompt snapshots) so oncall can go from alert -> hypothesis -> remediation in under 15 minutes.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated inference paths (same signal set, different thresholds).
- Focus on runtime surface: request ingress, routing, KV cache effectiveness, model execution, and response emission.
- Not covering long-term cost chargeback or offline eval pipelines (those are linked).

Principles (short):
1) Slice-first: dashboards and alerts should be built around a small set of high-value slices (customer-tier, route, model-variant, cold-cache) rather than global aggregates.
2) Alert finessing: prefer graded alerts + investigation scorecards vs single hard thresholds.
3) Observation as product: include example queries, a minimal replay harness, and a teardown checklist on every dashboard.

Important slices to onboard (initial):
- customer_tier=enterprise (high priority SLA)
- route=/chat/stream vs /chat/batch
- model_variant={gptx-8b, gptx-4b-quantized}
- kv_cache_warmth={hot,warm,cold} (defined below)
- tenant_concurrency_bucket={low,med,high}

Metrics definitions (canonical list, naming and intent):
- inference.request.count: counter. incremented on request ingress. tags: route, model_variant, customer_tier, tenant_id
- inference.tff.first_token_ms: gauge/histogram. time from request start to first token emitted. buckets: [50,100,250,500,1000,2500]
- inference.tff.nth_token_ms: histogram for downstream per-token latency (use for tail analysis)
- inference.model.exec.gpu_ms: histogram. GPU execution time broken out per-pass (include kv-hit flag)
- inference.kv.cache.hit_rate: ratio (0-1) evaluated per tenant/model_variant over sliding 5m
- inference.kv.cache.warmth_index: integer 0..100; computed as weighted recent hit_rate * request_frequency (heuristic described in appendix)
- inference.queue.wait_ms: histogram for time spent in scheduler queue
- inference.errors.rate: counter with tags error_type={timeout,oom,model-mismatch,invocation-error}
- inference.output.quality.regressions: export from quality-eval hook (occurs when eval set fails)
- observability.trace.sample_rate: exported for visibility into sampling controls

KV warmth heuristics (practical):
- warm: warmth_index >= 70 and hit_rate >= 0.8 over 5m
- warm-borderline: 50..69 or hit_rate 0.6..0.8
- cold: warmth_index < 50 or hit_rate < 0.6
Rationale: cache warmth correlates with TTF and per-token GPU time; use for adaptive batching and prefetch triggers.

Tracing annotations and span contract (lightweight):
Span names: ingress.request -> scheduler.queue -> model.exec -> emitter.stream -> exporter.kv_lookup
Required span tags: request_id, tenant_id, route, model_variant, kv_hit (true/false), batch_id (if batched), prompt_sha (hash of prompt prefix), token_count
Trace size policy: prefer compact spans; only include prompt_sha, not raw prompt. Prompt snapshots linked as external secure artifact when sample flagged.
Sampling policy prototype:
- Error traces: 100% capture for error_type != success
- High-latency: capture 50% where first_token_ms > p99 of slice
- Regular: 1% uniform sampling, with bias to enterprise tenants to 5%
Retention: full traces kept 30d, compact breadcrumb trace (no attachments) 90d

Dashboard composition (slice-first wireframe):
Top row (operational anchors): request rate (per-slice), p50/p90/p99 first_token_ms, error rate.
Second row (causality suspects): kv_cache.hit_rate, queue.wait_ms distribution, GPU exec_ms distribution.
Third row (investigation hooks): sample trace list (linked), recent prompt snapshot sample ids, active long-lived batches.
Fourth row (alert health): recent alerts fired, noise score, MTTR trend.
Widget best practices: 1) default to slice dropdown at top-left, 2) show both absolute and normalized (per-1000 reqs) views, 3) annotate with typical baseline ranges for each model_variant.

Alerting and finessing strategy (concrete):
- Strategy: avoid single global hard alert. For each slice, implement 3-level alerting:
  - P2 warning (informational): rolling 10m first_token_ms p95 > baseline*1.5 for 15m; notify #ops as low-urgency.
  - P1 degradation: p95 > baseline*2 for 10m OR error_rate increased by 5x sustained for 5m; page on-call.
  - P0 incident: service-level SLA breach (e.g., enterprise p99 > SLA), or sustained 50% request loss.
- Noise controls: require at least N tenants affected (default N=3) OR sustained absolute growth in requests in slice to avoid single-tenant flakiness spamming ops.
- Alert enrichment payload: include top 3 tenants by error rate, top 3 routes, last 10 sample prompt_shas, and a link to a pre-run investigation query.

Investigation scorecard (what oncall should collect quickly):
1) Snapshot: time window + tenant(s) involved + slice dropdown state
2) Quick metrics: p50/p95/p99 first_token_ms, kv_hit_rate, gpu_ms, queue_wait_ms, errors by type
3) Trace anchor: open a sampled trace with spans annotated by kv_hit, batch_id, prompt_sha
4) Reproduce: run replay harness (if safe) in staging with same prompt_sha and model_variant; check model.exec.gpu_ms delta
5) Rollback plan: if rollout suspected, failover route to known-good model_variant (automated rollback playbook link)

Instrumentation checklist (developer handoff):
- Emit request_id and prompt_sha on ingress span
- Increment inference.request.count with all defined tags
- Report kv_hit boolean on both span and metrics pipeline (so hit-rate can be computed without tracing)
- Export histogram buckets for first_token_ms and queue.wait_ms (use documented bucket boundaries)
- Add feature flag hooks to increase trace sampling for experiments

Operational runbooks to author next (owners):
- rollout-drift-investigation-runbook (owner: Sara Patel)
- kv-prefetch-triggering-playbook (owner: Diego Ramos)
- alert-noise-tuning-playbook (owner: Liam O'Connor)

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Should enterprise tenants have dedicated higher-sampling traces or just higher retention? (ops cost vs signal)
- Where to store prompt snapshots for privacy; do we always store prompt_sha only and require JIT retrieval?
- How conservative should noise de-dup be for low-volume tenants?

Appendix: quick SQL snippets (for dashboard queries)
- recent noisy tenants by error rate:
  SELECT tenant_id, sum(errors) as errs, sum(requests) as reqs FROM inference_metrics WHERE ts > now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY errs DESC LIMIT 10;
- kv warmth index (pseudo):
  warmth_index = round( 100 * (0.7 * hit_rate_5m + 0.3 * min(1.0, requests_5m / 100)) )

Next steps (this doc):
- Review with ops and SRE (schedule 30m sync)
- Create dashboard template from wireframe and push to staging (owner: Maya Chen)
- Prototype enriched alert payload with top-tenants and prompt_shas attached (owner: eng-observability)

Notes to self / scratchpad:
- Keep prompt snapshots out of traces by default; use an encrypted artifact store referenced by prompt_sha.
- Consider tie-breaker metric: p95 first_token_ms normalized by kv_hit_rate to quickly surface cache regressions.

description:
Summary: On 2026-03-13 we observed a repeatable capacity shortfall affecting a subset of Dedicated pools serving latency-sensitive routes. Customers saw throttled throughput and elevated tail latency; autoscaler failed to replenish headroom for ~18 minutes in the worst-impacted pools. This ticket consolidates the live triage notes, proposed short-term rollback/containment, forensic telemetry plan, and the longer-term resilience actions we will track in the postmortem.

incident_timeline:
2026-03-13T09:24Z - Alert: Dedicated pool headroom below 10% for pool: eu-west-2-dedicated-4. Alert surfaced from capacity-monitoring rule 'dedicated.headroom.low'.
2026-03-13T09:27Z - Autoscale controller reported repeated scale-up errors: 'quota_exceeded' and 'dealbreaker: kernel selection mismatch'.
2026-03-13T09:30Z - On-call rotation (SRE) started containment runbook; temporarily increased burst capacity for affected customers using reserve tokens.
2026-03-13T09:42Z - Manual rollback: rolled back runtime build runtime-1.21.7 -> runtime-1.21.4 on two affected zones; autoscaler recovered and headroom returned to >30% by 09:50Z.
2026-03-13T10:10Z - Stabilization: routing policy enabled temporary throttle for non-SLA routes; observability dashboards show token-level latency returned to baseline over next 20 minutes.

containment_steps_performed:
Enabled reserve headroom policy for top-10 impacted accounts (temporary config override).
Rolled back recent runtime image (runtime-1.21.7 -> runtime-1.21.4) in impacted zones to unblock autoscaler flow.
Applied emergency routing fallback to cheaper model variants for bursty routes to reduce token pressure.

forensic_hypotheses:
1) Kernel selection path regression in runtime-1.21.7 causes per-GPU resource skew, triggering quota_exceeded errors when autoscaler attempts to instantiate new replicas.
2) A change to continuous-batching thresholds increased effective active sequences per GPU, reducing headroom at typical request concurrency patterns.
3) Metric drift in our headroom estimator (recent change to the moving-window) caused delayed detection and inappropriate scale decisions.

forensic_plan:
Collect per-GPU allocation traces and kernel selection logs from 2026-03-13T09:00Z - 2026-03-13T11:00Z (ENG: telemetry team tag).
Extract autoscaler event stream and reconcile with cloud provider API responses (quota/limit codes) for failed scale attempts.
Replay representative traffic against runtime-1.21.7 in a staging cluster with identical batch/concurrency settings to reproduce the quota_exceeded condition.
Generate a timeline correlating model variant routing changes, batching metric changes, and headroom estimator outputs to identify the first causal deviation.

per-GPU active_sequence_count and kernel_selection_path
per-route token throughput and 99th/99.9th latency

description:
Issue summary: Customer reports SSE streaming sessions ending with a trailing silence and an incomplete final JSON object after an iOS client (managed device) reconnects. The client receives a partial JSON payload (closing bracket missing or truncated final text) but the stream does not emit an explicit terminal event. Impact: Customer's app shows 'incomplete' responses for ~5-15% of long-running streams on iOS 15/16 devices behind the Apple HTTP proxy used in their MDM. This affects Generation and Chat endpoints and causes user-visible corruption in message endings. Environment: prod-us-west, customer using our hosted API via SDK v1.12.0, mobile network: corporate Wi-Fi with Apple HTTP proxy/transparent caching. Observed: - Session logs show a short idle period then a socket rebind/hand-off from device path manager. - Edge logs include: "connection: id=sk-8765 partial_close=true late_fin=true" and serving-runtime logs show "stalled-flush: true" for the stream session. - Client-side: SDK reports reconnect, normal resume handshake, then receives no explicit "[DONE]"-like event or end-of-stream marker; final JSON block is truncated. Steps to reproduce (customer-provided): 1) Start a long streaming generation (>120s) on iOS device on corp Wi-Fi. 2) Background the app for ~10s then bring it to foreground. 3) Observe stream reconnect and final payload missing trailing characters. Expected: stream resumes and emits final terminal event or complete JSON. Observed: trailing silence and truncated final object. Additional notes: Issue more frequent when device OS performs a connection warm-up (path negotiation) or when Apple HTTP proxy inserts an intermediary probe. This appears different from standard proxy chunking issues we've seen previously because the connection close code sequence is unusual (delayed FIN coalesced with keepalive).

logs:
[edge-2026-03-12T14:02:11Z] x-request-id=7f9c2a session=ss-04f3
[edge-2026-03-12T14:02:12Z] connection: id=ss-04f3 partial_close=true reason=idle_probe_coalesce code=SOCKET_MIGRATE
[serve-2026-03-12T14:02:12Z] stream_id=ss-04f3 stalled-flush=true kvcache-primed=true last-frame-offset=18432
[client-logs] sdk.v1.12.0: reconnecting, resumeToken present
[client-logs] received chunk: "{\"choices\": [{\"text\": \"...and finally we recommend\"}\n\n(EOF)\n"

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: Apple HTTP proxy on managed networks sometimes coalesces an idle-probe FIN with a subsequent TCP migration, which the edge treats as a definitive stream close before the serving-runtime has flushed the trailing buffered tokens. Differences vs known issues: not classic proxy truncation or chunk reordering; here the edge emits partial_close marker and we see a stalled flush rather than an explicit RST. Reproducer verification: Support able to reproduce locally using an iOS device simulator + a transparent proxy that delays ACKs. Correlation: request ids with partial_close show higher incidence when keepalive interval on client > 20s. Temporary mitigation: instruct customer to enable websocket fallback in SDK or set keepalive to 15s. Observed workaround success: websocket fallback avoided truncation in 30 test runs (0/30 truncations).

Overview:
This playbook defines the Tribe Liaison role and the Status-Wire communication protocol used for coordinated incident response across teams (platform, runtime, SRE, customer success, and engineering tribes). It is intended for incidents with cross-team impact (multi-service degradation, multi-region latency spikes, or model-quality regressions affecting production).

Purpose:
- Reduce cross-team friction and duplicated messaging during incidents.
- Provide a repeatable activation workflow for public and customer-facing communications.
- Offer templates and checklists for rapid, consistent status updates and post-incident evidence collection.

When to activate the Status-Wire:
1) Any P0 or P1 incident declared by SRE / Incident Commander.
2) Sustained SLO deviation > 5 minutes affecting > 1 customer or > 10% of traffic.
3) Model-quality regression that causes repeated error responses or hallucination rates above threshold.

Roles & Responsibilities:
- Incident Commander (IC): overall incident authority; owns triage decisions and escalation to execs.
- Tribe Liaison (TL): single named engineer from each affected tribe. TLs consolidate technical findings and represent their team on the Status Wire. Responsible for:
  - Rapidly validating impact and proposed mitigations for their domain.
  - Contributing one-line status and next steps for each wire update.
  - Collecting evidence artifacts (logs, traces, perf snapshots).
- Bridge Operator: manages the incident bridge, recording timeline and action items.
- Communications Lead (Comms): drafts customer-facing updates, coordinates legal/compliance review if required.
- Customer Success Rep: prepares prioritized customer impact list and coordinates direct outreach where needed.

Activation checklist (first 10 minutes):
1. IC declares incident and sets severity.
2. Pager alert: On-call SRE acknowledges and opens bridge.
3. IC assigns an engineered TL per affected tribe (platform, runtime, model-infra, console).
4. Bridge Operator posts Status-Wire channel link (Slack #status-wire-<incident-id>) and pins initial incident summary.
5. TLs post immediate 1-line: "{team}: impact (yes/no), likely root area, immediate mitigation". Example: "Runtime: partial KV-cache eviction causing 40% increased tail latency; restarting cache nodes as mitigation"
6. Comms drafts and posts first customer notice (see templates).

Escalation matrix (quick reference):
| Role | Primary | Secondary | Escalation threshold | Contact method |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Incident Commander | SRE Lead on-call | Eng Director on-call | >30 minutes to containment | Pager / Phone |
| Tribe Liaison | Team on-call engineer | Team tech lead | No mitigation found in 20 minutes | Slack DM / Pager |
| Comms Lead | Support Ops | Head of CS | Customer SLA breach or regulatory impact | Slack / Email |

Runbook snippets (copy into service runbooks):
- inference-gateway:
  1) Check service health: curl -fsS https://health.redwood.internal/inference-gateway/metrics || true
  2) Query recent traces: otel-cli query --service inference-gateway --last 15m
  3) If error-rate > 2% and tail-latency > 800ms, toggle canary fallback: curl -XPOST https://admin.redwood.internal/route/fallback -d '{"route":"/generate","model":"gptx-small-fallback"}'
- kv-cache:
  1) Inspect eviction log: gcloud logging read "resource.labels.instance_id=\"kv-cache\"" --limit 200
  2) Rehydrate hot-keys from snapshot: /opt/tools/kv-rehydrate --snapshot s3://redwood-cache/snaps/latest --keys hot-keys.txt

Status-Wire messaging cadence:
- Initial (T+10m): Brief impact, services affected, immediate mitigations in progress, expected next update in 30 minutes.
- T+30m: Progress update including measurable signposts (error-rate, latency, traffic diverted) and next steps.
- Every 30—60m afterward: update until containment. Shorten cadence to 15 minutes if customer-impacting or high uncertainty.
- Containment achieved: merge into final incident summary and begin postmortem timeline.

Customer-facing templates (copy/paste-ready):
- Short status page entry (public):
  Title: "Degraded API latency for text generation — investigating"
  Body: "We are investigating increased latency affecting text-generation API requests in US-West. Impact: intermittent delays up to ~4s for a subset of requests. Current actions: rolling restart of KV cache nodes and routing a portion of traffic to fallback model variants. Next update: in 30 minutes. Affected customers will receive direct notices if they meet SLA thresholds."

- Email / CS message (for affected customers):
  Subject: "Service update: transient delays for Redwood text generation — {incident-id}"
  Body: "Hi {customer_name},

We are actively responding to an incident affecting text-generation latency in {region}. Some requests are experiencing elevated latency or transient errors. Our SRE and runtime teams have deployed mitigations (cache restarts and traffic routing) and are monitoring recovery. We will provide another update at {time} or sooner if status changes. We apologize for the disruption and will share a detailed post-incident report within 72 hours.

If you require escalation or mitigation assistance (e.g., pinning model variants or temporary throttling), reply to this message and your Customer Success lead will coordinate.

— Redwood Support"

Game day and simulation plan (quarterly):
- Objective: exercise cross-tribe coordination and Status-Wire to validate SLAs and communications.
- Frequency: quarterly for SRE + product-critical tribes; monthly light drills for new joiners.
- Duration: 90 minutes.
- Roles assigned in advance: IC, Bridge Operator, 3 TLs, Comms, CS.
- Scenario example: synthetic KV eviction at scale causing 30% tail latency increase and 5% error-rate.
- Success criteria: containment within 45 minutes, customer-facing update within 10 minutes, complete evidence capture (traces/logs/metrics) uploaded to incident ticket.

Post-incident evidence & postmortem template:
- Attachments required in postmortem: timeline (with T+ minute markers), logs (last 60 minutes per service), relevant traces (span IDs), Mitigation steps, Root cause analysis, Action items with owners and SLA for completion.
- Postmortem outline (use this header structure):
  *Summary*
  *Impact* (customers, SLOs)
  *Timeline* (bullet list with timestamps)
  *Root Cause*
  *Contributing factors*
  *Immediate remediation*
  *Long-term fixes*
  *Action items (owner + due date)*
  *Verification plan*

On-call rotation fairness & handoff checklist:
- Primary rotation length: 9 days (3-person rotation recommended for fairness).
- Shadowing: new on-call engineers shadow for 2 rotations.
- Handoff checklist (mandatory before shift end):
  1) Confirm no ongoing incidents assigned.
  2) Share any active mitigations, experiments, or rollouts in last 12 hours.
  3) Verify Escalation list and on-call contacts are up-to-date.
  4) If any open action items: add clear owner and ETA.

Bridge & tooling references:
- Incident bridge template: Zoom link pinned in channel; Google Doc timeline template: https://docs.internal.redwood/incident-timeline-template
- Dashboards:
  - SRE Living Dashboard: https://grafana.internal.redwood/d/ll1/sre-living-dashboard
  - Model Quality Monitor: https://grafana.internal.redwood/d/mq/model-quality
  - Token-level cost/latency: Console -> Observability -> Token Insights
- Runbook registry: Confluence runbook index (add link to service runbook pages).

Quick checklist for the Tribe Liaison (TL):
1) Join bridge and post one-line status.
2) Verify logs and traces for your domain and attach evidence to bridge notes.
3) Propose emergency mitigation and estimate time-to-contain.
4) Commit to follow-up artifact (e.g., heap dump, timeline snippet).

Appendix: sample Slack status-wire message (copy-paste)
```
[Status-Wire] Incident: INF-2026-842
IC: @sre-oncall
Services: inference-gateway (P), kv-cache (P)
Runtime: Restarting 2/3 cache replicas; expected partial recovery in ~12m. Error-rate peaked at 4.1%; tail latency 95p=950ms. Next update in 30m.
TLs: @runtime-tl (runtime), @platform-tl (platform), @modelinfra-tl (model)
```

Operational notes & governance:
- All incident owners must file a postmortem for P0/P1 incidents within 72 hours of containment.
- Action items must be tracked in the central incident board and have clear owners and due dates.
- Quarterly reviews: the Incident Review Council will audit a sample of postmortems for completeness and follow-through.

Related pages and references:
- Incident evidence collection standard, SLO definitions, Runbook registry.

- Primary owner: Leah Park (SRE, Incident Ops)
- Secondary owner: Marcus Chen (Runtime)

description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports intermittent stalls when streaming large model shard downloads and long-lived gRPC/http2 connections from their Private deployment. The problem started after an on-prem network change from their transit provider two days ago.

Impact:
- Models fail to fully stream for larger shards (>64KB) causing inference requests to stall and time out after ~30s.
- Affects production traffic for FinData Analytics (private deployment, single VPC peered to our control plane).
- Observed in us-east-1 only.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC) peered to Redwood control plane via TGW.
- Worker nodes: t3.large-equivalent instances with custom MTU 1500 by default.
- Presigned S3 artifact fetches used with range requests (HTTP/2 multiplexed).

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer):
1) Trigger a model load that requires range fetches (large model shard).
2) Observe initial TLS handshake completes. HTTP/2 connection established.
3) After a few KBs, the download stalls and the HTTP/2 stream is left in a half-open state; no further DATA frames from server are delivered.
4) Retry with smaller range window or reduce request size -> succeeds.

Observed behavior:
- tcpdump on worker shows server sending TCP segments but client stops ACKing after a certain MSS-sized segment. No ICMP "Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4)" is seen reaching the customer edge.
- When we instrumented a capture at the customer-VM side we do see an ICMP type 3 code 4 originating from the downstream router, but it disappears before reaching the customer's transit provider egress (suggesting provider filtering/rate limit).
- HTTP/2 stream state: initial SETTINGS/HEADERS exchange ok, partial DATA frames delivered, then stall; client eventually times out and triggers a reconnect.

Expected behavior:
- If path MTU requires fragmentation adjustments, ICMP "Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4)" should be delivered to endpoints so PMTU can adjust and streaming continues without stalls.

Additional logs / captures:
- Attached pcap snippets (provided by customer): "pcap_worker_side.pcap" shows server DATA up to a segment then no further ACK progression.
- Worker logs: serving-runtime reported repeated stream timeouts with code 14 (UNAVAILABLE) and downstream transport errors referencing ECONNRESET after timeouts.
- Console trace: Model shard fetch request id=shard-20260312-34 produced 0 bytes after 18s then retried and succeeded with MTU reduced.

Immediate customer workaround performed:
- Customer set worker node MTU to 1400 (temporary) — this prevented the need for ICMP fragmentation and streaming resumed successfully.

Notes:
- This only reproduces on large sequential downloads (range-based) or larger gRPC frame payloads; small requests and embeddings flows unaffected.
- The control plane auth and presigned URL generation are not implicated (we can generate working presigned URLs that still stall when path MTU issues present).


investigation_notes:
2026-03-12: Initial triage by Support (Aisha). Collected tcpdump + HTTP/2 trace. Customer confirms transit provider changed perimeter firewall/policy on 2026-03-11.
2026-03-12: SRE (Marco) requested pcap from customer and reproduced stalls by issuing range requests to the same object; pcap at worker shows missing ICMP fragments and stalled TCP sequence progression.
2026-03-13: We set up controlled repro from an EC2 in the customer's VPC and instrumented packet captures at three points: (a) worker VM, (b) customer edge router, (c) provider egress (captured by customer but provider did not provide mirrored capture). The VM saw ICMP type 3 code 4 originate from edge router; there is a gap at the provider handoff.
2026-03-13: Opened inbound ticket with customer's transit provider (ticket TP-44821) — provider response indicates they apply ICMP rate-limiting and drop some Type 3 messages under heavy NAT; they are investigating.
2026-03-14: SRE confirmed MTU-lowering on worker (1400) is an effective mitigation. We tested increasing TLS record granularity (server-side capping to 1200) and that also mitigates but requires runtime change.

Hypothesis:
- Transit provider's egress filtering/rate-limiting is preventing delivery of ICMP Fragmentation Needed messages to the customer's VMs, causing PMTU discovery to fail and resulting in a blackhole for packets larger than path MTU. HTTP/2/HTTP/2-over-TLS tends to push larger frames which triggers the failure more evident for large shard downloads.

Next steps / action items:
- SRE: Collect signed pcap evidence to include in provider escalation (assigned Marco Alvarez).
- Support: Document workaround steps for customer (MTU 1400 or server TLS record size cap).
- Customer: Keep transit provider ticket open and request allowing ICMP Type 3 Code 4 or otherwise enable PMTU transparency.
- Product: Consider adding an automatic fallback to smaller TLS record sizes for private deployments when PMTU probes fail (follow-up RFC).

comments:
2026-03-12 09:14 - Aisha Khan (Support): Customer reports repeated streaming stalls for large model loads. They rolled back a network change but problem persists. They've provided tcpdump and logs. Opening ticket and requesting captures from their edge.
2026-03-12 13:02 - Marco Alvarez (SRE): Reproduced locally inside customer's VPC. Captures show ICMP type 3 code 4 being generated at edge, but not propagated past provider handoff. Suspect provider-level ICMP filtering/rate limiting.
2026-03-13 08:23 - FinData NetOps (Customer): Provider confirms a firewall policy change on 2026-03-11 and acknowledges ICMP rate-limiting. They've opened TP-44821 with provider. Can confirm MTU workround helps.
2026-03-13 16:55 - Marco Alvarez (SRE): Applied temporary MTU 1400 to two worker nodes for customer testing; model shard fetches succeeded under load. Propose scripted mitigation and documenting for other customers.
2026-03-14 10:10 - Aisha Khan (Support): Customer requests guidance for permanent fix and asks if Redwood can detect PMTU blackholes and auto-fallback to smaller TLS records or throughput-mode that reduces frame sizes.
2026-03-14 14:30 - Marco Alvarez (SRE): Creating provider escalation bundle with pcaps + timeline. File attached to provider ticket TP-44821. Suggested product follow-up to product infra team: auto-detect PMTU failures and reduce record size.

resolution:
Workaround: Customer lowered worker MTU to 1400 which restored streaming. Alternative workaround: cap TLS record sizes/server-side chunking to avoid packets exceeding Path MTU.
Root cause: Provider-level ICMP (Fragmentation Needed) filtering/rate-limiting preventing PMTU discovery; provider ticket TP-44821 opened by customer.
Follow-up: SRE to push escalation to provider with signed pcap evidence. Product team to evaluate automatic TLS-record-size fallback for private deployments if PMTU probes fail.

description:
Design a compact, action-first incident card and an integrated rollout control surface for Private/VPC clusters that surfaces estimated cost impact, recommended rollback or model-variant actions, and one-click mitigations. The aim is to reduce time-to-mitigation for tenant-facing degradations while making cost trade-offs explicit to SREs and platform teams.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Incident cards appear in the Private Cluster 'Status' panel and show: incident title, severity, affected tenants, brief root-cause hints, and an estimated incremental cost delta (last 24h vs baseline).
2) Each card exposes primary actions: Add to Canary, Pause Rollout, Trigger Fallback Variant, Open Debug Shell (link), and Mark Investigating. Actions must include confirmation flows where destructive.
3) Rollout controls allow cost-aware canaries: step size, max cost delta per step, automated pause-on-cost-threshold.
4) Prototype validated in user testing with at least 5 SRE/platform engineers and 3 PM customers; task completion time for 'pause rollout and rollback' reduced by 40% vs current flow.
5) All links in cards resolve to existing tools: GitHub PRs, runbooks (Confluence), logs (Grafana/Loki), and the cluster-trace view.

design_notes:
- Use compact 3-line summary layout for cards to avoid vertical noise in the Status page.
- Cost metric uses internal 'delta-cost' calc from Optimize team (est. USD/hour) and shows color-coded delta: neutral (<1%), warning (1-5%), critical (>5%).
- Primary actions are contextual: if a rollout is active, show Pause/Abort; if model variant fallback exists, surface it with a confidence score.
- Add a small 'why this costs more' tooltip that lists contributors (batch size, fallback model, increased QPS).
- Mobile and tablet: collapse extra details behind a chevron; primary action must remain single-tap.
- Accessibility: each card must be navigable by keyboard, with ARIA labels for actions.

decisions:
1) Show estimated cost delta with two decimals and currency symbol (USD).
2) Implement color rules for delta bands as described above.
3) Action 'Trigger Fallback Variant' will call the existing runtime API implemented by ENG-2201; design will include a confirmation modal with rollback preview.
4) We will not surface raw billing numbers for multi-currency customers in this phase—only normalized USD deltas.
5) Rollout 'auto-pause on cost' default is OFF; turned on via cluster policy (PM decision).

tradeoffs:
- Surface financial signals too aggressively and we risk alert fatigue; too conservatively and teams miss cost regressions. We chose explicit deltas with thresholds to balance noise.
- Exposing cost numbers in the incident flow requires careful permissions; initial rollout restricts detailed cost drilldown to users with billing view permissions (de-scoped for current prototype).
- One-click mitigations accelerate fixes but increase risk of human error; mitigated via confirmation modals and brief runbook links.
