Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0240
Question: During a multi region switchover, what is causing some customers to get bursty too many requests and occasional service unavailable responses because different parts of the traffic gatekeeper disagree briefly on the time boundary used for quota calculations?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_5402831508734a51adf649603be4b075:
description:
Several customers (hosted + dedicated + private) escalated sustained 429/503 errors during a regional failover window. Initial triage shows that the rate-limiter's burst evaluation enters a transient jitter state when epoch anchors between proxy, orchestrator, and host-level rate controllers disagree. This leads to aggressive admission drops for a subset of tenants (capacity starvation) rather than graceful fallback. The goal of this ticket is to identify the root cause, implement a safe reconciliation path, and ship mitigations + tests to prevent recurrence.

impact_summary:
Multiple enterprise customers observed multi-minute spikes of 429 and some downstream 503s during scheduled failover and autoscaler activity. Customer requests were effectively throttled beyond configured quota; billing and SLAs were impacted for two Dedicated customers and one Private deployment. Pager escalations and CS tickets received during outage window.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Simulate region failover by toggling route priorities in staging multi-region env
2) Run sustained high-concurrency generator at 60% above target per-tenant sustained rate
3) Force orchestrator restart and proxy rolling restart to create misaligned epoch anchors
4) Observe per-tenant admission drops and token-pool drain events in orchestrator logs
5) Check metrics: tenant_admission_rejected, burst_claim_mismatch, quota_epoch_skew

investigation_notes:
2026-03-02: On-call (Luis) validated customer traces and correlated spike with a control-plane failover that overlapped proxy rolling restart.
2026-03-03: Reproduced in staging. Found a 200-800ms window where orchestrator computed burst credits using previous-epoch metadata while proxy used a freshly persisted marker; mismatch caused double-counting and premature eviction of tenant tickets.
2026-03-04: Heap of evidence shows race in policy evaluator: policy cache refresh is async and not versioned atomically with token epoch transitions.
2026-03-06: Confirmed that Private deployments using slower KMS and commit-confirmation had longer window of misalignment.
2026-03-08: Small hotfix deployed on hosted to introduce 250ms guard window; reduced severity but did not resolve root cause.
2026-03-10: Added additional logging and correlation IDs across proxy->orchestrator->host rate controllers to capture exact decision timelines.

root_cause_summary:
Race between epoch transitions and policy cache refresh. When a region failover or orchestrator restart occurs, different components evaluate burst policies against inconsistent epoch anchors. The evaluator treats missing/old anchors as 'no-burst' and aggressively evicts inflight capacity rather than deferring or reconciling, resulting in tenant capacity starvation.

short_term_mitigation:
1) Rollout guard-window (250-500ms) at proxy and orchestrator to ignore epoch flips for immediate decisions (deployed to hosted; pending dedicated/private rollout),
2) Enable diagnostic sampling for affected tenants to capture full decision traces for postmortem
3) Communicate to CS about temporary throttle behavior and mitigation timeline

long_term_fix_proposal:
A) Implement atomic epoched policy reads: annotate policy cache entries with epoch_id and ensure any admission decision reads a consistent epoch across proxy+orchestrator+host
B) Add idempotent burst-claim reconciliation: when epoch mismatch is detected, reconcile by computing conservative merged credit (min of claims) and schedule background rebalancing instead of immediate eviction
C) Introduce a degraded-mode path that favors availability for previously healthy tenants (soft-degrade) during control-plane transitions
D) Add cross-component integration tests and chaos test that exercises orchestrator/proxy restarts with high-concurrency workloads

acceptance_criteria:
Unit + integration tests that validate epoch-aligned policy reads
Chaos test in staging that shows no more than 5% extra rejections for affected tenants during simulated failover
Metric reductions: burst_claim_mismatch rate decreases by 95% in staging failover runs
Documentation updated for Dedicated + Private deployment runbooks
Release notes and customer communication prepared for runtime-2.4

implementation_plan:
1) Create tiny persistence field epoch_id on policy cache entries and plumb through RPCs (ENG-158240 will track RPC changes)
2) Implement conservative reconciliation algorithm in orchestrator admission path (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7852)
3) Expand guard-window to 500ms with feature flag, roll out to dedicated and private with staged canaries
4) Add end-to-end tests in policy-e2e harness; run against chaos monkey
5) Post-deploy telemetry check and 24h on-call monitoring window

Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0243
Question: In our GPU inference service that merges many request streams, what change was made to cut worst case latency spikes that happened when the attention memory footprint abruptly shifted during batch formation, while keeping median latency nearly flat?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_908e8464927742829dcdfe0c6165299b:
description:
Background and motivation: Production workloads show variance in per-channel activation distributions across prompts and token positions which makes static requant scales suboptimal. We observed systematic p99 latency spikes when the runtime switched between hot and cold KV cache footprints under continuous-batching; these were exacerbated by small batching jitter when multiple streams aligned. This PR implements a dynamic per-channel requant stage combined with a KV-cache-aware scheduling hint and a jitter-resilient continuous-batching policy to smooth throughput while keeping low tail latency. Scope: 1) A lightweight per-channel scale estimator that runs on the microkernel hot path and updates requant multipliers at configurable amortization windows. 2) A cheap, lock-free KV cache sizing hint that the scheduler uses to avoid abrupt prefix evictions during batch coalescing. 3) A jitter-resilient continuous-batcher that introduces minimal, adaptive hold windows to align requests from high-variance sources without increasing median latency. 4) Microkernel changes to expose a fused transform that applies requant multipliers inline with dequant/attn input packing to eliminate an extra copy. Design highlights and tradeoffs: - Estimator runs every N tokens (configurable per model) and uses exponential moving moments to remain stable across bursts. The goal is to reduce per-token compute overhead to <0.5% while adapting scales within 5-10k tokens. - Scheduler hint is advisory: it tags requests with estimated KV working set delta. The placement layer still enforces hard SLOs; the hint avoids placing requests that would cause a working-set jump on the same GPU within a short window. - Batcher employs an adaptive jitter budget: it only delays the head of a queue by up to X ms if the expected throughput improvement outweighs the added latency; X decays if p99 latency rises. Benchmarks (representative): - OPT-13B, INT8 hybrid (smoothquant + per-channel dynamic re-quant): throughput +10.8% on steady-state mixed sized prompts, median latency +2% (due to micro-batching alignment), p99 latency -14% on tail-heavy traces. - Llama-2-7B FP8 fallback: end-to-end token cost reduced by ~7% due to fewer KV evictions and reduced memory copies. - End-to-end e2e test with 500 simulated concurrent streams: observed 8-12% lower GPU-side memcpy time and 6-9% better sustained throughput. Implementation notes: - Runtime changes: src/runtime/quant/dyn_requant.h/cpp, src/runtime/quant/microkernel_requant.s, src/runtime/scheduler/kv_hint_scheduler.cpp - Batcher: src/runtime/batching/jitter_batcher.cpp, with a new config block in configs/batching.yaml - Tests: tests/quant/test_dyn_requant.cc (unit), bench/latency/bench_kv_jitter.py (integration traces) - Docs: docs/perf/quantization.md updated with configuration knobs and suggested Linear tasks for tuning. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for estimator accuracy and stability - [x] Integration benchmark harness with trace replay - [x] Backwards-compatibility: dynamic requant disabled by default; opt-in via runtime config - [x] Release notes draft included - [x] SRE smoke test run on dedicated cluster and passed Notes on safety and compatibility: This change touches kernel hot-paths; dynamic scaling is guarded behind a runtime flag and tuned conservatively out-of-the-box to avoid regression. We included an automatic rollback condition in the scheduler when p99 exceeds baseline by 20% during an experiment. Related work: ENG-2048 (per-channel requant research spike), PR #612345 (microkernel packing refactor) for reference. Next steps: 1) A follow-up PR to expose an admin dashboard for per-model scale drift metrics and recommended amortization windows. 2) Experiment with a learned estimator offline and compare to the EMA-based estimator used here.

Leah: EMA keeps the hot path cheap and is resilient to heavy tails; we add a debug mode to collect histograms offline and compare. Added test to validate estimator vs small histogram sample.
Rohit: Assembly changes look good but please add comment on register usage for AArch64.

Leah: We added cross-request dampening and a per-GPU dampening register to avoid opposite-direction flips. Also added a safety rollback in the scheduler if oscillation detected.

description:
Issue summary:
Users report that Access Request approvals show as 'Granted' in the Support Console but the target internal service (runbook/console) still returns 403. Happens after the recent Okta issuer domain swap (okta-old.redwood -> okta-new.redwood).

Impact:
- Internal engineers cannot escalate to runbooks or use the console automation tooling after approvals.
- Blocks oncall workflows during testing; affects ~12 engineers across multiple teams.

Environment:
- prod (us-east) - internal console + identity-proxy + okta-new.redwood

Steps to reproduce:
1) Submit Access Request for runbook elevation in Support Console using existing flow.
2) Approver approves the request (shows Granted in UI).
3) Attempt to open runbook — receives 403 with 'missing RBAC grant'.
4) Inspect auth logs on identity-proxy and console-service.

Observed logs/snippets:
- identity-proxy: "ERROR auth: issuer mismatch: token_iss=https://okta-old.redwood/oauth2/default, expected=https://okta-new.redwood/oauth2/default"
- console-service: "RBAC: no matching grants for principal: user:12345 issuer=https://okta-old.redwood"

Notes: This started after the Okta issuer domain migration rolled earlier this week; some tokens/approval links still carry the old issuer in their assertion/redirect flow.

comments:
2026-03-10 09:12 - Priya Shah: Reported by SRE oncall after two engineers couldn't escalate. Assigned to Ethan for initial triage.
2026-03-10 10:05 - Ethan Cole: Reproduced in prod. Token issuer mismatch seen in proxy logs. Hypothesis: approval tokens generated before migration still referencing old issuer; console and proxy validate against new issuer only.
2026-03-11 14:22 - Claire Wu (Identity): Confirmed Okta org swap completed; legacy issuer still active for 24h. We thought token exchange would normalize issuer during exchange but logs disagree.
2026-03-12 08:30 - Ethan Cole: Implemented temporary auth-layer allowance to accept old issuer for access-request assertion path. Rolling to prod canary (10%). Monitoring for unintended acceptance of stale tokens.
2026-03-12 12:00 - SRE oncall: Canary at 10% shows successful provisioning for previously-failing users. No obvious regression in other flows after 3h.
2026-03-12 15:40 - Priya Shah: Customer-facing note not required (internal only). Tracking follow-up to rotate any long-lived tokens that may contain old issuer references.

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: RBAC grant lookup keys include issuer, so any token with old issuer won't match grants issued under new issuer mapping.
Checked audit logs: Access Request approval events authored at 2026-03-09 23:xx still contain 'iss' set to https://okta-old.redwood. Approvals created after 2026-03-10 02:00 have new issuer.
Identity-proxy currently rejects tokens whose 'iss' does not match configured accepted_issuers list (single value).
Support Console's approval token generator signs a short-lived JWT with an 'iss' claim set to the Okta issuer configured at time of generation. Some queued approvals were created before migration and delivered post-migration.
RBAC datastore keys: grants are indexed by (principal_id, issuer). When issuer changes, previously-created grants are still stored under old issuer namespace; provisioning call attempts to read grants using issuer from assertion.
Attempted local repro by forging approval JWT with old issuer and calling provisioning endpoint — repro'd 403 with same logs as production.

resolution_notes:
Short term mitigation: Deployed identity-proxy update to accept both https://okta-new.redwood and https://okta-old.redwood on the access-request/provisioning endpoint only. This allowed in-flight approvals to complete normally without touching global token acceptance.
Medium term fix: Backfilled RBAC grants for recently-approved requests by running migration job that normalizes grant keys from old issuer to new issuer for approvals in the migration window (2026-03-09 22:00 -> 2026-03-10 04:00). PR: github.com/redwood-inference/rbac-tools/pull/57
Long term: Update approval token generation to include an 'orig_iss' claim and update provisioning to canonicalize issuer during lookup. Add explicit migration step to retirement playbook for future issuer changes. Added unit tests for multi-issuer acceptance in identity-proxy.
Follow-ups:
- Security to review acceptance window (Ethan & Claire).
- Rotate any long-lived service tokens that may embed old issuer references.
- Run additional audit to ensure no external tokens accepted accidentally.

description:
Motivation: multi-GPU tensor-parallel workloads show sporadic tail latency spikes when collectives are scheduled naively at layer boundaries. This PR introduces a wavefront-style collective scheduler that groups nearby collective ops into a compact execution wave and a compact_kernel_selector that prefers smaller, lower-latency kernels for short-sequence invocations. The goal is to reduce communication stalls, improve KV cache prefetch alignment with collectives, and give the runtime a low-overhead heuristic to pick kernels that minimize per-token latency for short and mixed-length batches. Work items: - implement wavefront scheduler with layer-aware grouping and interleaved compute/comm launch windows - add compact_kernel_selector with device-query and sequence-length histogram input - introduce a KV-shard prompter that prefetches KV shards for upcoming wavefronts (heuristic-based) - NCCL launch param autotuner that records performance fingerprints and falls back to conservative settings on regression - unit + integration tests and perf-canary workload validation Checklist: [x] scheduler core implementation and unit tests [x] kernel selector + device query [x] KV prefetch heuristic + metrics hooks [x] NCCL autotuner prototype [x] perf benchmarks against baseline [x] documentation and release note entry Context and motivation: customers running TP-4/8 models reported 10-30% 95/99 latency regressions after a recent batching change; root cause was misaligned collective launches interleaving with KV cache fills. This PR aims to reduce that variance without sacrificing throughput on large continuous-batching workloads.

Summary:
This playbook defines a measurable, evidence-driven process for offer evaluation and the automated triggering of role-specific onboarding pathways at Redwood Inference. It replaces ad-hoc offer decisions and fragmented onboarding handoffs with a single decision matrix, a negotiation and risk log, and concrete onboarding triggers tied to role risk, compliance needs, and ramp objectives.

Who this is for:
- Hiring managers
- Recruiters and Talent Acquisition
- HR Business Partners (HRBPs)
- People Ops specialists who build onboarding curricula
- Legal and Finance for offer approvals

Goals and principles:
- Make offer decisions transparent and auditable using a standardized scorecard.
- Reduce time-to-offer while preserving quality of decision-making (target: 48-hour typical offer SLA from verbal approval).
- Trigger onboarding pathways automatically based on objective signals (role, clearance, vendor status, critical deliverables).
- Record negotiation outcomes and commitments centrally for manager and HR ownership.

Key owners and roles:
- Recruiter: manage candidate communications, prepare initial offer package, populate scorecard.
- Hiring Manager: complete technical/cultural evaluation, set ramp objectives, confirm L4/L5+ approvals.
- HRBP: ensure compliance with compensation bands and local labor law; finalize benefits language.
- Finance: sign-off on salary above band midpoint + 15% (approval threshold).
- Legal: review for contractor/consultant engagements and NDAs.

Offer evaluation process (step-by-step):
1) Populate Offer Scorecard (required before verbal offer)
   - Responsible: Recruiter + Hiring Manager
   - Required fields: role level, base salary proposed, equity award, bonus eligibility, reason for hire, candidate score (0–5) across: technical fit, problem-solving, role-specific skills, team fit, ramp risk.
   - Attach: interview scorecards, reference-check notes, and compensation benchmarking snapshot.

2) Automated Decision Matrix applies
   - If candidate_score >= 4.0 AND proposed_comp <= band_midpoint + 10% -> auto-approve (Recruiter/HRBP finalize).
   - If candidate_score between 3.0–4.0 OR proposed_comp between band_midpoint + 10% and +25% -> HRBP + Hiring Manager sign-off required.
   - If candidate_score < 3.0 OR proposed_comp > band_midpoint + 25% OR offer contains atypical clauses -> Finance + Legal review and exec sponsor.

3) Negotiation and Risk Log (template)
   - Fields to capture: candidate_request (text), impact_on_budget (Y/N), manager_commitments (Y/N), date, negotiator name, final decision.
   - All negotiated deviations from the standard package must be recorded and stored in the candidate dossier.

4) Offer SLA targets
   - Verbal offer: within 48 hours of decision to hire.
   - Written offer (signed by HRBP/Legal): within 72 hours of verbal acceptance.
   - Exception path: roles requiring external contractor conversion, export control, or security clearance: review window up to 10 business days.

Offer Scorecard (required fields — flat table representation)
- candidate_name | role | level | technical_score (0-5) | problem_solving (0-5) | team_fit (0-5) | ramp_risk (low/med/high) | aggregate_score (0-5) | proposed_comp_pct_vs_band_mid | approvals_required

Decision and approval thresholds (examples)
- Aggregate score >= 4.0 and comp <= +10% => Recruiter + HRBP sign.
- Aggregate score 3.0–3.9 or comp +10%–+25% => Hiring Manager + HRBP required.
- Aggregate score < 3.0 or comp > +25% => Finance + Legal + Exec sponsor.

Onboarding trigger taxonomy
This section maps objective signals in the scorecard and offer to an onboarding pathway. Triggers are evaluated automatically by the People Ops intake system when the candidate signs the offer.
- Role risk triggers (immediately escalate): access to PII/PHI, admin network access, SOC2 high-impact role. => Trigger: Restricted onboarding pathway (security clearance checklist, 1:1 with Security engineer before first day).
- Compliance triggers: EEA employment, contractor vs. employee conversion, background check flags. => Trigger: Extended HR/Legal onboarding (pre-hire paperwork, local labor compliance steps).
- Ramp-critical triggers: role with measurable Q1 deliverables or cross-team dependencies. => Trigger: accelerated immersion track (prestart reading list, assigned buddy, condensed 30-day objectives).
- Remote/new-country triggers: candidate located outside primary region or requiring relocation. => Trigger: remote-localization packet and payroll/accounting enrollment steps.

Onboarding pathways (short descriptions)
- Core Standard Onboarding: baseline 90-day plan with security training, benefits enrollment, manager 30/60/90 goals and weekly 1:1 cadence.
- Restricted Onboarding: additional security orientation, expedited IAM provisioning, elevated audit logging for first 30 days.
- Accelerated Immersion: preboarding reading checklist, assigned project with narrow scope, daily standups first 2 weeks, weekly deliverable reviews.
- Compliance-Extended: staged paperwork, legal sign-offs, delayed access to production until checks complete.

Manager checklist (first 30/60/90 — condensed)
- Day 0–7: complete role-specific equipment and access; schedule 30/60/90 goal alignment; introduce to buddy; assign first-week small deliverable.
- Day 8–30: weekly check-ins; confirm completion of security and compliance training; evaluate initial pass/fail on deliverable; adjust ramp plan.
- Day 31–90: bi-weekly checkpoints; evaluate against three core KPIs defined at offer; formal 90-day calibration with HRBP.

Metrics and reporting:
- Offer conversion rate (verbal -> signed) target: >= 85%.
- Time-to-offer median: <= 4 days.

eval_reference.gold_answer:
Readiness checklist (eu-central-2) for an EKS cluster with GPU spot workers for batch inference:
1) Quotas: request ENI and IPv4 quota increases (and EIP if needed); verify ENI-per-instance for your target GPU type (e.g. `aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types p4d.24xlarge --query 'InstanceTypes[].NetworkInfo'`).
2) Networking: create a VPC with 3 AZ subnets (/24) and tag subnets/cluster for internal ELB (e.g. `kubernetes.io/cluster/prod-euc2=owned` plus ELB role tags).
3) Billing/allowlists: ensure GPU instance families (p3/p4) are approved in the billing console.
4) Cluster config: prepare an `eksctl` cluster YAML and nodegroups: a tainted/labelled SPOT GPU nodegroup (e.g. `role=gpu`, `capacityType=SPOT`, taint `spot=true:PreferNoSchedule`) plus a small on-demand infra pool.
5) GPU enablement: install the NVIDIA GPU Operator and device plugin (`kubectl create ns gpu-operator`, then apply the operator manifest).
6) Kubelet/node sizing: set any needed kubelet extra args and consider overriding `maxPods` on large GPU nodes to avoid IP exhaustion.
7) Security groups: allow required node traffic (intra-node SG TCP, 10250/TCP from control plane, NodePort range if needed) and lock down SSH.
8) Validation: after nodes are Ready, confirm GPUs are advertised (allocatable `nvidia.com/gpu`) and run a basic GPU check: `kubectl run gpu-check --image=nvidia/cuda:11.8-base --rm -it --restart=Never -- nvidia-smi`.
9) Finalize: run driver/inference smoke tests (and NCCL allreduce if multi-GPU), then hand off to oncall with logs.

Overview:

This playbook describes Redwood's responder rotation synthesis process and a lightweight Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol for incidents that meet defined criteria. It combines on-call scheduling practices, a structured bridge handoff procedure, and customer-facing messaging templates designed for speed and clarity. The goal is to reduce cognitive load during high-impact events and to ensure timely learning when full postmortems are not immediately practical.

Scope:
- Applies to: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, and Incident Response stakeholders.
- Excludes: low-priority alerts that resolve without human intervention (see 'Auto-resolved alerts' below).

Definitions:
- Responder rotation synthesis: periodic review and rebalancing of on-call shifts, handoffs, and escalation ladders to maintain equitable load and coverage.
- Deferred Postmortem (DPM): a time-boxed post-incident review that defers non-critical analysis until stakeholders are available, while still capturing root evidence and action items immediately.

Key principles:
1) Fast stabilization first: prioritize containment and customer impact minimization.
2) Minimal friction handoffs: standardized bridge transfer reduces repeated context overhead.
3) Continuous learning: short DPMs for low-severity incidents; full postmortems for Sev1/Sev2.
4) Equity in rotations: no responder assigned >36 hours continuous duty without relief.

On-call rotation design (synthesis process):
1. Quarterly synthesis review (owner: SRE lead):
   - Pull the last quarter's on-call logs and pager counts.
   - Calculate median and 95th percentile pager counts per responder.
   - Identify top-10% busiest windows and common root causes.
2. Rebalance rules:
   - Move noisy services to a dedicated micro-rotation if they account for >25% of pages.
   - Limit night-weekend primary duty to volunteers in the rotation unless emergency staffing required.
3. Local fairness check (monthly):
   - Team leads run a 15-minute review in the first week of each month to confirm schedule fairness and swap if needed.

Rotation constraints (config):
| Constraint | Value | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Max continuous on-call | 36h | Prevent fatigue and degraded decision-making |
| Minimum handoff overlap | 15m | Time to summarize bridge state and outstanding actions |
| Max weekly duty | 56h | Prevent single-responder overload across teams |
| Handoff notes retention | 90d | Auditability and incident reconstruction |

Bridge handoff procedure (step-by-step):
1) Pre-handoff checklist (outgoing):
   - Summarize incident timeline, current hypotheses, mitigation steps in progress, and customer impact.
   - Confirm runbook page(s) in Bridge tab are current and link to traces/log queries.
2) Live handoff (over bridge):
   - 5–15 minute verbal summary; ensure incoming acknowledges critical mitigations.
   - If unresolved customer-impacting work remains, assign an owner and ETA.
3) Post-handoff (incoming):
   - Record a 1-line status in the incident timeline and attach a minimum evidence set (logs, traces, alert IDs).

Incident lifecycle and DPM decision matrix:
- If incident is Sev1 or multi-tenant Sev2 -> full postmortem required within 72 hours of remediation.
- If incident meets ALL of the following, use DPM: single-tenant, <30 minutes customer-visible impact, known cause, effective mitigation applied at resolution.
- Otherwise triage for full postmortem.

Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol (when to use and how):
Purpose: capture essential facts and actions quickly when resource constraints or ongoing high operational tempo would make a full postmortem impractical in 72 hours.
DPM steps (owner: incident lead):
1) Within 8 hours of incident resolution: populate DPM template with
   - 1-line summary, impact window (start/end), services affected, severity, and customer impact.
   - Evidence snapshot (link to logs, runbook used, mitigation commands).
2) Create action items with clear owners and SLAs (default: 14-day action SLA).
3) Flag DPM for follow-up in the next synthesis meeting.
4) If DPM reveals systemic risk or unresolved unknowns, escalate to full postmortem.

DPM template (minimum fields):
- Title (1 line)
- Date/time window
- Affected services and teams (comma-separated)
- Immediate mitigations executed
- Evidence links (logs, traces, alert IDs)
- Action items (owner | due date | description)
- Decision to close DPM or escalate (yes/no)

Escalation and timeline expectations:
- Immediate: severity declaration and customer status update within 30 minutes of detection for Sev1/Sev2.
- Short window: initial triage and bridge stand-up within 60 minutes.
- DPM creation: within 8 hours.
- Full postmortem: published within 72 hours for Sev1/Sev2.

Customer communications templates (for bridge operator use):
- Initial status (first 30m):

Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench

What was the immediate mitigation applied at the request routing layer to prevent this kind of misrouting when a version lock is provided?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_df40f9a66b914f29839322d19f8922bb:
description:
Issue summary: During a synchronized canary roll for redwood-v1-large we observed that a small customer cohort lost explicit model pin state and was routed to the quantized variant (redwood-v1-large-q4). Impact: ~1400 requests over a 12m window returned lower-quality outputs and tokenization deltas; customer observed increased hallucination in 18% of affected responses (reported by customer and confirmed by telemetry). Environment: Dedicated tenant on prod:us-east-1. Steps to reproduce: 1) Start a weighted canary (10%) for redwood-v1-large across us-east-1 with prewarm enabled. 2) Trigger an orchestrator snapshot merge (scheduled merge job). 3) Send steady tenant traffic that relies on explicit version pin headers. Observed behaviour: A cohort of sessions lost model pin during the snapshot merge and were routed to redwood-v1-large-q4 (fallback path) instead of honoring tenant pin. Token counts and tokenizer fingerprints differed, leading to evaluation regression triggers from customer QA set. Expected behaviour: Tenant pin must be preserved across orchestrator snapshot merge; fallback routing should not select a different tokenizer family variant when pin is present. Relevant logs (trimmed): "2026-03-10T18:12:02Z control-plane: commit-snapshot nid=8792 merging epoch 412 -> 413" "2026-03-10T18:12:02Z orchestrator: cohort-signals: cohort=tn-998 lost-pin during merge window (prewarm=true)" "2026-03-10T18:12:03Z edge: route-resolver: selected target=redwood-v1-large-q4 weight=0.0->0.10" "2026-03-10T18:12:08Z serving-runtime: tokenization: tokenizer-hash mismatch from request header - expected 0x3b9f, got 0x8a2c" Additional notes: No 5xx spike, no autoscaler activity; issue correlates with coordinated snapshot/commit and edge prewarm probe timing jitter.

comments:
2026-03-10 18:25 - Ethan Park (Support): Customer Narrative Labs opened ticket after noticing quality regression. Provided initial logs and sample request IDs: req-82391, req-82402.
2026-03-10 18:40 - Priya Nair (SRE): Reproduced cohort loss in staging by forcing orchestrator snapshot merge during a prewarm window. Observed same edge route decision to q4 variant when pin header missing for ~12s.
2026-03-10 19:05 - Maya Chen (Customer Success): Confirmed with customer that they set explicit 'X-Model-Pin: redwood-v1-large' header; customer reports intermittent loss, not all requests affected.
2026-03-11 09:12 - Jordan Lee (Runtime): Tokenizer hashes differ between v1-large and v1-large-q4; should never be selected when pin present. Working on guard in route-resolver.
2026-03-12 11:30 - Priya Nair (SRE): Temporary mitigation deployed: route-resolver now verifies pin header at selection time and rejects fallback variants with differing tokenizer-family. Monitoring for false positives.

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis A: Orchestrator snapshot merge briefly cleared in-memory cohort pin map while control-plane applied new routing epoch, creating a window where edge route-resolver could not find a pinned mapping.
Hypothesis B: Edge prewarm probe timing (probe jitter ~30-50ms) caused a transient routing decision to include lower-cost q4 variant due to a race with weight application (weight transition 0.0->0.10).
Telemetry: Cohort loss aligns at 2026-03-10T18:12:02Z +/- 2s with snapshot commit event and prewarm probe spikes. No autoscaler preempt or GPU eviction recorded.
Control-plane review: commit-snapshot flow holds pin-delta writes, but a bug allowed a short-lived read-before-write window during epoch increments when prewarm flag true.
Edge analysis: route-resolver prioritizes explicit pin but falls back to best-available variant when lookup fails; it did not verify tokenizer-family equivalence before routing to quantized variant.
Repro: Deterministic in staging by inducing orchestrator merge while toggling prewarm and sending pinned header; reproduces cohort loss consistently when merge and first prewarm probe align within 60ms.
Customer impact: A subset of streaming chat sessions observed mixed-variant outputs; not all tenants affected because most flows had longer-lived pin leases (>30s).

resolution_notes:
Mitigation steps taken: 1) Edge route-resolver patch rolled to prod (hotfix) that enforces: if a requested pin exists in header, reject candidate fallback variants where tokenizer-family != pinned model. 2) Control-plane commit-snapshot flow patched to serialize pin-map flush before epoch activation (PR merged: orchestrator#2147). 3) Deployed a short-term canary throttle to delay weight transitions by 200ms during snapshot commits to avoid the probe/merge race. Outcome: Customer reports quality metrics returned to baseline within 1 hour after hotfix. Follow-ups: add end-to-end unit test for pin-map visibility during snapshot commit, add telemetry to count pin-resolve-failures, update canary playbook to include snapshot coordination.

description:
Issue summary:

Starting 2026-03-12 23:12 UTC, Acme Retail (dedicated tenant) reported a sustained elevation in 5xx responses for streaming/chat routes. Error pattern shows a stair-stepped increase in API gateway 502/503 responses lasting several hours with intermittent short recoveries. Customer impact: their storefront assistant fell back to degraded behavior (timeouts and truncated responses) across peak shopping hours.

Impact:
- Elevated 5xx rate (~12% of requests to streaming chat routes at peak).
- Increased tail latency for successful responses (+400ms p95).
- Customer-visible partial message truncation and reconnect loops.

Environment:
- prod:us-east (Dedicated capacity pool assigned to Acme Retail)
- Models: redwood-open-7B for chat, acme-embedder-v2 for on-the-fly embeddings

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) High concurrency burst from Acme's client at ~23:10 UTC with many long-lived streaming connections + a simultaneous bulk embedding upload job.
2) Ephemeral runtime prewarm subsystem begins spawning warmup workers and performing TLS handshakes to the proxy/acceptor.
3) API gateway accept queue depth rises, new connections see delayed accept or early RST.
4) Proxy returns 502/503 where gateway reports upstream unavailable.

Observed logs & traces (examples):
- api-gateway logs: repeated accept() latency spikes, backlog exceeded, upstream reset when handing to ephemeral-proxy.
- ephemeral-proxy logs: repeated TLS renegotiation failures "handshake timeout" for short-lived prewarm connections; many half-open sockets.
- serving-runtime logs: series of evictions/oom warnings shortly after prewarm wave; KV cache writes spiked and NVMe write latency increased (iowait).
- kernel metrics: netstat shows SYN_RECV/SYN_SENT queue growth and increased orphan sockets.
- kernel backlog: somaxconn / net.core.somaxconn counts reached limit on several nodes.

Initial hypotheses tested:
- Hypothesis A: API gateway threadpool starvation from large-sidecar healthchecks. (ruled out after thread pool metrics remained within normal ranges)
- Hypothesis B: Autoscaler activity removed warmed workers mid-prewarm causing handshake storms and connection churn. (partial evidence: scale-in events correlate with start of 5xx staircase)
- Hypothesis C: Local NVMe IO saturation due to ephemeral runtime KV-cache snapshotting created backpressure, causing worker OOMs and upstream restarts. (strong evidence: correlated nvme latency spikes and increase in runtime evictions)

Investigation notes:
- Correlated timeline across systems indicates the initial trigger is a coordinated arrival of long-lived streaming connections + a bulk embedding job from the tenant. The prewarm subsystem responds by launching warmers that perform multiple short TLS handshakes to the proxy layer. When autoscaler concurrently scales in to save costs (based on memory-util thresholds), there is a window where warmers are being torn down while new warmers spin up — increasing handshake churn and SYN backpressure at the acceptor.
- NVMe write amplification was observed at the time of the spike: frequent small writes from the runtime's KV-cache checkpointing increased iowait which in turn delayed worker threads, increasing connection hold time and accept queue growth.
- Kernel backlog tuning (somaxconn) on affected nodes was at default; raising backlog would temporarily reduce accept failures but not address root cause.

Temporary mitigations applied (timeline):
- 2026-03-12 23:40 UTC: Routed Acme tenant traffic to a reserved warm pool (fallback pool) to reduce prewarm pressure; immediate 5xx reduction to ~1.5%.
- 2026-03-12 23:55 UTC: Reduced prewarm concurrency for Acme's tenant from 8 -> 2 per node and disabled aggressive KV-cache snapshotting for the affected runtime group.
- 2026-03-13 01:10 UTC: Increased somaxconn on edge acceptor nodes as short-term relief.

Permanent remediation plan (work items):
1) Autoscaler policy change (ENG-998): modify scale-in thresholds to avoid concurrent scale-in during active prewarm phases for dedicated tenants (canary patch in staging).
2) Prewarm handshake backoff (RUNTIME-1421): implement exponential backoff and connection reuse for prewarm workers to reduce SYN bursts.
3) KV-cache snapshot batching (RUNTIME-1422): reduce small-file NVMe write amplification by batching checkpoints and using async fsync.
4) Kernel/infra tuning (OPS-776): formally increase accept backlog and tune net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog on acceptor tiers for dedicated pools.
5) Observability: add an alert rule that correlates prewarm spawn rate, NVMe iowait and accept queue depth to catch emergent patterns early (MON-312).

Resolution notes / current status:
- Customer traffic was stabilized by routing to reserved warm pool and adjusting prewarm concurrency. No data loss observed.
- Engineering owners assigned for remediation items 1-4. Estimated ETA for full rollout of fixes: 2 weeks after code review and staging validation.

Follow-up actions for CS/Support:
- Schedule a joint postmortem session with Acme on 2026-03-18 to review mitigations and planned changes.
- Offer temporary traffic smoothing guidance and safe concurrency knobs to the customer until permanent fixes land.

References & cross-links:
- Live dashboards: /dashboards/tenant/Acme-Retail/accept-queue-backpressure
- Kernel backlog notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/accept-queue-backpressure-runbook
- Related internal ticket: INT-3301 (autoscaler scale-in timeline investigation)

## Overview
This page defines the **offline bundle** file format used to install or upgrade **Redwood Private** in **air-gapped / offline** environments. It specifies:
- Bundle layout (directory structure + required artifacts)
- The **bundle manifest** (schema + hashing requirements)
- SBOM inclusion/pointers
- Compatibility rules (forward/backward)
- Size and packaging constraints for common offline transport workflows

This page is the source of truth for what the installer expects on disk. Signing and verification behavior is defined in the design doc and ADR (linked above).

---

## Goals
1. Enable offline install/upgrade with **no network fetches** (installer must operate fully from the bundle).
2. Provide a deterministic, machine-verifiable inventory of contents (hashes + versions).
3. Support cryptographic signing of the manifest (integrity + provenance).
4. Support incremental evolution of the bundle format without breaking older installers.

## Non-goals (initial phase)
- Customer-provided signing roots / customer-signed bundles (tracked as a future plan).
- Fully standardizing on one container transport format for all customers; we support a small set with clear rules.

---

## Terminology
- **Bundle**: The offline artifact delivered to customers (a directory or an archive that expands to a directory).
- **Bundle root**: Top-level directory containing manifest and artifact subdirectories.
- **Manifest**: Canonical file inventory and metadata; is the unit that is signed.
- **Build ID**: Unique identifier for the release build producing the bundle.

---

## Bundle root requirements
The bundle MUST expand to a single directory (the bundle root) containing the following top-level files:
- `manifest.json` (required)
- `manifest.sig` (required for signed bundles; optional only for explicitly approved break-glass bundles)
- `README.txt` (required; short human instructions, version, and support pointers)

Optional:
- `manifest.certchain.pem` (optional; included when verification expects an embedded certificate chain)
- `SBOM/` directory (optional; when SBOM is embedded rather than referenced)

The installer MUST be pointed at the bundle root directory (not at an archive). Customers may transport bundles as an archive (e.g., `.tar.zst`) but MUST extract prior to install.

---

## Directory structure (bundle layout)
### Required directories
A valid bundle contains the following directories under the bundle root:

1) `install/`
- Contains installer entrypoints and helper binaries/scripts used by Redwood Private installation and preflight.

2) `charts/`
- Helm chart tarballs (`.tgz`) required for Redwood Private components.

3) `images/`
- Offline container images in one of the supported forms (see “Container images” section).

4) `artifacts/`
- Redwood runtime artifacts required for on-prem serving (e.g., engine plugins, tokenizer assets, compatibility shims).

5) `config/`
- Offline install configuration defaults, schema files, and example values.

### Optional directories
- `models/` (optional in initial phase; when present, includes model weights or model bundles for customers approved for offline model transport)
- `deps/` (optional; OS/package dependencies only when explicitly required for a specific on-prem installer path)
- `SBOM/` (optional; embedded SBOM documents)

### Example tree
The following is an illustrative example. Exact filenames vary by release.

Bundle root:
- `manifest.json`
- `manifest.sig`
- `README.txt`
- `install/`
  - `redwood-private-installer-linux-amd64`
  - `redwood-private-installer-linux-amd64.sha256` (optional convenience checksum; not a substitute for manifest hashes)
  - `plugins/` (optional)
- `charts/`
  - `redwood-private-1.32.0.tgz`
  - `redwood-observability-1.32.0.tgz`
  - `redwood-gateway-1.32.0.tgz`
- `images/`
  - `oci-layout/` (preferred)
    - `index.json`
    - `blobs/sha256/...`
  - `images.lock` (required; references image digests; also included in manifest)
- `artifacts/`
  - `runtime/`
    - `engine-plugins-2026.01.0.tar.zst`
    - `tokenizers-2026.01.0.tar.zst`
  - `compat/`
    - `k8s-migrations-2026.01.0.tgz`
- `config/`
  - `values.schema.json`
  - `values.offline.example.yaml`
- `SBOM/` (optional)
  - `sbom.spdx.json`
  - `sbom.cyclonedx.json`

---

## Supported artifact types and rules
### Installer artifacts (`install/`)
Required:
- Exactly one platform installer binary is REQUIRED for supported platforms (initial support: Linux amd64; Linux arm64 optional by release).
- Any required helper binaries MUST be included locally; the installer must not download dependencies in air-gapped mode.

Rules:
- Filenames are included in manifest and MUST match exactly (case-sensitive).
- Executable bit must be preserved by the customer’s transfer/extract tooling. README.txt includes extraction guidance.

### Helm charts (`charts/`)
Required:
- Helm chart tarballs (`.tgz`) for all components referenced by the release.

Rules:
- Chart versions and `appVersion` MUST align with the bundle `release.version` metadata in `manifest.json`.
- The installer reads charts from this directory only; it must not attempt to pull charts from remote repos.

### Container images (`images/`)
Required:
- An offline image store plus a lock file.

Supported formats (one of):
1) **OCI image layout** (preferred)
   - Stored under `images/oci-layout/`
   - The manifest MUST include the top-level `index.json` hash plus blob hashes.
2) **Docker image tar archives** (supported only for customers with existing docker load workflows)
   - Stored as `.tar` under `images/docker-archives/`
   - The manifest MUST include sha256 hashes for the tar files and the expected image digests.

Lock file:
- `images/images.lock` is REQUIRED.
- It contains the authoritative list of image references and immutable digests (e.g., `registry.redwoodinference.com/redwood/gateway@sha256:...`).
- The lock file itself is hashed and listed in `manifest.json`.

Rules:
- Tags are allowed in lock entries for readability but digests MUST be present and treated as authoritative.
- The bundle MUST include all images referenced by charts/values for the default offline install path.

### Runtime artifacts (`artifacts/`)
Required:
- Runtime-dependent assets needed for the release (engine plugins, tokenizer assets, migration packages, etc.).

Rules:
- Artifacts must be referenced by exact filename and sha256.
- Where possible, artifacts should be compressed using `.tar.zst` for size efficiency.

### Config assets (`config/`)
Required:
- Offline example values files and schemas used for validation.

Rules:
- These files are treated as install inputs and MUST be hashed.

### SBOM (`SBOM/` or external reference)
SBOM is REQUIRED at the release level, provided either:
- Embedded in the bundle at `SBOM/` and referenced from the manifest with hashes, OR
- Referenced externally via a pointer in the manifest (pointer MUST include content hash), for customers who prefer separate SBOM distribution channels.

---

## Manifest: required files and signing
### Files
- `manifest.json` (required)
- `manifest.sig` (required for normal releases)

The signature covers the canonical bytes of `manifest.json` (canonicalization rules are owned by ADR-0147; this page specifies the semantic schema).

---

## Manifest schema (semantic specification)
`manifest.json` MUST be a UTF-8 JSON document.

### Required top-level fields
- `schema_version`: Version of the manifest schema (e.g., `"1.0"`).
- `bundle`: Bundle identity fields (id, format version).
- `release`: Redwood Private release metadata (version, channel).
- `build`: Build provenance metadata (build id, timestamps, repo SHAs).
- `artifacts`: List of all files/artifacts covered by the manifest, including their hashes.
- `sbom`: SBOM pointer(s) and hashes.

### Recommended/optional top-level fields
- `compatibility`: Installer version constraints and upgrade/downgrade rules.
- `notes`: Human-readable summary (kept short; do not include secrets).

### Required per-artifact fields
Each artifact entry MUST include:
- `path`: Relative path from bundle root using `/` separators.
- `sha256`: Lowercase hex sha256 digest of the file content.
- `size_bytes`: File size in bytes.
- `type`: One of: `installer`, `helm_chart`, `image_lock`, `image_store`, `runtime_artifact`, `config`, `sbom`, `model`, `dep`, `other`.

Optional per-artifact fields (when applicable):
- `media_type`: Helpful descriptor (e.g., `application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json`, `application/gzip`).
- `image_digests`: For image stores/archives, a comma-separated list of image digests expected to be present.
- `chart`: For charts, `name` and `version` as a single string `"<name>@<version>"`.

### SBOM section
The manifest MUST include at least one SBOM reference:
- `sbom.primary_path` (relative path) OR `sbom.primary_uri` (external location)
- `sbom.primary_sha256`

Optional:
- `sbom.formats` as a comma-separated list (e.g., `spdx-json,cyclonedx-json`)
- `sbom.secondary_paths` as a comma-separated list of additional embedded SBOMs

### Compatibility section
If present, `compatibility` MUST include:
- `min_installer_version`: Minimum installer version required to verify/install this bundle.
- `max_tested_installer_version`: Highest installer version validated during CI for this release (informational).
- `downgrade_policy`: `forbid` or `allow_with_flag` (default: `forbid`).

---

## Manifest example (illustrative)
(For readability, formatted here; actual file must follow canonicalization rules for signing as defined in ADR-0147.)

{
  "schema_version": "1.0",
  "bundle": {
    "format": "redwood-private-offline-bundle",
    "format_version": "1",
    "bundle_id": "rbwpriv-2026.01.0+build.18492",
    "created_at": "2026-01-12T03:41:22Z"
  },
  "release": {
    "product": "redwood-private",
    "version": "2026.01.0",
    "channel": "stable"
  },
  "build": {

  },

    "min_installer_version": "1.18.0",
    "max_tested_installer_version": "1.19.2",

  },

---

## Hashing requirements
- `sha256` is the required hash algorithm for all artifacts.
- Hashes MUST be computed on the exact bytes of the file as stored in the bundle.
- For archives (e.g., `.tgz`, `.tar.zst`, `.tar`), hash the archive file itself (not expanded contents).

Common transfer pitfalls to call out in support:
- Repackaging archives can change bytes and invalidate hashes.
- “Smart unzip” or antivirus tools can modify files or strip executable bits.

---

## Backward/forward compatibility policy
### General rule
- Installers MUST fail closed if required fields are missing or any required artifact hash mismatches.
- Installers MUST ignore unknown fields (forward-compatible) unless the field is explicitly declared “critical” by installer version.

### Manifest schema versioning
- `schema_version` uses `MAJOR.MINOR` semantics.
  - MINOR increments may add optional fields or new artifact types.
  - MAJOR increments may introduce breaking changes; will require a new minimum installer version.

### Bundle format versioning
- `bundle.format_version` is an integer representing the on-disk layout expectations.
- The installer MUST check `bundle.format` and `bundle.format_version` and error if unsupported.

### Artifact type extensibility
- New `type` values may be added. Installers should treat unknown `type` values as `other` for display/inspection, but still enforce hash verification for those files if they are referenced in `artifacts`.

---

## Size and packaging constraints
### Practical constraints (customer environments)
Air-gapped customers frequently move bundles via:
- Secure file transfer to a staging host inside the enclave
- Removable media with filesystem limits (notably FAT32 4 GiB file limit)
- Offline scanning/ingestion systems with maximum object size policies

### Redwood guidance
- Target bundle size (typical release, excluding optional models): **≤ 60 GiB**.
- Hard limit for standard supportability: **≤ 120 GiB**.
- If a release would exceed 120 GiB, Release Engineering must:
  - Provide a documented split-bundle strategy OR
  - Obtain explicit Product + Security approval with customer-specific guidance.

### Split bundle policy (when needed)
If split delivery is used, the following rules apply:
- Each part must be independently hashable and referenced from the manifest.
- The installer must support a deterministic reassembly method (documented in README.txt).
- Split bundle mechanics MUST NOT change the bytes of `manifest.json` post-signing.

Note: Current default path is single bundle directory; split delivery is supported only for approved customers and must be coordinated with Solutions/PS.

---

## README.txt requirements (customer-facing summary)
`README.txt` MUST include:
- Product + release version
- Bundle ID + build ID
- Minimum installer version
- Simple extraction guidance (including preserving executable bits)
- Primary verification command (e.g., `installer inspect --verify`)
- Log locations for verification failures
- Support escalation pointers

Do not include secrets, internal URLs that won’t resolve in air-gapped environments, or customer-specific tokens.

---

## Validation checklist (what CI and local tooling must enforce)
A bundle is considered well-formed if:
1. Required top-level files exist: `manifest.json`, `manifest.sig`, `README.txt`.
2. All `artifacts[].path` entries exist on disk and are within the bundle root (no `..` traversal).
3. All artifact hashes and sizes match.
4. `schema_version`, `bundle.format`, and `bundle.format_version` are supported.
5. `images/images.lock` exists and is included in `artifacts`.
6. SBOM is present (embedded or pointer) and hash is verifiable.
7. No network fetch is required for default offline install path.

---

## Open items / future extensions
- Standardizing model transport under `models/` (including chunking and license attestation).
- Optional inclusion of per-artifact `sha512` for customers requiring dual-hash policies.
- Formal definition of “critical unknown fields” (installer behavior) tied to schema version.

---

## Ownership
- Format/layout + installer expectations: **Eng Private Deployments** (Ethan Park)
- Manifest schema + canonicalization: **Deterministic policy/manifest engineering** (Jordan Lee) in collaboration with Release Eng
- Signing and key management: **Release Engineering / Security Engineering** (Connor O'Brien, Marcus Lin)
- Docs and customer guidance: **DevEx** (Kira Thompson)

Document dsid_fa1c733deb77445da7bc55dc472d233d:
description:
Summary: Introduces a neon-orchestrated hybrid attention path that combines a lightweight FlashAttention-style fast path with a tiled microkernel fallback. The patch adds a tiler that decides at runtime between (1) the optimized Flash micro-path for dense short sequences and (2) a new neon-prefetch tiled kernel for long contexts and odd sequence-lengths. Additionally this PR implements a lazy-KV streaming integration: instead of allocating/evicting large KV pages eagerly, the runtime streams KV slabs on demand and performs background prefetch with priority hints from the batcher. Motivation: our production traces show two dominant sources of per-token latency and cost: kernel selection overhead for mixed-length workloads and expensive full-KV swaps on long-context workloads. The hybrid path reduces kernel dispatch overhead and keeps the fast Flash path density benefits while the tiler maintains throughput on longer sequences. Design notes: - Kernel Tiler: a lightweight heuristic that computes tile sizes based on seq_len, k/v cache hits, and device utilization. Tiler exposes hints to the scheduler (tile_size, prefetch_priority, use_flash_path). - Flash micro-path: minimal changes to the existing Flash bridge to support neon-friendly memory layout and allow partial-row processing for non-4x head dims. - Neon tiled kernel: a new microkernel optimized for moderate tile sizes (32..256) with streaming prefetch and FP16 accumulation; includes an in-kernel rotary index remap to avoid extra memory passes. - Lazy-KV streaming: KV is broken into logically contiguous slabs. When a request needs a slab not present, we schedule an async prefetch and continue with partial KV (best-effort) to maintain tail latency. Background prefetching uses LRU+priority hints from the tiler. - Scheduler integration: continuous-batcher emits per-request hints (hot_token_prefix, expected_future_tokens) so the runtime favors coalescing requests that share KV slabs. - Fallback semantics: graceful fallback to the tiled kernel if flash_path fails or when the tiler estimates minimal benefit. Implementation touches: serving/runtime/tiler/* (core tiler & heuristics), serving/runtime/kvcache/streamer.* (lazy slab manager + prefetch worker), serving/runtime/kernels/neon_tiled_attn.* (new kernel), serving/runtime/kernels/flash_bridge adjustments, tests/perf/bench_attn_tiler.py, docs/attn_tiler.md. Testing & benchmarks: - Microbenchmarks across sequence lengths 8..16384, heads 8..64, model dims 1024..6144. - Canary on dedicated pools (pool-attn-4g). Results (canary): p50 latency -6%, p95 latency -12% on mixed-length workloads (avg seq ~512), throughput +18% on long-context workloads, token-cost -9% (due to fewer KV churns). Rollout plan: canary to 5% dedicated capacity for 48h, monitor tail latency, KV cache miss rate, memory OOMs. If no regressions, gradual increase over 7 days. Migration notes: no API changes. Config flags: runtime.tiler.enabled (default: true), kvcache.lazy_streaming (default: false) — kvcache.lazy_streaming off by default during initial rollout. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-1842) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Perf harness runs - [x] Canary plan - [x] Docs update - [x] Security review (no new surface) Known limitations: streaming introduces additional background IO which can increase memory churn under extreme concurrency; tiler heuristics are intentionally conservative and will be tuned as we gather telemetry. Backwards compatibility: existing model pins and rollouts remain unaffected.

Dataset: EnterpriseRAG-Bench
Question ID: qst_0263
Question: In the GPU inference runtime that mixes tiny chat requests with very long prompt processing, what is the target reduction for worst case per token latency on the latency sensitive traffic while keeping overall throughput loss under about ten percent?

Document dsid_061c09d8eef649eba85cd1421e28a41a:
description:
Motivation: Our continuous-batching pipeline currently prioritizes throughput, but under certain request mixes (short chat turns mixed with long-prefills) we see tail latency spikes and unfair slowdown of latency-sensitive routes. This ticket implements a graceful backpressure and latency isolation layer in admission control plus lightweight batch shaping hints so kernel selection and attention optimizations remain performant at the tail. The goal is to reduce 99.9th token latency for latency-sensitive routes by 35-50% without losing >10% aggregate throughput on heavy mixed workloads.

Scope: admission scoring, soft priority queues, prefill-aware shape hints emitted to the batcher, and a small runtime admission policy that can trigger compact kernels or decode-only fast paths. This work should be orthogonal to autoscaling and focused on per-GPU runtime scheduling and request admission.

Non-goals: changing global QoS for Dedicated customers, implementing persistent per-customer reservations, or adding billing changes. Those are follow-ups managed under Reserved Capacity roadmap.

acceptance_criteria:
1) End-to-end e2e test shows 99.9th token latency improvement >= 35% for latency-tagged route under mixed synthetic workload (short chat probe + long prefill).
2) P99 and P99.9 for throughput-only benchmarks degrade by <10% vs baseline.
3) No regressions in unit tests; integration tests for kernel fallback exercised.
4) Feature flag gated and can be toggled per-cluster; rollout doc merged.
5) Github PR with runtime + admission unit tests merged and performance dashboard linked.

design_notes:
High-level design: add an admission scorer computed at request enqueue time: score = alpha * latency_sensitivity + beta * prefill_length_norm + gamma * cache_hit_priority. Requests with score above threshold go to a fast-path soft-queue with small max batch size and strict latency timer; lower scored requests enter throughput queue where the batcher shapes larger batches. The scoring is additive and configurable by route.

Kernel interaction: fast-path queues trigger compact-kernel selection (fewer fused attention kernels, minimal KV routing) to reduce per-token latency; throughput queues prefer wide-kernels and aggressive batching. We will expose a 'batch_hint' metadata field from admission to the kernel selector runtime that can be used to prefer FP16-fused kernels for latency peers and quantized kernels for throughput peers.

Attention optimization: for latency-tagged requests we will enable early-attention pruning (heuristic based on prefix similarity) to reduce attention compute for long prefills when safe. This is implemented as a costed decision that falls back if model logits change above a threshold.

Trade-offs considered:
- Setting too-small fast-path batch sizes reduces throughput; choose conservative defaults and tune via canary.
- Kernel switching adds overhead; amortize by caching kernel choices per (model, seq_len_bucket, batch_hint).
- Attention pruning can change outputs; limited to routes with regression guards and eval prompt sets.

Document dsid_876b1a31bcc7409ab560b9ccbe5a0d41:
description:
Issue summary: Several customers (notably LumenHealth) report that historical dashboard panels (time ranges > 30 days) intermittently show zeroed or stale metric counts and their trace links are missing. The problem is transient: panels become correct again after ~10-30 minutes without user action. Impact: dashboards with SLA and usage rollups show incorrect historical values; alerting based on those rollups can under- or over-fire. This affects customer trust in console analytics and can mask billing/usage anomalies. Environment: production us-east region. Affected customers reported on enterprise tier; observed across multiple orgs.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Open Console -> Dashboards -> choose a dashboard with weekly/monthly rollups (time range > 30 days). 2) Observe counts for a low-cardinality metric (e.g., route_success_rate, total_tokens) and trace-link anchors. 3) Rapidly change time window back and forth (e.g., 90d -> 30d -> 90d) and refresh. 4) Some panels will render with zeroed or very old counts and trace-link buttons show 'No traces' instead of opening the trace view. 5) Wait 10-30 minutes; panels recover without manual cache clear. Repro is intermittent (~1 in 10 attempts during retention compaction windows).

observed_logs:
console-frontend: panel-render: query=rollup_v2 start=2025-12-01 end=2026-03-01 shard=warm-compact read_mode=primary; retention-indexer: compaction job id=cmp-2026-03-12-08 warmup=true; indexer-lag: lag=18m; kv-cache: miss-rate spike to 78%. Trace-hook service logs show O(200) missing anchors during query window. No 5xx in api-gateway. No token auth errors. Relevant links: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/retention/indexer-run-03-12, https://kibana.redwood.internal/app/discover#/logs?q=cmp-2026-03-12-08

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: retention compaction warmup job is causing a temporary partition state where rollup queries hit compacted partitions that are in 'read-repair' mode; dashboard renderer treats empty result as zero and trace-hook anchor resolution returns empty. Confirmed with SRE that a compaction job ran with warmup=true and indexer lag spiked ~18 minutes. Queries during warmup hit a mix of old and compacted store replicas; read-repair and backfill to hot replicas happen asynchronously. Observed that the console frontend does not fallback to hot-replica read-path when primary returns empty for rollups, so panels show stale/zeroed values. Trace-links are resolved by joining rollup keys to trace-anchor index which is being reindexed during compaction; when anchor index is temporarily empty, UI shows 'No traces'. Repro correlates strongly with compaction windows and indexer backfill events.

impact_and_scope:
- Affects historical panels (>30d) across multiple enterprise orgs in us-east during retention compaction windows.
- Observed on ~4 orgs in last 72h, including LumenHealth and 2 other enterprise accounts.
- Alerts relying on those rollups may be suppressed or show incorrect counts for the duration of compaction warmup.
- No data loss: data is present after reindex/backfill; this is a read-path consistency/window problem.

workaround:
Short term: ask customer to (a) avoid rapidly toggling large time windows during the scheduled compaction window, or (b) use a narrower time range (<=30d) which reads from hot partitions. Support can also force a panel refresh via console 'Force reload' (admin button) which triggers a hot-replica read. We have provided LumenHealth with instructions for forced refresh and notified them of the scheduled compaction window.

root_cause_summary:
Race between retention compaction warmup and dashboard read-path: compaction marks partitions compacted while the indexer backfills the hot replica asynchronously. Dashboard queries hitting compacted-but-not-yet-backfilled partitions return empty rollups; UI treats empty as zero. Trace-anchor index reindex causes temporary absence of anchor joins. No write-side data loss.

proposed_fix:
1) Frontend: treat empty rollup responses as 'retry with hot-replica' instead of rendering zero. 2) API layer: add fallback read-path to hot replicas when compaction-warmup flag is set for the partition. 3) Indexer: reduce warmup aggressiveness and emit explicit 'warmup-in-progress' header that the API can use to select fallback. 4) Add an observability alert for 'rollup-empty-during-compaction' so SRE is alerted earlier. Implementation PR: https://github.com/redwood/reindexer/pull/1189 (adds warmup header); https://github.com/redwood/console/pull/4712 (frontend retry).

Document dsid_415b72b7d40a405e87b9671946e894d8:
description:
Context: Multiple SDKs exposed slightly different streaming iterator ergonomics and credential refresh hooks which made cross-language examples and platform integrations brittle. This PR introduces a lightweight SessionDecorator abstraction and a small set of shared semantics (ResumeToken v2 + telemetry markers) to harmonize behavior across Python/TypeScript/Go. Goal: make stream consumers simpler to implement, provide a single place for automatic credential rotation and graceful resume, and add telemetry points to measure reauth/backpressure heuristics.

What this changes (high level):
- Add SessionDecorator (py/ts/go) that wraps an existing stream handle/iterator and: automatically refreshes credentials on auth failures, exposes a simple resume_token API, and emits telemetry events for: credential_refresh_attempt, credential_refresh_success, resume_attempt, resume_success, resume_fail.
- Introduce ResumeToken v2 semantics: small stable opaque token returned at stream checkpoints; safe to persist short-term for fast reconnection.
- Unify async iterator ergonomics: all SDKs now offer .stream() returning an async/pullable iterator with a single .resume(resume_token) helper. This removes previously divergent push/pull naming.
- Add backpressure hint optional argument (hint: "latency" | "throughput") to stream factory to allow runtime routing optimizations in Dedicated/Hosted.
- Deprecate older streamResume and token-swap callback signatures; provide compatibility shims for one release cycle.
- Bump SDK versions: python -> 0.42.0, typescript -> 1.12.0, go -> 1.7.3.
- Tests: unit coverage for decorator edge cases, integration tests exercising auth rotation against the dev auth-proxy, and cross-SDK interoperability smoke tests.

Implementation notes:
- Python: session_decorator.py implements an async generator wrapper that catches AuthExpired errors, triggers the provided credential_provider.refresh() and retries from a resume_token. Adds small coordination via an async Lock so concurrent reauth attempts coalesce.
- TypeScript: sessionDecorator.ts implements an async iterable class that mirrors the Python contract, exports a withSessionDecorator factory that preserves stream typing.
- Go: session_decorator.go adds a StreamDecorator type with Resume(ctx, token) and Start(ctx) iterator model; uses channels to translate push->pull where necessary.
- Telemetry: lightweight events emitted to existing "sdk.stream" namespace with fields: event_type, sdk_lang, duration_ms, error_class. These are instrumented behind a toggle so customers can opt into increased telemetry retention.

Checklist: [x] design doc (Linear ENG-2159) linked [x] unit tests added [x] e2e smoke tests added [x] docs updated in /docs/sdk/streams.md [x] version bumps for all three SDKs [x] feature flagged telemetry

Related: Linear ENG-2159, ENG-2164, support ticket SUP-4721. Docs: https://internal.redwood.ai/docs/sdk/streams#session-decorator (internal).

akshay: Dropped a short perfdump in the thread. Key points: compaction time is dominating when we try to coalesce many tiny free ranges, and the allocator spends cycles scanning buckets. CPU-side kernel selection flips to the fallback kernel mid-request because workspace estimate grows.

ell en: Can you share the KV cache hit distribution? Might be related to eviction churn.
akshay: KV hit rate is fine overall (~82%) but there are hot streams that continuously touch new blocks, causing fragmentation. The paged block reuse allocator tries to salvage partial blocks but our compaction threshold triggers full copy compaction too often.

paul: Ideas: 1) implement a "salvage-first" opportunistic reclaim that extracts contiguous subranges without full compaction; 2) add a lightweight bitmap to each block to speed free-range detection; 3) introduce a watermark to prevent kernel fallback by reserving a tiny extra workspace for worst-case transient growth.
maria: I prototyped (2) a while back — bitmap reduced compaction scan by ~40% in microbench. We didn't hook it to the eviction policy though.
akshay: Sketching a combined approach: salvage-first + soft-evict watermark + adaptive block_sizing on hot streams. Pseudocode for the eviction heuristic I tested:

```
if fragment_pct > 30% and active_streams < 4:
  salvage_contiguous_ranges()
elif fragment_pct > 60%:
  schedule_full_compaction(async=true)
else:
  prefer_block_reuse()
```

paul: Also saw that batching heuristics exacerbate it — large batches cause longer-lived KV entries so eviction churn overlaps with slow compaction. We should bias batch packing to prefer requests with higher KV hit probability when fragmentation is high.
maria: Agree. We can add a batch_score = hit_prob - frag_penalty and let the scheduler prefer higher score in that pool.

Question ID: qst_0268
Question: In the March 2026 production incident where long streamed chat replies started arriving chopped up and in the wrong order and the customers usage charges jumped because their client kept reissuing the same request, what was identified as the underlying platform cause?

Context Documents:
Document dsid_a990e708840f481795741cfd3fb55691:
description:
Issue summary:

During a peak traffic window on 2026-03-09 17:22 UTC, Cinder Labs began seeing partial/stale streaming responses, token reordering for long chat sessions (>4096 tokens), and a surge in client retries that amplified upstream throughput. This led to increased 5xx rates from serving nodes, transient throttles from the API gateway, and an unexpected billing delta for the customer.

Impact:
- Multiple customer endpoints experienced truncated streams and out-of-order token sequences (~1200 user sessions affected).
- Observed 5xx rate peaked at 6.3% for the customer’s traffic window.
- Billing spike estimated at +42% for the affected 2-hour window due to retry amplification.
- Customer escalated to enterprise support and requested immediate mitigation, crediting and a post-incident review.

Environment:
- Production (us-east-1) serving cl-13b-v1-quant behind api-gateway v2.13.
- Dedicated routing policy: enterprise-reserved-us-east.

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1. Create a multi-turn chat session pinned to cl-13b-v1-quant with >4096 token context and stream responses.
2. Induce a partial runtime eviction (simulate KV cache evictions / kernel reselect) while continuing to stream.
3. Observe token gaps and client-side automatic retries causing multiple inflight requests for the same session.

Observed behavior:
- When a serving shard dropped the KV prefix during a background compaction, subsequent token continuation resumed from an earlier cache state and produced overlapping token sequences.
- Client SDKs retried idempotently but without session-affinity checks, creating duplicate in-flight completions.
- API gateway detected elevated error rates and began conservative throttling; some requests received 429s while others returned 5xx from the runtime.

Initial mitigation and timeline:
- 17:28 UTC: Support opened escalation and notified SRE and Serving Runtime teams.
- 17:35 UTC: Temporary routing policy change to route Cinder Labs traffic to a healthy pre-warmed pool (bypassed recently-updated autoscaler rules).
- 17:42 UTC: Disabled aggressive client-side retry guidance sent to Cinder Labs; asked temporary SDK toggle to backoff.
- 18:10 UTC: Rolling kernel-selection rollback (PR linked) deployed for us-east pool which stopped KV prefix evictions during active streaming.
- 19:00 UTC: Error rates returned to baseline; streaming behavior normalized.


investigation_notes:
Timeline and findings:
- 2026-03-09 17:22 UTC: first elevated 5xx and streaming truncations for Cinder Labs observed (api-gateway metrics + their telemetry).
- Root cause hypothesis: interaction between a recent kernel-selection tweak (PR 4821) and aggressive KV compaction led to transient state loss for long-lived sessions.
- Evidence: heap/kvcache flush logs on serving nodes show compaction events coincident with affected session IDs.
- Replay of workload on staging reproduced token reordering when compaction was force-triggered during active streaming.
- Throttle amplification: client SDK retry logic started new requests that did not enforce session-affinity, creating fanout and repeated token generation for the same logical conversation.
- Billing delta analysis: aggregated request counts for Cinder Labs during the window were 2.4x baseline; cost-weighted tokens increased proportionally.
- Contrib factors: recent autoscaler tuning reduced pre-warmed buffer by 20% in us-east pool, increasing likelihood that compaction/eviction occurred under pressure.


comments:
Support (Maya Chen) — 2026-03-09 17:30 UTC: Customer reported truncated streams and repeated partial messages. Opened incident and paged SRE.
SRE (Arjun Patel) — 2026-03-09 17:38 UTC: Identified KV compaction entries correlated with session IDs. Temporarily rerouted traffic to healthy pool.
Customer (Elena Ruiz, Cinder Labs) — 2026-03-09 17:45 UTC: Confirmed temporary improvement after reroute; requested timeline and credit for billing spike.
Eng (Tomasz Novak) — 2026-03-09 18:05 UTC: Rolled back kernel-selection change (PR 4821) in us-east as mitigation; monitoring for regressions.
Billing (Priya Shah) — 2026-03-10 09:12 UTC: Preliminary credit calculation prepared; recommended 50% credit for the affected window pending final audit.
Support (Maya Chen) — 2026-03-11 11:02 UTC: Sent post-incident summary and next steps to Cinder Labs; scheduled follow-up review on 2026-03-12.
Customer (Elena Ruiz) — 2026-03-11 15:40 UTC: Appreciated rapid response; requested concrete SDK guidance to avoid amplification in future.

resolution_summary:
Root cause: interaction between a kernel-selection optimization and KV compaction behavior on serving nodes caused transient session state loss for long chat contexts, leading to token reordering. Secondary amplification: client SDK retries without enforced session-affinity produced duplicate inflight completions and a billing spike.

Fixes applied:
- Rolled back kernel-selection tweak in us-east (PR 4821) and deployed a guarded kernel rollout that disables compaction during active streams.
- Temporary routing to pre-warmed pool restored stability during the rollout.
- Issued a targeted billing credit to Cinder Labs (50% of the two-hour delta) and submitted final audit for adjustment.

Status: Mitigation deployed, monitoring in place, customer credited; incident closed after validation period.

follow_up_tasks:
Implement server-side session-affinity enforcement for streaming continuations (owner: Eng/Serving Runtime) — ETA 2026-04-07
Add a compaction-safe flag to the runtime that prevents KV prefix eviction during active streams (owner: Eng/Serving Runtime) — ETA 2026-03-25
Enhance SDKs to surface and opt-in to conservative retry modes for enterprise tiers (owner: DevX/SDK) — ETA 2026-04-01
Create billing audit dashboard to detect anomalous retry amplification per customer (owner: Finance/Platform) — ETA 2026-03-20
Run tabletop with top enterprise customers to validate failover behaviors and communication playbooks (owner: Support/GTM) — ETA 2026-04-15

description:
Goal: Design a compact, information-dense inspector panel for the Private Console that surfaces tenant-level mesh connectivity, recent path health, and safe rollback actions. This panel should live as a collapsible strip in the tenant overview and expand into a transient overlay when operators need details. It must be usable by SREs and Platform Engineers to make fast triage decisions (isolate region, trigger rollback, estimate cost impact) without drilling into multiple screens.

Scope: initial MVP for single-tenant view, covers cross-region connectivity map (simplified), last-5-heartbeats visualization, top-3 failure signals (e.g., packet loss, high retransmit rate, control-plane lag), suggested mitigations (restart agent, reroute traffic to region B, initiate rolling upgrade rollback), and a compact cost delta estimator showing estimated additional egress and reserved capacity cost for failover.

Out-of-scope: full multi-tenant graph, packet-level trace replay, deep topology editor. Those will be follow-ups if MVP is validated.

acceptance_criteria:
Compact panel fits within 340px height in tenant overview in collapsed state
Panel expands to overlay with per-path details and last-5-heartbeat sparkline
Top-3 signals are algorithmically ranked and human-readable (label + severity color)
Quick actions available: Open runbook, Trigger safe rollback (requires two-step confirm), Route traffic to alternate region (preview cost delta)
Design handoff artifacts (Figma frames, interaction spec) provided and validated by ENG lead
Analytics events defined for expand/collapse, action clicks, and confirm steps

decisions:
Show only top-3 signals by default to keep surface scannable — full list accessible in expanded overlay
Cost estimator shows a conservative 95th-percentile delta pulled from cost-service rather than live billing to avoid surprising numbers
Rollback action will be a controlled two-step flow that triggers a canary first (safety requirement from Eng) — design includes both canary and global rollback options
Compact visual language uses small sparklines + status pill (green/amber/red) rather than large heatmaps to preserve density
Panel will default to collapsed in tenant overview; tenants with active incidents auto-expand up to 30 seconds after page load

constraints_and_risks:
Backend needs new summary API (ENG-28901) to drive top-3 signals and cost estimate — latency and rate limits need to be validated
Security teams require audit logs for rollback and routing actions — UI must surface confirmation and note that actions are audited
Mobile and very narrow viewports will show only the status pill and an overflow menu linking to full overlay
Cost estimator accuracy limited until cost-service supports per-tenant reserved-capacity breakdown (work in separate ENG ticket)
